title: `geom_line/hline/abline` won't add a line if X-axis is a single value and `expand = FALSE`
description:
This might be sort of a corner case: adding an horizontal line on a graph with a single X value. Simple example here that works:

```r
library("ggplot2")

dd <- data.frame(
    x = 1,
    y = 0.3
)

ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.75) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1))

```
![works1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4000337/180976353-f53bf558-5aac-450b-8150-a67682d9dc5b.png)

Now, if we restrict the coordinates strictly to our definitions, using `expand = FALSE`, this does not work anymore:

```r
ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.75) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE)
```
![does-not-work1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4000337/180976674-4ef77deb-d902-4c37-95b3-f78b74dd8a8c.png)

Variations with `geom_line()` or `geom_abline()` behave in the same way:

```r
ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.75) +
    geom_abline(slope = 0, intercept = 0.75) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) # Does not work

ll <- data.frame(x = c(-Inf, Inf), y = 0.75)
ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line(data =  ll, aes(x, y)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) # Does not work
```

One solution I found was to set limits on the X-axis explicitly:

```r

ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.75) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1), xlim = c(0.95, 1.05), expand = FALSE)
```
![works2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4000337/180976981-f8064877-3e22-4a80-9339-13ea23a50e94.png)

But it's not as elegant: the drawback is that we don't have a nice X-axis with a single value anymore. 

I can see why `geom_line/hline/abline` don't like this (and can't see a line on non-continuous and virtually non-existent X-axis), but I wonder if there's a way to circumvent it, as all I want is to draw this line!

title: Add 'row.names' into ggplot_build(...)$data very useful for grouped geom_boxplot
description:
Hi.
After seeing in my boxplot that I may have some uncomplete groups of data under certain customer_ids, I wanted to see how filtering them out would change the behavior of all the rest.

My first idea was to gather the already calculated values in the drawn boxplot and filter the dataframe in order to draw it again.

Having successfully gathered the $data, I realized that my customer_ids are not listed on any column of the resulting dataframe. Instead, I saw a $y column with numeric values, which just guessing represents the order of the grouping variable.

Probably the plot object contains the grouping labels, but the "data" structure does not and it would help to have it.


----------

Next code is meant to confirm that no labels are shown in $data, and finally assign them.

I had to confirm that the sequence of $y matched the order of the group, which is a factor() type.
I did that by fixing the seed and inspecting the resulting order in Rstudio.
However, this is not optimum as I don't have knowledge on how sorting and data types are handled internally.
The ideal is to preserve the original grouping names.

```{r}
set.seed(111)
DF = data.frame(
  id  = factor( rep(LETTERS[1:5], 100), levels=LETTERS[1:5] ),
  COL = sample(1:20, 100, replace=TRUE)
)

# A     B       C     D      E
# 6.0   12.0    8.0   12.5   10.0  <-- xmiddle / ¿median?

bp = ggplot( DF , aes( COL, id ) ) + geom_boxplot();   
bp

# === SEARCH FOR Categorical-labels + Median values ===

# Getting boxplot data
Qggbp  = ggplot_build( bp )$data;         
typeof(Qggbp)    # list
Qggbp # gets converted into DF
row.names(Qggbp) # -> (nothing)
Qggbp$y          # -> null

# Getting boxplot data
Qggbp  = Qggbp[[1]]
typeof(Qggbp)    # list
Qggbp # gets converted into DF
row.names(Qggbp) # -> [1] "1" "2" "3" "4" "5"

# Realising tha they are numbered instead of labeled
Qggbp$y          # -> [1] 1 2 3 4 5   /  attr(,"class")  /  [1] "mapped_discrete" "numeric"
Qggbp$y %>% as.numeric # -> [1] 1 2 3 4 5

# Setting the names row-names to which they are associated.
row.names(Qggbp) <- levels( DF$id )
Qggbp

```

When writing this I found [this question of 5 years ago](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41435641/how-does-the-group-column-from-ggplot-build-correspond-to-the-original-factor-le)

title: Natively Cap the Axis Lines, as featured on the lemon package (feature)
description:
---- Feature Request:  Natively Cap the Axis Lines ----

It would be amazing to have the option to cap the axis lines, such as featured on the `lemon` package. The `lemon` package, however, requires to remove the ggplot2 default axis lines so that new ones can be drawn:
>  In order to manipulate the axis lines, they must be drawn. Modify the theme so the panel.border is not drawn (it will be on top of the axis lines), and have the axis lines drawn.

Therefore, it would be nice being able to cap the axis lines natively (without getting rid of the original axis lines).

Please find below a reprex of an example chart with capped axis lines:

```r
# one can install the `lemon` package from CRAN.
# install.packages('lemon')
library(tidyverse)
library(lemon)

set.seed(2)
letters_data <- purrr::map_dfr(
  letters,
  ~ data.frame(
    idx = 1:400,
    value = cumsum(runif(400, -1, 1)),
    type = .,
    flag = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), size = 400, replace = TRUE),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
)

letters_data %>% 
ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(idx, value, colour = type)) +
  coord_capped_cart(bottom = "both", 
                    left = "both",
                    ylim = c(-50,25)) +
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(legend.position="none",
        axis.ticks.length = unit(.25, "cm"), 
        axis.line = element_line()) + 
  coord_capped_cart(bottom=capped_horizontal(), 
                    xlim = c(0, 400),
                    ylim = c(-40, 20),
```

title: Remove random ggplot2 startup messages
description:
I might be a little conservative in my opinions, but generating unnecessary messages upon loading packages is bad practice. While I understand the intentions behind these messages, I for one, would hate if multiple future packages would print their own tips, every time I would start a new session.

```r
library(ggplot2)
```


Maybe consider generating a function that enables user to selectively add these tips to their sessions - perhaps upon loading `tidyverse`.
One might consider to generate a tips package that enable the user to select whether or not to receive tips e.g. `tips::tip_of_the_day(enable = TRUE)`, or alternately integrate into existing packages e.g. `usethis::tip_of_the_day(enable = TRUE)`

title: Simplify alignment for column geoms
description:
Currently the alignment of columns is always centre, which may not always be desired. E.g. in the following case, values of `date` always give the first of the month, but are used to indicate the whole month (as is fairly common practice):

```
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(lubridate, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- tibble(
  month = as_date(c("2020-01-01", "2020-02-01", "2020-03-01")),
  value = 1:3
)

ggplot(df, aes(month, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d")
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17475731/177399041-7ff49399-2ad7-40e7-a15b-680235652a5c.png)

In this case an `align` argument to `geom_col()` would be really useful to align the columns with the first of each month. `align` could accept values `"centre"` (the default), `"right"` and `"left"`, which would be the option used here. The current alternatives are to use `position = position_nudge()`, which is fairly esoteric for such a simple task (and wouldn't always work that well, e.g. since February only has 28 days), or to instead use `geom_rect()`, which again seems much too complex for such a simple task.

If you agree that this sounds like a useful feature I'd be happy to submit a PR.

As always, thanks for the hard work on this beautiful package! 

(N.B, this example is a bit contrived due to the use of `scale_x_date()` but it's the simplest example I could think of)

title: arrows are (mis-)plotted using geom_line()'s linetype styling
description:
Plotting arrows with `geom_line()` creates weird or broken looking arrowheads when `linetype` is non-solid and `size` is increased. It seems, arrowheads are plotted by re-using the line's linetype, e.g. a dashed line, which can result in arrowheads that look like they have pieces missing. The issue does not appear when using `linetype="solid"`.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x, y), data = data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = c(3)), linetype = "solid", size = 1.0, arrow = arrow()) +
  geom_line(aes(x, y), data = data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = c(2)), linetype = "dashed", size = 1.0, arrow = arrow()) +
  geom_line(aes(x, y), data = data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = c(1)), linetype = "dashed", size = 1.0, arrow = arrow(type = "closed"))
#> size aesthetic has been deprecated for use with lines as of ggplot2 3.4.0
#> ℹ Please use linewidth aesthetic instead
#> This message is displayed once every 8 hours.
```

title: whisker limits on geom_boxplot do not accord with documentation
description:
---

Box plot doc states "The upper whisker extends from the hinge to the largest value no further than 1.5 * IQR from the hinge (where IQR is the inter-quartile range, or distance between the first and third quartiles). The lower whisker extends from the hinge to the smallest value at most 1.5 * IQR of the hinge. Data beyond the end of the whiskers are called "outlying" points and are plotted individually." 

When you run the ggplot the red and green lines are at the whisker limits stated in the documentation they are not where ggplot boxplot draws the pictures.

Can the documentation be brought up to date to align with the ggplot boxplot?

```r

library(ggplot2)
library(triangle)

myTriangle <- data.frame(y=(rtriangle(1000,.5)-.5)^4)

myTriangle[1,1] <- -.1  # make own outliers
myTriangle[2,1] <- .1



quantile(myTriangle$y,c(.24,.5,.75,.95,.99))

IQR <- quantile(myTriangle$y,.75)-quantile(myTriangle$y,.25)
low <- quantile(myTriangle$y,.25) - IQR*1.5
high <- quantile(myTriangle$y,.75) + IQR*1.5


#doc
# The upper whisker extends from the hinge to the largest value no further than 1.5 * IQR from the hinge (where IQR is the inter-quartile range, or distance between the first and third quartiles). The lower whisker extends from the hinge to the smallest value at most 1.5 * IQR of the hinge. Data beyond the end of the whiskers are called "outlying" points and are plotted individually.

myTriangle %>%
  ggplot(aes(y=y)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=low),color="green")+
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=high),color="red")


```

title: About the name and the default value of `rename_aes`
description:
@thomasp85 
Sorry for bothering you. Re-reading #3672, I found I don't have clear answers to the following points. Can we discuss here?

1. Why is the default value of `rename_size` `FALSE`? I'm afraid it would feel a bit inconsistent that the extension packages that don't catch up with this change would behave differently, while we are very careful not to introduce breaking changes on ggplot2 itself by setting `rename_size = TRUE` everywhere necessary. What about
    a. using `rename_size = TRUE` by default for the first release, or
    b. making the default value of `rename_size` as an option or an edition? In this case, the user can choose the behavior they prefer, and the developer can use `rename_size = FALSE` (or `TRUE`) if they think it's inappropriate to expose it as an option.
3. Can we have another word than "rename"? It seems "rename" sounds like the original one is removed (c.f. https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/4884#issuecomment-1159863428), like dplyr's `rename()`, while `rename_size = TRUE` actually keeps the `size`.

description:

``` r
library("ggplot2")
library("sf")
#> Linking to GEOS 3.9.1, GDAL 3.3.2, PROJ 7.2.1; sf_use_s2() is TRUE
nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
indices <- which(nc$CNTY_ID >= 1820 & nc$CNTY_ID <= 1830)
nc <- nc[indices, ]

p <- ggplot(nc, aes(fill = NAME)) +
  theme_bw(15)

p + geom_sf(size = 3)
```

Changing `linewidth` does affect linewidth:

``` r
p + geom_sf(linewidth = 3)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/kW7vaDs.png)

This breaking change isn't documented in the NEWS.md file and according to the discussion in https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/3672 it doesn't seem like such a "breaking change" was intended until after proper deprecation?:

@yutannihilation wrote:

> Just curious, will this eventually change the behavior of size on Geoms that actually have both size and linewidth? I know there's no breaking change here, but https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/4872 made me think this might need some consideration to avoid ambiguity.
>
> For example, in the case of geom_pointrange(), it's not clear what to do when we want to increase only the size of the points. Does specifying only size achieve this? Or, will this increase both the size of the points and that of the lines? I feel the former behavior is right, but it would be a breaking change.

and @thomasp85 replied:

> At this point the ambiguous geoms will not differentiate but I think we would do that down the line after proper deprecation

title: Can we deprecate fatten arg of geom_pointrange()?

In my understanding, `fatten` was a workaround for the inability of controlling the point size and the line width differently. So, now that https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/3672 gets merged, I think `geom_pointrange()` no longer needs this parameter.

title: Issue with geom_contour_filled when the z values are too close together
description:
There seems to be a bug in the function `geom_contour_filled` where it fails in some simple cases.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

#Generate some data
data = crossing(x = 1:10, y = 1:10) %>% 
  mutate(z = (x+y)/4)

#Works great
ggplot(data) + geom_contour_filled(aes(x, y, z = z))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/6bGAOZr.png)

``` r
#Make a minor tweak and it fails
data2 = data %>% mutate(z = z + 100)
ggplot(data2) + geom_contour_filled(aes(x, y, z = z))
#> Warning: Computation failed in `stat_contour_filled()`:
#> factor level [4] is duplicated
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/MWgqJQN.png)


Looking into it, I believe the problem is with the legend names (more specifically the function `pretty_isoband_levels`). If the z values are close, you can get different levels with the same names because it only uses 3 digits (eg. "(101, 101]" and again "(101, 101]").

title: Tidiverse
function to save the data frame used to make a plot
description:
I often send results to customers in the form of plots. The customers themselves are familiar with R and would like to change some stylistic aspects. It would be very handy to send the (minimal) data that was used for creating the plot along with the plot. The original data is often in a much larger data frame which has gone through a few steps of manipulation before it is ready for passing to a `ggplot` function.

Thus, it would be very useful to have something like this:

```
g <- ggplot() + ...
ggsave(g, filename = "plot1.png")
ggdatasave(g, filename="plot1.RDS")
```

Does such a function already exist? I am aware that this can be achieved in different ways, but I thought this could be a nice feature.

title: Manual scales: not dropping and need exact order to merge with other aesthetics
description:
Setting a manual color scale via `scale_color_manual` doesn't drop unused factors (this could be a feature and not a bug but it is not documented on the help page), and unless they are in the same exact order as other aesthetics the legends are not merged.

I wish there were some kind of check and reorder the scales to see if they match. I'm not sure how easy is to do this, but I think it would make ggplot2 slightly more user friendly.

I didn't find this mentioned previously on any other issue but I might have missed them. 

``` r
library("ggplot2")
packageVersion("ggplot2")
#> [1] '3.3.6'
p <- ggplot(iris) +
  geom_point(aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, col = Species, shape = Species))
```

# Manual scale

``` r
p + scale_color_manual(values = c("setosa" = "red", "versicolor" = "green", "virginica" = "blue"))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/YXh1WFF.png)

# Manual scale with extra values

``` r
p + scale_color_manual(values = c("setosa" = "red", "versicolor" = "green", "virginica" = "blue", "Other" = "black"))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/qeziiKs.png)

drop doesn’t seem to work with manual values

``` r
p + scale_color_manual(values = c("setosa" = "red", "versicolor" = "green", "virginica" = "blue", "Other" = "black"),
                     drop = TRUE)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/7LREmEn.png)

# Manual scale with different order

``` r
p + scale_color_manual(values = c("versicolor" = "green", "virginica" = "blue", "setosa" = "red"))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/yyUXKzg.png)

The legends are not merged into a single one.

title: Expand documentation for coord_flip
description:
Hello

First of all, I have used `ggplot` pretty much every working day for I don't know how many years now, so I should use this opportunity to say thank you for the essential package / nice community / responsive authors / all the things that make it great 🤗 

In general I find the documentation of `ggplot` functions good, with good conceptual background and pretty thorough examples. However whenever I try to understand the tricksy bits of `coord_flip`, I find myself consistently frustrated by the pretty thin coverage. Questions I have wished were answered:

- How does `coord_flip` interact with `facet`s? i.e. does the `facet` x match to the flipped or unflipped x `aes`?
- How does `coord_flip` interact with `scale`s? i.e. does the `scale` x match to the flipped or unflipped x `aes`?
- How does `coord_flip` interact with axis-related params in `theme`?
- Do the `xlim` and `ylim` parameters in `coord_flip` refer to the axes before or after the flipping?
- I'm sure there are others...

It would be great to have an expanded **Details** section for the `coord_flip` documentation, going over the concepts here. Maybe even a little diagram! It could also be an opportunity to describe some cases where `coord_flip` doesn't work so well, or common pitfalls.

Thanks again!
Will

title: Lines with alpha values disappear in legend in some situations.
description:
---

When I make a lineplot with colour groupings and some alpha value I noticed the legend lines would disappear when plotted in RStudio, though when I make a reprex they still show up:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
    ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1,2,1,2), y=c(3,2,1,2), z=c("A","A","B","B"))) +
        aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z) +
        geom_line(size=2L, alpha=0.6)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/jM3Xdmv.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-05-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

This is what I see inside RStudio however:

![](https://i.imgur.com/8snXzSU.png)

So I investigated how to add the lines again using `guides()`. I found that setting `alpha=1` brings the lines back for me, and so does `alpha=0.999`, but `alpha=0.9` hides them again. I then went down a rabbit hole of doing a "does work/doesn't work" sort of binary search on each digit to learn that the threshold seems to be `0.99803921568627457230` which I noted has an interesting floating point representation. Curiously, `0.9980392156862745723` (without the 0 at the end) doesn't show lines in the legend, nor will anything lower, but anything higher will show them. This is again *not* reflected in the image in the following reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2) 
    ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1,2,1,2), y=c(3,2,1,2), z=c("A","A","B","B"))) +
        aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z) +
        geom_line(size=2L, alpha=0.6) +
        guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 0.9980392156862745723)))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/WJScVI2.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-05-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Versus anything higher (including for some reason concatenating a 0) which *is* reflected in the following reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2) 
    ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1,2,1,2), y=c(3,2,1,2), z=c("A","A","B","B"))) +
        aes(x=x, y=y, colour=z) +
        geom_line(size=2L, alpha=0.6) +
        guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 0.99803921568627457230)))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/XVRMNKc.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-05-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I'm not really sure what to make of this. I suspect someone with a deeper understanding of R's internal number representation could figure it out. Let me know if you want more information from me.

title: Legend for `geom_col()`'s size does not correctly depict change in size
description:
I'm not sure if this is related to issue #3729 at all, but here it is: when using the `size` aesthetic for a bar/col geometry, the corresponding legend does not match differences in sizes in the plot like e.g. a point geometry would. This is especially true if the `colour` aesthetic is also mapped to a variable from the dataset, as the outline completely disappears from the legend and therefore the audience might think that it's the darker area that depicts the size:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
# coloured outline (continuous)
exp_df <- data.frame(x = letters[1:4], y = 1:4)
ggplot(exp_df, aes(x, y, size = y, colour = y)) +
  geom_col()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/uqJSMHS.png)

``` r
# coloured outline (discrete)
ggplot(exp_df, aes(x, y, size = y, colour = x)) +
  geom_col()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/nhN7agM.png)

``` r
# transparent fill
ggplot(exp_df, aes(x, y, size = y, colour = y)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/FvOfbnl.png)

``` r
# single colour
ggplot(exp_df, aes(x, y, size = y)) +
  geom_col(colour = "red", alpha = 0)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/kjOHZq7.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-05-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

title: Helper stat for `geom_area()`
description:
I realised it would be pretty easy for us to automatically handle non-aligned data. Sketch of approach below

``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- tibble::tribble(
  ~g, ~x, ~y,
  "a", 1, 2,
  "a", 3, 5,
  "a", 5, 1,
  "b", 2, 3,
  "b", 4, 6,
  "b", 6, 7
)
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = g)) + geom_line()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/vWEA4py.png)

``` r
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, fill = g)) + geom_area()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/5fyFn0r.png)

``` r

all_x <- sort(unique(df$x))

completed <- df |> 
  split(df$g) |> 
  lapply(function(grp) {
    y_fun <- approxfun(grp$x, grp$y, yleft = 0, yright = 0)
    
    data.frame(
      g = grp$g[[1]],
      x = all_x,
      y = y_fun(all_x))
  }) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows()

ggplot(completed, aes(x, y, fill = g)) + geom_area()
```

title: Incorrect plot of geom_bar() for factor variables when using ..prop.. (+ workaround)
description:
When I was trying to produce a grouped barplot using `geom_bar()` with proportions on the Y axis (`aes(y = ..prop.., fill = ...)`), I got a totally weird output (see example). With or without faceting, (the latter using `position = "dodge"`), every factor level of each group has a bar of 100%.

As a workaround, I converted the factor to numerical data and used the factor levels as limits in `scale_x_discrete(limits = levels(...))`.

```r
#### EXAMPLE DATA ####

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)

# table
dat <- tibble(Gender = sample(c("female", "male"), 1000, TRUE), 
              Musicality = ordered(sample(c("none", "low", "moderate", "much"), 
                                          1000, TRUE, c(0.3, 0.1, 0.4, 0.2)),
                                   c("none", "low", "moderate", "much")))

#### INCORRECT BEHAVIOUR FOR FACTOR DATA (+ WORKAROUND) ####

# plot overall distribution (as proportions) of Musicality, using 'dodge'
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Musicality, fill = Gender)) + 
  geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop..), position = "dodge")
```
![geom_bar bug 1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/85945308/168257113-f6dfefa5-9450-4734-b346-20b7964a76fd.png)
```r
# Obviously a bug! Expected to look like this (but with percentages on the Y axis):
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Musicality, fill = Gender)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```
![geom_bar bug 1 expected like](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/85945308/168257106-4a93dcc9-08cd-4d9b-88fb-2eb39812f2da.png)
```r
# Workaround:
ggplot(dat, aes(x = as.numeric(Musicality), fill = Gender)) + 
  geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop..), position = "dodge") + 
  scale_x_discrete(limits = levels(dat$Musicality))
```
![geom_bar bug 1 workaround](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/85945308/168257111-699739b3-fdfa-4b75-b927-4cea844ac21a.png)
```r
# plot gender-wise distribution (proportions) of Musicality with faceting
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Musicality, fill = Gender)) + 
  geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop..)) +
  facet_grid(~Gender)
```
![geom_bar bug 2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/85945308/168257120-2f7d21a9-a5a5-46ef-91c4-76ccf4dc8944.png)
```r
# Obviously a similar bug! Workaround:
ggplot(dat, aes(x = as.numeric(Musicality), fill = Gender)) + 
  geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop..)) +
  facet_grid(~Gender) + 
  scale_x_discrete(limits = levels(dat$Musicality))
```
![geom_bar bug 2 workaround](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/85945308/168257115-04ed4528-973f-45b6-92e2-7f9562b32554.png)

title: Feature request: Support variable strip height
description:
I use `facet_wrap` with `ncol = 1` to present many barplots of likert-type data from a survey. The survey topic usually embraces several items that are too wide to be used as simple axis labels. This approach works well generally and in the case of item labels being too wide even for a facet label, I wrap them with `stringr::str_wrap()` or by using `strip.text = ggtext::element_textbox_simple()` in the `theme()` call. However, one single facet label spanning two lines makes the rest of the facet labels taller, resulting in the waste of space. AFAIK, this was not always the case in ggplot2 (I've seen plots from `{likert}` that accomplished that exactly, but the package seems broken).

Maybe it is more suitable for some ggplot2 extension, but my thoughts are that even ggplot2 itself could provide some argument enabling this behaviour. It makes sense to me only for single-column faceting, but it can be generally done for any layout.

The implementation seems straightforward as only `assemble_strips` requires the edits, starting with: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/21df8dc88e9b736a136bc39362defe2943008767/R/labeller.r#L570

What do you think about it? Are you familiar with any existing solution to this problem?

Here is some reprex for illustration:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

data.frame(x = c("a", "b")) |>
  ggplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ x, ncol = 1)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/tBigtCq.png)

``` r

data.frame(x = c("a", "a\nb")) |>
  ggplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ x, ncol = 1)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/vSSkhIb.png)

title: labeled breaks for binned color scale malfunction when show.limits = T
description:
---

When formatting labels for breaks in color scales, ggplot returns an error for the length of label vector if _show.limits = T_. This error appears even if the breaks and labels vectors are the same length. 

This may be because limits and breaks are passed to different vectors before compiling the final plot and therefore the user cannot easily write labels for limits and breaks together. An example is provided here: [https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71976832/custom-labels-for-limit-and-break-values-when-using-scale-color-binned-in-r-ggpl](url)

Is it possible to integrate limits and breaks in a more streamlined way to avoid the error message and not have to define labels with a custom function that circumvents the issue?

```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy, color = year)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_binned(limits = c(1999, 2008),
                    breaks = c(2000, 2002, 2004, 2006),
                    labels = c('2', '3', '4', '5'),
                    show.limits = F) # labels work

ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy, color = year)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_binned(limits = c(1999, 2008),
                    breaks = c(2000, 2002, 2004, 2006),
                    labels = c('2', '3', '4', '5'),
                    show.limits = T) # method fails when limits are activated

    # Error in f(): ! Breaks and labels are different lengths

```

``` r
library(tidyverse)
```

title: Feature Request: Monotonically Ordered Positions For Points
description:
It would be nice to be able to specify one keyword and get ordered dots, e.g. `geom_point(position = "ordered")`. I know this can be achieved with hacks like ordering the sample names' factor levels on the x-axis by increasing y-axis values and using facetting, but this proposed option would greatly simplify the goal. Example figure from _Science_ journal.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/631218/166630774-227cf721-9952-49a3-b40c-e8f986d26c29.png)

It could become as simple as:

```r
mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl, mpg)) + geom_point(position = "ordered")
```

and be a cleaner alternative to jittering, which doesn't have a 100% guarantee that two points will not overlap after jittering.

title: Evaluation of If Else in Aesthetics Error
description:
The example seems to be evaluating the else part, even though the if condition is true, and so it probably shouldn't be evaluated.

``` r
characteristicsList <- list(x = "Classifier Name")
ggplot2::aes(fill = if(is.null(characteristicsList[["fillColour"]])) NULL else !!rlang::sym(characteristicsList[["fillColour"]]))
#> Error in `rlang::sym()`:
#> ! Can't convert NULL to a symbol.
```

<sup>Created on 2022-05-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I sought feedback on R-package-devel mailing list and [a former R Core member thought it looks like a bug in ggplot2](https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-package-devel/2022q2/008009.html). The overall aim of this code is that I am creating a function that allows the end-user to specify what to place on the x-axis, and what variable (if any) to use for line colour and what one for fill colour. Also, being robust to spaces in column names in case end-user has those.

title: `ggsave()` doesn't render custom fonts when saving (+workaround)
description:
I've been using a few scripts that save plots with custom fonts loaded via [extrafont](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/extrafont/index.html). This was working fine up until a few days ago, when ggsave stopped saving the plots w/the custom font (I update this plot daily, so I can see from the commit history that on 4/27 it was working & on 4/28 it wasn't). 

For example, this renders in the IDE correctly:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.1.2
library(ggtext)
extrafont::loadfonts(device = "win")

ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(x = hp,
           y = qsec)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(plot.title = element_markdown(family = "Vivaldi")) +
  labs(title = "Here is a title rendered with **markdown**")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/5XYbPBd.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-04-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

but when I save w/ggsave, here's what appears:

![tmp](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/31866288/165965326-3063bb3d-d250-49ac-a482-71510300ab93.png)

Rendering in the IDE is fine, & saving by exporting from the IDE is fine, it's just when I call ggsave. I found a workaround that seems to do the job - specifying the device in both the filename *and* device fields, but it feels a bit clunky:

```r
# doesn't work
plot %>%
  ggsave("plot_without_font.png")

# works
plot %>%
  ggsave("plot_with_font.png",
         device = png)
```

Not sure what the difference is between a few days ago & now (I haven't updated packages in the past few days, so I'm assuming there's some latent issue in my environment or session), but thought I'd highlight in case anyone else is running into the same issue!

title: Mismatched fill colour with geom_dotplot
description:
When using `geom_dotplot` and specifying a `fill` aesthetic, we get a different output depending on whether `fill` is specified inside the function `aes` or as a separate vector. In the example below, I would expect all points below x~12 to be the same colour in both graphs.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# Use 'dose' inside aes
gg1 <- ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = len)) +
    geom_dotplot(aes(fill = factor(dose)),
                 binwidth = .5) +
    guides(fill = "none") # Remove legend

# Create separate vector for fill
dot_cols <- as.integer(factor(ToothGrowth$dose))
gg2 <- ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = len)) +
    geom_dotplot(fill = dot_cols,
                 binwidth = .5)

gg1 + gg2
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/BOeNdgU.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-04-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

As we can see, on the right, there are about 5 points between x=10 and x=12 that should be black but are actually red. 

As far as I can tell, this could be a consequence of the data being sorted with respect to x, which means that the rows of the dataset no longer match the elements of the vector `dot_cols`. As a proof of concept, I recreated the second graph but I sorted the data first (I also used the `group` aesthetic to try to get as close as possible to the original graph):

``` r
library(tidyverse)

# Repeat last graph but reorder data first
ToothGrowth2 <- arrange(ToothGrowth, len)
dot_cols2 <- as.integer(factor(ToothGrowth2$dose))
ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = len, group = factor(dose))) +
    geom_dotplot(fill = dot_cols2, 
                 binwidth = .5)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/TQqoaui.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-04-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Now all points below x~12 are black, as expected.

title: coord_polar _ remove extra grid line
description:
The issue has been discussed on https://stackoverflow.com/questions/72005238/scale-y-axis-on-a-polar-plot-in-ggplot/72005779#72005779 from which I copy the exchange:

When plotting the following,

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

foo <- tibble(theta = c(0, 10, 20), r = c(10, 30, 90))

ggplot(foo) +
  geom_point(aes(x = theta, y = r)) +
  coord_polar() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = 90) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 360), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = c(0, 90, 180, 270)) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "red")
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/5YUTYYl.png)

the Y-axis (= radius) expands to 100 instead of 90. In addition there are two circles corresponding to major grid elements, one at 90 as required and one at 100. I added the "theme" statement to demonstrate that both correspond to major grid lines.

A workaround proposed by user Allan Cameron was

``` r
ggplot(foo) +
  geom_point(aes(x = theta, y = r)) +
  coord_polar() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = 90) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 360), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = c(0, 90, 180, 270)) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = c("red", NA))
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/UdyOYDX.png)


... which works, but is hardly satisfactory ! Quoting A.C. :
"There is no outer axis line in coord_polar, and a grid line seems to be used in its place, without respecting axis.line theme elements."

title: [question] Adding rasterGrobs to specific facets systematically
description:
Hi everyone,

I'm opening this mostly as a "question issue", hoping to get some directions that would help me to solve another issue efficiently (see https://github.com/exaexa/scattermore/issues/8).

In short, we've got a package called `scattermore` that helps in certain very specific plotting workflows (mostly scatterplots with millions of points combined with Shiny) by being able to plot simple stuff very quickly. Internally, it processes points to a raster bitmap using some simple C code, and then just pastes the raster bitmap (created by `as.raster`) to the plotting area.

We have added some adaptors that allow using the functionality also from ggplot (instead of the base R), which has gained some attention and usage (the method is now used e.g. in [seurat](https://github.com/satijalab/seurat/)), despite the current implementation ss a bit of a quick hack (seen at https://github.com/exaexa/scattermore/blob/master/R/scattermore.R#L160 and briefed at https://github.com/exaexa/scattermore#quick-how-to).

Naturally, I'd love this to cooperate better with the rest of ggplot. One of the open issues is how to guess a "correct" raster or point size (in raster pixels) for plotting of the bitmap; but that can be "fixed" on the user side using a bit of guesswork. Recently, we found another issue (https://github.com/exaexa/scattermore/issues/8) with plotting data that do not go through the ggplot "data system" into the facets. The main question here is whether there would be a way to systematically use the faceting machinery of a given plot to split "external" data used by `geom_scattermost()` into facets, and add individual rasters into the right facets. In particular:

- is it possible to somehow access the computed facet dimensions during the plotting process, or is there functionality to compute per-facet minima and maxima for "fake data" as done here? https://github.com/exaexa/scattermore/blob/master/R/scattermore.R#L257-L261
- how do I put a `rasterGrob` to a specific facet? i.e., if I'm able to extract data for a given facet and I know what facet it is, how do I assign my bitmap to that asset in a code like this? https://github.com/exaexa/scattermore/blob/master/R/scattermore.R#L296

Many thanks for any help/opinions/hints :]
-mk

title: `scale_*_reverse()` should not be limited to continuous data
description:
`scale_*_reverse()` should allow discrete data that we have comparators for (or anything we can reorder using `desc`). For instance, strings can be ordered alphabetically. `scale_*_reverse()` would be the the most intuitive choice one would think about when trying to reverse their axes. However, running it with discrete data yields the following error:

```r
baz <- tibble(foo = c(0, 1, 2), bar = c("b", "a", "c"))
ggplot(baz, aes(x = foo, y = bar)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_reverse()
```

```Error in -x : invalid argument to unary operator```

Replacing the last line with `scale_y_reverse(NULL)` also returns the same error.

If `scale_*_reverse()` cannot be changed in such a manner as to be able to accept discrete data, perhaps a simple function `scale_*_reverse_discrete()` may be helpful, rather than the current workaround below:

```r
ggplot(baz, aes(x = foo, y = bar)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)
```

(inspired by https://stackoverflow.com/questions/28391850/reverse-order-of-discrete-y-axis-in-ggplot2)

EDIT: Fixed formatting, removed extraneous NULL

title: geom_point() and geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0) have different behaviors for zero values in scale_y_log10()
description:
I'm using ggplot2 3.3.5 and found that `geom_point()` and `geom_jitter(height = 0, width = 0)` have different behaviors for dealing with zero values in log-transformed axes.  In particular, geom_point() represents zeros as dots lying on the x-axis whereas geom_jitter() does not plot the zeros at all.  For me, this is relevant, because sometimes I want the jitter width to be non-zero, but height to be zero, and I don't want my dots to disappear!  Right now I work around the issue by setting the zeros to some small value I choose to make the plot nice.

```
data = data.frame(x = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2), y = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3))
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + scale_y_log10()
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_jitter(height = 0, width = 0) + scale_y_log10()
```

title: Feature requests: Composable mappings
description:
Hi ggplot2 team,

In brief: I think it would be neat if it was possible to do `aes(x = 1, y = 2) + aes(colour = class)`, and get the equivalent of `aes(x = 1, y = 2, colour = class)`. In effect, I'm suggesting that the `aes()` mappings might be composed, much like the layers of a plot.

Why might this be neat? I'm probably not the only one who writes out small novels in most `aes()` calls. Most of them are pretty repetitive among layers or plots, but not exactly repetitive enough to warrant assigning the mapping to a variable for reuse. 

Consider the example below, wherein we might want to recycle the `colour` mapping to other plots/layers as well. For instance, another dataset with different column names, which renders the `fill` part invalid, or another layer with similar but not duplicated mappings.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, disp)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(fill   = factor(cyl),
        colour = after_scale(colorspace::darken(fill, 0.3))),
    shape = 21, size = 3
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Ek9WJUn.png)

What I'm suggesting is to write some mechanism wherein parts of mappings can be easily combined. For example:

``` r
`+.uneval` <- function(e1, e2) {
  if (!inherits(e2, "uneval")) {
    rlang::abort("Appropriate message here")
  }
  ans <- ggplot2:::defaults(e2, e1)
  class(ans) <- class(e1)
  ans
}
```

This then allows you to set the `colour` outside of the plot, combine it with the mapping of the layer, and reuse it elsewhere at a later point.

```
dark_outline <- aes(colour = after_scale(colorspace::darken(fill, 0.3)))

ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, disp)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(fill = factor(cyl)) + dark_outline,
    shape = 21, size = 3
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/9deSk3Q.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-03-31 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Thank you for your work and consideration of this FR!

title: Non-linear scale changes geom_density values
description:
It is often useful to use `geom_density()` and `geom_function()` together, to compare data to a model. This is even an example in the `geom_function()` [man page](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_function.html#ref-examples). However, the density values output by `geom_density()` change when a logarithmic axis is used, making such comparisons difficult.

I suspect that `geom_density()` is performing the kernel density estimation upon the data _after_ the scale transformation has been applied. This will yield smoother curves in the logarithmic scale. However, it also reduces the distance between points, and this increases the density value.

If this is what's going on, perhaps we can find a way to apply an inverse transformation to the density values?

``` r
library(tidyverse)

p <- tibble(x = rnorm(1000, mean = 10)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x)) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 10), color = "red")

p + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, NA))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/khtrOzH.png)

``` r
p + scale_x_log10(limits = c(1, NA))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/eztvayq.png)

title: editing ggplot2-generated graphics in Adobe Illustrater / Affinity Photo
description:
Dear Support Team,

I am frequently generating graphics using ggplot2 in R. These graphics are then being edited using either Adobe Illustrator or Affinity Photo.
When importing those figures, they show white lines through the middle of a bar, violin or dot, which seem to mark the boundaries of adjacent objects. Another problem is that text is often grouped in non-intuitive ways. It becomes basically impossible to edit the figures / export them in a way so that the original graphic is being maintained.
This problem is especially daunting when dealing with scatterplots or barplots with many elements. Do you know a way with which I can reduce the amount of complexity/layers when exporting a ggplot to a postscript?

---

When opening ggplot-generated postscripts in a graphics editor, the plots show a lot of layers that destroy the image.

```r
ggsave(filename = "plot.ps,
         plot = my_plot, device = cairo_ps,
         dpi = "retina", height = 3.5*5, width = 3.5*5, units = "cm")
```

title: Feature request: Set theta limits in `coord_polar()` for partial plots

- The alignment of the axis is set by the `coord_polar(start = )` argument.
- The range of the values on the theta-axis is controlled by the underlying data / geoms / etc.

Currently, when plotting polar plots, the resulting plot gives the full "circle".
It would be nice if the "range" or "limit" (not which terminology fits here) of theta could be controlled to allow for partial plots.

For example to allow the following plots:

Etc....

---

The user facing mechanism for this would probably be to specify the range -- along theta -- the underlying plot should be mapped onto, defaulting to `c(0, 2*pi)` for the full circle.

Under this mechanism, the above plots would have the following values:

2. `c(325, 35)*pi/180`

title: Can't pass `n` argument from `geom_line` to `stat_density`.
description:
I'm trying to make a plot that draws one kernel density estimate (KDE) per group. There are many groups, so I'd like to turn the `alpha` down.  I call `geom_line(stat = "density", ...)` as I want just the line and the ability to control its `alpha`. I'd like to increase the number of points at which the KDE is evaluated with the `n = ` argument of `stat_density`, but doing so from `geom_line` yields an error. The error does not occur for other arguments passed to `stat_density` from `geom_line`

Looking at the reprex, first I draw the baseline plot:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

plot_df <- data.frame(
  x = rnorm(n = 2 * 5e2),
  group = rep(c("1", "2"), each = 5e2)
)

ggplot(
  data = plot_df
) +
  geom_line(
    mapping = aes(x = x, group = group),
    stat = "density",
    alpha = 0.2
  )
```
![](https://i.imgur.com/HtfaMqE.png)

Say I decide I want more `n`:

``` r
# trying to change the 'n' argument of stat_density yields an error
ggplot(
  data = plot_df
) +
  geom_line(
    mapping = aes(x = x, group = group),
    stat = "density",
    n = 2^10,
    alpha = 0.2
  )
#> Error in `remove_missing()`:
#> ! `na.rm` must be logical
```

An error. To check if this is something to do with the passing of arguments from `geom_line` to `stat_density` I try another argument, the `adjust` argument:

```r
# but the 'adjust' argument works
ggplot(
  data = plot_df
) +
  geom_line(
    mapping = aes(x = x, group = group),
    stat = "density",
    adjust = 3,
    alpha = 0.2
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/SjiwMs6.png)

This is what as I expected.

Trying the other way around -- that is calling `stat_density` with `geom = "line"` -- produces a plot, but not normalised as I would expect (but googling suggests that this is expected):

``` r
ggplot(
  data = plot_df
) +
  stat_density(
    mapping = aes(x = x, group = group),
    geom = "line",
    n = 2^10,
    alpha = 0.2
  )
```

title: Request for improved documentation of `geom_bar` and `geom_col`
description:
Hi All,

I would like to request that the documentation for `geom_bar` and `geom_col` indicate it's behavior when duplicated x/y are present in the data. There is nowhere in the documentation that indicates that the maximum value is taken when this situation occurs and additionally, no warnings are emitted to indicate that data is dropped. 

Arguably, this situation should cause an error since there is no way to plot "identity" of multiple values. 

In addition, this issue gets compounded when `position = "fill"` since the length of the segments now reflect the proportion of the group maximums. 

I've included a reprex below for clarification. 

```r
# Begin reprex --------------
reps <- paste0("rep", 1:3)
res <- lapply(reps, \(x){
    data.frame(x = paste0("sample", 1:3), 
                       y1 = abs(rnorm(3)),
                       y2 = abs(rnorm(3)),
                       y3 = abs(rnorm(3))) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = where(is.numeric))
}) %>% do.call(rbind, .)

ggplot2::ggplot(res, ggplot2::aes(fill = name, y = x, x = value)) +
    ggplot2::geom_bar(position = "dodge", stat = "identity")

# show the 3 values associated with the top bar in the plot 
dplyr::filter(res, name == "y3", x == "sample3")

# End reprex --------------
```

title: Easy way to split one field into n facets
description:
I often create a heatmap that is too long to display on one chart. I have to scratch my head each time to figure out how to break it into columns. I eventually end up with some integer division solution `x %/% y` like here:
Code ```r library(tidyverse) library(scales) df <- USJudgeRatings |> as_tibble(rownames = "y") |> gather(x, fill, -y) |> mutate( x = fct_reorder(x, fill, mean), y = fct_reorder(y, fill, sum, .desc = FALSE) ) |> print() # number of columns for plot n_col <- 2 # separate into columns and keep factor order plot_prep <- df |> mutate( y_order = as.integer(y), max_rows = ceiling(n_distinct(y) / n_col), facets = (-y_order %/% max_rows) # needs something to facet on, need '-' to keep highest values on left ) |> print() # plot p <- plot_prep |> ggplot(aes(x, y, fill = fill)) + facet_wrap(~facets, ncol = n_col, scales = "free_y") + geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.5) + scale_fill_stepsn(breaks = breaks_pretty(6), colours = viridis_pal()(5)) + theme( strip.background.y = element_blank(), strip.text = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(size = 7) ) p + theme(aspect.ratio = 1) # identify aspect ratio aspect <- plot_prep |> select(x, y) |> summarise_all(n_distinct) |> mutate(ratio = y / x / n_col) |> print() p + theme(aspect.ratio = aspect$ratio) # <------ fixed 1:1 size ```

title: stat_summary with geom_vline: Improve documentation?
description:
I find that the documentation of `stat_summary` is very much tailored to the default case of `geom = "pointrange"`. However, `stat_summary` is also useful with other geoms.

In my application, would like to mark quantiles in a density plot using vertical lines.  I figured out one way to do it within ggplot2 (and without generating a separate data.frame containing the quantiles) using stat_summary as follows:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg)) + geom_density() +
  stat_summary(aes(x = 0, y = mpg),
               fun.data = function(x) data.frame(xintercept = quantile(x, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))),
               geom = "vline")
```

Now a couple of questions occurred to me: First, is this a legitimate use of `stat_summary`? I am asking because the documentation of `stat_summary` is very much tailored to the default case of `geom = "pointrange"`. For example, the documentation of the argument `fun.data` explains:

> fun.data A function that is given the complete data and should return a data frame with variables ymin, y, and ymax.

This seems to be wrong: In my example, it suffices if `fun.data` returns a data.frame with all required aesthetics.

If my example is a legitimate use of `stat_summary`, I would suggest that the documentation should be updated. I would be glad to contribute to this, but before that I would like to make sure that I understand the philosophy behind `stat_summary`. Is it correct to say the following?

1. `stat_summary` computes summary statistics of the values of `y` stratified according to the value of `x`.
2. To explain the argument `fun.data`: A function that is given the complete data (for a single value of `x`) and should return a data.frame that contains all aesthetics that are needed by `geom`. For example, when `geom = "pointrange"`, `fun.data` should have variables `ymin`, `y`, and `ymax`.
3. I find the section about the argument `orientation` a little misleading and not precise enough.  In any case, one could add: `orientation` does not affect the computation of the summary statistics, which will always be done on values of `y`.

One could also add the above example to the documentation.

Finally, it is a little unfortunate that in this example, `stat_summary` has to be given two aesthetics, including the "dummy aesthetics"; however, at the moment, I don't have any idea how to simplify this.

title: Add the possibility to have guides lines when using coord_polar()
description:
# Request
So here is my feature request: Add a way to draw simple lines when using coord_polar() so that one can a) add them as guides to make the plot more readable and b) draw them behind other geoms so they are not obstructing the view. 

# Longer version
Dear ggplot2 maintainers,
I want to create polar histograms with ggpot2 and off the bat I think they look great in ggplot.  However there is one issue with the type of plot I created below (code if necessary can be found at the end)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17894303/158505158-35672613-9d56-4c0a-adb7-88dd487c1ebd.png)

and that is that this type of plot is that it is very difficult to read. More specifically it is difficult to map the count (or more generally speaking the y-axis) ticks and tick labels to the distance from the circles. That's why I would love to add guides lines from the ticks to the vertical axs of the circle. I have added an example for reference that I have done following a suggestion from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71476327/add-guide-lines-for-y-axis-when-using-coord-polar-for-polar-histogram

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17894303/158505502-9fa95048-2518-4d24-8d07-940eb451fb25.png)

So far, I have only been suggested a very hacky way of adding these lines and preferably it would be good to have the lines behind the geoms (e.g. the histogram in my case), which doesn't seem to work.  I am also aware of another hack to draw straight lines when using coord_polar() (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66196451/draw-straight-line-between-any-two-point-when-using-coord-polar-in-ggplot2-r) but the issue with that solution is that you cannot seem to draw from the tick because if the lines is too long it just disappears. 

# Code to reproduce
```r
library(ggplot2)
# Seed
set.seed(20220315)

# Create random data from 0 to 360
example_dat <- data.frame(rot_y = runif(1000, min = 0, max = 360))

# Create polar plot
ggplot(example_dat, aes(x = rot_y )) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 15, boundary = -7.5, colour = "black", size = .25) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,360),
                     breaks = seq(0, 360, by = 60),
                     minor_breaks = seq(0, 360, by = 15))  +
  coord_polar() +
  labs(title = 'Polar histogram of y rotation',
       y = 'Count',
       x = '')
```

title: log10 transformation gives the wrong scales with geom_bar
description:
Hello, 

When there is more than one entry per x value for geom_bar, `scale_y_continuous(trans="log10")` (or equivalently `scale_y_log10()`) labels the y-axis incorrectly. In this example, the max value should be 5e3, but the axis label goes up to 1e7. 

Expected behavior with simple data:
```r
df = data.frame(x=1:5, y=c(2, 20, 200, 400, 5000))

ggplot(df, aes(x=factor(x), y=y)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity") +
  theme_classic() +

```
![simple](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/32148717/156818829-e59a5a33-718b-441a-b21c-c9d75bf4d736.png)


Bug with more complex data: 
```r
df = data.frame(x=rep(1:5, 2),
                y=rep(c(1, 10, 100, 200, 2500),2), 
                group=rep(letters[1:5], each=2))

ggplot(df, aes(x=factor(x), y=y)) +
```

It is also a bit odd that the log10 transformation seems to be applied per entry, i.e. there is a total value of 2 for x==1, but it shows up as 0 because log10(1) + log10(1) = 0, whereas I would expect it to show log10(1+1).

title: Consider making `add_ggplot` as an S3 generic
description:
Would it be possible to make `add_ggplot` as an S3 generic? 
Currently we have to resort to overwriting `"+.gg"`  if we want to adopt a different method based on the class of `e1`, e.g. [`GGally`](https://github.com/ggobi/ggally/blob/master/R/ggpairs_add.R#L46:L69) is a prime example of this. This allows developers to fix issues like #4304 .

The fix, as below, will be relatively simple, but the downside is that you do have to export another function.

```r
#' @export
add_ggplot <- function(p, object, objectname) {
  UseMethod("add_ggplot")
}

#' @export
add_ggplot.ggplot <- function(p, object, objectname) {
  if (is.null(object)) return(p)
  
  p <- plot_clone(p)
  p <- ggplot_add(object, p, objectname)
  set_last_plot(p)
  p
}
```

title: ggplot with different types of shapefiletyps in one legend by using "colour" and "fill" argument as astetic to same time
description:
Hello,

I have a problem with drawing the legends in a ggplot. I have already searched the net for hours for a solution but have not found anything yet.

I am trying to create a ggplot with different line and polygon shapefiles. I draw the shapefiles with the function geom_sf().  The drawing is not a problem. My problem is related to the legend creation.

The goal is to create a plot that has a single legend and has all the different shapefile types including their colors and or fill astetic. That means, a line-shape should be represented in the legend as a simple line and a polygon-shape as a simple polygon. I have managed to do all that. 

The main difficulty is that one of the polygonshape (for better readability) not only uses the "fill" argument as astetic but also the "color" argument. 

If I create a plot where all polygonshapes always use the fill argument as astetic and all lineshapes always use the color argument as astetic everything works fine. But as soon as I include a polygonshape in the plot which uses both arguments at the same time, it destroys the whole legend structure. In this case, for example, the symbols for the line shapefiles suddenly have a frame and/or background although they should not have one. 

Is it not possible to build something like this with ggplot or am I just being clumsy?

Summary:

Analogous to the minimal example created below, I would like to create a single legend in this plot where:

A = a polygon symbol is without border (as it can be seen in the plot)
B = a polygon symbol is with border (as seen in the plot) and 
C = a simple line without border or background (as it can be seen in the plot).

How do I get this to work?

```
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

poly1 <- cbind(lon = c(5, 6, 7, 5), lat = c(52, 53, 51, 52))
poly2 <- cbind(lon = c(3, 5, 7, 3), lat = c(50, 52, 50, 50))

poly1 <- st_sf(st_sfc(st_polygon(list(poly1))))
poly2 <- st_sf(st_sfc(st_polygon(list(poly2))))
line <- st_sf(st_sfc(list(st_linestring(cbind(lon = c(5.5, 4.5), lat = c(53.5, 54.5))))))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = poly1, 
          aes(fill = "A"),
          colour = NA,
          show.legend = "polygon") +
  geom_sf(data = poly2, 
          aes(fill = "B", 
              colour = "B"),
          show.legend = "polygon") +
  geom_sf(data = line, 
          aes(colour = "C"), 
          show.legend = "line") +
  scale_fill_manual(name="Legend", 
                    values = c("A" = "yellow", "B" = "green"), 
                    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(linetype = c("blank","blank"), shape = NA))
                    ) +
  scale_colour_manual(name="Legend",values = c("B" = "blue", "C" = "purple"),
                     guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(linetype = c(0, 1)))) +
  theme_bw() 
```

title: Legend glyphs for geom_pointrange do not follow their plotted direction
description:
*(This is super similar to this past issue https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/1389, but the addition of bidirectional geoms in v3.3.0 have changed the circumstances of that original issue)*

---
 
Since ggplot2 3.3.0, geoms like `geom_boxplot()` and `geom_pointrange()` work with either the x or the y aesthetic, thus eliminating the need for packages like {ggstance} for horizontal point ranges:

```r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3)

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(x))) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = x - 1, xmax = x + 1))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Rba1ANw.png)


Currently, however, the legend keys for point ranges show vertical lines regardless of the direction of the actual point range. There are ways to adjust the legend keys by either [modifying some of the underlying grid grobs](https://stackoverflow.com/a/41475858/120898), or by adding an empty `stat_summary()` layer in combination with `geom_point()` and `geom_line()` ([example](https://stackoverflow.com/a/40229390/120898)), but these are fairly hacky.

In a previous issue #1389, [the official recommendation from Hadley was to use **ggstance**](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/1389#issuecomment-336525032), but now that `geom_pointrange()` can go an any direction now since v3.3.0, it would be neat if the legend glyphs matched the direction of the geoms for things like point ranges and box plots. I have no idea how feasible or difficult that would be though.

Thanks!

title: Discourage use of `position = "stack"` with non-linear scales.
description:
This issue is very similar to #257, but since it has been a while, I thought the topic is ripe to revisit.
In the example below, the plot with the log axis has the same exact values as the one without it. However, from interpreting the data, it appears as if group A has the value 90.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = "Z", y = 10, group = c("A", "B"))

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack")
p
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/47G3aNL.png)

``` r
p + scale_y_log10()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/12uzqTo.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-02-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

While I understand that the position adjustments are made after scale transformations, I think it would be nice if a user would be made aware that the plot has some perceptual problems. Therefore, I'm suggesting to do one of the following:

1. Throw a warning when a user tries to stack in non-linear space. However, I don't know if the architecture of ggplot2 would allow it, with most components being agnostic about one another.
2. Explicitly document in `?position_stack` that the position adjustments are made after scale transformations, with the warning that this can cause perceptual problems with non-linear scales.

Thanks for reading!

title: Way to apply custom function to labels and variables in a plot (similar to rename_with for a tibble)
description:
I have found that there are very many situations where it is useful to update both the labels and variable values that are used in a `ggplot` plot using a function mapping `character()` -> `character()`. A very typical use case is when a variable is named `total_population` but the axis label should read *Total population*. Currently some suggested solutions I have seen/used are:

* Setting labels manually, which is very flexible, but needs to be repeated for every label in every plot, and can lead to errors if a variable is replaced in a plot but one inadvertently neglects updating the label.
* Renaming variables prior to plotting. Although this is possible, it requires the use of quotes in the case of spaces, and can require updating the variable name in many places in generating the plot in the case when one simply wants to change the displayed text on the plot.

To address this issue, I have written a function that takes a `ggplot` object and an arbitrary function that maps one `character` vector to another. It then applies the function to text elements of the plot. The function also takes arguments to determine if the function should be applied to labels used in the plot, to variables (works on factors and strings), and allows choosing subsets of either labels or variables. An ellipsis argument allows additional parameters to be passed to the mapping function.

A reprex demonstrating the use of this function to plot mass against height using the `starwars` data set is included below.

The feature request is to add this function or an adaptation of it to the `ggplot2` package. I should note that due to limited familiarity with the ggplot object system, this function is not currently implemented as a standard `ggplot` function that is added to a plot using `+`. Instead, it has to be used separately, using a pipe or direct function call. It would probably be desireable to rewrite it so that it fit with regular usage.

I have searched widely for a solution for this problem, in case there is already a good way to do this, then my apologies for the noise :-)

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(snakecase)

# The proposed function
gg_apply <- function(p, fun, ..., .labs=TRUE, .vars=TRUE) {

  # Calculate new label values, and test that fun returns a sane result
  labels_new <- lapply(p$labels, fun, ...)
  stopifnot(
    all(sapply(labels_new, is.character)),
    length(labels_new) == length(p$labels)
  )

  # If .labs is true, we replace the labels in p
  if ( isTRUE(.labs) ) {
    .labs <- names(p$labels)
  }
  if ( isFALSE(.labs) || is.null(.labs) || all(is.na(.labs)) ) {
    .labs <- character()
  }
  stopifnot(is.character(.labs))

  # .labs is now a character vector of labels to replace
  for ( lab_name in .labs ) {
    p$labels[[lab_name]] <- labels_new[[lab_name]]
  }

  # Process non-character list values for labs.
  # If neither of these conditions is true, vars MUST be a
  # character vector, or we bail.
  if ( isTRUE(.vars) ) {
    .vars <- names(p$data)
  }
  if ( isFALSE(.vars) || is.null(.vars) || all(is.na(.vars)) ) {
    .vars <- character()
  }
  stopifnot(is.character(.vars))

  # .vars is now a character vector of variables to replace
  for ( var_name in .vars ) {

    # Process a character variable and do some sanity testing
    if ( is.character(p$data[[var_name]]) ) {
      var_new <- fun(p$data[[var_name]], ...)
      stopifnot(
        is.character(var_new),
        length(var_new) == length(p$data[[var_name]])
      )
      p$data[[var_name]] <- var_new
    }

    # Process a factor variable and do some sanity testing
    if ( is.factor(p$data[[var_name]]) ) {
      var_fct_old <- p$data[[var_name]]
      var_chr_new <- fun(as.character(var_fct_old), ...)
      levels_new  <- fun(levels(var_fct_old), ...)
      stopifnot(
        is.character(var_chr_new),
        length(var_chr_new) == length(var_fct_old)
      )
      p$data[[var_name]] <- factor(var_chr_new, levels=levels_new)
    }

  }

  p
}

# Example usage of the function
p <- starwars %>%
    filter(mass < 1000) %>%
    mutate(species = species %>% fct_infreq %>%  fct_lump(5) %>% fct_explicit_na) %>%
    ggplot(aes(height, mass, color=species, size=birth_year)) +
    geom_point()
p %>% gg_apply(snakecase::to_sentence_case)
#> Warning: Removed 23 rows containing missing values (geom_point).

```
![](https://i.imgur.com/HQb2bCb.png)

In the plot, note that all the labels are formatted using sentence case, as one would expect in a publication. Also note that any function can be used. For example, to create representations of a plot in multiple languages, one could use a lookup function that maps variable names to different language representations.

title: Feature Request: Excel-Like "Display Units" functionality
description:
In Excel, there is an option to choose the units when making a plot. For example, if you select "Millions", the axis tick values are all divided by 1 million and the word "Millions" appears next to the axis indicating the units. This is very useful because the units are indicated and the plot looks better without ,000,000 at the end of all the y-axis numbers.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11261404/152703925-81af29a7-5fdf-4d97-b4b0-a623e8a73c39.png)

I can get there in ggplot2 by working out the right `x` and `y` position for annotate so that the label is in the top left and not obstructing anything, and then giving the right function to labels in `scale_y_continuous`. But, it would be nice to have a ggplot function for this. The label ("Millions") and function (./1e6) can be user-supplied, the big pain is just figuring out the right x and y values for each plot and each time you resize a plot.

```{r}
df <- 
  structure(list(date = structure(c(18628, 18659, 18687, 18718, 
  18748, 18779, 18809, 18840, 18871, 18901, 18932, 18962), class = "Date"), 
      y = c(6105750.57579939, 6119933.22024793, 4020995.18830257, 
      6935125.38889255, 12647068.2650316, 6810926.72861688, 10050003.3378196, 
      12234936.8401193, 9163733.44758565, 11271291.6355059, 7451434.07531243, 
      8564463.78746752)), row.names = c(NA, -12L), class = "data.frame")
 
ggplot(df, aes(x = date, y = y)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  annotate("text",
    x = min(df$date) - 36, max(df$y) - 1e6, label = "Millions", hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
    angle = 90, color = "grey40"

  coord_cartesian(xlim = range(df$date), clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) x / 1e6)
```

title: scale_colour_manual() silently ignores drop = TRUE
description:
This might be expected behavior but it seems to conflict with the documentation:

## Reprex

### As Expected

```r
library(tidyverse)

df <- mutate(mtcars, cyl = factor(cyl, levels = as.character(c(2,4,6,8))))

p <- ggplot(df, aes(mpg, wt, color = cyl)) + geom_point()
p + scale_colour_discrete(drop = TRUE)  # omits "2" from legend, as expected
p + scale_colour_discrete(drop = FALSE) # puts "2" in legend, as expected
```

### Unexpected

```r
# imagine this is a palette being used widely across an organization
my_global_palette <- c("2" = "black", "4" = "orange", "6" = "blue", "8" = "darkgreen") 

# puts "2" in legend, even though it's not in the levels that appear in the data
p + scale_colour_manual(values = my_global_palette, drop = TRUE) 
```

## Description

`?scale_manual` says:

> `drop`
>   Should unused factor levels be omitted from the scale? The default, `TRUE`, uses the levels that appear in the data; `FALSE` uses all the levels in the factor.

`scale_colour_manual(..., drop = TRUE)` silently accepts the `drop` argument, but in the last example above, the factor level "2" is still shown in the legend.

Maybe the intent is for `values` to take precedence over the `drop` argument, but (a) this is unclear from the documentation, and (b) I think a case could be made against it. A user may wish to define and reuse a default palette without all elements of that palette appearing every time. (Maybe that's achievable in some other way?)

title: Axis ticks reserve space, even when absent
description:
Hi there,

I've come across a few cases on SO where some confusion was created by axis ticks creating whitespace around the plot, even when `axis.ticks = element_blank()` ([example 1](https://stackoverflow.com/q/70945828/11374827), [example 2](https://stackoverflow.com/a/70924084/11374827)). I'm not sure whether this is intentional or not, but I found it to be a bit counterintuitive. To illustrate:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, cty)) +
  geom_point()

p +
  theme(
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.length = unit(2, "cm") # exaggerated for clarity
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/PZHWcsX.png)

There are other ways to arrive at the same plot without the involvement of axis tick length, so it doesn't seem like the axis tick lengths are a necessary part for this purpose.

``` r
p +
  theme(
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x.bottom = element_text(margin = margin(t = 2, unit = "cm")),
    axis.text.y.left   = element_text(margin = margin(r = 2, unit = "cm"))
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/348b1SQ.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-02-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

If the ggplot2 maintainers agree with me, I could draft a PR to remove the empty space when the axis ticks are blank.

title: `annotate()` with hline and vline geoms
description:
I was adding other annotations to a plot, and wanted to add reference lines. I was in the mindset of `annotate()`ing thigs, so I tried to use it with `"hline"` and `"vline"`, but discovered that nothing happened. For example:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(data.frame(x = 1, y = 1), aes(x, y)) + geom_point()

p +
  annotate("hline", yintercept = 0) +
  annotate("vline", xintercept = 0)
```

What I expected:

``` r
p +
  annotate("segment", x = -Inf, xend = Inf, y = 0, yend = 0) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = -Inf, yend = Inf)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/laYjbuG.png)

I realize the “solution” here is to use the geoms directly with fixed values:

``` r
p +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
```

But `annotate()` not working seems like an unexpected inconsistency.

title: Reversed legend order when geoms are horizontal
description:
When flipping the orientation of a geom (e.g., geom_bar or geom_errorbar), the order of the color/fill/etc groups are flipped, but not the order of those groups within the legend. The ideal behavior would be that by default the legend order always matches the order in the plot.

```r
ggplot(mpg, aes(y = class)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = drv)) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

title: scale_x_datetime limits with histogram/stat_bin: warning message about missing values
description:
When using scale_x_datetime to set limits on the axis with a histogram, a warning message is produced:

```r
d1 <- lubridate::now()
tibble(date = d1) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(date)) + 
    geom_histogram() + 
    scale_x_datetime(limits = c(d1-1, d1+1))
```

produces:

```
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (geom_bar).
```

There is only 1 row of data.  Often with geom_histogram() this warning happens when a bin/bar is excluded from the plot (not a row from the original data).  But in this case, there should only be one bin/bar.  What are the extra bars/values that are missing?  The plot appears normal: there is one bar as there should be.  Initially I thought it was because bins is set to the default of 30.  

The warning message changes if you explicitly set bins=1 

```r
d1 <- lubridate::now()
tibble(date = d1) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(date)) + 
    geom_histogram(bins = 1) + 
    scale_x_datetime(limits = c(d1-1, d1+1))
```

produces:

```
Warning message:
Removed 1 rows containing missing values (geom_bar).
```

And if the limits are increased enough, the warning message goes away:

```r
d1 <- lubridate::now()
tibble(date = d1) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(date)) + 
    geom_histogram(bins = 1) + 
    scale_x_datetime(limits = c(d1-10, d1+10))
```

This happens with more observations as well, and you get the same warning message whether or not bars are actually excluded:

```r
d1 <- seq(lubridate::now(), by=1, length.out=10)
tibble(date = d1) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(date)) + 
    geom_histogram() + 
    scale_x_datetime(limits = c(min(d1), max(d1)))  # limits too small - min and max bars not drawn
```

```r
d1 <- seq(lubridate::now(), by=1, length.out=10)
tibble(date = d1) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(date)) + 
    geom_histogram() + 
    scale_x_datetime(limits = c(min(d1)-1, max(d1)+1))  # larger limits - all bars show
```

This seems to be misleading and inconsistent.  With real data, the warning about 2 missing values appears regardless of the limits I set.

I tried to track this through stat_bin, but I couldn't find a point where it seemed like this would be caused.

``` r
  x = pillar::num((1:10) / 100, fixed_exponent = -3, notation = "eng"),
```

title: Provide filled counter-part for geom_step
description:
To visualize discrete state change progressions, it would be great if `geom_step` could be extended to also provide a filled counter-part (similar to `geom_area`).

For a discussion ( including some rather tedious workarounds) see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/21887088/generate-a-filled-geom-step

Currently, with geom_area we get 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/200952/145805739-ecfa7d6b-6b3a-4e98-9eeb-58b7202ce1d2.png)

Because of the way geom_area works there are linear interpolations between subsequent points, which are incorrect as they are not reflected in the step-wise nature of the data.

Since the state changes are discrete in nature, geom_step gives a more precise (but visually flawed) picture
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/200952/145805850-06abb349-55d7-4d5f-9744-8aa785ac3e16.png)

Example data:
[filled_step_data.csv](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/files/7703479/filled_step_data.csv)

Example code:
```r
require(tidyverse)

read_csv("filled_step_data.csv") %>%
      ggplot(aes(timestamp, accu_moves)) +
     # geom_step() +
     geom_area()
```

title: should legend styling elements within guide_* instead be within theme?
description:
I've noticed that legends are not able to be styled completely within a theme, and instead need arguments provided to a guide_* layer.

This seems sub-optimal, as you are unable to have all styling aspects of a plot within 1 theme.

For example, say you wanted to always have black frame and black ticks around plots with colorbar legends, you then need to always add a guide_colorbar layer. It would preferable that if in theme, you could add colourbar.frame and colourbar.ticks arguments etc. in the same way that you would do for axis.line or axis.ticks. 

Is it possible to move legend styling aspects from guide_* to theme*? Or to have them in both? 

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)

custom_theme <- theme_minimal()

p <- ggplot(penguins) +
  geom_point(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, col = flipper_length_mm)) +
  custom_theme

p +
  guides(col = guide_colorbar(frame.colour = "#323232", ticks.colour = "#323232"))
```
