However, adding a geom (either before or after adding the secondary axis) fixes the issue:
```r
plot + ggplot2::geom_point(data = data.frame(x = 0.5, y = 0.5), mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y))
```

Best,
Frantisek

title: Add filter param within aes()
description:
`ggforce` has a filtering param in the `aes()` mapping that I find really helpful. ([examples](https://ggforce.data-imaginist.com/reference/geom_mark_rect.html#examples), [source code](https://github.com/thomasp85/ggforce/blob/1f17eb3cdb0ef54a6ed5dcb77ef5fecb195c90e4/R/mark_ellipse.R#L83-L89)) With 4.1, I'm trying to phase out `%>%` in as many places as possible. I can use the `magrittr` pipe like this `geom_text(data = . %>% filter(a == b))` but I can't use this `geom_text(data = filter(., a == b))` or `geom_text(data = . |> filter(a == b))` -- I know this is expected this to fail
Would it be possible to add a filter param so that I could write `geom_text(aes(filter = (a == b)))`
This is a common workflow that lets me avoid adding objects to my global environment. I use `. %>% filter()` to keep the factor levels and aggregations that I established ```r library(tidyverse) mpg |> count(class) |> mutate(class = fct_reorder(class, n)) |> ggplot(aes(n, class, label = n)) + geom_col(fill = "lightblue") + geom_text(data = . %>% filter(n %in% range(n))) ``` ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14003618/121685332-cb9a0400-ca8d-11eb-8425-50881f504fcd.png) With `ggforce`, filtering looks like this: ```r ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy)) + ggforce::geom_mark_rect(aes(filter = hwy > 40)) + geom_point() ``` ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14003618/121687082-ee2d1c80-ca8f-11eb-9f40-30b9eca45a20.png)

title: Cannot detect geom orientation in draw_key anymore
description:
In {ggdist} I have been detecting the orientation of the geom when drawing legends inside `draw_key()`. I do this by checking the value of `params$orientation`, which has been working fine. However, I was just testing with the dev version of ggplot2 and this no longer works; `params$orientation` is now returning `NA` inside `draw_key()` unless it is set explicitly by the user.

## Expected output

Specifically, here is the github version of {ggdist} (`remotes::install_github("mjskay/ggdist")`) with the CRAN version of {ggplot2} (3.3.3):

``` r
library(ggdist)    # CRAN version or remotes::install_github("mjskay/ggdist")
library(ggplot2)   # CRAN version

ggplot(
  data.frame(g = c("a","b"), x = rnorm(1000, c(1,2))),
  aes(y = g, x = x, color = g)
) + 
  stat_pointinterval()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Xqkk2la.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-06-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>


Note the orientation of the intervals in the legend matches the auto-detected orientation of the intervals in the geom.


## incorrect output on dev version of ggplot2 

Here is the output on the dev version of ggplot2, which appears to be because `params$orientation` is `NA` inside the key function (even though it is detected correctly in `setup_params()`):

``` r
library(ggdist)    # remotes::install_github("mjskay/ggdist")
library(ggplot2)   # remotes::install_github("tidyverse/ggplot2")

ggplot(
  data.frame(g = c("a","b"), x = rnorm(1000, c(1,2))),
  aes(y = g, x = x, color = g)
) + 
  stat_pointinterval()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/pW3TmhO.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-06-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>


## workaround

It is possible to work around this by manually setting the orientation:

``` r
library(ggdist)    # remotes::install_github("mjskay/ggdist")
library(ggplot2)   # remotes::install_github("tidyverse/ggplot2")

ggplot(
  data.frame(g = c("a","b"), x = rnorm(1000, c(1,2))),
  aes(y = g, x = x, color = g)
) + 
  stat_pointinterval(orientation = "y")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/t2w9RE9.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-06-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

Is there another (more correct) way to detect geom orientation in `draw_key`? Or is this not a thing that should be done in the first place?

title: How to add non-scientific p values on ggplot2 ?
description:

```
transPvalue=function(p0){

  if(p0<0.01){
    p0=formatC(p0, format="e", digits=2);#p0 #"1.2e-52"

title: Problem with `geom_ribbon` and alpha combined with `coord-cartesian` in R 4.1.0 on Windows
description:
Since upgrading to R 4.1.0, I've run into an issue with `ggplot2` on Windows where setting an `xlim` using `coord_cartesian` can result in a `geom_ribbon` being suppressed altogether. I've been able to reproduce this on two different Windows 10 machines running R 4.1.0, both inside RStudio and RGui. Running the code below without the `coord_cartesian` works fine on all machines I've tested. With the `coord_cartesian`, it produces a plot with no ribbon on my two Windows 10 machines using R 4.1.0, but works fine on R 4.0.5 on Windows 10 as well as R 4.1.0 tested using Ubuntu 20.04. Note removing the `alpha` parameter makes the issue go away even on R 4.1.0 on Windows 10.

I first ran into this using the `survminer` package, but I've managed to get a reprex now which occurs just in `ggplot2`.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:10, ymin = 1:10, ymax = 10 + 1:10), aes(x)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), alpha = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(c(1, 9))
```

title: GeomTile should have a non_missing_aes with xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax
description:
Similarly to `GeomBar` and `GeomCol` that use `GeomRect` to draw, I believe `GeomTile` too should  declare a `non_missing_aes` member for xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax variables.

For example in `GeomBar` I see this:
```
  # These aes columns are created by setup_data(). They need to be listed here so
  # that GeomRect$handle_na() properly removes any bars that fall outside the defined
  # limits, not just those for which x and y are outside the limits
  non_missing_aes = c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax"),
```

I stumbled to this, using `geom_bin2d` (which uses `GeomTile`) where it may produce data with NA in any of xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax. Here is a reprex showing that result grob contains NAs.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(x, y)) + xlim(4, 10) + ylim(4, 10) + geom_bin2d()
g <- layer_grob(p, 1)[[1]]
#> Warning: Removed 478 rows containing non-finite values (stat_bin2d).
any(is.na(g$x)|is.na(g$y))
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2021-05-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

Adding the `non_missing_aes` fixes this.

description:
Came across [this StackOverflow post](https://stackoverflow.com/q/67735115/680068), when numeric values are stored as character, the order of first paired bars are flipped.

Data:
```R

                                          1L, 2L, 3L, 4L),
                                        .Label = c("Mar-2021", "Jun-2021", "Sep-2021", "Dec-2021"),

                       Key = c("Previous Forecast", "Previous Forecast", "Previous Forecast", "Previous Forecast",

                       Value = c("3.1", "3.4", "3.3", "3.0",

title: Layers inheriting aesthetics at the stage or whole aesthetic level
description:
Hi, everyone. I don't think there is an answer per se to this question, but I ran across an issue when I wanted to create the following side-by-side jitter and boxplot:
``` r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(iris, 
       aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length)) + 
  geom_jitter(aes(x = stage(start = Species, after_scale = x - 0.1)), 
              width = 0.05) + 
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, 
               position = position_nudge(x = 0.1), 
               outlier.alpha = 0)
```

![d874462b099af08a086c219bc3d07ccf5dd3e4a7](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4877315/119919893-60065180-bf39-11eb-89a4-face4eda6a38.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-05-24 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

Basically, I wanted the plots to be centered on the tick marks, which required a nudge in opposite directions for each. The boxplot was easiest with the use of `position_nudge`. The stripchart was a little more difficult, given the fact that there is no built-in `position_jitternudge`. The fairly recent addition of our ability to manipulate the aesthetic mapping stages makes this possible, however, by specifying a manual nudge in the `after_scale` step. Notice, however, that I have to repeat the `start` aesthetic mapping, even though aesthetic inheriting is on for the `geom_point` layer (by default). To illustrate that I need to specify it, here's a reprex of just specifying the `after_scale` part (this was my initial try at the plot, where I incorrectly assumed the `start` stage would be inherited):

``` r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(iris, 
       aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length)) + 
  geom_jitter(aes(x = after_scale(x - 0.1)), 
              width = 0.05) + 
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, 
               position = position_nudge(x = 0.1), 
               outlier.alpha = 0)
#> Error: geom_point requires the following missing aesthetics: x
```

<sup>Created on 2021-05-24 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

In summary: it appears that *aesthetic inheritance, and overriding them, happens at the whole mapping level, rather than at the individual stage level*. So here's my question: Would it make sense to allow for overriding inherited aesthetics at the individual stage levels to avoid duplicate mapping specifications?

title: Accreditation of Author in `stat_ellipse()` Documentation
description:
Hello everyone, 

I hope this finds you well.

I noticed that the authors mentioned in the `stat_ellipse()` function are  the authors of the `car` package and not specifically not those who made the function it was inspired from (`car::dataEllipse())`

I have attached a screenshot of the documentation below.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/46410142/119870690-a2a33c00-beef-11eb-9889-2e5027dd976f.png)

The other two authors of the given function (besides for John Fox) are [Georges Monette](https://github.com/gmonette) and [Michael Friendly](https://github.com/friendly) who were the ones together with Fox help develop the idea and the function. 

Attached is the relevant documentation from the `car` package showing their contributions:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/46410142/119871641-a71c2480-bef0-11eb-8d39-34d8e55d735c.png)

As a student of Georges I think it would be appropriate to give him as well as Dr. Friendly a mention in the `stat_ellipse()` documentation as they both together with Fox founded and elucidated the idea of data ellipses (besides for being developers for the `dataEllipse()` function).

The relevant paper on the concept of data ellipses written by Monette, Fox and Friendly is [here
](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistical-science/volume-28/issue-1/Elliptical-Insights-Understanding-Statistical-Methods-through-Elliptical-Geometry/10.1214/12-STS402.full)

I understand that you may just want to attribute the package authors and not the relevant contributors but I thought it would be worthwhile trying to get them both mentioned in the documentation as well. 

Looking forward to hearing back.

title: Suggestion: Replace Jitter's Random Noise with Quasi-Random Noise
description:
A small suggestion for an improvement to `geom_jitter`. `geom_jitter` is good for small numbers of points, but with large numbers of points, particles will still tend to overlap. Instead of adding a small amount of random noise, we can use a low discrepancy sequence to slightly perturb points in a way that reduces the overlap between points by more than random noise. As an example, you can look at a two-dimensional linear congruential generator based on the plastic ratio on the top left. Compare this to the results of randomly jittering points, which can be seen on the bottom right.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/71727937/119757070-468dd880-be59-11eb-83b3-80233aef9d6a.png)

It's immediately clear that there's a lot less overlap and the space is being used much more efficiently. Obviously you'll never be able to completely eliminate overlap, but I think this should be able to push it back further so that it doesn't become as big an issue until you get larger sample sizes.

title: n.breaks for sec_axis
description:
Suggestion for improvement:

When using a continuous scale I find the `n.breaks` argument very useful and intuitive to use. However, when using the `sec.axis` argument to simply duplicate the existing axis I run into the issue that:

1. The labels/ticks of the original axis are not actually duplicated, rather the labels prior to any manipulations are duplicated.
2. The `sec_axis` function does not have a similar `n.breaks` argument.

I believe it would be very useful if the secondary axis could have the `n.breaks` argument and/or duplicate the primary axis that utilised this argument.

title: breaks and labels different lengths error with scale_size_binned()
description:
---

It isn't clear how to set labels and breaks for scale_size_binned() - as you can see in the reprex, the breaks and labels are, in fact, the same length, yet it's still throwing an error.  This works if you remove limit=c(1,10). 

```r
set.seed(10)
t.dat <- data.frame(x=runif(100),y=runif(100),value=runif(100,1,10))
ggplot(t.dat,aes(x=x,y=y))+
  geom_point(aes(size=value))+
  scale_size_binned(breaks=c(1,2,5,10),
                    labels=c("1","2","5","10"),
                    limits = c(1,10))
Error: Breaks and labels are different lengths
```

title: Add option to jitter outliers in a boxplot
description:
I would like to be able to add a small amount of jittering to outliers in a boxplot or alternatively stack the points to avoid having them overlap.

Here is an example of where points in a boxplot overlap:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# outliers are overlapping
ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, cty)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/PzsKZII.png)

To add jittering to these outliers, we currently have to result to the following hack, by creating a separate dataset of outliers and plotting them using `geom_jitter()` manually.

``` r
# adding jittering to outliers is a bit of work
outliers <- 
  mpg %>%
  group_by(drv) %>%
  filter(cty > quantile(cty, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR(cty) | 
           cty < quantile(cty, 0.25) - 1.5 * IQR(cty))

ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, cty)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0, width = 0.1, data = outliers)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/66YKeYh.png)

I understand that the `position` argument in `geom_boxplot()` is already "occupied", so maybe the simplest solution would probably to just add a new argument `outlier.jitter = c(0, 0)` (for x and y coordinate jittering respectively).

An even better solution would of course be to incorporate the beeswarm algorithm from **ggbeeswarm**:

``` r

library(ggbeeswarm)

ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, cty)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_beeswarm(data = outliers)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/vfF9qme.png)

log_breaks <- function(maj, radix = 10) {
  function(x) {
    minx <- floor(min(logb(x, radix), na.rm = TRUE)) - 1
    maxx <- ceiling(max(logb(x, radix), na.rm = TRUE)) + 1
    n_major <- maxx - minx + 1
    major_breaks <- seq(minx, maxx, by = 1)
    if (maj) {
      breaks <- major_breaks
    } else {
      steps <- logb(1:(radix - 1), radix)
      breaks <- rep(steps, times = n_major) +
        rep(major_breaks, each = radix - 1)
    }
    radix^breaks
  }
}

scale_x_log_eng <- function(..., radix = 10) {

    trans = log_trans(radix),
    breaks = log_breaks(TRUE, radix),

  )
}

title: Document computed variable `n`  in `stat_density()`.
description:
Today I was surprised by the following. I wanted to compute proportional densities of two groups. This is doable by using `y = after_stat(count / nrow(df))`, but I had precomputed `n <- nrow(df)` and used it as below:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(
  x = c(rnorm(1000, -1), rnorm(100, 1)),
  group = rep(c("A", "B"), c(1000, 100))
)

n <- nrow(df) 

ggplot(df, aes(x)) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count / n),
                   fill = group))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/W47N2F3.png)

Both densities above integrate to 1, whereas I wanted the sum of density areas to be 1. I can fix this by using another symbol for the number of observations.

``` r
random_symbol <- n

ggplot(df, aes(x)) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count / random_symbol),
                   fill = group))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Vvhxsyh.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-05-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I don't think the behaviour is problematic, but it would be nice if `n` was documented as a computed variable in `?stat_density`.

As a side note, the note in `?after_stat` reads:
> Evaluation after stat transformation will only have access to the variables calculated by the stat.

Though in the second plot, I can use `random_symbol` from the global environment.

title: Documentation tweak for stat_function xlim argument
description: Current documentation for `stat_function` xlim argument is "Optionally, restrict the range of the function to this range." However, xlim can be used to _widen_ the _domain_ of the function beyond the original data mapping.

description:
This is question related to inter-operation between packages and how to best achieve it. I have made a pull request for 'ggrepel' trying to easy this problem. During the exchange of ideas with @slowkow who is the author and maintainer of 'ggrepel' we thought best to ask here the opinion from the maintainers of 'ggplot2' before releasing some new features in 'ggrepel' and 'ggpmisc'. 

Originally `geom_text_repel()` and `geom_label_repel()` did not have a `position` parameter and nudging was handled by a private version of `position_nudge()`  currently exported as  `position_nudge_repel()` . The repulsive geoms need  as input both the nudged `x` and `y` positions and the original `x` and `y` positions to be able to draw a segment or arrow connecting them. The current naming used by  `position_nudge_repel()` for the variables holding these positions is different to that used by 'ggplot2' position functions. My proposal as currently implemented in my pull request is to use `x` and `y` for the nudged positions for consistency with 'ggplot2' and in addition I propose calling the variables holding the original positions `x_orig` and `y_orig`. These last two names are the main concern of this issue.

Why I think it is important to agree on suitable names is that I have written some new position functions that I wish can be used both with the repulsive geoms from 'ggrepel' and geoms defined in 'ggplot2' and its extensions, even if in this case the original positions are ignored. In addition I think consistency in the naming of the variables used to store the original positions would easy the development of non repulsive geoms that draw connecting segments based only on nudging. From my tests using a more sophisticated approach to nudging than that available in 'ggplot2' can in some cases make repulsion more effective or even unnecessary.

I am not sure whether changing the position functions in 'ggplot2' so that they save the original `x` and `y` positions makes sense at this early stage, but agreeing on a naming convention that would be acceptable  in the future could avoid compatibility headaches.

Preliminary versions of the new nudge functions are available in my 'ggpmisc' package, from which I show four example plots that use nudging (automatically computed)  instead of repulsion to position text labels. (For this approach to work well with longer text labels also the justification needs to be computed in coordination with the nudging, but the implementation of the justification is still at at early stage.)

![position_nudge_line-6](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2743159/117195028-74997300-aded-11eb-8a62-ffcefe44fa9e.png)

![position_nudge_line-12](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2743159/117195085-8713ac80-aded-11eb-8091-ddb88e15baf6.png)

![unnamed-chunk-77-1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2743159/117195450-f4274200-aded-11eb-9e79-8024e77d664d.png)

![unnamed-chunk-64-1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2743159/117195360-dce85480-aded-11eb-8a03-40239f690920.png)

Thanks in advance for any ideas or suggestions.

title: Discrete and continuous color scales have different logic in using options values
description:
See discussion in #4456: The question is whether settings for `fill` should be applied to `colour` and vice versa or not. Currently discrete scales do so, continuous scales do not.

Related: #4149

I am not sure what is causing this problem, so I uninstalled R from my MacBook Pro (macOS Catalina 10.15.6) and then reinstalled R (4.0.5) and ggplot2, but the problem persists. title: New `stat_adjbox` based off of `robustbase::adjboxStats`
description:
Hi!

I implemented a `stat_adjbox` based off of `robustbase::adjboxStats` and `robustbase::adjbox`. 
This is probably not the best place to share this, but I don´t know exactly where/how to contribute.

Does this could/should be implemented in `ggplot2` or perhaps in `robustbase`?

reprex:
``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(glue)
library(rlang)

# temp
new_data_frame <- ggplot2:::new_data_frame
has_groups <- ggplot2:::has_groups
warn <- ggplot2:::warning_wrap



stat_adjbox <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL,
                         geom = "adjbox", position = "dodge2",
                         ...,
                         coef = 1.5,
                         na.rm = FALSE,
                         orientation = NA,
                         show.legend = NA,
                         inherit.aes = TRUE) {
  layer(
    data = data,
    mapping = mapping,
    stat = StatAdjbox,
    geom = geom,
    position = position,
    show.legend = show.legend,
    inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list(
      na.rm = na.rm,
      orientation = orientation,
      coef = coef,
      ...
    )
  )
}


StatAdjbox <- ggproto(
  "StatAdjbox", Stat,
  required_aes = c("y|x"),
  non_missing_aes = "weight", #ignored!
  setup_data = function(data, params) {
    data <- flip_data(data, params$flipped_aes)
    data$x <- data$x %||% 0
    data <- remove_missing(
      data,
      na.rm = params$na.rm,
      vars = "x",
      name = "stat_adjplot"
    )
    flip_data(data, params$flipped_aes)
  },
  
  setup_params = function(data, params) {
    params$flipped_aes <- has_flipped_aes(data, params, main_is_orthogonal = TRUE,
                                          group_has_equal = TRUE,
                                          main_is_optional = TRUE)
    data <- flip_data(data, params$flipped_aes)
    
    has_x <- !(is.null(data$x) && is.null(params$x))
    has_y <- !(is.null(data$y) && is.null(params$y))
    if (!has_x && !has_y) {
      abort("stat_adjbox() requires an x or y aesthetic.")
    }
    
    params$width <- params$width %||% (resolution(data$x %||% 0) * 0.75)
    
    if (is.double(data$x) && !has_groups(data) && any(data$x != data$x[1L])) {
      warn(glue("Continuous {flipped_names(params$flipped_aes)$x} aesthetic -- did you forget aes(group=...)?"))
    }
    
    params
  },
  
  extra_params = c("na.rm", "orientation"),
  
  compute_group = function(data, scales, width = NULL, na.rm = FALSE, coef = 1.5, flipped_aes = FALSE) {
    data <- flip_data(data, flipped_aes)
    qs <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
    
    adjbx <- robustbase::adjboxStats(data$y)
    
    stats <- adjbx$stats
    names(stats) <- c("ymin", "lower", "middle", "upper", "ymax")
    
    outliers <- data$y < adjbx$fence[1] | data$y > adjbx$fence[2]
    
    if (length(unique(data$x)) > 1)
      width <- diff(range(data$x)) * 0.9
    
    df <- new_data_frame(as.list(stats))
    df$outliers <- list(data$y[outliers])
    
    
    df$x <- if (is.factor(data$x)) data$x[1] else mean(range(data$x))
    df$width <- width
    df$flipped_aes <- flipped_aes
    flip_data(df, flipped_aes)
  }
)




# reprex
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:glue':

#>     collapse
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

require(boot)

data(coal, package = "boot")

coaldiff <- diff(coal$date)
df <- tibble(a=coaldiff, b=-coaldiff) 

# for comparison
df %>% robustbase::adjbox()
```

title: `stat_binhex` hexagons appear extremely stretched if all data points fall in a single bin on y dimension
description:
If all data points are in a single bin on the y axis (e.g. if they are all equal to 0) the hexagons appear extremely stretched vertically. 

Minimal reprex:
```r
data <- tibble(x = rnorm(1000, 20, 20), y = rep(0,1000))

data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y))+
  stat_binhex(bins = 100)+
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-100,100))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-100,100))
```

title: misleading error message thrown by `cut_interval()`
description:
`cut_interval()` throws a misleading error message when the user does not specify exactly one of `n` or `length`. In the worst case, if the user supplies `width` instead of `length` (as they would for `cut_width()`, you get a very fun error 😀 

``` r
ggplot2::cut_interval(x = 1:10, width = 10)
#> Error: Specify exactly one of n and width
```

<sup>Created on 2021-05-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

The error gets thrown by `breaks()` [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/87e9b85dd9f2a294f339d88a353d0c11c851489d/R/utilities-break.r#L96). Looks like an easy fix. Happy to send a PR if you don't want to bother doing it yourself 🙂

title: Build in support for brailleR
Switch digest::digest() to rlang::hash()?
description:
As of version 0.4.10, rlang has `hash()`. We previously discussed about the alternative of `digest::digest()` (c.f. https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/4247#issue-728905266), and this seems the one, while at the moment we don't have strong motivation to migrate. I don't want to include this in the next release, but let's revisit here when it's done. I think `rlang::hash()` is good in that

* it seems faster than `digest::digest()` for our usages, and
* we'll have less dependencies since we already have rlang in Imports.

Here's the benchmark:

``` r
library(base64enc)
library(rlang)
library(digest)

x <- list(
  "z",
  as.character(1:6),
  data.frame(
    colour = scales::viridis_pal()(300),
    value  = seq(1, 6, length.out = 300)
  ),
  "colourbar"
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  digest_w_colon  = digest::digest(x),
  digest_wo_colon = digest(x),
  digest_xxhash32 = digest::digest(x, "xxhash32"),
  digest_xxhash64 = digest::digest(x, "xxhash64"),
  serialize_ascii = serialize(x, NULL, TRUE),
  serialize_bin   = serialize(x, NULL, FALSE),
  rawToChar       = rawToChar(serialize(x, NULL, TRUE)),
  rlang_w_colon   = rlang::hash(x),
  rlang_wo_colon  = hash(x)
)

title: Non-deterministic behavior regarding legend order
description:
While preparing a teaching example, I noticed that the legend order changes when I supply a different labeling function. To me it seems that the labeling of the values should not affect the order of the different legends. In the first two plots below, see how the "continent" and "Population" guides change order, although the only difference is the labeling of the population values. Of course, it's easy enough to fix the order, but possibly the example is still of interest. I wasn't able to narrow down the exact details of why this happens, but if there's interest in fixing this I'd dig deeper.

``` r
library("ggplot2")
library("gapminder")
million <- function(x) paste0(scales::comma(x / 1000000), "m")

p <- ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent, size = pop)) + 
    geom_point()

p + scale_size(name = "Population", labels = scales::comma)

title: Feature request: Set constant aesthetics in initial ggplot layer
description:
Apparently, only aesthetics that are mapped via `aes()` in the initial `ggplot()`-layer are used in subsequent layers. 
In effect, setting aesthetics manually, e.g. by `col = "blue"` for multiple layers becomes impossible without some workarounds.
These examples should explain what I mean:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.0.4
# The way I would like to set the constant aesthetics in all layers
ggplot(
  data = NULL,
  col = "blue", 
  fill = "orange", 
  alpha = 0.35,
  size = 1
) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0.5, xmax = 2, ymin = 1.75, ymax = 4)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 1.5, xmax = 3, ymin = 1.25, ymax = 3)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0.25, xmax = 2.25, ymin = 0.75, ymax = 2.5)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 4), ylim = c(0, 4))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/RVV8Dm4.png)

``` r


# Workaround 1 by setting scale
ggplot(mapping = aes(col = "blue", fill = "orange", alpha = 0.35)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0.5, xmax = 2, ymin = 1.75, ymax = 4)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 1.5, xmax = 3, ymin = 1.25, ymax = 3)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0.25, xmax = 2.25, ymin = 0.75, ymax = 2.5)) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_alpha_identity() +
  scale_size_identity() 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/rnd5UH9.png)

``` r

# Workaround 2 by using variables and duplicate code
my_col <- "blue"
my_fill <- "orange"
my_alpha <- 0.35
my_size <- 1

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = 0.5, xmax = 2, ymin = 1.75, ymax = 4),
    size = my_size,
    col = my_col,
    fill = my_fill,
    alpha = my_alpha
  ) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = 1.5, xmax = 3, ymin = 1.25, ymax = 3),
    size = my_size,
    col = my_col,
    fill = my_fill,
    alpha = my_alpha
  ) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = 0.25, xmax = 2.25, ymin = 0.75, ymax = 2.5),
    size = my_size,
    col = my_col,
    fill = my_fill,
    alpha = my_alpha
  ) 
```

title: `direction` argument to `scale_fill_fermenter` does not behave as documented
description:
Thank you for maintaining ggplot! I'm really enjoying using it in slides and Rmarkdown files as part of my reporting workflow.

I've been using the ColorBrewer palettes, and recently noticed that I'm not able to reverse their directions as expected. For example, the`scale_fill_fermenter()` function with a `PuOr` palette places purple on the low end and orange on the high end. I expected that setting `direction = -1` argument would reverse the direction of the palette. 

Instead, `scale_fill_fermenter()` behaves identically for `direction = 1` and `direction = -1`. I can get my desired behavior by setting `direction = "horizontal"`, but this isn't in the docs.

I did a quick search for this behavior in open issues, but the closest thing I could find (tidyverse/ggplot2#4364) seemed different, so I'm opening the issue. It's not breaking my workflow, but I thought updating the docs or function might save others some time. If the fix is something a new contributor could tackle, I'm happy to give it a shot with a nudge in the right direction!

I've noticed this behavior in ggplot2 version 3.3.3, running in R version 4.0.2., and have a quick trio of examples below.

``` r
set.seed(2349)
library(ggplot2)

# Generate some data to plot
n = 100
tb = data.frame(x = runif(n),
                y = runif(n))

# Example 1
# Expected: discrete palette, with high values in orange and lows in purple.
# Actual: as expected.
ggplot(tb,
       aes(x = x, y = y, fill = y - x)) +
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = 'PuOr') +
  geom_point(pch = 21, 
             color = 'white')
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/5OU8lRE.png)

``` r

# Example 2
# Expected: discrete palette, with high values in *purple* and lows in *orange*
# Actual: same result as example 1. Highs are in *orange*.
ggplot(tb,
       aes(x = x, y = y, fill = y - x)) +
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = 'PuOr',
                       direction = -1) +
  geom_point(pch = 21, 
             color = 'white')
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/V7WH6uh.png)

``` r

# Example 3
# Expected: unknown! Found a stackoverflow answer that suggested this,
#           but it's not in the docs.
# Actual: discrete palette with purple on the high end, as desired.
ggplot(tb,
       aes(x = x, y = y, fill = y - x)) +
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = 'PuOr',
                       direction = 'horizontal') +
  geom_point(pch = 21, 
             color = 'white')
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/JDOXnrY.png)

title: Weighted density not working in ggplot2 3.3.3 (R 4.0)
description:
---

Weighted density appears to be not working in **version 3.3.3** of **ggplot2** (built with **R 4.0** under Linux fedora 32). I am trying to plot results of clustering in distributions composed of different subgroups. I want the plots of clusters (sub-distributions of groups) to be weighted according to their relative size in the total population, in order to compare them and with the global distribution. This **was possible with ggplot2 version 3.2** (despite an spurious warning), using `aes(weight=1/nrow(df))`. However, with **ggplot version 3.3.3** (R 4.0) there is no reaction to weight (neither a value nor a column of calculated `weight = n() / nrow(df)` . I hope I'm not doing something stupid!

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)


# Height of two groups of people, by gender (unequal size of groups)
set.seed(1234)
df01 <- data.frame(gender=factor(rep("F", 900)),
           height=round(rnorm(900, mean=165, sd=4))
  )
df02 <- data.frame(gender=factor(rep("M", 600)),
           height=round(rnorm(600, mean=185, sd=4))
  )

# The two groups combined in a single data frame
df <- rbind(df01,df02)

# histogram and density of full (global) distribution 
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x=height)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..), colour="black", fill="white") +
    geom_density(alpha=.2, fill="#FF6666")

# histogram and density colored according to gender (not weighted)
p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x=height, color=gender, fill=gender)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..), alpha=0.5, position="identity") +
    geom_density(alpha=.2)

# Overlap of Global distribution plus not weighted density, grouped by gender
p3 <- p1 +
     geom_density(inherit.aes = FALSE,
              aes(x=height, group=gender, color=gender, fill=gender),
              alpha=0.2, size = 1.5)

# Overlap of Global distribution plus **weighted** density, grouped by gender
# Weight calculated as "1/nrow(df)"
# This gives expected results (**weighted** density) using R version 3.6
# (ggplot2 3.2.1 ), with already known warnings about sum(weights) !=1...
# But, with R version 4.0 (ggplot2 3.3.3) result is **not weighted**,
# identical to p3

p3w <- p1 + 
     geom_density(inherit.aes = FALSE,
              aes(x=height, group=gender, weight=1/nrow(df),
              color=gender, fill=gender),
              alpha=0.2, size = 1.5)


# Overlap of Global distribution plus **weighted** density, grouped by gender
# Weight calculated as a new column of values w= n() / nrow(df)
# This gives **not weighted** graphs (identical to p3) with R v4.0, ggplot2 3.3.3
# and weighted, but much too amplified graphs for R v3.6, ggplot2 3.2.1
    
# New column with weights by gender      
df <- df %>% group_by(gender) %>% mutate(w = n() / nrow(df))

p4w <- p1 +
     geom_density(inherit.aes = FALSE,
              aes(x=height, group=gender, weight=df$w,
              color=gender, fill=gender),
              alpha=0.2, size = 1.5)
```

title: Some levels don't get unique colors, starting at 48 levels
description:
At different number of unique levels, starting with level number 48, ggplot2 surprisingly reuses an existing color in the palette.

While 47 different colors are already more than you can differentiate, it is surprising behavior which can break assumptions. For example https://github.com/kassambara/survminer/issues/526 seems to be caused by assuming that each level gets a unique color.

```r
library(tidyverse)

num_generated_colors <- function(num_requested_colors) {
  g <- data.frame(
    var = as.character(seq_len(num_requested_colors))
  ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(var, 1, fill = var)) +
      geom_col()
  
  p <- ggplot_build(g)
  
  n_distinct(p$data[[1]]$fill)
}

num_generated_colors(47) # Gives 47 colors
num_generated_colors(48) # Again gives 47 colors
num_generated_colors(49) # Gives 48 colors
num_generated_colors(50) # Gives 49 colors
```

For 1 through 300 levels in data, the points where we lose one more unique color are:

```r
tibble::tibble(
  requested_colors = 2:300
) %>%
  mutate(generated_colors = map_dbl(requested_colors, num_generated_colors)) %>%
  filter(generated_colors == lag(generated_colors, default = 1))
```

which gives the following points (tsv):

title: alpha in geom_label() only works correctly if data.frame is provided
description:
Creating a plot with geom_label and specifying alpha works if the label is specified in a separate data.frame:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

# Working example
df <- data.frame(
    x = 1.75,
    y = 32,
    text = c("(a)")
  )

ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_label(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y, label = text), colour="white", alpha=0.25)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/xl4e9uN.png)

However, the plot looks different, if the label is added directly (without aes() specifications):

``` r
# This does not work
ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_label(x=1.75, y=32, label="(a)", colour="white", alpha = 0.25) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/DRQqhRj.png)

A work-around is setting the alpha-value lower:

``` r
# but works with different alpha setting
ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_label(x=1.75, y=32, label="(a)", colour="white", alpha = 0.05) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/b6txjvy.png)
```
But, I guess this a small bug in ggplot2::GeomLabel(), which is easy to fix.

title: position_dodgev() is obsolete without replacement
description:
ggstance was [superseded by ggplot 3.3.0](https://github.com/lionel-/ggstance) on the grounds of full support for horizontality in ggplot. However, `position_dodgev()` or a general equivalent does not appear to be present in ggplot and the legacy ggstance `position_dodgev()` only dodges non-overlapping y intervals. The latter restriction is problematic as it means `position_dodgev()` doesn't support what seem to be mainline use cases for asking ggplot to dodge labels. In special cases `position_stack()` or `position_fill()` may offer a solution but I haven't yet encountered a plotting need where either has been helpful.

In practice, I've yet to find I need to dodge horizontally and regularly working around ggplot and ggstance's limitations by coding manipulations of individual y values leaves something to be desired. It would therefore be helpful if vertical dodging could receive at least a minimal amount of support. `position_jitter()` isn't useful as I need deterministic placement. `position_nudge()` provides only constant shifts and therefore keeps overlapping labels overlapping.
```r
# position_stack()'s use of vjust as a fixed y coordinate multiplier behaves poorly here
# label for 0 overlaps the point, labels near 1 are easily read for an adjacent point
# geom_text()'s vjust argument appears to be overridden
data = tibble(x = c(0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875, 0.9375, 0.96875, 1)) %>% mutate(y = x)
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = x), position = position_stack(vjust = 1.05), vjust = -0.2)
```

title: Clarify that `fullrange = TRUE` extends range to the axis limits, not the whole plot.
description:
There's some understandable confusion about `geom_smooth(fullrange = TRUE)` not making the smooth line go all the way to the axis lines. (Two example posts on Stack Overflow: [1](https://stackoverflow.com/q/66959036/903061), [2](https://stackoverflow.com/q/55307921/903061))

The current argument description in `?geom_smooth` is:

> `fullrange`    Should the fit span the full range of the plot, or just the data?

I suggest modifying the documentation for clarity, something like this:

> `fullrange` If `TRUE`, the fit will extend to the axis limits, potentially beyond  the data. (It will not extend into the padding of the limits configured by `expansion()`.)

title: How to avoid the connection lines using stat_summary_bin with geom = "line" when there is no data?
description:
# Problem
I want to compute a window average over a times series I employed `stat_summary_bin`  for that. My time series has a period where no data was recorded. As seen in the example below, when using `geom = "line"` the gap with no data was connected.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2)

tibble(x = 0:100, 
       y = c(rnorm(31), rep(NA, 15), rnorm(55))) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  stat_summary_bin(fun = mean, geom = "point", breaks = seq(0, 100, 10), color = "red") +
  stat_summary_bin(fun = mean, geom = "path", breaks = seq(0, 100, 10), na.rm = FALSE)
#> Warning: Removed 15 rows containing non-finite values (stat_summary_bin).

#> Warning: Removed 15 rows containing non-finite values (stat_summary_bin).
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/QvSh17T.png)

Checking the data computed with `stat_summary_bin` it is possible to see that the bin with no data was no created, that is the reason points were connected.

``` r
layer_data(last_plot(), 3)
#> Warning: Removed 15 rows containing non-finite values (stat_summary_bin).

#> Warning: Removed 15 rows containing non-finite values (stat_summary_bin).

#>  bin           y ymin ymax  x width flipped_aes PANEL group colour size linetype alpha

#>2   2  0.34708727   NA   NA 15    10       FALSE     1    -1  black  0.5        1    NA
#>3   3  0.15990531   NA   NA 25    10       FALSE     1    -1  black  0.5        1    NA
#>4   5 -0.05227375   NA   NA 45    10       FALSE     1    -1  black  0.5        1    NA
#>5   6 -0.21015714   NA   NA 55    10       FALSE     1    -1  black  0.5        1    NA
#>6   7 -0.28512254   NA   NA 65    10       FALSE     1    -1  black  0.5        1    NA
#>7   8  0.28080004   NA   NA 75    10       FALSE     1    -1  black  0.5        1    NA

```
# Solution

To solve this problem I found a solution [here](https://www.javaer101.com/en/article/36245471.html).
``` r

        y = c(rnorm(31), rep(NA, 15), rnorm(55))) %>%

   geom_line() +
   stat_summary_bin(fun = mean, geom = "point", breaks = seq(0, 100, 10), color = "red") +
   stat_summary_bin(fun = mean, geom = "path", breaks = seq(0, 100, 10), na.rm = FALSE)

title: Add a warning in geom_bar when mapping of a continuous variable to the fill aesthetic is not possible?
description:
Consider the following plot:

```r
demo <- diamonds[1:10, ] 
ggplot(data = demo, mapping = aes(x = cut, fill = price)) +
  geom_bar()
```

Among the 10 diamonds in the "demo" datasets, there is only one diamond with a "Fair" cut and one diamond with an "Ideal" cut. Each of these diamonds has a price and the corresponding bar is colored based on this price using a color scale, in agreement with the aes_colour_fill_alpha documentation. Bars for the other cuts, however, represent several diamonds which all have different prices, making such mapping impossible, and the corresponding bars are consequently plotted in the default gray color.

This behavior tends to be confusing to the user as there is no explanation for why the mapping of prices to the fill aesthetics happens for some bars but not others. This gets even more confusing when no mapping happens at all, as for instance with:

```r
ggplot(data = diamonds, mapping = aes(x = cut, fill = price)) +
  geom_bar()
```

I think usability could be improved by printing an informative warning message in situations where continuous variables cannot be mapped to the fill aesthetics, and by updating the aes_colour_fill_alpha documentation to indicate the expected behavior in such situations.

title: geom_jitter documentation for width and height arguments is misleading
description:
The width and height arguments have distinct, yet identical definitions in the geom_jitter documentation, as follows:

> width Amount of vertical and horizontal jitter. [...] so a width or height [...]
> height Amount of vertical and horizontal jitter. [...] so a width or height [...]

This is misleading as it sounds that width is used to specify the amount of both vertical and horizontal jitter, and so is height.

These definitions are inherited from the position_jitter documentation where the two arguments are defined together, in which case the wording makes sense.

I suppose the issue could be addressed by providing distinct definitions for width and height in position_jitter, but this solution would have the inconvenience of duplicating text and increasing wordiness. Alternatively, the behavior of Roxygen when building the geom_jitter definition could be altered so that width and height share the same definition, similar to the position_jitter documentation, but I am not sure how this can be achieved.

title: inconsistency in print.ggplot documentation
description:
`?ggplot2::print.ggplot` currently includes:

```
Value:

     Invisibly returns the result of 'ggplot_build()', which is a list
     with components that contain the plot itself, the data,
     information about the scales, panels etc.
```

but the code itself is returning `invisible(x)`, not `invisible(data)` (where `data <- ggplot_build(x)`).

If I am interpreting this correctly, then an easy fix might be from:

1. Change the documentation from `result of 'ggplot_build()'` to `the original plot`; or
2. Change from `invisible(x)` to `invisible(data)`.

(Personally I prefer the second, but that might be a breaking change and require more changes than just one line, e.g., testing and/or notification of a future breaking change.)

I'm willing to submit a PR for this if there is interest.

description:
Hi Team

I'll set off the next couple of months for working on and preparing a ggplot2 patch release. Hopefully this will not include any breaking changes (or only a modest amount), and can get released without much hassle...

You are of course welcome in joining me ironing out bugs (I know some one you do that on the daily 🙌), but I don't expect anyone to set aside any extra time.

After this the road is paved for a more exciting feature release, so if you have anything big brewing you can begin to think about that and maybe tagging them so we know what we want to work on. Best

title: The future of vars()
description:
`vars()` have been deprecated in the rest of tidyverse and is now in an odd position in ggplot2. Due to the non-standard semantics of facet specifications there are no real way to avoid some type of collector function with the same semantics as `vars()` so the current plan is to let it exist purely as a ggplot2 thing, but switch back to promoting formula notation in documentation examples etc... `vars()` will then only be promoted as a utility for programming with ggplot2 and not for interactive use.

Feedback from the maintainer team on this is very welcome - I've never really used `vars()` myself so my attachment to it is very limited

title: scale_y_continuous() 'sec.axis' and Warning min(x) max(x)
description:
In a ggplot I am using a secondary Y-axis to display additionnal labels to my plot.
I use it like this :
```
scale_y_continuous(
      expand = c(0, 0),
      breaks = seq(0, N.rows, length.out = n.grad),
      labels = function(x) format(x, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE),
      sec.axis = sec_axis(
        trans = ~.,
        breaks = dt.data[right.y.hiden == FALSE]$right.y.label.pos,
        labels = dt.data[right.y.hiden == FALSE]$sample.string))
```
in `sec_axis()` breaks and labels are queried in a data.table `dt.data`:

- If multiple breaks and labels are selected from the data.table -> no problems.
- If there is only 1 break and 1 label queried from the data.table, displaying the plot returns this warning (I guess this is the matching translation from the language I use):
```
Warning messages:
1: In min(x) : no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf
2: In max(x) : no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
```
The plot returned is fine : it totally matches my expectation.
But I don't understand why these warnings are printed.

So I basically have to questions:
1. Why those warnings are printed when there is only 1 break & label ?
2. Is there something I should mention in `sec_axis()` or elsewhere to get rid of these warnings ?

I don't know if it is reproducible, but from what I experienced, if you give just a single value to `breaks` and `labels` in `sec_axis()` such has:
`sec.axis = sec_axis(trans = ~., breaks = 125, labels = "awesome single label")`
This should trigger the warnings.

title: legend box border thickness inconsistencies for legend.box = "horizontal"
description:
When there are guides for two scales, and they are placed horizontally (`legend.box = "horizontal"`), the border around the two guides together has inconsistent width.  This appears to be the result of one guide being smaller than the other, and the individual guides overlapping the joint bounding box border in some but not all places due to the size inconsistency.  Even if the legends are the same size, if there is a gap/margin between them, the border is thicker for this region.

* I've set the size to 2 below to exaggerate the effect, but it occurs whether or not the size is explicitly set. 
* I've also explicitly set the fill to red below to highlight what might be the underlying issue, but removing this doesn't change the thickness issue.
* Moving the legend does not seem to change this

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gapminder)

gapminder %>% 
  filter(year == 1982) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = lifeExp, y = gdpPercap)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = pop, color = continent)) +
  theme(legend.box = "horizontal",
        legend.box.background = element_rect(color="black", size=2, fill="red")
  )
```

title: Layer orders with differing fill Aesthetic Mappings on Density Geometries affect resulting legend
description:
EDIT: This is again related to #3804 
EDIT2: feel free to delete as this is completely redundant to an issue I posted back in July 2020 (Amazing how you can forget about bugs you discover).


I happened upon a strange behavior in ggplot2 today.
If you add two `geom_density` layers to a `ggplot`, one with `fill` assigned and one with `fill` left as default, the order in which these layers are called will produce different results. Consider this reproducible example.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

#global fine
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class, fill = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_density(aes(x = after_stat(scaled))) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/WHMCixK.png)

``` r

#fill only assigned to last layer - unexpected behavior - an additional guide appears
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_density(aes(x = after_stat(scaled))) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(density), fill = class))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/lB3IV7N.png)

``` r

#fill assigned before last
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(density), fill = class)) +
  geom_density(aes(x = after_stat(scaled))) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/KOvy20q.png)

``` r

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(density), fill = class)) +
  geom_density(aes(x = after_stat(scaled), fill = class))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/CdcFthd.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-03-04 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

I would assume this is a bug and the issue only pertains to the case when the second `geom_density` has a `fill` aesthetic assigned where as previous ones are using `default_aes`.

I haven't been able to reproduce this in other geometries, although I have not tested all of them.

title: Add error to `direction` argument of guide_*()
description:
The `direction` argument of `guide_*()` functions can only be "horizontal" or "vertical". At present an unhelpful error message is returned in case of error:

```r
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(quakes,
       aes(x = long,
           y = lat,
           colour = mag)) +
  geom_point() +
  guides(colour = guide_colorbar(direction = "horiz"))
#> Error in if (!g$title.position %in% c("top", "bottom", "left", "right")) {: argument is of length zero
```

In line with the tidyverse style guide an error like this would be more suitable:

```r
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(quakes,
       aes(x = long,
           y = lat,
           colour = mag)) +
  geom_point() +
  guides(colour = guide_colorbar(direction = "horiz"))
#> Error: The direction argument of guide_colorbar() must be either "vertical" or "horizontal"  
```

title: Issue a message when fill aesthetic is used with GeomPoint and shape is not "filled"
description:
I've spend an hour or so of `ggplot2` debugging to find out that `fill` aesthetics is simply ignored when `shape` of the point is not 21:25, i.e., not "filled". `grid::grid.point`, which is used, documents this case quite well, but `ggplot2` gives a hint only through the example that could be "hidden" from the user that struggles with, e.g., boxplot ouliers fill modification (as in my case).

title: Poor compatibility with R 4.1 pipe |>
description:
The planned native R pipe `|>` in R 4.1 currently interacts poorly with `ggplot()`. `|>` prohibits any symbols with special parsing rules on the RHS of the pipe, including `+`, `(`, and `{`. That makes it really hard to work with `\>` and `ggplot()` in a way that feels natural. See reprex below for some approaches that fail and work. 

Enabling a more natural workflow would require either an update to the ggplot2 API to make it pipeable or a change in the `|>` parsing rules to permit, for example, `(` or `{` on the RHS of `|>`. Do you have some connections with the R development team to raise this issue? 

```r
stopifnot(R.version$major == "4" & R.version$minor == "1.0")
library(ggplot2)

# Drop-in replacement of %>% with |>
## Doesn't work
mtcars |>
  ggplot() + 
      aes(x = as.factor(cyl), y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl)) +
      geom_jitter(height = 0, width = .2) + 
      stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, size = 1, color = "black") +
      theme_classic()

# Wrapping ggplot() chain in parentheses
## Doesn't work
mtcars |>
  (ggplot() + 
      aes(x = as.factor(cyl), y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl)) +
      geom_jitter(height = 0, width = .2) + 
      stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, size = 1, color = "black") +
      theme_classic()
  )

# Wrapping ggplot() chain in squiggly brackets
## Doesn't work
mtcars |>
  {ggplot() + 
      aes(x = as.factor(cyl), y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl)) +
      geom_jitter(height = 0, width = .2) + 
      stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, size = 1, color = "black") +
      theme_classic()
  }

# Wrap pipe chain and initial ggplot() in parentheses
## Works, but confusing
(mtcars |>
  ggplot()) + 
      aes(x = as.factor(cyl), y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl)) +
      geom_jitter(height = 0, width = .2) + 
      stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, size = 1, color = "black") +
      theme_classic()

# Write ggplot call as an anonymous function
## Works, but confusing
mtcars |>
  dplyr::mutate(cyl = as.factor(cyl)) |>
  (\(d) ggplot(d) + 
      aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, color = cyl) +
      geom_jitter(height = 0, width = .2) + 
      stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, size = 1, color = "black") +
      geom_density() +
      theme_classic() )()
```

title: negative axis labels use hyphens rather than minus signs
description:
This is a minor, low priority issue. In some contexts, hyphens (U+002D) and minus signs (U+2212) are not interchangeable since, for example, the appearances of -1 (hyphen) and −1 (minus sign) are somewhat different. From a typesetting perspective the use of a minus sign is correct. This is a [known ggplot issue since at least 2015](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/34931258/true-minus-sign-on-x-axis-variable-labels-in-ggplot2) but, as searches of this repo yield no hits, it's unclear if it's been considered for a fix.

In most cases a simple workaround seems likely to suffice.
```r
# with hyphens
qplot(c(-2, 0), c(-2, 0))

# workaround posted by @Rosen Matev on Stack Overflow
# https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14780860/fix-typography-in-axis-labels
unicode_minus = function(x) sub('^-', '\U2212', format(x))
qplot(c(-2, 0), c(-2, 0)) + scale_x_continuous(labels = unicode_minus) + scale_y_continuous(labels = unicode_minus)
```

Egor

```r

title: guide_legend ignores legend.spacing.(x/y) depending on byrow
description:
Hello there,

I apologise in advance if I submit issues too frequently; I do really appreciate all the good work you put into ggplot2.
By default, a legend appears to ignore the `legend.spacing.y` theme setting.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, fill = as.factor(cyl))) +
  geom_density() +
  theme(legend.spacing.y = unit(0.5, "cm"))
p
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/3aq6L4s.png)

However, when `byrow = TRUE` in the guide, the `legend.spacing.y` is applied as expected.

``` r
p + guides(fill = guide_legend(byrow = TRUE))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/RJP1AYA.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-02-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

For horizontal legend layouts, `legend.spacing.x` is ignored when `byrow = TRUE`, which is opposite to the vertical case. 

``` r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, fill = as.factor(cyl))) +
  geom_density() +
  theme(legend.spacing.x = unit(0.5, "cm"),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(label.position = "top",
                             byrow = TRUE))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/ri1A1bU.png)

I was surprised by this as I would have expected the `legend.spacing` to be applied regardless of the layout order of the keys, but I'm likely not aware of the considerations going in to this. I believe the [code](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/R/guide-legend.r#L448-L578) controlling the legend spacing and gaps sometimes `interleave()`s the label/key sizes with spacings, and sometimes doesn't, conditional on the `byrow` argument. 

In an earlier comment (https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3587#issuecomment-546700387), it was proposed to get rid of the legend spacing, but I think there is a use-case for the spacing for the keys (the text margins maybe less so). Would it be a good idea to always interleave the spacing regardless of the `byrow` argument?

title: Colors don't appear in legend when specifying alpha with lines
description:
The colors in the legend disappear when specifying line transparency (alpha) within geom_line, geom_path, etc. The colors in the legend do show up if you either 1) remove the alpha specification, or 2) use alpha with a different geom (like geom_point).

```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg, color=factor(cyl))) +
  geom_line(alpha=.5)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg, color=factor(cyl))) +
  geom_line()

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg, color=factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(alpha=.5)
```

title: Old bug resurfaced - annotate does not work when x axis is date
description:
When using annotate on plot with date x axis, annotate throws `Error: Invalid input: date_trans works with objects of class Date only`. Both the data for x axis and the x coord for annotate are supplied as lubridate `Date` objects. The same goes for if both objects are supplied as `POSIXct` objects, but the error asks for `POSIXct`. If the x axis data is `Date` and x coord is `POSIXct`, the error asks for `Date` and vice versa.

My ggplot2 version is 3.3.2, the latest on CRAN.

In trawling the internet for answers, I found this: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/18796386/how-to-use-ggplot2s-annotate-with-dates-in-x-axis and this: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/859 both referencing an old, similar bug. Perhaps it is back?

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)

df <- tibble(
  date = sample(seq(as_date('2020-05-01'), as_date('2020-10-08'), by="day"), 100),
  sample = runif(100, min = 0, max = 100)
)

ggplot(df, aes(date,sample)) + geom_line() + annotate('text',x = c(as_date('2020-07-24'), as_date('2020-08-07')), y = c(50,70),c('hey!','listen!'))
```

title: Idea to easily use facet_wrap with geom_sf
description:
Like other issues and several Stack Overflow questions have revolved around, I would like to raise the issue of implementing an easy way to use `facet_wrap` with `geom_sf`. This would enhance the experience of spatially visualising data with `ggplot`. Thanks for all your work on the package.

Currently, like this [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62560181/r-facet-a-map-with-ggplot2) shows, when using `facet_wrap` with `geom_sf`, the problem is that the axes do not adapt to the different bounding boxes of each group. For example, one country may be in Africa and another in the Middle East, but the `facet_wrap` does not allow for `scales = "free"` to adapt the bounding box to each facet (see picture below).

This issue has been raised before. Thanks for all your hard work. The intention of this issue is to bring up the great potential of adding this feature.

Here is a short `reprex`:
```
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(raster)

# Load data
chile  <- getData("GADM", country = "Chile",level=1)

# Convert to sf and simplify for speed
chile_sf <- st_as_sf(chile) %>%
  st_simplify(., dTolerance = 0.1)

# Subset regions
regions <- chile_sf %>%
  mutate(NAME_1 = as.character(NAME_1)) %>%
  filter(NAME_1 %in% c("Atacama",
                       "Valparaíso")
  )

# Plot
ggplot(regions) +
  geom_sf() +
  facet_wrap(~NAME_1) +
  labs(title = "Notice that each facet considers the combined bounding box of both regions")

```

![facet_dont_work](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/55885264/108286344-321aaf80-7189-11eb-8584-7ca276776d82.png)

Link to SO question: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62560181/r-facet-a-map-with-ggplot2

title: theme_update - Error: No method for merging x into y
description:
I'm trying to reproduce the example shown here: https://community.rstudio.com/t/custom-ggplot2-theme-that-capitalizes-title/39688

The goal being to create a ggplot2 theme that would capitalise all desired texts. 

The original example I linked to above uses: `update_theme()`, but since I think the name has been changed, I changed it to `theme_update()`.

This produced the issue which I traced the issue in the debugger to the function: 

```r
> ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp)) +
+   geom_point() +
+   labs(
+     title = "My plot title"
+   ) +
+   new_theme()
Error: No method for merging list into element_line
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

Since it's request I include a minimal example here it is:

```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot_add.my_theme <- function(object, plot, object_name){
  plot$theme <- ggplot2:::theme_update(plot$theme, object)
  plot$labels$title <- stringr::str_to_upper(plot$labels$title)
  plot
}

new_theme <- function(){
  out <- theme_bw()

  out <- out %+replace% theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

  class(out) <- c("my_theme", class(out))

  return(out)
}


# works
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "My plot title"
  ) +
  new_theme()
```

I was testing around and the use of `theme_replace()` works ONCE. This I believe because it is replacing the `theme_bw()` function. This does not work on subsequent executions. 

To be honest this is reaching the limits of my R knowledge. I don't really fully grasp the chunk above; maybe I'm not understanding something which could easily be fixed.

Could someone be so kind as to explain this chunk as well please?

title: Better error message when using coord_map() without {maproj} installed
description:
It seems that the {mapproj} package is required for `coord_map()` to work. The documentation for the function does talk about {mapproj} but doesn't explicitly say that the package is required.

Using the example from the function documentation this is what I get:

```
library(ggplot2)
library(maps)
nzmap <- ggplot(map_data("nz"), aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "white", colour = "black")
nzmap + coord_map()
``` 

`Error in loadNamespace(name) : there is no package called ‘mapproj‘`

When running this function in isolation it's easy enough to understand I need to install the package. However when this is part of a large codebase that runs on one machine and then is attempted to run on another machine, the error has no indication of where it came from. When uploading a shiny app to shinyapps.io, shinyapps did not pick up that it needs to install {mapproj}, and looking at the error log did not make it clear where in my app {mapproj} is needed.

title: Plotting order: `geom_sf()` vs `geom_point()`
description:
I'm trying to figure out how to get `geom_sf()` to behave like `geom_point()` when it comes to plotting order. 

I understand there's no longer an option to use `aes(order = ...)`. Is there another way to prevent `geom_sf()` from re-ordering the points (rows) of its input, whilst still colouring by some attribute? 

When all the points belonging to one class are plotted on top of all the others, it's hard to form an "unbiased" picture of the relative spatial distributions of the different classes. (In this reprex, they're nothing special, but with real data, the differences are meaningful.)

This seems like a bug, insofar as the behavior of `geom_sf()` should be consistent with that of `geom_point()`. But maybe I'm overlooking something? Thank you for your time and attention, and for this wonderfully useful package.
 
    library(sf)
    #> Warning: replacing previous import 'vctrs::data_frame' by 'tibble::data_frame'
    #> when loading 'dplyr'
    #> Linking to GEOS 3.7.2, GDAL 2.4.2, PROJ 5.2.0
    library(ggplot2)
    library(tibble)

    # This can be any polygon, really
    nc <- sf::st_read(
      system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"),
      quiet = TRUE)

    # Sample a lot of points inside the polygon
    N <- 10000
    sampled_points <- st_sample(
      st_transform(nc, 32119), # NC state plane, m
      size = N)

    # Assign each point a random value: "Apple", "Banana", or "Cherry"
    # (stored as attribute `fruit`)
    labeled_points <- st_sf(
      geometry = sampled_points,
      fruit = sample(
        c("Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"),
        size = N,
        replace = TRUE))

    # `geom_sf()` plots all blue points ("Cherry") on top,
    # even though the rows of `labeled_points` are not sorted
    # with respect to `fruit`.
    ggplot(data = labeled_points) +
      geom_sf(aes(colour = fruit), size = I(3))

![](https://i.imgur.com/e6pITRo.png)


    st_as_xy <- function (points) {
      tibble(
        as_tibble(st_coordinates(points)),

    # `geom_point()`, in contrast, seems to plot points in the
    # order in which they appear in the data (as desired!).
    ggplot(data = st_as_xy(labeled_points)) +

title: Default width of geom_bar/geom_col under facetting
description:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/dbd7d79aa35c49b4eab200cf5f7a084a7748e776/R/geom-bar.r#L132

^ This line shows how the default width for `geom_bar` and `geom_col` is selected as "By default, set to 90% of the resolution of the data." I recently came across a situation where I was making a facetted column chart and the resolution of the data (across all groups) was very small. So small, that I could not see the columns. Manually setting the `width` solved the issue until I realized what was happening. The resolution within groups was much larger. I'm suggesting it may be better to compute the resolution for each group, then perhaps take the minimum resolution. 

This should illustrate the issue:

```
> library(tidyverse)
-- Attaching packages ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ tidyverse 1.3.0 --
v ggplot2 3.3.3     v purrr   0.3.4
v tibble  3.0.6     v dplyr   1.0.3
v tidyr   1.1.2     v stringr 1.4.0
v readr   1.4.0     v forcats 0.5.1
-- Conflicts --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- tidyverse_conflicts() --
x dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
x dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
```

I start by creating a `tibble` where the resolution without considering `group` is 0.1.

```
my_tibble <- tibble(x = c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5,
                          1.6, 2.6, 3.6),
                    y = c(10, 9, 8,
                          20, 19, 18),
                    group = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 3))

> resolution(x = my_tibble$x, zero = FALSE)
[1] 0.1
```

Then making my facetted plot creates strangely narrow columns. I believe this should illustrate the problem. If the values within each group have a reasonable resolution for plotting, but the resolution of all data is very narrow plots look funny (or in my real-data case, do not show up at all).

```
ggplot(data = my_tibble, mapping = aes(x = x, y = y, fill = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(group))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53956863/106405117-b8e63300-63fa-11eb-973d-cb7ffe59333e.png)

Here is one possible way to determine a more appropriate width:

```
desired_width <- 0.9*my_tibble %>% 
  group_by(group) %>% 
  summarise(res = resolution(x = x, zero = FALSE)) %>% 
  select(res) %>% 
  min()

> desired_width
[1] 0.9
```

Overriding the default `width` provides a more natural ggplot.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53956863/106405244-301bc700-63fb-11eb-9eb3-ac0b8603d3d2.png)

title: Cannot specify quantiles in custom summary statistic
description:
Reproducible example:

This works:

`df <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), y=as.factor(c(rep("A", 50), rep('B',  50))))

data_summary <- function(x) {
  m <- mean(x)
  ymin <- m-sd(x)
  ymax <- m+sd(x)
  
  return(c(y=m,
           ymin=ymin,
           ymax=ymax))
}

ggplot(df, aes(x=y, y=x)) +
  geom_violin() +
  stat_summary(fun.data=data_summary)`


But this doesn't:

`
data_summary <- function(x) {
  m <- mean(x)
  qu <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, .75), na.rm=T)

  ymin <- qu[1]
  ymax <- qu[2]

  return(c(y=m,
           ymin=ymin,
           ymax=ymax))
}


ggplot(df, aes(x=y, y=x)) +
  geom_violin() +
  stat_summary(fun.data=data_summary)
`

There seems to be some ggplot2 bug, because the function above with the quantile seems to be fine.

Thanks!

Jonas

title: check_overlap argument not accepted in geom_label()
description:
The `geom_label()` is not accepting the `check_overlap` argument, although it appears to be a valid option according to the `geom_label` documentation (`ggplot2` version 3.3.3):

> Arguments `check_overlap` 	
If `TRUE`, text that overlaps previous text in the same layer will not be plotted. `check_overlap` happens at draw time and in the order of the data. Therefore data should be arranged by the label column before calling __`geom_label()`__ or __`geom_text()`__.

In another section of this documentation, there's no explicit reference that this specific argument is not supported:
> geom_label()
Currently `geom_label()` does not support the `angle` aesthetic and is considerably slower than `geom_text()`. The `fill` aesthetic controls the background colour of the label.

### Reprex
#### `geom_label()`
The plot is generated with a warning:
```r
mpg %>% 
  ggplot(aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_label(aes(label = class), check_overlap = T)
#> Warning: Ignoring unknown parameters: check_overlap
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12656725/106171413-cb116880-6191-11eb-8b00-ff021558659b.png)

#### `geom_text()`
* `geom_text()` default behavior: overlapping text
```r
library(tidyverse)

mpg %>% 
  ggplot(aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = class))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12656725/106170959-4e7e8a00-6191-11eb-9e7a-755572f46c72.png)

* `geom_text()` with `check_overlap = TRUE`: overlapping text removed
```r
mpg %>% 
  ggplot(aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = class), check_overlap = TRUE)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12656725/106170800-22fb9f80-6191-11eb-9881-a2667057dd52.png)

title: point is misplaced if width = 0 is used in position_dodge2 with geom_point

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df <- tribble(~dimension, ~group, ~value,
              "dim 1", "A", 0.6,
              "dim 1", "B", 0.7,
              "dim 2", "A", 0.4,
              "dim 2", "B", 0.5)

plot <- ggplot(data = df,
               mapping = aes(x = dimension,
                             y = value,
                             color = group))  

# point in wrong column (point of 'dim 1' 'B' appears in column of 'dim 2'
plot +  geom_point(
             position = position_dodge2(width = 0))
```

``` r

title: Boxenplots
description:
This is a feature request to include boxenplots as a new layer or as an extension. I assume it would be a function like `geom_boxenplot()`. Boxenplots were introduced by a trio of authors (Heike Hofmann and Karen Kafadar and Hadley Wickham) in 2011 and were created to improve boxplots for modern (bigger) data. [The paper](https://vita.had.co.nz/papers/letter-value-plot.html) describes the mathematical definition, and it's implemented in [seaborn](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.boxenplot.html) for Python.

Unfortunately, it doesn't look like there are any results for a boxenplot function anywhere in the R ecosystem.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10804060/105781296-9605db80-5f2f-11eb-82a7-2addd7190874.png)

I also did not see anything in the ggplot extensions for boxenplots. It seems like ggplot2 would be the place to have this, although an extension would work too.

title: `geom_contour` documentation is misleading
description:
The documentation for `geom_contour` says:

> Contouring
> tends to work best when \code{x} and \code{y} form a (roughly) evenly
> spaced grid.

but in fact, as issue #4320 and its discussion describes, there are much more stringent requirements. Exactly what the requirements are is a little unclear to me; the code to do it is in `isoband_z_matrix()` here:  https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/9741da5050f81b7b5c012c56d02f45fc93d68f89/R/stat-contour.r#L224  It's something like "Contouring requires the `(x, y)` pairs to be a large subset of the grid of all possible pairs of unique values of `x` and `y`, with no repeats."  

It would also be helpful to add an example using `akima::interp()`, the usual way to produce the grid of values from irregular data.

title: In geom_rect, axis ticks do not correspond to factor levels of dataframe
description:
When using geom_rect with a dataframe that consists of xmin (factor), xmax (factor), ymin (numerical), ymax (numerical) and a fill variable (here called length), the x-axis does not get ordered according to the factor levels of xmin and xmax. Even when the levels are similar in both xmin and xmax. Instead they get ordered alphabetically.

```r
library(ggplot2)
xmin <- factor(c("iter0", "iter6", "iter12", "iter19", "iter23", "iter29", "iter37", 
                 "iter44", "iter50"), 
               levels = c("iter0", "iter6", "iter12", "iter19", "iter23", "iter29", "iter37", 
                          "iter44", "iter50"))
xmax <- factor(c("iter5", "iter11", "iter18", "iter22", "iter28", "iter36", 
                 "iter43", "iter49", "iter63"),
               levels = c("iter5", "iter11", "iter18", "iter22", "iter28", "iter36", 
                          "iter43", "iter49", "iter63"))
plotdf <- data.frame("xmin" = xmin,
                     "xmax" = xmax,
                     "ymax" = 3+(1:9),
                     "ymin" = (1:9),
                     "length" = seq(2, 10)) 

p <- ggplot(plotdf) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xmin,
                 y = ymin,
                 col = "red"))
p2 <- ggplot(plotdf) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xmin,
                 y = ymin,
                 col = "red")) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, 
                xmax = xmax,
                ymax = ymax,
                ymin = ymin,
                fill = length))

ggpubr::ggarrange(p, p2)
```

title: fullrange makes fit line shorter instead of longer in geom_smooth and throws warnings
description:

Warning message:
Removed 59 rows containing missing values (geom_smooth). 
```
The number depends on the specifics of the data set being plotted, of course.

  stat_summary(data=df, aes(y=val, group=1, size=10), fun=mean, color='red', geom='point') +
  geom_smooth(data=df, aes(y=val, group=1), method='loess', se=TRUE, formula=y~x, fullrange=FALSE) +

title: guide_axis(n.dodge)
description:
When using `guide_axis(n.dodge)` in a faceted plot, the first label of each facet always starts in the top line, instead of the dodging being continuous across the facets. Depending on the number of axis labels, this can cause labels to be next to each other & overlap instead of on alternating lines.

Example:
```r
df <- tibble(x = rep(c("a long axis label", "another long axis label", "the third long axis label"), 2),
             y = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1),
             z = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3))

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(z))
```
