description:
Hello there,

This is just a minor inconsistency, but in case this wasn't noticed yet, here it is. Apparently, `guide_colourbar()` uses the `ticks.linewidth` and `frame.linewidth` parameter as-is, while in the rest of ggplot2 (as far as I can tell), almost every parameter for linewidth is calculated as below:

```
# Right before handing `supplied_value` to grid
lwd = supplied_value * .pt
```

Here is a reprex with exaggerated line sizes. You can notice when comparing the width of `geom_line()` versus the colourbar guide ticks. The lines appear of the same width when you adjust `ticks.linewidth = 5 * .pt`.

``` r

library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = c(0.5, 0.5))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = x)) +
  geom_line(size = 5) +
  scale_colour_gradientn(
    colours = c("white", "white"),
    guide = guide_colourbar(ticks.colour = "black", ticks.linewidth = 5)
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/tkrddYa.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-01-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Thanks for reading!

title: Allow scale name to be a function.
description:
I think it might be useful to have the possibility of passing a function to scale names like so:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- expand.grid(X1 = 1:10, X2 = 1:10)
df$value <- df$X1 * df$X2
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(X1, X2)) + geom_tile(aes(fill = value))

p1 + scale_fill_continuous(function(x) base::toupper(x))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/lVvyRgF.png)

``` r
# With function shorthand
p1 + scale_fill_continuous(~ base::toupper(.x))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/iA4Pi4a.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-01-11 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Something like this would make code snippets more portable. In my case, I have a function that makes a plot and I had to define the title outside the plot depending on the function arguments. With this, I could've defined a global dictionary which translates column names to actual (human readable) variable names and re-use that all over my report. 

To produce the code above I just added this

```r
  if (is.formula(name)) {
    name <- as_function(name)
  }

  if (is.function(name)) {
    make_title <- name
    name <- waiver()
  } else {
    make_title <- super$make_title
  }
```


before this line: 

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/R/scale-.r#L107

And then added `make_title = make_title` to the ggproto construction. 

All tests pass, so changing this should be safe.

title: Error with date scale and Infinity (geom_segment)
description:
To emphasize a certain point, you might want to actually draw its coordinates using `geom_segment()`.

When using  `geom_segment()`, you can use `Inf` if the mapping so that the segment will start on the edge of the plot.

However, if you use `Inf` like this on an axis of class `Date`, it will throw an error:

> `Error: Invalid input: date_trans works with objects of class Date only`


Here is an example with a simple workaround:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
set.seed(1234)
last_month <- ymd("2020-12-01") - 29:0

df <- data.frame(
  date = last_month,
  price = runif(30)
)
max_y = max(df$price)
max_x = df$date[df$price==max(df$price)][1]

base <- ggplot(df, aes(date, price)) +
  geom_line(color="red")

base+
  geom_segment(aes(x=max_x, xend=max_x, y=-Inf, yend=max_y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=-Inf, xend=max_x, y=max_y, yend=max_y))
#> Error: Invalid input: date_trans works with objects of class Date only

base+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=ymd("2020-11-01", "2020-11-10", "2020-11-20", "2020-12-01")) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=max_x, xend=max_x, y=-Inf, yend=max_y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=-Inf, xend=max_x, y=max_y, yend=max_y))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/EtALmmp.png)

<sup>Created on 2021-01-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


As you can see, adding a `scale_x_continuous()` call solves this issue without breaking the date labels so maybe this error is not mandatory.

title: Points don't inherit font family
description:
I expect that the font-family specified in the theme is applied to all applicable graphical content. However, when specifying some unicode characters for the shape scale I get empty boxes instead of the characters. Point geometries can use arbitrary characters for the shape scale, but not all characters are available in all font families. While constructing the points grob, `GeomPoint` omits the `fontfamily` `gpar` parameter, which means that there is no way to specify a font family that contains the desired characters. The standard ways of specifying a font family for the quartz device don't work for the gpar fontfamily (`quartz(family =`, or  `quartzFonts(sans = quartzFont(…`).

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_family = 'Apple SD Gothic Neo'))

p = ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3, shape = factor(0:2)), aes(x, y)) + geom_point(aes(shape = shape), size = 4) + scale_shape_manual(values = c('0' = '\u2013', '1' = '◀', '2' = '\u25B6')) + theme(text = element_text(family = 'Apple SD Gothic Neo'))
print(p)
data = ggplot_build(p)
gtable = ggplot_gtable(data)
grid.draw(gtable)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/lv0ezb5.png)

``` r
# add family to gpar for points grob
gtable$grobs[[6]]$children[[3]]$gp$fontfamily = 'Apple SD Gothic Neo'
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(gtable)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/O63iuIq.png)

<sup>Created on 2020-12-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


I get the behavior I want by adding the font family `gpar` parameter to the correct grobs as above or to the gtable itself:
```r
data = ggplot_build(p)
gtable = ggplot_gtable(data)
gtable$gp = gpar(fontfamily = 'Apple SD Gothic Neo')
grid.draw(gtable)
```

From a user perspective, I think this could be fixed by either adding a family parameter to `scale_shape` or inheriting the family from the theme or device.

title: Using emojis in geom_text causes last letter of character to be repeated on macOS
description:
I was experimenting with adding emojis to `geom_text()` labels, and I didn't expect my code to work as is (the unicode placeholders weren't surprising), but I was surprised by the text being altered.

Adding an emoji to the label results in the last character of the label being repeated, and the number of characters repeated is equal to the number of emojis. This happens regardless of where the emoji is, beginning or end of text.

I think this might be a macOS specific problem, I don't see the same issue when I run the same code on RStudio Cloud (which is running Ubuntu 16.04.7) or on an RSP instance (running Ubuntu 20.04).

``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2, 3),
  y = c(1, 2, 3),
  grp = c("hi", "hello", "jello")
)

# one emoji, one character repeated
ggplot(data = df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("😊", grp)))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/meoeCaV.png)

``` r
# two emojis, two characters repeated (and so on...)
ggplot(data = df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("😊😊", grp)))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/EhtN7M9.png)

``` r
# emoji at the end, it's repeated
ggplot(data = df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(grp, "😊")))
```

title: coord_flip should support something other than axis-mirroring
description:
`coord_flip()` causes axes to be mirrored across a diagonal that intersects (0,0).

This is undesirable behavior in a lot of cases. An example is where the original x axis was a categorical variable whose left-to-right order was meaningful. When we do `coord_flip()`, the new y axis--the former x axis--would need to reflect the old x-axis's left-to-right order in a top-to-bottom order to maintain the same meaning. Instead, its default is bottom-to-top.

It would be helpful if an argument was present that permitted the new y axis to maintain an expected order, which means its top-to-bottom order is the same as the original x axis's left-to-right order.

Reproduceable example:

Note the order of the x-axis:
```
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) + 
  geom_bar()
```

Now note the order of the y-axis appears to be flipped:
```
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) + 
  geom_bar() + coord_flip()
```

A Google search on this issue shows tons of hacky workarounds.

title: tag position inside plot borders
description:
Some peer-reviewed journals (e.g. Oecologia) require figure panel labels to be _inside_ of plot borders (although they seem to enforce these requirements inconsistently).  It would be nice if there were an option like `theme(plot.tag.position = "topleftinner")` to place a label at the upper left corner of the inside of plot borders.  Currently, I think I have to kludge this by tweaking `theme(plot.tag = element_text(vjust = , hjust = )`, but it's inconsistent, so I have to do this tweaking for every panel individually.  Maybe there's an easier way that I don't know about?

Related to: https://github.com/thomasp85/patchwork/issues/222

``` r
library(ggplot2)
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars) + geom_point(aes(mpg, disp)) + labs(tag = "a)")
p1 + theme(plot.tag.position = c(0,1),
           plot.tag = element_text(vjust = 1.5, hjust = -2.85))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/qWKrEqC.png)

``` r
# left of "a" just touching plot border

p3 <- ggplot(mtcars) + geom_smooth(aes(disp, qsec)) + labs(tag = "b)")
p3 + theme(plot.tag.position = c(0,1),
           plot.tag = element_text(vjust = 1.5, hjust = -2.85))
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/jZHfEyH.png)

``` r
# "b)" is slightly further in with same theme()
```

title: Patch release of ggplot2
req: delay "unknown aesthetic" warnings until plot
description:
`ggplot2` extensions may introduce new aesthetics to the grammar. One such topic I'm considering is the breakout of `color` to support `hue`, `saturation`, `lightness` (for various reasons, not just for "two color scales" as supported by several extension packages).

If I start building a grob and include the aesthetic before it is properly handled by any custom extension function:

```lang-r
gg <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = hp)) +
  geom_path(aes(lightness = hp))
# Warning: Ignoring unknown aesthetics: lightness
```

It is obvious that I can suppress the warnings individually, but if this is going into a package, I'd rather not suggest the users must do that every time they want the extension. The premise of the warning is correct, but I suggest that the timing of it is not.

Is it feasible to delay the unk-aesthetic warning until the plot rendering? That way, iteratively-built grobs don't warn about missing aesthetics until all processing has been completed?

title: dup_axis guide parameters don't apply to the right axis with coord_flip
description:
If you use `dup_axis()` to duplicate an axis and don't want to repeat the title of the axis, then flip the coordinates with `coord_flip` you have the "new" x axis title that disappears and not the y axis one (as expected). If you change the guide argument to something like `angle = 45` then it correctly applies to the duplicated axis.

Sorry if the problem is not explained very well, here is a reprex demonstrating it.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

mtcars %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = mpg, y = cyl)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(sec.axis = dup_axis(guide = guide_axis(title = NULL))) +
  coord_flip()
```

title: remove_missings(..., finite = TRUE) removes everything if there is a character column
description:
In base-R, character values are not "finite" (i.e. `is.finite("a")` is `FALSE`).  Therefore, if `remove_missings()` with `finite = TRUE` encounters a character column, it throws away everything. Thus, the first of the following two lines raises a warning and returns an empty data.frame, while the second line preserves the input data.frame:
```r
remove_missing(data.frame(foo = "bar", stringsAsFactors = FALSE), finite = TRUE)
remove_missing(data.frame(foo = "bar", stringsAsFactors = TRUE), finite = TRUE)
```

For me, this led to the following problem that I found extremely difficult to debug: I had a custom `stat` with `required_aes = c("x", "colour")`.  If the colour-aesthetic was mapped to a factor column, everything worked as expected - non-NA-values of factor variables are finite.  If the colour-aesthetic was mapped to a character column, the layer was dropped.

Minimal example:
```r
StatXMean <- ggplot2::ggproto(
  "StatXMean", Stat,
  compute_group = function(data, scales, params, na.rm = FALSE) {
    dplyr::summarize(dplyr::group_by(data, colour),
                     xintercept = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  },  required_aes = c("x", "colour")
)

stat_x_mean <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL, geom = "vline",
                        position = "identity", na.rm = FALSE, show.legend = NA,
                        inherit.aes = TRUE, ...) {
  ggplot2::layer(
    stat = StatXMean, data = data, mapping = mapping, geom = geom,
    position = position, show.legend = show.legend, inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list(na.rm = na.rm, ...),
  )
}

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point() + stat_x_mean()

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = as.factor(drv))) +
  geom_point() + stat_x_mean()
```

title: geom_histogram: Use center=0.5*binwidth to avoid missing bars when xlim is set.
description:
This issue is associated with #3332 but directed to #2887. Here, I want to reproduce the case in #2887.

```r
d <- data.frame(x = 1:3)
p = ggplot(d) +
  geom_bar(aes(x)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 3))
p
```
>#two bars are missing
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5996084/101124441-0f6d0600-3632-11eb-88ad-ccd40071e481.png)

If you check the plot data you will see two NA rows, one missing xmin, one missing xmax:
```r
ggplot_build(p)$data
#[[1]]
#  y count   prop x flipped_aes PANEL group ymin ymax xmin xmax colour   fill size linetype
#1 1     1 0.3333 1       FALSE     1    -1    0    1   NA 1.45     NA grey35  0.5        1
#2 1     1 0.3333 2       FALSE     1    -1    0    1 1.55 2.45     NA grey35  0.5        1
#3 1     1 0.3333 3       FALSE     1    -1    0    1 2.55   NA     NA grey35  0.5        1
```

As proposed by @clauswilke, setting the limits wide enough will solve this problem. 
Similarly, for `geon_histogram`, when `xlim` is set and `binwidth` is used to set bins, bars could be missing (#3332). Here is an example:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

testdata = data.frame(num = c(0:4, 2:6), var = rep(c("A","B"),each=5))

plot1 = ggplot(testdata, aes(num, fill = var)) + 
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "dodge", binwidth = 3) + 
  xlim(0,6) +
  ggtitle("binwidth = 3") 

plot2 = ggplot(testdata, aes(num, fill = var)) + 
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "dodge", binwidth = 3, center=1.5) + 
  xlim(0,6) +
  ggtitle("binwidth = 3, center=1.5") 

plot3= ggplot(testdata, aes(num, fill = var)) + 
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "dodge", breaks = seq(0, 6, 3)) + 
  xlim(0,6) +
  ggtitle("breaks = seq(0, 6, 3)")

plot1 / plot2 / plot3
#Warning message:
#Removed 2 rows containing missing values (geom_bar). 
```

plot1 is missing two bars, similarly, two rows are NA-contained in the plot1 data. When setting `center=`0.5*binwidth, the bars are recovered (plot2), however, this is not the default of `center`. Users may not aware of this setting since the warning message is not helpful to identify plausible solutions.

title: Hash for guide_train should take colours into account
description:
When using [ggnewscale](https://github.com/eliocamp/ggnewscale), legends can disappear if they have the same title and breaks:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(ggnewscale)

data <- expand.grid(y = 1:4, x = 1:4)
data$z <- c("a", "b")

ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(data = ~.x[.x$x == 1, ], aes(fill = z)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = 1) +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_tile(data = ~.x[.x$x == 2, ], aes(fill = z)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = 2) 
```
![](https://i.imgur.com/wcxTZER.png)

What's going on is that ggplot2 is merging both guides because they have the same title and labels. Changing the name of each scale makes them distinct. 

``` r
ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(data = ~.x[.x$x == 1, ], aes(fill = z)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(name = "1", palette = 1) +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_tile(data = ~.x[.x$x == 2, ], aes(fill = z)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(name = "2", palette = 2) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/tsXBUXq.png)

The problem is that `guide_train.legend` computes the hash using the title, labels, direction and name: 

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/12e61dfcf9151c2094536294a8ef42ddffdca9ef/R/guide-legend.r#L229

In the first example, all of those characteristics are the same, and the guides are merged. Ideally, the hash should include information on the colours included in `key[[aes_column_name]]`

This small hack is a small proof of concept of how it would work:

``` r
my_guide <- function(...) {
  guide <- guide_legend(...)
  class(guide) <- c("my_guide", class(guide))
  guide
}

guide_train.my_guide <- function (guide, scale, aesthetic = NULL) {
  guide <- NextMethod("guide_train")
  
  guide$hash <-  with(guide, 
                      digest::digest(list(title, 
                        key$.label, direction, name, key[, 1]  # should be `key[[aes_column_name]]`
                                                 )))
  guide
}

ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(data = ~.x[.x$x == 1, ], aes(fill = z)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = 1, guide = my_guide()) +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_tile(data = ~.x[.x$x == 2, ], aes(fill = z)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = 2, guide = my_guide()) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/amxCg2A.png)

title: Default colour aesthetic in geom_polygon() set to string "NA"?
description:
There might be a bug in the default aesthetics for `geom_polygon()`.  It appears to be set to the string "NA" rather than NA.  Here's a minimal reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

geom_polygon()$geom$default_aes
#> Aesthetic mapping: 
#> * `colour`   -> "NA"
#> * `fill`     -> "grey20"
#> * `size`     -> 0.5
#> * `linetype` -> 1
#> * `alpha`    -> NA
#> * `subgroup` -> NULL
```

title: Map_data() documentation has what seems like a typo
description:
This is not a complicated problem. In the reference page for the function `map_data()` ([here](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/map_data.html)), the example has the following call:
```r
ggplot(choro, aes(long, lat)) +
  geom_polygon(aes(group = group, fill = assault)) +
  coord_map("albers",  at0 = 45.5, lat1 = 29.5)
}
```
And then later, there is something slightly different.

However, the call `coord_map()` should have `lat0` instead of `at0` as an argument (in both examples):
``` r
ggplot(choro, aes(long, lat)) +
  geom_polygon(aes(group = group, fill = assault)) +
  coord_map("albers",  lat0 = 45.5, lat1 = 29.5)
}
```
It works either way, since the name doesn't seem to matter here, but it's rather confusing.

I hope I'm doing this right. I've never used GitHub before, so maybe I'm wrong about something (maybe I'm filing it in the wrong place)... I just think this should be pointed out somewhere.

title: Feature request: better text placement with inward facing axis ticks
description:
Hello there,

Currently you can set inward facing axis ticks by setting the `axis.ticks.length` to a negative unit. However, doing this naively causes the axis text to be placed awkwardly.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.ticks.length = unit(-5, "pt"))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/jdHgFe7.png)

You could fix this awkward text placement by giving the axis text wider margins, but takes extra effort in looking up what the current theme's axis text margins are and adding your own.

``` r

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.ticks.length = unit(-5, "pt"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = unit(7.2, "pt"))),
        axis.text.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = unit(7.2, "pt"))))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/NoCTrZA.png)

<sup>Created on 2020-11-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I haven't got unit arithmetic to work within the `margin()` function, so the conversion is more difficult if `axis.ticks.length` is defined in `"cm"` and the margins in `"pt"`. For example `margin(t = unit(1, "mm") + unit(1, "pt"))` throws an error, whereas `unit(1, "mm") + unit(1, "pt")` does not.

The piece of code responsible for measuring the sizes of axis elements is found here: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/12e61dfcf9151c2094536294a8ef42ddffdca9ef/R/guides-axis.r#L283

From a quick test, I got correct placement of the labels (as in the second plot) by replacing that line with the following:

```
grob_dims <- unit.c(max(tick_length, unit(0, "pt")), label_dims)
```

I think I have heard it mentioned that the guide system at some point will be converted to the `ggproto` class, so this feature might be something to keep in mind when that update happens.

Thanks for reading!

title: user-defined transformation results in "NAs not allowed" error
description:
The article mentioned in [this link](https://rpubs.com/huanfaChen/squash_remove_y_axix_ggplot) describes how to squash a part of a (positional) axis with a user-defined transformation. 

In it, one uses `scales::trans_new` with appropriate `transform` and `inverse` arguments to do so.

However, running the code results in 
```
# Error in x[isq] <- from + (x[isq] - from) * factor :
#   NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments
```

The article contains output without errors, thus it may have worked in an older version.

Here is the full code

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

dat <- data.frame(group=rep(c('A', 'B', 'C', 'D'), each = 10), 
                 value=c(rnorm(10), rnorm(10)+100)
                 )

squash_axis <- function(from, to, factor) { 
    # A transformation function that squashes the range of [from, to] by factor on a given axis 

    # Args:
    #   from: left end of the axis
    #   to: right end of the axis
    #   factor: the compression factor of the range [from, to]
    #
    # Returns:
    #   A transformation called "squash_axis", which is capsulated by trans_new() function

  trans <- function(x) {    
      # get indices for the relevant regions
      isq <- x > from & x < to
      ito <- x >= to

      # apply transformation
      x[isq] <- from + (x[isq] - from)/factor
      x[ito] <- from + (to - from)/factor + (x[ito] - to)

      return(x)
  }

  inv <- function(x) {

      # get indices for the relevant regions
      isq <- x > from & x < from + (to - from)/factor
      ito <- x >= from + (to - from)/factor

      # apply transformation
      x[isq] <- from + (x[isq] - from) * factor
      x[ito] <- to + (x[ito] - (from + (to - from)/factor))

      return(x)
  }

# return the transformation
  return(trans_new("squash_axis", trans, inv))
}

ggplot(dat,aes(x=group,y=value)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = squash_axis(5, 95, 10))

```

title: Set common scale parameters outside of the scale function
description:
A problem that pops up repeatedly in different contexts is that we may want to adjust certain scale parameters without explicitly calling a scale function. We already have some support for this, e.g. with `xlim()` to set limits on the x position scale or `xlab()` to set its title, but there are numerous other scenarios where the same problem arises. Here are some examples:

- We may want to set scale expansions: #3962 
- We may want to set breaks or limits, including for non-position scale functions: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/3973#issuecomment-621879755
- We may want to specify `drop = FALSE` on discrete scales: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/4268#issuecomment-729224543

It would be good if we could come up with a generic approach to these issues. I note that `xlim()` and `xlab()` use entirely different implementation approaches currently, so that's not promising:

- `xlim()` and `ylim()` use the `ggplot2:::limits()` function to automatically generate a scale function and give it the appropriate parameter settings:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/3be0acce79dc295d5470d949c60de1b9c84a6fc9/R/limits.r#L112-L160

- `xlab()` and `ylab()` ultimately feed their info to the `update_labels()` function, which writes to a special `plot$labels` field that the layout reads from:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/3aa29375167946b970692e42241e9aabaee3ae03/R/labels.r#L13-L17
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/660aad2db2b3495ae0d8040915a40d247133ffc0/R/plot-build.r#L170
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/b76fa9639215785f8e94874d3bdf02225bae898a/R/layout.R#L107-L113

Neither approach generalizes directly to the other use cases. I also have concerns about the way `xlim()` and `ylim()` are implemented, because the fact that they add explicit scales functions is not obvious and can lead to strange behavior.  See e.g. the following reprex, where in the first plot the call to `scale_x_continuous()` overwrites the `xlim()` call but in the second plot the `xlab()` call is not overwritten:

    library(ggplot2)

    ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
      geom_point() +
      xlim(100, 300) +
      scale_x_continuous(name = "Displacement")
    #> Scale for 'x' is already present. Adding another scale for 'x', which will
    #> replace the existing scale.

![](https://i.imgur.com/o6emEot.png)


    ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
      geom_point() +
      xlab("Displacement") +
      scale_x_continuous(limits = c(100, 300))
    #> Warning: Removed 16 rows containing missing values (geom_point).

![](https://i.imgur.com/YhDgWHA.png)

<sup>Created on 2020-11-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

title: Inconsistent colours in filled contour plot
description:
This bug was reported in https://stackoverflow.com/q/64873086/2554330 where the user couldn't get colours consistent across two graphs.   Code here is basically what was posted there.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

v <- list()
v[[1]] <- ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, z = density)) + stat_contour_filled(breaks=(0:10)*0.005)
v[[2]] <- ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, z = 1.1*density)) + stat_contour_filled(breaks=(0:10)*0.005)

do.call(grid.arrange,  v)
```
![Screen Shot 2020-11-17 at 12 28 57 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1935680/99425504-eb3ec480-28d0-11eb-9132-84c0e702ac22.png)

Notice that neither graph lists all bins between the specified breaks, and they are inconsistent about assigning colours to corresponding bins, most obviously at the top end where the first graph leaves out 2 bins and the bottom graph leaves out one.

What I would expect is that if the `breaks` are specified explicitly, the colour would depend on the specified bins, not just the non-empty ones.

title: Suggestion: Point out which continuous/discrete value was wrongly supplied to which discrete/continuous scale
description:
When working with very complex plots, with many different values, mappings, and scales, it often happens that I mix something up and accidentally supply a continuous value to a discrete scale, or vice versa. In this case, while ggplot does tell me which way the mix-up occurred, it does not tell me *which value* was specifically wrongly supplied to *which scale*. Instead, I have to figure this out myself, often by frustrating trial-and-error if it is not immediately obvious from the code.

I would love it if the error message included:

- the name of the scale which a continuous/discrete value was wrongly supplied to,
- the aesthetic which is mapped to this scale,
- and the value which is mapped to this aesthetic.
- Possibly even more useful information that is available internally, that I am not aware of?

Here is some reproducible code to illustrate my problem:

```r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(0)

df = tibble(col1 = rnorm(6) * 100,
            col2 = factor(c(100, 100, 101, 101, 102, 102)),
            col3 = rnorm(6),
            col4 = factor(c(1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 2)))

df %>% ggplot(mapping = aes(x = col1, y = col2, fill = col3, colour = col4)) +
  geom_point(pch = 21, size = 10, stroke = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis") +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "magma")
```

When I run this, I get the dreaded:

```
Error: Continuous value supplied to discrete scale
```

However, finding out which scale would be changed—in this case, to be continuous—requires reading and understanding the code. (Of course, in this case, it is the `fill` scale, but can you see this at first glance?) It is even harder to do if:

- the plot is assembled at distant code locations; for example when a "barebones" plot only with geoms is constructed, and then "finished off" with scales/labs/etc. further down in the script; especially if the same plot can be "finished off" in multiple different ways
- the same aesthetic has multiple values mapped to multiple scales (using something like `ggnewscale`)
- there are scales involved where it is not immediately obvious whether they are discrete or continuous, particularly if they are supplied by another external module
- binned scales are involved
- you are new to `ggplot2` and don't even know what the error message is trying to tell you in the first place...
- and so on

Now my simple suggestion would be to amend the error message, so it reads for example:

```
Error: Continuous value (col3) supplied to discrete scale ("viridis") for aesthetic "fill"
```

I'm sure the exact wording can be improved; this is just an idea. I don't know how much effort this would be to implement, but it would certainly improve my quality of life a lot, and perhaps even that of others.

title: No US-alias for scale_colour_viridis_b()
description: Most (all?) `ggplot2` functions allow for both US and British spelling. title: "scale_y_log" with "jitter_dodge" misbehavior (using color to create 3 plots at one x value)
description:
Hello! I have this plot in a Shiny app and so there are a lot of possibly combinations and one of my users pointed this out to me today. In the Real World this x axis is timepoints, and I've just pulled one out for the reprex.

Basically, for a given x value, I want 3 boxplots so I used `aes(color)` to make them. When one of my factors only has zero as a value, and I apply a log10 transform (thus creating a -Inf) it throws off the x position of the dodge. This does not happen when `x` and `color` are the same value.

``` r
library(reprex)
library(ggplot2) # ggplot2_3.3.2

df <- data.frame(cat_id = as.character(1:22),
                 species = "cat",
                 color = c("tabby", rep("tortie", 20), rep("black", 1)),
                 floofiness = c(runif(21, 1, 10), 0),
                 nose_warmth = c(runif(22, 1, 10)))
```

# Expected behavior
``` r

title: [Feature Request] Add options "ggplot.ordinal.color" and "ggplot.ordinal.fill" scales defaults
description:
`ggplot` exposes options for [setting default scales](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/95ba60bd9c70cdcada44ad805728fff9b54596db/R/scale-colour.r#L43-L54), but but this mechanism of setting a default scales function [isn't available for ordinal scales](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/2bc493e20556a40a4adb46a05e36f7d671c810d4/R/scale-viridis.r#L58-L66) (which is a direct alias for the viridis scales). 

When using [`thematic`](https://github.com/rstudio/thematic) to automatically set color schemes, this means that plots with ordinal color scales will always revert to a viridis color pallet, contrasting with other plots in the same theme. This has been raised in [thematic#59](https://github.com/rstudio/thematic/issues/59) and [thematic#62](https://github.com/rstudio/thematic/issues/62)

It would be wonderful if these ordinal scales got the same default color scales treatment so that they can be themed consistently without needing any uncouth `ggplot` namespace modifications to inject this behavior.

title: Geoms switch locations on dodged chart when color set in aes()
description:
So this is a weird and very specific bug that I've noticed for quite some time. 

The issue occurs when I create a bar chart using `geom_col(position = "dodge")`, create a second geom like `geom_text(..., position = position_dodge(width = .9)`, and in that second geom define a color or fill inside of `aes`.

As I said, very specific!

Some examples. Here's a simple chart with two dodged geoms that works exactly as intended:

```r
mtcars %>%
	group_by(cyl) %>%
	summarize(mpg = mean(mpg), hp = mean(hp)) %>%
	pivot_longer(-cyl) %>%
	ggplot(aes(x = as.character(cyl), y = value, fill = name)) +
	geom_col(position = "dodge") +
	geom_text(aes(label = name), position = position_dodge(width = .9), vjust = -0.1)
```

But if you add `color` to the aesthetics of the geom_text, the text switches horizontal locations across the dodge!

```r
mtcars %>%
	group_by(cyl) %>%
	summarize(mpg = mean(mpg), hp = mean(hp)) %>%
	pivot_longer(-cyl) %>%
	ggplot(aes(x = as.character(cyl), y = value, fill = name)) +
	geom_col(position = "dodge") +
	geom_text(aes(label = name,
				  color = case_when(value < 30 ~ "black", TRUE ~ "blue")), 
			  position = position_dodge(width = .9), vjust = -0.1) +
	scale_color_identity()
```

This does NOT hold true if you change other aesthetics in `aes()`, like `vjust`. Only `color` (and `fill`) that I've noticed. It's not specific to `geom_text()`, either — you can change it to `geom_point()` and the same thing happens, the dots switch sides.

I encounter this in my work semi-regularly, when I'm trying to combine direct labels with a complex graph. I can work around it, by switching to a faceted graph or applying direct annotations, but it'd be nice if this worked, or if I knew what I needed to do to prevent this from happening.

title: `axis.text.y.right` does not inherit from `axis.text.y`
description:
In the [{ggplot2} documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/theme.html) it says that:

> axis.text.*.* inherits from axis.text.* 

And while this is true for `axis.text.x.top` which inherits from `axis.text.x`, the same does not hold for `axis.text.y.right` which seems not to inherit from `axis.text.y`. 

Below (first plot) is an example using `element_text(hjust = 1)` which works for `axis.text.x`, but does not work for `axis.text.y`. The problem can be solved (second plot below) when explicitly specifying `axis.text.y.right` whereas it is not necessary to specify `axis.text.x.top`.

 I have illustrated the problem in this [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/64539478/align-y-axis-labels-inward-when-y-axis-position-is-set-right) and it was also the root for this [issue in {ggiraph}](https://github.com/davidgohel/ggiraph/issues/182).


``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)


p <- mtcars %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = cyl, y = gear)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    position = "top",
    labels = c("few", "", "", "", "many")
    ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    position = "right",
    labels = c("few", "", "", "", "many")
    ) 

# x labels are hjust = 1 
# y labels do not respond to `hjust`,
# axis.text.y.right does not inherit from axis.text.y
p +
  theme(
    axis.text.x =
      element_text(
        hjust = 1),
    axis.text.y = 
      element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1 # does not affect plot no matter which value is set
    )
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/WtQIcZD.png)

``` r

p +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = # axis.text.x.top is not needed!
      element_text(
        hjust = 1),
    axis.text.y.right = # this fixes the problem
      element_text(
        angle = 90,
        hjust = 1
      )
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/LTjBrrC.png)

title: Drop support for R 3.2
description:
As I commented on https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/4242#issuecomment-714070558, digest package now requires R >= 3.3. `digest::digest()` is used for hashing guides so that we can merge overlapped guides by `guides_merge()`.

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/7e51849b010b34cf07f1e4995d7e64e6e1cd5b55/R/guides-.r#L231-L244

Since the hashing we need is very simple, it's probably possible to implement another hashing function (Maybe `paste()` with some nice separator is enough...?), but I'm not sure if it's worth. I feel it's time to consider dropping support for R 3.2. If this sounds good, I'll prepare a pull request.

title: Integer data might get non-integer breaks
description:
This is related to #3222. I agree with @thomasp85 that he said:
> _I think the fact that few users are aware of integer/numeric difference and whether their data is one or the other will make adding this a source of confusion..._

But for analyses with values that are really not divisible like the number of patients, plants or buildings, this is sometimes a problem (even if you set the column to be `integer`):

```r
df
#> # A tibble: 90 x 4
#>    age_group location group   n_patient
#>    <ord>     <chr>    <chr>       <int>
#>  1 0-17      A        Group 1         0
#>  2 0-17      A        Group 2         0
#>  3 0-17      M        Group 1         0
#>  4 0-17      M        Group 2         0
#>  5 0-17      M        Group 1         0
#>  6 0-17      M        Group 2         0
#>  7 0-17      N        Group 1         0
#>  8 0-17      N        Group 2         0
#>  9 0-17      O        Group 1         0
#> 10 0-17      O        Group 2         0

ggplot(df) + 
  geom_col(aes(x = age_group, y = n_patient, fill = group)) + 
  facet_wrap("location", scales = "free")
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/31037261/96688546-95ced080-1381-11eb-8ed0-d0bacb151af3.png)

As you can see, the `n_patient` column is of class `integer`, but still locations N and O have decimal breaks. In #3222 the question was to basically to let `waiver()` check if all values are equal to `floor(values)` in all cases, but I am wondering if `waiver()` could be edited so that if the data contains true integer values, the breaks will never be non-integer.

What do you think?

title: labs should ignore trailing comma
description:
Many `ggplot2` functions accept (that is, ignore) a trailing comma. A few don't, such as `ggplot::labs`:

```r
df <- data.frame()
ggplot2::ggplot(
    df,
    ggplot2::aes(
        x = x,
        y = y, # trailing comma
    ), # trailing comma
) +
    ggplot2::labs(
        x = "x",
        y = "y", # no trailing comma allowed. Error: Argument 3 is empty
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme(
        , # trailing comma
    )
```

title: Why are you re-licensing ggplot2?
description:
@hadley said:

> We are systematically re-licensing tidyverse and r-lib packages to use the MIT license, to make our package licenses as clear and permissive as possible. To do so, we need the approval of all copyright holders, which I have found by reviewing contributions from all all non-RStudio contributors.

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/4232#issue-719518370

I asked:

> Could I please ask if you might provide some context about the reason for the change of license?

I'm afraid my comment was not visible, so I'm posting a new issue here, where I hope ggplot2 users and contributors might learn more about the plan to re-license. I would like to please ask if someone might be willing to provide some context regarding the reason for the change of license. Is that OK?

ggplot2 is available under the terms of the Free Software Foundation’s GNU General Public License (GPL). https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/LICENSE

That's the [same license that the R Project uses](https://www.r-project.org/about.html):

> R is available as Free Software under the terms of the Free Software Foundation’s GNU General Public License in source code form.

For those of you who are not familiar with software licenses, you might consider reading [this recent post](https://plausible.io/blog/open-source-licenses) from a company that re-licensed their code from from the MIT to a newer licensing scheme called GNU Affero General Public License V3 (AGPLv3).

For example, one reason to re-license code from GPL to MIT might be to give permission for a corporation that is interested to take the ggplot2 (and other tidyverse and r-lib) code and use it in closed-source proprietary products.

title: geom_label + summary: after_stat but before scale
description: I'm using stat summary to compute statistics directly in the graph and show a label for it, for example showing the 90% percentile. The computed value is passed to the label aesthetic using `after_stat` and that works fine when there are no axis transformations, but with a log10 transformation the label is in the right place but the text is after the transformation and but before the transformation. From the documentation I would expect after_stat to be before any scale transformation. Works fine with regular scale: ```r library(ggplot2) ggplot(cars) + geom_step(aes(x = speed), stat = "ecdf") + geom_label(aes(x = speed, y = 0.9, label = after_stat(x)), orientation = "y", stat = "summary", fun = quantile, fun.args = list(probs = 0.9)) ``` Wrong text with log10 transformation: ```r library(ggplot2) ggplot(cars) + geom_step(aes(x = speed), stat = "ecdf") + geom_label(aes(x = speed, y = 0.9, label = after_stat(x)), orientation = "y", stat = "summary", fun = quantile, fun.args = list(probs = 0.9)) + scale_x_log10() ```

title: Incorrect guide type and keys when type paremeter to scale_fill_binned() is a function
description:
When a function is passed to the `type` argument of `scale_colour_binned()`, the plot has the colourscale guide, not the bins guide it presumably should have.

Second and more importantly, when the binned guide is forced, its colour values differ from those in the geom - a colour at one end of the scale is missing. This only occurs for some lengths of/values in the data, presumably because of the binning transformation, but I was not able to diagnose when exactly it occurs beyond the two contrasting examples below.

This does not occur when `"viridis"` is passed to the `type` parameter instead of `scale_colour_viridis_c`. My expectation was that these are equivalents and should behave identically.

Reprex below using `geom_point()` and the colour aesthetic; I've also reproduced the issue with `geom_sf()` and the fill aesthetic.

Reproduced using current github master branches of {ggplot2} and {scales}.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
df <- data.frame(a = 1:100, b = 1:100)

ggplot(df[1:11,]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = b, x = a, y = b)) +
  scale_colour_binned(type = scale_colour_viridis_c)
```
First problem: an incorrect guide type is produced - colour bar instead of colour bins.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1666657/95793893-eb064480-0ce6-11eb-984b-f31b4c4ca2cf.png)

When I force colour bins, the bottom bin colour (bright yellow) is missing from the guide:

```
ggplot(df[1:11,]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = b, x = a, y = b)) +
  scale_colour_binned(type = scale_colour_viridis_c, guide = "bins")
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1666657/95793877-e04baf80-0ce6-11eb-95bf-2720162e1a84.png)


(This also occurs when `type = scale_fill_distiller` and when `guide = "coloursteps"`.)

However this only occurs with some data - if I only take the first 10 rows, the guide is correct (but still has to be forced):

```
ggplot(df[1:10,]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = b, x = a, y = b)) +
  scale_colour_binned(type = scale_colour_viridis_c, guide = "bins")
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1666657/95793856-d0cc6680-0ce6-11eb-99d2-c74509658812.png)

The colour values issue does not occur with either input data when `type = "viridis"`:

```
ggplot(df[1:10,]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = b, x = a, y = b)) +
  scale_colour_binned(type = "viridis")
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1666657/95793827-bdb99680-0ce6-11eb-8f57-e497ead28385.png)

```

ggplot(df[1:11,]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = b, x = a, y = b)) +
  scale_colour_binned(type = "viridis")
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1666657/95793804-ae3a4d80-0ce6-11eb-84d2-0acd89009c5c.png)

Though the guide type (shape?) is still perhaps unexpected? This seems to be a coloursteps fill guide, not a colour bins guide. Also its direction is reversed, on which see #4210. 

In any case, if I again force the bins guide, its colour range is correct:

```
ggplot(df[1:11,]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = b, x = a, y = b)) +
  scale_colour_binned(type = "viridis", guide = "bins")
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1666657/95794659-b3000100-0ce8-11eb-9ee9-d1ab297cb77b.png)

title: annotation_raster icw/ scale_y_reverse() is upside-down on some devices
description:
People have reported a [issue in magick](https://github.com/ropensci/magick/issues/266) which is due to a bug in `annotation_raster`, or perhaps something underneath.

The problem is that `ggplot2::annotation_raster` seems to revert the y scale so that the picture is upside-down for most graphics devices, except for xquartz (i.e. the default on MacOS).

```r
# Test data
test <- as.raster(matrix(hcl(0, 80, seq(50, 80, 10)), nrow = 4, ncol = 5))

# For comparison
plot(test)
```

Plot the same raster in ggplot2:

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(
  data.frame(x = 0, y = 0), ggplot2::aes_string("x", "y")) + 
  ggplot2::geom_blank() + 
  ggplot2::theme_void() + 
  ggplot2::scale_y_reverse() + 
  ggplot2::coord_fixed(expand = FALSE, xlim = c(0, 5), ylim = c(0, 4)) + 
  ggplot2::annotation_raster(test, 0, 5, -4, 0, interpolate = TRUE) + NULL
```

On MacOS I see the correct picture using the default xquartz png device

![out](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/216319/95747263-71476a00-0c98-11eb-803a-dbb8e9b8db93.png)

However on Windows and Linux (or on macos with type="cairo") it is upside-down!

![linux](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/216319/95747305-88865780-0c98-11eb-876e-f0187b39770a.png)

title: facet_grid margins=TRUE seems to malfunction with geom_col

title: geom_dotplot don't put dots at proper locations.
description:
I'm not sure if I'm trying to do something not meant to, but suspect there may be a bug in the function.  Instead of describing the issue, I just post the script in its entirety so you can run it and see what I meant.  This script will create one pdf file (attached) with three pages.  The first one and third one have plots with dots placed at expected locations, but the second one has plots with dots placed incorrectly (at least not as expected).  The only difference between codes for the first page and codes for the second page is the value for x in aes(), x=dose vs. x=supp. I may have missed some options that should correct the problem, but I've searched around and found no solutions.  Thanks.
[violin.pdf](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/files/5357648/violin.pdf)

```
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript

library(ggplot2)

plotit <- function(p)
{
    p <- p +
      geom_violin(width=0.7, alpha=0.8, position=dodge) +
      geom_dotplot(binaxis='y', stackdir='center', dotsize=0.2) +
      geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.2, color= "black", outlier.size=0.5, position=dodge) +
      stat_summary(fun=mean, colour='red', geom="point", size=2, position=dodge) +
      labs(fill="dose") +
      ylim(0, 40) +
      ggtitle('Tooth Growth') + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) +
      scale_fill_hue()+scale_color_hue()

    print(p)
}

d <- ToothGrowth
d$dose <- as.factor(d$dose)
dodge <- position_dodge(width=0.7)

file <- 'violin.pdf'
unlink(file)
pdf(file)

p <- ggplot(d, aes(x=dose, y=len, fill=factor(dose, levels=c('0.5', '1', '2'))))

plotit(p)

p <- ggplot(d, aes(x=supp, y=len, fill=factor(dose, levels=c('0.5', '1', '2'))))

plotit(p)

p <- ggplot(d, aes(x=supp, y=len, fill=factor(dose, levels=c('0.5', '1', '2')))) +
    geom_violin(width=0.7, alpha=0.8, position=dodge) +
    geom_jitter(alpha=0.4, size=0.7, color="red", position=dodge) +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.2, color= "black", outlier.size=0.5, position=dodge) +
    stat_summary(fun=mean, colour='red', geom="point", size=2, position=dodge) +

    ylim(0, 40) +
    ggtitle('Tooth Growth') + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) +
    scale_fill_hue()+scale_color_hue()

print(p)

dev.off()

title: Feature request: ggsave takes multiple filenames
description:
I often make one plot with ggplot and then want to save it as a .png (for dropping into Google Docs) and as a .pdf (for dropping into Word documents or email attachments). Saving with default dimensions isn't hard:

```
ggsave("fig.png", plot = plot)
ggsave("fig.pdf", plot = plot)
```

But things become a bit of a copy-paste pain when I have more keywords:

```
ggsave("fig.png", plot = plot, height = 4, width = 4, units = "cm")
ggsave("fig.pdf", plot = plot, height = 4, width = 4, units = "cm")
```

I sometimes define a function to handle this case:

```
ggsave_multiple <- function(fns, ...) map(fns, function(x) ggsave(x, ...))
ggsave_multiple(c("fig.png", "fig.pdf"), plot = plot, height = 4, width = 4, units = "cm")
```

But it would be nice if ggplot did this by default, but currently this throws an error:

```
ggsave(c("fig.png", "fig.pdf"), plot = plot)
# Error: `device` must be NULL, a string or a function.
```

Alternatively,

```r
labeling::extended(1e250, 2e250, 3, only.loose = FALSE)
#> Error in if ((w[1] * sm + w[2] * cm + w[3] * dm + w[4]) < best$score) break: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

The work-arounds offered in the previous issue are to either divide all values by an amount so that the labeling tool doesn't overflow, or to not have labels, but these don't get to the underlying issue. 

A better work-around would be to add 

```
+ scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(min(your_y_values), max(your_y_values), length.out=5))
```

which at least fixes the problem on the user side.

title: geom_segment() is up to an order of magnitude slower than geom_abline()
description:
The repex illustrates a 4x slowdown on my machine from using `geom_segment()` to produce slightly tidier plots than `geom_abline()` when drawing over a geom_raster(). This is strange as `geom_segment()` has somewhat fewer pixels to draw than `geom_abline()`. I would also expect the time to render a line a default resolution to be a few milliseconds, not several seconds.

With my full working case the `geom_abline()` version renders in 5 seconds and `geom_segment()` takes 45 seconds. This seems excessive given the ggplot render thread is the only active consumer of CPU on the machine. Based on the workaround of using a second, single row tibble I wonder if this might be a `geom_segment()` equivalent of the issue with `geom_text()` where it responds to scalar input by repeating the single draw that's required `nrow(data) ` times and therefore runs in O(N) time when it should run in O(1).

```r
library(gridExtra)
library(magrittr)
library(tidyverse)

data = crossing(x = seq(0, 100), y = seq(0, 75, by = 0.5))
data %<>% mutate(field1 = x + y, field2 = x + 0.5 * y, difference = field1 - field2, percentDifference = 100 * (field1 = field2) / field1)
plot1 = ggplot(data) + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = field1)) + geom_abline(slope = 1)
plot2 = ggplot(data) + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = field2)) + geom_abline(slope = 1)
plot3 = ggplot(data) + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = difference)) + geom_abline(slope = 1)
plot4 = ggplot(data) + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = percentDifference)) + geom_abline(slope = 1)

title: Feature request: support for tibble aesthetics
description:
I'm developing a ggplot2 extension where it would be helpful to pass a tibble column as an aesthetic.

As a simple motivating example, you could imagine a `geom_box()` layer with a `bounds` aesthetic that expects a tibble with columns xmin, ymin, xmax and ymax. Then I could simply do `geom_box(bounds = bbox)` and the layer will use the nested columns to draw the box.

To do this, we need to make use of nested tibbles (i.e. a tibble column within a tibble).

``` r
library(tidyverse)

dat <- tibble(a = tibble(x = 1:5, y = 6:10))

# works fine
ggplot(dat) +
  geom_point(aes(x = a$x, y = a$y))
```

So far, so good. But these aesthetics are still just vectors. Let's try using the tibble column `a`.

(Obviously, `geom_point()` doesn't expect a tibble column for its `x` aesthetic, but it _does_ generate the relevant error.)

``` r
ggplot(dat) +
  geom_point(aes(x = a, y = a$y))
#> Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type tbl_df/tbl/data.frame. Defaulting to continuous.
#> Error: Aesthetics must be either length 1 or the same as the data (5): x
```

The warning can be removed with a new `scale_type`. But the error is generated by this line: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/813d0bd8c7d4df3b3cba170de54233076b346c1c/R/geom-.r#L211

The length of a data frame is the number of columns (2) instead of the number of rows (5), so we get this error. This is the same problem that `vctrs::vec_size()` addresses.

Would it be possible to simply avoid this error by replacing `length()` with `nrow()`, `NROW()` or `vec_size()`? Or would there be other repercussions?

title: `print.ggplot2` for loops and functions
description:
I don't understand how the print system works, and I couldn't find anywhere if this is explained in detail. I [found](https://stackoverflow.com/a/27201707/2886003) gpplot2 overloads the print method, but I'm not sure what it means and how does it affect to not working on a loop or function. Could be possible to avoid using explicitly `print` on a loop? Maybe calling `NextMethod` or `UseMethod`?.

I'm sure I'm missing a lot, but I would appreciate your comments. Thanks

I found this "surprising" effect of pipetting and printing, not sure if related, but it actually prints/shows the plot. 

```r
library("ggplot2")
library("magrittr")
{ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
     geom_point() %>% 
     print()}
```

Upon further reading I found it is mentioned on the [R FAQs](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/FAQ/R-FAQ.html#Why-do-lattice_002ftrellis-graphics-not-work_003f):
 
> The most likely reason is that you forgot to tell R to display the graph. Lattice functions such as xyplot() create a graph object, but do not display it (the same is true of ggplot2 graphics, and Trellis graphics in S-PLUS). The print() method for the graph object produces the actual display. When you use these functions interactively at the command line, the result is automatically printed, but in source() or inside your own functions you will need an explicit print() statement.

title: awkward behavior from scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log")
description:
Three interrelated issues:
1. Log transformation of zero values for a continuous fill produces a warning about infinite values in a discrete y axis. This warning could be more clearly worded since the fill is neither discrete nor a y axis. There also appears to be differentiation of NaN from -Inf, leading to a cryptic NaN warning from negative fill values.
2. There doesn't appear to be any way to tell ggplot these fill values are expected in order to suppress the warnings. The closest I can see is something like  `scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "transparent", trans = "log")`, which plots fine since apparently -Inf, NaN, and NA are treated interchangeably but is orthogonal to warning generation.
3. The resulting labels on the fill colorbar include 8+ decimal places, which is a curiously verbose default, though `format_format(digits = n)` provides a simple mitigation.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(magrittr)
library(scales)
library(tidyverse)

data = crossing(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), y = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100))
data %<>% mutate(value = x - y)
ggplot(data) + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = value)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log")

Warning messages:
1: In self$trans$transform(x) : NaNs produced
2: Transformation introduced infinite values in discrete y-axis 

# change for more concise labeling
ggplot(data) + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = value)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = format_format(digits = 2), trans = "log")
```

Observed on R 4.0.2 with tidyverse 1.3.0 (ggplot 3.3.2). I suspect this might also occur with other scale_fill functions.
![ggplot scale_fill_viridis_c](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9359341/91611293-ccfba500-e92f-11ea-9432-ab97a4e5e9c5.png)

title: Suggestion: fatten parameter for geom_point
description:
In `geom_pointrange()`, the `fatten` parameter allows scaling the point to some factor larger than the line. Several other geometries, such as `geom_linerange()` also use a `fatten` parameter. An issue that has come up in several contexts (e.g., https://stackoverflow.com/questions/34893760/how-to-scale-the-size-of-line-and-point-separately-in-ggplot2) is the desire to set the proportionality between point size and line size in plots where the point and line sizes are mapped to a continuous or discrete (factor) variable.

Fatten would be a nice way to address this and would have consistency in nomenclature with other geometries.

    library(tidyverse)

    # You can't see the points because they're the same size as the lines
    mtcars %>% 
      mutate(cyl = ordered(str_c(cyl, " cylinders"))) %>% 
      ggplot(aes(x = disp, y = mpg, size = cyl, color = cyl)) + 
      geom_line() + 
      geom_point() + 
      scale_size_manual(values = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5))

![](https://i.imgur.com/8KkU4z6.png)


    # Kludge to make pointrange only plot a point.
    # Use fatten to make points twice as fat as the lines so they can be
    # seen easily.
    mtcars %>% 
      mutate(cyl = ordered(str_c(cyl, " cylinders"))) %>% 
      ggplot(aes(x = disp, y = mpg, size = cyl, color = cyl)) + 
      geom_line() + 
      geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mpg, ymax = mpg), fatten = 2) + 
      scale_size_manual(values = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5))

![](https://i.imgur.com/DYax5VR.png)

<sup>Created on 2020-08-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I find the second chart, the one created with `geom_pointrange()` easier to read, and it would be nice to have a `fatten` parameter for `geom_point` to make it possible to generate this kind of geometry without the kludge.

title: Map cut on the “eges” of x-axis using Aitoff projection
description:
I am trying to plot with ggplot2 (v3.3.2) data points on a map using a specific projection (called aitoff), which is useful especially for sky plots.

```
skydata <- data.frame(RA=c(0,180,360), Dec=c(0,10,20))
ggplot(skydata) + 
    geom_point(aes(RA,Dec)) +
    coord_map(projection="aitoff",orientation=c(90,180,0)) + 
    scale_y_continuous(breaks=(-2:2)*30,limits=c(-90,90)) +

title: In `stat_density()`, the calculated `count` aesthetic should take weights into account
description:
The weight should sum to one, ignoring color or fill aesthetics. That was the behavior before as can be seen here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/20342494/density-of-each-group-of-weighted-geom-density-sum-to-one
In the way that geom_density is now there is no way to make the sum of both areas be equal to one.

Example:
```r
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2movies) 
m <- ggplot()
m + geom_density(data = movies, aes(rating, weight = votes, colour = factor(Action)))
```
The plot above is equal to 

```r
m + geom_density(data = movies[movies$Action == 0, ], aes(rating, weight = votes/sum(votes)), fill=NA, colour="black") +
    geom_density(data = movies[movies$Action == 1, ], aes(rating, weight = votes/sum(votes)), fill=NA, colour="blue")
```
I would expect a much smaller area for Action == 1 in the first plot, as less than 10% of the movies are action movies.

title: Harmonize width and location of horizontal bars across facets with different number of bars

I regularly make plots like the one below. While it conveys all the necessary info, its format is (imho) not really fit for publication.

What bothers me is that 
a) bar widths are not the same (=should all have the width of the bars in the facet with most bars, i.e. europe), 
b) that the bars in the different facets are not horizontally aligned (i.e. the bar BR in the facet south america should have the same vertical position as the bar ES in the facet europe). I would have hoped that facet_row would do the trick, but it seems not to be the case.

title: Allow passing arguments to the custom labelling functions
description:
In the discrete scales (e.g. `scale_y_discrete()`), we are allowed to specify a vector of values, NULL, `waiver()` or any function that takes the breaks and returns the labels desired. The last option is especially neat as it gives the user plenty of possibilities. However, the breaks are passed only as the first argument of the function. When I want to gain any control, I have to "wrap" my function with `function(x) my_function(arg_1, arg_2)`. In other words, labels argument of a scale layer can only handle function "name/object" and not a function call.

Another and quite a similar issue concerns `facet_wrap` and `facet_grid` layers; this time, a special `labeller `function is introduced for labelling and there is even documented `as_labeller` function. This works great, but again, when I construct `my_function` labeller, it cannot be specified as a function call with arguments. Again, when wrapped with `as_labeller(function(x) my_function(arg_1, arg_2))` it does the job as intended.

Is there any workaround that I am missing? If not, I would highly appreciate the option to pass additional arguments to my labelling function. Maybe it could be accomplished with some `labs_args` list user can specify within a scale/facet layer or possibly, it would be even nicer to have `purrr `style recipe, like `~ my_function(.x, arg_1, arg_2)`.

Thanks a lot!

title: Add error message for when `ggplot2()` is used instead of `ggplot()`
description:
I have seen a lot of people, especially those who are starting out with R/`ggplot` use `ggplot2` as the function name and then get confused at the (somewhat cryptic) error message
```
Error in ggplot2(...) : 
  could not find function "ggplot2"
```

Can we add a dummy function (maybe to [`R/plot.r`](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/R/plot.r)) to show a more helpful error message to the user?
```r
ggplot2 <- function(...) {
  # Show a helpful error message if ggplot2 is used accidentally
  abort(glue("
    You have accidentally called `ggplot2` instead of `gglot`.
    Please note that while the name of the package is `ggplot2`, the function itself is called `ggplot`.
  "))
}
```

I will be happy to submit a Pull Request to implement this.

---

Reprex
```r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot2()
```

title: geom_line with data parameter has high memory usage, apparently unfreed after usage
description:
After running the following code:

```r
library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame( x1 = runif(1e6))
df$y = df$x1

ggplot() + geom_hline( data = df, mapping = aes( yintercept = 1))

gc()
```
...Windows Task Manager shows 1.2 GB of memory usage on my machine. I would expect the ```gc()``` call to make this go down to something around 200 MB. But no amount of calling ```gc()``` or clearing objects from memory (e.g., ```rm( list = ls())```) will get that number down. Restarting R does: ```.rs.restartR()```. So I worry that this memory will never get freed up & might contribute to out of memory errors in other situations. Less-focused related discussion [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/63236265/r-geom-smooth-geom-hline-makes-memory-usage-explode).

Similar behavior is observed with ```geom_vline``` & ```geom_abline```. Using ggplot2 version 3.3.2, R version 4.0.2, Windows 10.

Thank you for all of your work.

title: Possible bug in `stage()`/`after_stat()` with scale transformations.
description:
I think I might have found a bug with either the scales or the `stage()`/`after_stat()` functions in combination with dates. 
I came across this when making a custom stat where I wanted to put `default_aes = aes(xmin = after_stat(start), xmax = after_stat(end))` in the ggproto methods, where `start` and `end` are computed variables.

What happens is that when I try to apply a `stage()` or `after_stat()` to a date variable, it gives me an error that the date transformation is invalid. I don't think it is a problem with stats, as it also shows up with `stat_identity()`.
The attempted plot below is not very interesting, but it is the most minimal example I could come up with.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics) +
  geom_point(aes(x = stage(date, after_stat = x), 
                 y = unemploy))
#> Error: Invalid input: date_trans works with objects of class Date only
```

The error above doesn't happen for integer or numeric data.
```
ggplot(economics) +
  geom_point(aes(x = stage(as.integer(date), after_stat = x), 
                 y = unemploy))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/soRUYWn.png)

And also the error can be rescued by formatting the output as a date again, but this seems overly verbose and seems difficult to anticipate in a custom stat.
``` r
ggplot(economics) +
  geom_point(aes(x = stage(date, after_stat = structure(x, class = "Date")), 
                 y = unemploy))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/ZSc1vZP.png)

The same is true for other geoms and aesthetics as well. Here are similar examples with `after_stat()` instead of `stage()`.

``` r
ggplot(economics) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = date, xend = after_stat(x + 30),
                   y = unemploy, yend = unemploy))
#> Error: Invalid input: date_trans works with objects of class Date only
```

```
ggplot(economics) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = as.integer(date), xend = after_stat(x + 30),
                   y = unemploy, yend = unemploy))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/JIY7UhP.png)

``` r
ggplot(economics) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = date, xend = after_stat(structure(x + 30, class = "Date")),
                   y = unemploy, yend = unemploy))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/IoNHYnm.png)

title: Discrete example in stat_summary doesn't work after 3.3.2
description:
The example "Orientation follows the discrete axis" in stat_summary (lines 55 to 58) doesn't demonstrate what it claims to after the ggplot2 update to v3.3.2 (it did work in 3.3.0). The example doesn't actually follow the discrete axis. In order for it to demonstrate what it claims to, cyl should be replaced with factor(cyl) or a similar discrete datatype. See details below.

```r
# install / load ggplot2 v 3.3.0
# run below example

# Orientation follows the discrete axis
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) +
 geom_point() +
 stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_boot", colour = "red", size = 2)
```
You will get a plot that summarizes mpg by groups of cyl, this is the presumed desired behavior based on the title of the example
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44787126/88719754-c6d89580-d0f1-11ea-9e4e-3760a386b6f9.png)

```r
# install / load ggplot2 v 3.3.2
# run below example

# Orientation follows the discrete axis
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) +
 geom_point() +
 stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_boot", colour = "red", size = 2)
```
Now you will get a plot that summarizes cyl by mpg, 
but this doesn't match the behavior implied by the title for the example "Orientation follows the discrete axis"
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44787126/88719587-85e08100-d0f1-11ea-8d79-2eae993cb175.png)

In order for this example to work with v 3.3.2, the y-mapped variable has to result in a mapped_discrete datatype
For example, you could update the example as follows (replacing cyl with factor(cyl)):
```r
# Orientation follows the discrete axis
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, factor(cyl))) +
 geom_point() +
 stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_boot", colour = "red", size = 2) 
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44787126/88719935-0f904e80-d0f2-11ea-9875-5b3f31844db4.png)

title: New ggplot2.discrete.fill option doesn't work with ordered factor columns
description:
I have found what I think is an issue with the new ggplot2.discrete.fill options, although it may be my understanding of what exactly "discrete" means and this may be by design. When using the option it works correctly for character columns, or as in the example factor(char_column)'s, but does not appear to work for already existing factor columns as this uses the default colours instead.

As I said this may be by design in that factors are treated different in plotting and I haven't realised, but this isn't clear in documentation anywhere I looked. I am using ggplot2 version 3.3.2, and R version 3.6.1.

title: axis.text.x margins are not applied with scale_x_discrete position set to "top"
description:
The closed issue [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2425) (#2425) includes a simple reprex and the issue is still present in 3.3.2. Here's another reprex for reference:

```R
data <- data.frame(category = c("1", "2", "3"), value = c(10, 5, 15))

ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
	geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
	scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
	theme(axis.text.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 50, b = 50), debug = TRUE))
```

If you run the above and then switch `scale_x_discrete(position = "top")` to `scale_x_discrete(position = "bottom")`, you can immediately see the issue.

I'm also not convinced that #1502 (margins not being applied to the legend) was actually the same issue as was suspected in the discussion on #2425. The legend margin issue appears to have been fixed in #2556, but this axis text margin bug is still very much present as of 3.3.2.

But the output image gets reversed when I add scale_y_log10.

```r

df <- tibble(
  x = 1:10,
  y = seq(0.1, 1, 0.1)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_log10()
```

title: Bug: Unexpected fill guides with multiple geom_density layers

title: Strange warning from `position_dodge()` when using `geom_smooth()`
description:
When using `position_dodge()`, I get a confusing warning about overlapping x intervals that I don't get with `geom_line()`. 
Seems like it might be a bug? The dodging is useful to prevent the error bars from being on top of one another.

``` r
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))

data_1 <- tibble(y = 1:10 + runif(10), x = seq_along(y), set = "one")
data_2 <- tibble(y = 2:11 + runif(10), x = seq_along(y), set = "two")
data <- bind_rows(data_1, data_2) %>% 
  mutate(y_upper = y + abs(runif(seq_along(y))),
         y_lower = y - abs(runif(seq_along(y))))

ggplot(data, aes(x, y, colour = set)) + 
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = y_lower, ymax = y_upper),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/gMA1edZ.png)

``` r
  
ggplot(data, aes(x, y, colour = set)) + 
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  geom_smooth(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4), 
              method = "loess", formula = "y ~ x", se = FALSE) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = y_lower, ymax = y_upper),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10)
#> Warning: position_dodge requires non-overlapping x intervals
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/EgBkkiX.png)

  labs(x = bquote(.(sym(a))[.(sym(b))])) +

title: multiple arrows in geom_path if color specified, but only one arrow otherwise
description:
### Summary

When using `geom_path` I find that

* if I use only `geom_path(arrow = arrow())`, the result is a single arrow at the end of the path, but
* if I add a colour aesthetic, `geom_path(aes(colour = t, arrow = arrow()))`, the result is an arrow on each segment.


### Minimal reproducible example

To reproduce, I set up some points on a circle and used a `geom_path` with and without a `colour` aesthetic.  

```
library('ggplot2')

t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, by = pi / 12)
x <- cos(t)
y <- sin(t)
df <- data.frame(t = t, x = x, y = y)

plot1 <-
  ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path(arrow = arrow())
plot1 

plot2 <-
  ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path(aes(colour = t), arrow = arrow())
plot2 
```

Here's `plot1`.

![plot1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3383807/87227337-52b79700-c368-11ea-9e7e-99fee2f93df9.jpg)

Here's `plot2`:

![plot2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3383807/87227348-5f3bef80-c368-11ea-9747-059659535781.jpg)

### Related issue

This is related to #2280 (geom_path should support intermediate arrows), which was marked won't fix because of difficulty.

title: geom_histogram does not warn about absurdly large number of bins
description:
When the range of the data is large and the binwidth is small, such that an absurdly large number of bins are required to plot the histogram, geom_histogram fails with an uninformative warning.

```r
> ggplot(tibble(x=c(1, 1e12)), aes(x)) + geom_histogram(binwidth=1)
Warning message:
Computation failed in `stat_bin()`:
'by' argument is much too small 
```

This is in contrast to the case where a large (but not absurdly so) number of bins are required. In this case, a sensible and descriptive warning message is thrown.

```r
> ggplot(tibble(x=c(1, 1e6)), aes(x)) + geom_histogram(binwidth=1)
Warning message:
Computation failed in `stat_bin()`:
The number of histogram bins must be less than 1,000,000.
Did you make `binwidth` too small? 
```

Which is strange, because one would expect that 1e12 breaks would behave the same as 1e6 breaks, based on the snippet below:

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/dcad61a07d67e7339a94b18a5976079a89429fb8/R/bin.R#L90-L96

I think that the warning message for e.g. 1e6 breaks should be consistent with that for 1e12 breaks.

---

My use case: I have data with range of about [0, 1e23]. Most of the data is distributed at around [0, 5] and the distribution there is shown best at a bin width of about 0.1. Following the advice written [here](https://groups.google.com/d/msg/ggplot2/jSrL_FnS8kc/MvzM_2_jiSIJ), I intended to plot the whole histogram from [0, 1e23] with bin width 0.1, but zoom in on [0, 5] using ggforce::facet_zoom. Obviously, that didn't work. My workaround now is to subset the data from [0, 1e23] to [0, 1e5], then doing the facet_zoom.

title: improve geom_bar() and geom_col()'s linetype aesthetic's default behaviour
description:
Using the `fill` aesthetic with a categorical variable works as expected in `geom_col()` and `geom_bar()`, but `linetype` with the same variable gives a results that looks like it is fails.

The reason why it looks like it is failing is that the bar chart border is by default invisible (is that accurate?). To make the change visible, one has to change the `colour` value for the bar/col geometry.

The second issue is that the area surrounded by the line is not what might be expected by most users when using `stat = "identity"` (`geom_col()`'s default). The `fill` aesthetic will make each colour look like one single block, but using the `linetype` aesthetic will draw each case's border separately.

Seeing this result, one might try to find a different `stat_*()` function to use, and logically might try `stat_sum()`, to end up with a sum of all values that have the same categorical level (i.e. ending up with one single case, and one single area to draw a border for). However, `stat_sum()` is used for something completely different: mainly to draw an alternative to a scatterplot when there is exact overlap. Using it for a bar chart results in an interestingly glitchy plot.

I have to admit I haven't thought much of the potential drawbacks and side-effects of (1) improving the default `colour` of the bar/col geometries when the `linetype` aesthetic is used, and (2) the modification of the default behaviour of the border drawing when `linetype` is used with `stat_identity()`, but is there maybe some room for improvement?

``` r
library(ggplot2)
## (1) linetype aes looks like it does not work
# using linetype looks like it fails
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(Titanic),
       aes(x = Class, linetype = Survived)) +
  geom_bar()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/aZXAk2g.png)

``` r
# one has to change the colour to see the effect
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(Titanic),
       aes(x = Class, linetype = Survived)) +
  geom_bar(colour = "black")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/AkO7jmx.png)

``` r

## (2) linetype aes with identity stat won't group cases
# count stat (default for bar chart): the whole area is bordered
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(Titanic),
       aes(x = Class, linetype = Survived)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count", colour = "black")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/fZk02Vd.png)

``` r
# identity stat (geom_col()'s default): each case has a separate border 
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(Titanic),
       aes(x = Class, y = Freq, linetype = Survived)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", colour = "black")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/N9CNUat.png)

``` r
# ...whereas identity stat + fill aesthetic works out fine visually
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(Titanic),
       aes(x = Class, y = Freq, fill = Survived)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/pv1Jjj6.png)

``` r
# sum stat, maybe? No, it is used for something else.
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(Titanic),
       aes(x = Class, y = Freq, linetype = Survived)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "sum", colour = "black")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/1g1sGh6.png)
