```r
plot_data <- dplyr::storms %>%
  dplyr::group_by(year) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(wind = round(mean(wind), 2)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(year = lubridate::dmy(paste0("01-01-", year)))

ggplot(plot_data, aes(year, wind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) 
```

title: Error with coord_flip with geom_bar: attempt to replicate an object of type 'environment'
description:
I have a simple plotting code that works well without `coord_flip`, but fails with it.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

test_data = tibble(measurement_concept_id = c('a', 'b', 'c'),
                   n=1:3)

# this works
test_data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(as.factor(measurement_concept_id), n)) + geom_bar(stat='identity') +
  scale_y_log10() 

# this fails
test_data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(as.factor(measurement_concept_id), n)) + geom_bar(stat='identity') +
  scale_y_log10() %>%
  coord_flip()
```
Any idea what can go wrong here?

title: Check if the visual tests actually run
description:
(Moved from https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/3922#issuecomment-607288487)

Visual tests are so sensitive that it fails even with the subtle changes between R versions that we cannot detect with our eyes. So, it's a common practice to run the tests only on the latest stable version of R. But, sometimes we mistakenly set the CI to skip visual tests on all the versions. Since visual tests are important to detect regressions, we need some way to ensure they actually run.

@lionel- says this might require a new feature on vdiffr's (and testthat?) side after R 4.0:

> Maybe vdiffr could signal a special condition class when a test is not run. Then a calling (not exiting so other tests keep running) condition handler could transform the condition to an error that would be caught by testthat.
> 
> With R 4.0 it would be easy to do this with a global condition handler, without any change in the ggplot2 sources. On older R we'd need to install the handler around test_check() with withCallingHandlers(), conditionally on some environment variable indicating that the tests should really be run (but then you run into the same issue i.e. is this envvar correctly defined... So the global handler approach is a little more appealing).

title: Too much space reserved for axis labels when using facets
description:
ggplot2 seems to reserve too much space for axis labels in non-english languages (non-ASCII characters?) when using facets.

Problem seems to be locale dependent as it appears with default "Russian_Russia.1251" locale and does not appear with "en_US.UTF-8".

---

``` r
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(1L)
test_df <- data.frame(
  cat = sprintf("cat%s", rep(1:3, each = 3)),
  subcat = sprintf("subcat_subcat_subcat_subcat%s", rep(1:3, times = 3)),
  subcat_ru = sprintf("субкат_субкат_субкат%s", rep(1:3, times = 3)),
  amount = runif(3*3, 25, 40)
)

ggplot(test_df, aes(y = subcat, x = amount)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(cat ~ .)
```
Plot renders fine with english characters.

![test_plot_en](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1351765/78250083-01da0c00-74f8-11ea-9e2e-f8c808b16751.png)

``` r

ggplot(test_df, aes(y = subcat_ru, x = amount)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(cat ~ .)
```
But breaks when using russian.

![test_plot_ru](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1351765/78250287-4fef0f80-74f8-11ea-841c-6a99cf13cd71.png)

title: Discrete scale broken with negative limits
description:
I recently reinstalled my R/Rstudio due to the issue with one of the packages, and during this process, I also (1) downloaded and installed R development tools and libraries (clang and gfortran) from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/tools/ (2) downloaded and installed gfortran compiler for R from https://github.com/fxcoudert/gfortran-for-macOS/releases/tag/6.3 (3) uninstalled Java/JDK 14 and installing Java/JDK 11 version; and (4) ran “R CMD javareconf” comman on the terminal. All of these actions were taken to resolve the error associated with one of the packages requiring Java connection.

However, during theses resolution steps, something else seemed to be messed up because the existing function/package/script started working inappropriately (it worked before I tried the resolution steps above). So the problem is (and this problem is SEPARATE from the package problem that I was trying to solve with the resolution steps mentioned above): I run this script that utilizes several packages including ggplot2, tibble, dplyr, etc. to generate my graphs. Just several days ago when I tried to generate these graphs, the script worked fine (see below picture, on the left labeled as a "good example"). 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62915812/78048637-0069e180-7348-11ea-988e-f743f2d1e092.png)

But after all the resolution steps that I took as discussed above, the exact same script no longer works properly (see above picture, on the right side labeled as a "bad example" that I'm getting now). I used the exact same script, same packages to generate these graphs but now the graphs are being generated strangely…It seems like the tickmarks on the y axis are now not getting evenly spaced out throughout the whole y-axis and the problem starts at the stage where I create "Plot."

Does anyone have any idea what might have gone wrong during the resolution that could have damaged R (or its associated packages) to cause this problem? I want to go back to the ggplot2 that used to create that "good example"

The data that I used are basically table of different cell numbers in each well ("Number_of_Objects) in 384-well plate and I tried to depict the data using the heatmap approach as shown in the figure. The figure shows the collection of small rectangles corresponding to each well in 384-well plate and they are colored on gray gradient based on the cell density (darker, the greater density). The code that I used to plot this is:

```r
library("tidyverse")
library("stringr")
library("ggplot2")
library("ggpubr")

#Table corresponds to the data table of 384-well plate that will be analyzed#

Plot=ggplot(Table, aes(x=Column, y=-Row)) + theme_classic()+
    scale_x_discrete(limits=c(1:24), name="") + 
    scale_y_discrete(limits=c(-1:-16), labels=LETTERS[1:16], name="")
  
  
  pShape=Plot + ggtitle("Number of non-border cells") +
    geom_tile(aes(fill=Number_of_Objects)) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "black", high = "gray80", name="")
``` 

I used the exactly the same script both times and both times the script runs without any error but generates completely different graphs. How can I fix the issue so that I can go back to the "good example" graph state? 

During install/reinstall, some of those packages might have been updated as well. I checked the updates on all the packages that were installed and except for "tibble," which is a package that gets called along with those libraries when I load "tidyverse," everything was up-to-date. title: Show secondary axis lines without specifying secondary axes
description:
I'm trying to make a plot with a border around the entire panel and also with tick marks at the very ends of the axes. Unfortunately, regardless of theme this means the tick marks don't line up with the panel border. This is especially apparent when you have a larger `base_size`:

```r
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10,50), expand = c(0,0)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=24)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7232514/77961322-4880f980-729f-11ea-9d4f-11467e7d00c1.png)
(note the 10 and 50 y axis tick marks do not line up with the panel border)

Now, this makes sense, because the panel border is actually supposed to be within the axes, so let's just put some axes on:

```r
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10,50), expand = c(0,0)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=24) +
    theme(axis.line = element_line(lineend = "square"))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7232514/77961676-cf35d680-729f-11ea-99ec-628b4fb3a20b.png)

Well, that's not really what we want, because the panel border still doesn't line up with the axes. But how can I add right and top axes? The only way I know of is as follows:
```r
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10,50), expand = c(0,0), sec.axis = sec_axis(~.)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=24) +
    theme(axis.line = element_line(lineend = "square"), axis.text.y.right = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y.right = element_blank())
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7232514/77962056-80d50780-72a0-11ea-984c-07c441f1b29f.png)

But that feels pretty hacky to me. So my questions is: is there a way to add such an axis line without specifying sec.axis and then removing everything I don't want? Ideally the defaults for the the secondary axis theme elements would be element_blank() when there is no sec.axis specified, then the user could just turn them on as desired, e.g.:
```r
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10,50), expand = c(0,0)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=24) +
    theme(axis.line = element_line(lineend = "square"), axis.line.y.right = element_line(lineend = "square"))
```

title: geom_text add option for coordinate related angle ('slope') rotation
description:
It would be helpful to have the option to rotate text (when using e.g. geom_text) providing a 'slope', so that you can annotate a 1:1 line with 1:1 correctly rotated.
The following example should indicate the issue:
```r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(f = rep(letters[1:4], 10), x = rnorm(40), y = rnorm(40))

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
	geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) + 
	geom_point() +
	facet_wrap(~ f, scales = "free_x") +
	geom_text(x = 0, y = 0, label = "1:1", angle = 45)
```

title: ggupset breaks with version 3.3.0
description:
Hi,

I noticed yesterday that with the new version of ggplot, my extension [ggupset](https://github.com/const-ae/ggupset) breaks when I add a `scale_x_mergelist()`.
On the positive side, the main functionality of the package is still intact and my replacement combination matrix axis still works. 

However, I have a helper function `scale_x_mergelist()` that converts a list column into a character vector with `paste(..., collapse = "-")`.  Previously, the collapsed string was shown on the x-axis, now it is blank:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(ggupset)
ggplot(tidy_movies, aes(x = Genres)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_mergelist(sep = "-")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/tSWbxhw.png)

title: coord_cartesian() fails without reversed limits with scale_y_reverse()
description:
In 3.3.0 (including latest dev version), there is odd behavior when combining `coord_cartesian()` with `scale_y_reverse()`.

This is fine:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 35), ylim = c(50, 350))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/322716/77412129-9619e400-6e11-11ea-9be7-9348aa44036d.png)

This also is fine:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  scale_y_reverse() + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 35))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/322716/77412213-af229500-6e11-11ea-9e6e-08b2a3517541.png)

This breaks. I'm inclined to see it as a bug, because even if you think I *should* reverse the lower and upper limit of `ylim` given the use of `scale_y_reverse()`, why should that error make the axis ticks, etc. disappear altogether for the y axis?

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  scale_y_reverse() + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 35), ylim = c(50, 350))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/322716/77412247-bb0e5700-6e11-11ea-88ec-77b0beeaf3de.png)

Interestingly, this is fine again.

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  scale_y_reverse() + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 35), ylim = c(350, 50))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/322716/77412410-f4df5d80-6e11-11ea-98c2-308ffacb52cb.png)

title: geom_rect rectangle disappears when used together with coord_sf in R
description:

I have tried to create the rectangle using `geom_rect` function, but whenever I include `coord_sf` function in the code chunk, the rectangle disappears. Below are the maps I got with the following codes. Classes of zone_map and ecoregion_polygon objects are "sf" and both are read in using `st_read` function.

      geom_sf(data = ecoregion_polygon, color = "black", fill = burlywood1_transparent) +

title: geom_contour incompatible with scale_x_log10 and scale_y_log10
description:
`geom_contour` seems to be incompatible with log scales, generated with `scale_x_log10` or `scale_y_log10` (or both).

```r
library(ggplot)
v <- ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, z = density))
v + geom_contour() + scale_x_log10()
```

This produces a warning message, below, and an empty plot.

```
Warning message:
Computation failed in `stat_contour()`:
Number of x coordinates must match number of columns in density matrix.
```

Use of `scale_y_log10` yields a similar result, with the warning message about `y` coordinates.

title: stat_function disregards log and possibly other scale
description:
stat_function() seems to disregard scale_y_log10() and similar. There has been a PR #1011 that is (as far as I understand) supposed to have fixed this issue, merged in 2015 and released in 1.0.1.9000.

However, I can observe the following behavior in ggplot2 3.2.1 and 3.3.0 (did not test others):

``` r
library(tidyverse)
fn <- function(x) {exp(x)}
data <- tibble(x = c(1:10), y=exp(x))
data %>% ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + stat_function(fun=fn)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Muzqyqj.png)

This (above) looks as expected, nothing was rescaled, the function matches the data points.

``` r
data %>% ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + stat_function(fun=fn) + scale_y_log10()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/TGEPs1Q.png)

The problem can be observed here, while the data points were adapted to a logscale y axis, the function wasn't. 

``` r
data %>% ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + stat_function(fun=function(x){log10(fn(x))}) + scale_y_log10()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/nsK9acX.png)

This is what I would the plot to look like (just without the workaround of applying the extra log10()).

<sup>Created on 2020-03-21 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

title: Allow position aesthetics other than x and y?
description:
This is an issue so that we remember to come back to this. As noted by. @clauswilke here: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3561#issuecomment-599091916 , constructing ternary diagrams using ggplot requires a lot of copying of ggplot2 code, which has resulted in the current breaking of the ggtern package.

At the heart of the issue is that a ternary diagram is a transformation of 3 variables, rather than 2. Currently, x- and y-scales are hard-coded in the `Layout` and other places, which makes adding an additional aesthetic that should be treated as a position aesthetic impossible (see https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2540#issuecomment-570737499 ). I can't find the thread, but this came up in the context of `coord_sf()`, where `geometry` is also sort of a position aesthetic (that only sort of acts like one).

One approach would be to allow coords to define what is a position aesthetic. Currently there are a lot of definitions of "what is a position aesthetic" (#3342). If I remember correctly, this will break Coord and possibly Facet subclasses that are passed `scale_x` and `scale_y`.

Anyway, not pressing, just something that should be considered when coords are revisited.

title: arrow in geom_segment misoriented for length-zero segments
description:
The expected behavior when `geom_segment()` is given a segment of __length 0__ (`xend == x`) is probably not to draw anything at all. But when an `arrow` is specified, the arrowhead is fixed so that it points left. See the "C" arrow below.  

I want it to  produce no arrowhead at all just for" C", or at least it should draw it so that it is oriented towards the aesthetic given (either pointing from `x` to `xend`, or pointing from `y` to `yend`, depending on what is specified).

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(patchwork)

dat <- tribble(
  ~letter, ~start, ~end,
  "A", 0.0, 0.10, 
  "B", 0.0, 0.01, 
  "C", 0.0, 0.0,   # this segment will have length 0
)


# expected behavior 
g0 <- ggplot(dat, aes(y = letter)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = start, xend = end, yend = letter))

# unexpected behavior, arrow drawn but going left
g1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(y = letter)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = start, xend = end, yend = letter), arrow = arrow())

# arrow goes left, regardless of orientation of the segment itself
g2 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = letter)) +
  geom_segment(aes(y = start, yend = end, xend = letter), arrow = arrow())


g0 + g1 + g2
```

title: Filled contours don't play well with faceting
description:
This is technically a bug report against my PR #3864, but the bug isn't caused by that PR, it's just revealed by it. The same bug exists with `geom_contour_filled()`, just requires more code to generate a reprex.

I have noticed that when I draw filled density contours across facets, the color levels in the legend get jumbled. (Carefully look at the levels in the legend, and you'll see they're not even in order.)

``` r
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(4393)
dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 1000), ]

ggplot(dsmall, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_density_2d_filled() +
  facet_grid(. ~ cut)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/BvsSpRs.png)

What happens is that the breaks are calculated separately for each facet, and then they don't match across facets. It's possible to work around this by manually specifying breaks, but I think the default settings should work with facets.

Fundamentally, the problem is that the `level` variable for contour bands is an ordered factor specifying the bin boundaries:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/db58364f9d95b7596249feb01b34420b7b4483b5/R/stat-contour.r#L111

By contrast, the `level` variable for contour lines is a numeric:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/db58364f9d95b7596249feb01b34420b7b4483b5/R/stat-contour.r#L86

I think instead we should return a numeric value for `level` in all cases and by default map that to fill for filled contours. We can still return the ordered factor as well as an option, under a different name. The numeric value I would use for `level` would be the mid-point between the lower and the upper level boundary. This is consistent with other binning approaches, e.g. the placement of bars in histograms.

The result would be something like the following (but without the `aes(fill = ...)` statement needed):
``` r
ggplot(dsmall, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_density_2d_filled(aes(fill = after_stat(level_high))) +
  facet_grid(. ~ cut) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/OUQGn3h.png)

This will be consistent with how contour lines work already:
``` r

ggplot(dsmall, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_density_2d(aes(color = after_stat(level))) +
  facet_grid(. ~ cut) +
  scale_color_viridis_c()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/k2iqgl0.png)

If we agree on this approach I'll incorporate it into #3864.

title: Binned scales don't use na.value
description:
The new binned scales in v3.3.0 don't appear to use `na.value`, though `na.value` is included in the documentation (`?scale_fill_steps`) and ostensibly has a default of `grey50`.

Here's a reprex. `scale_fill_gradient()` works with `na.value`, but binned scales like `scale_fill_viridis_b()` and `scale_fill_steps()` do not:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(x = rep(1:3, 2), y = rep(1:2, 3), z = 1:6) %>% 
  mutate(z = ifelse(x == 1 & y == 1, NA, z))

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = z))

p + scale_fill_gradient(na.value = "red")
```

``` r
p + scale_fill_viridis_b(na.value = "red")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/7Pq83EA.png)

``` r
p + scale_fill_steps(na.value = "red")
```

title: default_aes not used in compute_*() methods
description:
While writing about extensions I noticed that the content of `default_aes` in a stat is not added to the data before it is passed through the `compute_*()` mill. This effectively renders it useless for anything but defining mappings for the geom.

The current code reflects this as it has all sorts of code around extracting non-required aesthetics from the data, e.g. in StatBinHex

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/1223de2d6841be4276b5b398aff747672797c1b9/R/stat-binhex.r#L45-L65

we set a default `weight`, but still has to guard it with `data$weight %||% rep(1L, nrow(data))` when using it in `compute_group()`

I cannot see any meaningful reason why this is so, and the fix seems obvious. Have I missed an underlying reason @hadley?

title: Change function signature of Geom$draw_layer()
description:
Several distinct issues have arisen where `Geom$draw_layer()` needs more info than it is currently given. Specifically, it looks like it would be good to hand it a new object called `layer_params` (https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3116#issuecomment-465756191) as well as the theme (https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/2749#issuecomment-595045228). Is there anything else that we should add, while we're add it?

The current signature is as follows:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/83c8123d15ef5f50d6c357ad388b7514e083c51c/R/geom-.r#L74

I propose the following signature:
```
  draw_layer = function(self, data, params, layout, coord, theme, layer_params, ...) 
```
The `...` future-proofs this in case we are still missing something.

@paleolimbot @thomasp85 Are you guys still on board with `layer_params` as discussed here: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3116#issuecomment-465756191 or has your thinking evolved since then?

We could also now make the function signature 
```
  draw_layer = function(self, data, params, layout, coord, theme, ...) 
```
and leave the `layer_params` issue for a future date.

title: Warning filter component in ggplot2
description:
I recently created a plot using ggplot2 within a function, and this plot generates warnings when being printed.  
Currently to suppress all warning on a ggplot2 plot you have to do something like this:
```r
suppressWarnings(print(my_ggplot2_plot))
```

I recently made a function which allow R users to filter warnings returned by a function they use:
```r
warn.handle <- function(pattern, ...){
  withCallingHandlers(..., warning = function(warning){
    condition <- conditionMessage(warning)
    if(grepl(pattern, condition)){ invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }
  })
}
```
Example:
```r
warn.handle(pattern = "a character string that will match in a warning", function_that_returns_warnings())
```

So I can use it on a ggplot2 plot when printing it (see 1st chunck of code), but if my plot is part of a plotting function I create, and that I add additionnal ggplot2 components to it, warnings will be displayed anyway:

```r
function_to_make_plot(){
  #create a plot
  my_ggplot2_plot<-ggplot() + <additionnal stuff...>
  #return
  return(
    warn.handle(pattern = "a character string that will match in a warning",
                         print(my_ggplot2_plot))
  )
}

function_to_make_plot() #Filtering warnings works.
function_to_make_plot() + xlab("My X-Axis Title") # All warnings will be printed.  
```

So my question is more like, is their any plan to create a ggplot2 component that would be able to do such thing ?
Something like that for example:

```r
my_ggplot2_plot<- ggplot() +
  <additionnal stuff...> +
  filter.warnings(pattern = "a character string that will match in a warning", ...)
```
`filter.warnings()` could be stored in `my_ggplot2_plot` so that if new components are added afterward, printing the final plot will still filter the unnecessary warnings.
It is just an idea, but I think it would helpful for some of us.

title: Facet_wrap and scale="free" unexpectedly centers y-axis at zero in ggplot2
description:
From this dataframe
```

     df <- data.frame(cat=c(rep("X", 20),rep("Y", 20), rep("Z",20)), 
                         value=c(runif(20),runif(20)*100, rep(0, 20)), 
                         var=rep(LETTERS[1:5],12))
```

i want to create facetted boxplots. One facet would contain only Zeros.
    
  ```
  library(ggplot2)
    

    p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(var,value)) + geom_boxplot() + facet_wrap(~cat, scale="free") 
    p1

```

The results is aesthetically dissactisfactory as it centers the y-axis of the empty panel at zero. Note, that "scale="free"" causes this. I want to start all y-scales at zero. I tried several solutions found on the web:

```
    p1 + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) # not working
    p1 + expand_limits(y = 0) #not working
    p1 + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA)) ## not working
    p1 + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,100)) ## partially working, but defeats scale="free"
    p1 + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,max(df$value))) ## partially working, see above
    p1 + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,max(df$value))) + expand_limits(y = 0)## partially working, see above
```

One solution would possibly be to replace the zero's with very tiny values, but maybe you can find a more straightforward solution. Thank you.

title: Error when using geom_vline() with facet_grid()
description:
If data is not defined within the `ggplot()` call (but in subsequent geom calls) , using `geom_vline()` throws an error but only if used with `facet_grid()` (Example 1 in reprex). If the call to `facet_grid()` is removed, there is no error and it works fine (example 2). Alternatively, if we define data within the `geom_vline()`, it works fine (example 3). 

This seems inconsistent to me. I would expect either 1 and 2 to both work or both throw an error, so I think this might be a bug?

```r
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Breaks
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = cyl)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0)) +
```

title: In stat_summary_hex and stat_binhex, hexagons overlap when z values are factors
description:
Issue #826 (June 28, 2013) has never been fixed, so `stat_summary_hex()` and `stat_binhex()` are not working correctly.

I need this feature to work, so I will try to post working code snippets here as a workaround to this bug.

Over time, I hope that we can eventually create a new pull request to fix this issue.

---

# Demonstration

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(scico)
library(tidyverse)
library(hexbin)
```

Generate two-dimensional data. Some objects are TRUE and some are FALSE.

``` r
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(
  x = rnorm(1000),
  y = rnorm(1000),
  z = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), size = 1000, replace = TRUE)
)
```

# Problem

For each hexagonal bin, we’d like to know the proportion of TRUE objects.

The `stat_summary_hex()` function seems like a good choice. Let’s try it.

``` r
ggplot(d) +
  aes(x = x, y = y, z = z) +
  stat_summary_hex(size = 0.1, color = "black", fun = mean, bins = 30) +
  scale_fill_scico()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/0LuYXRU.png)

We get something unexpected:
* One set of hexagons for TRUE objects.
* Another set of hexagons for FALSE objects.

Let’s try `stat_binhex()` instead.

``` r
ggplot(d) +
  aes(x = x, y = y, z = z) +
  stat_binhex(size = 0.1, color = "black", bins = 30) +
  scale_fill_scico()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/c4cpfgs.png)

We get something different, but unexpected:
* Multiple sets of overlapping hexagons.

# Solution

Instead of using ggplot2 functions, let’s write our own code to compute the proportion of TRUE objects in each hexagon.

``` r
hex <- hexbin::hexbin(d$x, d$y, xbins = 30, IDs = TRUE)
x <- table(hex@cID, d$z, useNA = "always")
x <- x[seq(nrow(x) - 1),]
x <- as.data.frame.matrix(x)
colnames(x) <- c("false", "true", "na")
x <- cbind(x, data.frame(hexbin::hcell2xy(hex), hex = hex@cell, count = hex@count))
head(x)
#>     false true na           x         y hex count
#> 12      0    1  0 -0.50799600 -3.253220  12     1
#> 22      1    0  0  1.76477910 -3.253220  22     1
#> 45      0    1  0  0.06019778 -3.054242  45     1
#> 74      1    0  0 -0.50799600 -2.855264  74     1
#> 102     1    0  0 -1.07618977 -2.656287 102     1
#> 106     1    0  0 -0.16707973 -2.656287 106     1
```

Now we can display the number of TRUE objects in each hexagon:

``` r
ggplot(x) +
  aes(x = x, y = y, fill = true) +
  geom_hex(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_scico()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/UIH52yC.png)

Or the number of FALSE objects in each hexagon:

``` r
ggplot(x) +
  aes(x = x, y = y, fill = false) +
  geom_hex(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_scico()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/q709wQv.png)

Or the proportion of TRUE objects in each hexagon:

``` r
ggplot(x) +
  aes(x = x, y = y, fill = true / count) +
  geom_hex(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_scico()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/ZVBC64p.png)

title: geom_bar()/geom_col() should provide clearer warning when dropping data due to axis limits and column width
description:
Consider the following plot:

```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = carb)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "count") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(2, 4))
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4790348/75587164-ba5ced80-5a2a-11ea-93d4-e294e2639037.png)

The bars centered at `2` and `4` are dropped. As documented in https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2887, this is because the limits are not adjusted for the `width` of the bars. The bar centered on `2` actually extends back to ~`1.5`, and the bar centered on `4` actually extends to `4.5`. Users do get some warnings:
>Warning messages:
1: Removed 9 rows containing non-finite values (stat_count). 
2: Removed 2 rows containing missing values (geom_bar). 

The second warning alludes to the bars being dropped because they extend outside the specified axis limits. However, this isn't a sufficient explanation of what is happening because users may be specifying limits because they *want* bars outside of the axis limits to be dropped (and thus they expect to see the warnings), but don't understand why columns that appear to be *inside* the axis limits are also dropped.

**suggestion**: Improve the error message to note when columns are dropped because the column *width* is outside of the range (e.g. the column centered on `2`), as opposed to when the *entire column* is outside of the range (e.g. the column centered on `1`).

Finally, consider this solution to the issue:
```r

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = carb)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "count") +
  # expand axis limits to accommodate column width
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1.5, 4.5))
```
> Warning message:
Removed 9 rows containing non-finite values (stat_count). 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4790348/75587890-576c5600-5a2c-11ea-8299-29192f90731e.png)


Is this solution the *preferred* approach to resolving the issue, or is this relying on undocumented/unreliable behavior?

title: axis.title.x overrides axis.title in theme()
description:
This appears to be new behavior in 3.3.0, where if you add a "more specific/child" theme element to a plot, and then also modify the "parent" theme element, the "child" element theme setting is used. This seems like something related to #3039, and I'm not sure if the old behavior was just a bug (that I happened to make use of!).

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(size = 16)) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank())
```

``` r

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank()) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(size = 16))
```

title: geom_bar: some Y axis breaks change the width of the bars/the plot
description: The bars of a barplot where the maximum Y axis label is two digits (eg. 20, 40, 60) will be wider than the bars of a barplot where the maximum Y axis label is three digits (eg. 20, 40, 60, 100), regardless of `geom_bar(size=)` parameter. Does this have a good reason to be the case? This makes aligning barplots vertically quite challenging. ```r # creating an example dataframe scrap <- as.data.frame(cbind(seq(1, 100, 10), seq(1, 100, 10))) colnames(scrap) <- c('x', 'y') # plotting barplot without setting breaks (i.e. will automatically put a break at 100) plot_nobreaks <- ggplot (data = scrap, aes (x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar (stat = 'identity', size=0.5) + # note that size of the bars is set theme_minimal() + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0, 100)) # plotting barplot with set breaks (i.e. will not put a break at 100) plot_breaks <- ggplot (data = scrap, aes (x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar (stat = 'identity', size=0.5) + # note that size of the bars is set theme_minimal() + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0, 100)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(20, 40, 60)) # exporting ggsave('nobreaks.pdf', plot=plot_nobreaks, width=50, height=50, unit='mm') ggsave('breaks.pdf', plot=plot_breaks, width=50, height=50, unit='mm') ``` Now, here is how the two plots look aligned in Illustrator. Notice how the width of the bars is inconsistent, even though `geom_bar(size=)` was set. This makes it very difficult to align barplots vertically, even when they have the same number of bars.

title: Feature request: more lenient check_nondata_cols
description:
Currently data.frame columns are dropped when they don't satisfy the checks of `check_nondata_cols` which looks like the following:

```
check_nondata_cols <- function(x) {
  idx <- (vapply(x, function(x) is.null(x) || rlang::is_vector(x), logical(1)))
  names(x)[which(!idx)]
}
````

The reason I would like it to be more lenient is such that vector-like columns which technically aren't vectors could be accepted, specifically for the virtual `S4Vectors::Vector-class` (and non-virtual classes containing this). This would open up channels to have Bioconductor work with ggplot2 more naturally, provided some extra infrastructure is implemented at the scale/coordinate level (which could befit a ggplot extention package).

I would propose to change `check_nondata_cols` to the following:

```
check_nondata_cols <- function(x) {
  idx <- (vapply(x, function(x) is.null(x) || rlang::is_vector(x) || inherits(x, "Vector"), logical(1)))
  names(x)[which(!idx)]
}
```

Thanks you for reading and considering!

title: Can't set theme(axis.title.x) after theme_void()
More configurable continuous colorscale defaults
description:
`scale_[fill/colour]_[continuous/binned]` have a `type` argument which provides an entrypoint for customizing the scale's default. Currently, `type` only supports `gradient` and `viridis`. It seems reasonable that it could also support an arbitrary function, which would make the default much more configurable. For example:

```r
library(ggplot2)
scale_colour_custom <- function(...) {
  scale_colour_gradient(..., low = "white", high = "green")
}
options(ggplot2.continuous.colour = scale_colour_custom)
qplot(1:10, 1:10, color = 1:10)
```

title: Improvements to qualitative color scaling
description:
`scale_[fill/color]_discrete` currently default to `scale_[fill/color]_hue`. While this is a great default when there are a large number of levels to encode, it's not a great default there are just a few (i.e., it's not colour-blind safe or aesthetically pleasing compared to carefully chosen qualitative palettes like colorbrewer or [Okabe-Ito](https://jfly.uni-koeln.de/color/)). In the event there isn't already a "blessed" ggplot2 scale (e.g., `scale_colour_brewer()`), the usual way to override the default is with a custom qualitative colorscale is to use `scale_[fill/color]_manual()`, but this also isn't ideal for situations where you don't want to make any assumptions about the number of levels to encode (i.e.,  `scale_[fill/color]_manual()` errors if there are more levels than color codes).

I'd like to propose that `scale_[fill/color]_discrete` gain a new argument, say `codes`, that would accept a vector of color codes. In the event `codes` is longer than the number of levels to encode, it would effectively be `scale_[fill/color]_manual`; otherwise, it would effectively be `scale_[fill/color]_hue`. Moreover, I think it would make sense for `codes` to default to something sensible like Okabe-Ito.

It seems the implementation for this would be relatively straight-forward ([see here](https://github.com/cpsievert/ggplot2/commit/bafa5361eb602bdee2cdfcfb97661d4eb9979bef) for a proof-of-concept). If there's interest in pursuing this idea, I'd be happy to start a PR.

title: Change default for bw arg of stat_density() and stat_ydensity()
description:
In the [`?density`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/topics/density) help page, the description for the `bw` argument states:

> The default, `"nrd0"`, has remained the default for historical and compatibility reasons, rather than as a general recommendation, where e.g., `"SJ"` would rather fit, see also Venables and Ripley (2002).

`stat_density()` and `stat_ydensity()` use `density()`'s default of `"nrd0"`. Since ggplot2's philosophy is to provide the "best" default wherever possible, it seems like a good idea to change the default for these functions to `bw = "SJ"`.

I'm not an expert in KDE algorithms, so I can't verify if the claim in the `?density` page is true or not, but I thought it worth opening up the discussion.

If you decide to change the default for those functions, it also needs changing in the `compute_group()` and `compute_density()` methods of the `StatDensity` and `StatYdensity` ggproto objects.

title: Clarify the current status of fortify()
description:
(Originally commented at https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/3802#issuecomment-583852613)

In my understanding, there are 2 purposes of `fortify()`.

1. User-facing utility to convert an object to data.frame, which otherwise the users don't know how to.
2. API for developers that let the custom objects handled nicely in the internal of ggplot2 by tweaking the object at the very first stage.

For purpose 1, ggplot2 now provides 2 types of methods, both of which are becoming less important:

* Convert model objects, which is superseded broom package. In addition, ggfortify covers much wider range of objects.
* Convert geospatial objects (of sp and maps), which is being superseded by sf package and `geom_sf()`.

So, we can and should deprecate (or at least discourage) this type of usages.

On the other hand, for purpose 2, I think `fortify()` still plays a somehow important role. For example, `fortify.tbl()` ensures `tbl` is `collect()`ed. 

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/0137a4d7a25f6ffa3c80cd3e9626a9b0dbc22482/R/fortify.r#L19-L24

### Suggestions

I suggest

- [x] Deprecate `fortify.lm()`, `fortify.glht()`, `fortify.confint.glht()`, `fortify.summary.glht()` and `fortify.cld()`. Replace examples using `broom::augment()` and `broom::tidy()`.
- [x] Deprecate `fortify.<sp-object>` and `fortify.map()` after ensuring `geom_sf()` supersedes `geom_map()`.
- [x] Merge the docs of `fortify()` to `autoplot()` and `autolayer()`, and explain how developers of some custom objects can implements these methods so that the users can use ggplot2 to visualize the objects painlessly (#3721).

Note that this issue is not very high priority as maintaining `fortify()` doesn't seem a heavy burden, at least at the moment. I filed this issue just because it seems we need some place to discuss to avoid confusion. Anyway, I believe it's a right move to encourage users to use broom and sf.

title: ggsave() can't be used with devices taking `file` as argument instead of `filename`
description:
In `ggsave()`, if `device` is specified and the device takes the `file` argument instead of `filename`, ggsave fails with an error: `unused argument (filename = filename)`

```r
library(ggplot)
p <- qplot(cars[[1]], cars[[2]])
ggsave("plot.pdf", p, device = pdf)
```

For the `grDevices` devices that take `file`, ggsave customizes the call to use `file` instead, but this doesn't work for devices from other packages, such as `devEMF::emf` or `Cairo::CairoSVG`.

This appears to be caused by these changes to remove partial argument matching.
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2355
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/2364

It would be nice if ggsave automatically caught this error, then retried with `file` instead of `filename`.

title: Utility function to strip plot_env to keep only items that are used
description:
There is an ongoing problem of ggplot objects saving superfluous items when being written to disc as it saves its calling environment. See:

https://github.com/ropensci/drake/issues/882
https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/2016-July/072925.html
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3619
https://github.com/traversc/qs/issues/31

This comment (https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3619#issuecomment-552340703) suggests that there is nothing that can be done but surely something can be done.

My proposal is to create a utility function that will look through a ggplot function for dependencies then strip the superfluous items out of `plot_env`. Users (or the `drake`/`qs` authors) could run this immediately before saving a ggplot object. Perhaps ggplot could even overwrite `saveRDS` to make this automatic.

It would work something like this:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
save_size_rds <- function (object) {
  tf <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
  on.exit(unlink(tf))
  saveRDS(object, file = tf)
  file.size(tf)
}

normal_ggplot <- function(){
  junk <- rnorm(1e+06)
  input <- iris
  ggplot(input) + 
    geom_point(aes(x = Sepal.Width, y = Sepal.Length))
}

strip_junk_from_environment <- function(ggplot_object){
  # Code here to scan the ggplot call
  used_objects <- c("input")
  
  rm(list = setdiff(names(ggplot_object$plot_env), used_objects), 
     envir = ggplot_object$plot_env)
  ggplot_object
}

save_size_rds(normal_ggplot())
#> [1] 7709833

save_size_rds(strip_junk_from_environment(normal_ggplot()))
#> [1] 30763
```

title: Support units for `offset` argument of `breaks_width()`
description:
The `breaks_width()` function supports units in the `width` argument (e.g. `"3 months"`) but not in the `offset` argument.  This makes it difficult to label time series by fiscal year, e.g. in the UK the fiscal year runs from April to March.

Here is an example of using `breaks_width("1 year", 3)`, which offsets the breaks by 3 days rather than 3 months.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Set up some example monthly data, from April 2015 to March 2018
set.seed(1)
df_months <- seq(as.Date("2015-04-01"), as.Date("2018-03-01"), by = "1 month")
df <- tibble(date = df_months,
             month = month(df_months, label = TRUE),
             value = runif(length(df_months)))
df
# # A tibble: 36 x 3
#    date       month  value
#    <date>     <ord>  <dbl>
#  1 2015-04-01 Apr   0.266
#  2 2015-05-01 May   0.372
#  3 2015-06-01 Jun   0.573
#  4 2015-07-01 Jul   0.908
#  5 2015-08-01 Aug   0.202
#  6 2015-09-01 Sep   0.898
#  7 2015-10-01 Oct   0.945
#  8 2015-11-01 Nov   0.661
#  9 2015-12-01 Dec   0.629
# 10 2016-01-01 Jan   0.0618
# # … with 26 more rows

# Function to create fiscal year labels like "14/15" for the 2014/15 fiscal year
fiscal_year <- function(x) {
  year_number <- lubridate::year(x)
  paste(substr(year_number, 3, 4),
        substr(year_number + 1, 3, 4),
        sep = "/")
}

ggplot(df, aes(date, value, label = month)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text() +
  scale_x_date(labels = fiscal_year, # Use the function to create the labels
               breaks = scales::breaks_width("1 year", offset = 3)) # offset by 3 days
```

![temp1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3522552/72899373-c6fc7080-3d1d-11ea-9411-70e411c618f5.png)

Here is another example, using `breaks_width("1 year", offset = 90)` to offset the breaks by approximately 3 months.  It can never be exactly 3 months, because February is sometimes 28 days and sometimes 29 days.

```r
ggplot(df, aes(date, value, label = month)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text() +
  scale_x_date(labels = fiscal_year, # Use the function to create the labels
               breaks = scales::breaks_width("1 year", offset = 90)) # offset by ~3 months
```

![temp2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3522552/72899691-6b7eb280-3d1e-11ea-895b-a7bbe5c7ebeb.png)

I would propose the syntax `breaks_width("1 year", offset = "3 months")` instead.

title: Unrecognised aesthetic text changes geom_violin grouping
description:
I'm not sure whether this is a bug or a feature but I thought I would point it out anyway. I wanted to create a Plotly graph using `ggplotly()` with custom tooltip text. The way to do this is to set the `text` aesthetic of the ggplot and then specify to use this as the tooltip content when calling `ggplotly()`. My initial approach to this gave the following error:

```
Warning in max(data$density) :
  no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
Error in order(data[["y"]], decreasing = TRUE) : 
  argument 1 is not a vector
```

After some debugging, I realised that setting the `text` aesthetic for my plot (even though this is not recognised by `geom_violin()`) was affecting the `group` aesthetic. Since each value of `text` was unique, I was then trying to create a violin plot for each individual data point which is obviously impossible. Manually specifying the group fixed this but it seems like a strange thing to have to do. Below is a reprex to illustrate my point.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(magrittr)
library(plotly)

example_data <- tibble(
  target = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:2], each = 4)),
  error = runif(8, -1, 1),
  model = factor(rep(c('Model 1', 'Model 2'), times = 4)),
  type = factor(rep(rep(c('Type 1', 'Type 2'), each = 2), times = 2))
)

p <- example_data %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(model, ' (', type, ')')) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = target, y = error, text = label)) +  # only works if we add `group = target`
    geom_violin() +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
    coord_flip()
  
ggplotly(p, tooltip=c('text'))
```

Is this intended behaviour?

title: Feature request: warning for  fill/colour mismatch between aes() and scale...()
description:
Custom legends are sensitive to whether it's a "fill" or "colour" aes. Switching between one and the other with essentially the same data is common. 

Currently, if you forget to change e.g. "colour" to "fill" for your custom legend / colour scheme, ggplot2 ignores your colour scale / custom legend (since the "colour" aes is not specified) and uses the default for the colours / legend (since no information is provided for the "fill" aes).

Below, p1 uses "colour". p2 uses "fill" but the user forgot to update "scale_colour...".  

```
library(ggplot2)
library(RColorBrewer)

p1 = ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, colour = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_colour_brewer(
    name = 'Dude which plant',
    palette = 'Set2'
    )

p2 = ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_colour_brewer(
    name = 'Dude which plant',
    palette = 'Set2'
    )

```

p2 uses default legend and colour scheme without telling the user.

For p2, it might be useful to have a warning saying "you used scale_colour but didn't specify a colour aesthetic." or something like that.

May be related to #2691 / #2239.

title: Inconsistency geom_abline <-> geom_hline for log10 transformation
description:
In case a transformation is applied, the `geom_hline` function takes the intercept in the initial scale, contrary to the other geoms.

```{r examplePlot}
p1 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) + geom_point() + scale_y_log10()
```

The line is created if the intercept is specified in the original (non-transformed) scale in `geom_hline`:
```{r hline-intercept-raw}
p1 + geom_hline(yintercept = 30)
```
![ggplot_hline_intercept-raw](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15339154/72598199-a0020100-390f-11ea-9ef7-bd972d3b6365.png)

Contrary to the `geom_abline` behaviour:
```{r abline-intercept-log10}
p1 + geom_abline(intercept = log10(30), slope = 0)
```
![ggplot_abline_intercept-log10](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15339154/72598174-95476c00-390f-11ea-8f2a-e26a6dbf3ed6.png)

title: Conditional axis.text to change font size and font face creates unwanted margin
description:
This issue was raised yesterday in [this Stackoverflow thread](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/59757585/conditional-change-of-axis-text-font-family-and-font-size-creates-unwanted-gap/59759697#59759697)

This happens not only when using `ifelse()`, but also when manually changing the fonts, e.g. with a named vector. 

In my reprex, I used `coord_flip`, because this was originally shown by the OP in SO, but the same applies without `coord_flip` (albeit not that obvious), and also with `axis.text.x`

The weird thing to me is that this indeed seems only to happen with font size and font family.
``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(iris, aes(Species, Petal.Length)) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(family = ifelse(levels(iris$Species)=="setosa","sans","mono"))) +
  coord_flip()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/VcpXRGB.png)

This also happens without `ifelse`
``` r
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(iris, aes(Species, Petal.Length)) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = c(setosa = 10, virginica = 20, versicolor = 20))) +
  coord_flip()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/jmhDmRA.png)

Adding `margin` helps, but only with specified units:
``` r

ggplot(iris, aes(Species, Petal.Length)) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(family = ifelse(levels(iris$Species)=="setosa","sans","mono"),
                                   margin = margin(r = -2, l = 0.8, unit = 'in'))) +
  coord_flip()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/F9tN6Gb.png)

title: geom_sf() plotting issues with zm geometry
description:
When using sf point data with z or zm geometries (example below only contains z geometry), geom_sf() does not plot the right number of points and the points are located in the incorrect position. This can also lead to perplexing output for various aesthetics (colour included in example). I have tried swapping in different values for the z geometry, and can't quickly discern a pattern to the output.

```r
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)

data <- data.frame(fence = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
                   plot = c(1, 2, 1, 2),
                   treatment = c('control', 'warming', 'control', 'warming'),
```

title: Legends should not use after_scale()ed values
description:
(Originally commented at https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3725#issuecomment-573745316)

Currently, legends reflect the value of `after_scale()`. But, it's not always possible because the expression of `after_scale()` might refer to the variable unavailable at the stage of drawing legends.

For example, I think it is a proper usage of `stage()` to modify scaled `colour`s by combining other aesthetics. But, the following example has two problems:

1. `x` is not available on drawing legends
2. even if we manage to make `x` available, it's not clear what legends should be drawn because the scaled `colour`s are discrete but the `after_scale()`ed values are continuous.

Especially because of the problem 2., I think legends should use the raw scaled values, not the `after_scale()`ed ones.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(88)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(9), y = runif(9), g = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), each = 3))
p <- ggplot(d) +
  geom_point(aes(x, y, colour = stage(g, after_scale = alpha(colour, x))), size = 10)

# fail
p
#> Error in alpha(colour, x): object 'x' not found

# ok
p + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/fHQ3qu7.png)

<sup>Created on 2020-01-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

title: Change in behaviour of manual scales in release candidate
description:
In previous ggplot2 versions, the following was valid:

``` r

df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3)
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, col = factor(x))) +

  scale_colour_manual(values = c("red", "green", "blue", "teal"), breaks = factor(1))
```

title: Mark geom_map() as superseded
description:
I believe we are already in the mood of moving away from `geom_map()` as `geom_sf()` almost superseded it. But, AFAIK, this hasn't been discussed formally so far. Considering we keep developing many codes around `geom_sf()`, I think it's good to mark `geom_map()` soft-deprecated before we face difficulties about the different behaviors between them.

Here I file this issue to discuss what functionalities are missing from `geom_sf()` and its related functions, which might drive people to fall back to `geom_map()`. Any thoughts?

Edit: to be clear, I don't think we can remove `geom_map()` considering its wide spread usages (so I chose the word "soft-deprecated"). Still, I believe we can discourage the usage of `geom_map()` to prevent further confusions by improving `geom_sf()` or providing some alternatives.

title: Theme-related bug in release candidate
description:
I just found an annoying theme-related bug in the release candidate. Not sure if there's still time to fix it. I don't want to risk messing anything else up.

The issue is: When rendering axis labels, any element properties that are not available in `element_text()` will get stripped out in this code block:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/94b5a16ce0b508e4ad67ae1aa504660221830327/R/guides-axis.r#L195-L199

The intent is clearly to work with elements other than `element_text()` (even the comments state this), but in practice it doesn't work.

Reprex:
``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(ggtext)

ggplot(mpg, aes(class)) + 
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    name = "vehicle *class*",
    labels = c("2seater", "*compact*", "midsize", "**minivan**", "pickup", "<sub>sub</sub>compact", "suv")
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title.x = element_markdown(
      linetype = 1, fill = "cornsilk", r = unit(5, "pt"), padding = margin(4, 4, 4, 4)
    ),
    axis.text.x = element_markdown(
      # these properties get stripped
      linetype = 1, fill = "cornsilk", r = unit(5, "pt"), padding = margin(4, 4, 4, 4)
    )
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Lqxa8hM.png)

<sup>Created on 2020-01-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

(The axis tick labels should be enclosed in boxes, just like the axis title. This doesn't happen, because `linetype`, `fill`, etc. get stripped. We can see, though, that the tick labels are rendered as markdown, as requested.)

The problem is that `merge_element()` doesn't keep any properties of the old element that aren't defined in the new element:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/47a06183c4aa1fe8c4d8c68921c148e6fb9e0cdd/R/theme.r#L633-L640

A fix is theoretically simple, I just don't know immediately off the top of my head whether `merge_element()` is behaving incorrectly or whether the code that overrides axis text properties should not use `merge_element()` to combine the elements.

@paleolimbot @thomasp85 Thoughts? Can this be fixed before the release? I'll let it sit for a few hours and then see if I can prepare a PR.

title: better documentation for map related functions?
description:
Here are several comments, They're linked but I'm happy to split them into several issues if it's preferable.

## `geom_map()`

The titles and descriptions of `geom_map` are : 

> Polygons from a reference map
> This is pure annotation, so does not affect position scale

I think this could be clearer, `geom_map` wraps the functionalities of `geom_polygon` to plot maps. the difference being that we provide a reference map through the `map` argument, which takes care of the `x` and `y` aesthetics and allows us to use a more convenient `data` argument.

The description of the `map` argument doesn't mention the `map_data()` function (only an example does), tough it will probably be useful in most cases. Instead it says : 

> Data frame that contains the map coordinates. This will typically be created using fortify() on a  spatial object. It must contain columns x or long, y or lat, and region or id.

## `fortify()`

If we follow to fortify's page we read : 

> Rather than using this function, I now recommend using the broom package, which implements a much wider range of methods. fortify may be deprecated in the future.

It doesn't say what `fortify()` does, says we shouldn't use it anyway, and refers to *broom* without telling us which functions from *broom* we should use (we might think it's just `broom::fortify()` but it doesn't exist).

## `map_data()`

The `map` argument is described as : 

> name of map provided by the maps package. These include maps::county(), maps::france(), maps::italy(), maps::nz(), maps::state(), maps::usa(), maps::world(), maps::world2().

But none of these functions exist.

From examples we can infer that we can use a string such as "state", but the doc seems to hint that we might have more choice than what's in this list, and doesn't tell us where to look. The following argument hints that we can look at `?maps::map`, and there we find that we can infer the list of available maps by looking `help(package='maps')`. I think it is very convoluted and we would benefit from having these maps enumerated in the *ggplot2* doc.

## `coord_map()`

The `projection` argument is forwarded to `mapproj::mapproject` so I understand that you decide to redirect the user there, but again, once there we need to read and scroll to get a list of possible values and it all adds up for a user who "just wants to draw a map", as this one : https://twitter.com/calvinmdewilde/status/1215116524798636032.

So here as well, could we have in *ggplot2*'s doc the list of available projections ?

## a map vignette ?

I believe a vignette focused on maps would be extremely helpful. It could showcase all the projections and a couple cases of maps (world, US). At the moment if I google "ggplot maps" I find mostly references discussing `geom_polygon()` so it seems that `geom_map()` is under-advertised, which I think is unfortunate as map charts are very popular these days.

title: Improve documentation of arguments to `xlim`/`ylim`
description:
Currently, `xlim` and `ylim` are documented together with `lims`.  Thus, the argument `...` to all three functions is described as:

    A name-value pair. The name must be an aesthetic, and the value must be either a length-2 numeric, a character, a factor, or a date/time.

Which is not correct for `xlim`/`ylim`.

Suggested text:

```
For `xlim` and `ylim`: Two numeric values, specifying the left/lower limit and the right/upper limit of the scale. If the larger value comes first, the scale will be reversed. You can leave one value as NA to compute from the range of the data.

For `lims`: A name-value pair. The name must be an aesthetic, and the value must be either a length-2 numeric, a character, a factor, or a date/time.

A numeric value will create a continuous scale. If the larger value comes first, the scale will be reversed. You can leave one value as NA to compute from the range of the data.

A character or factor value will create a discrete scale.

A date-time value will create a continuous date/time scale.
```

Alternative would be to move some of this to the details section.

title: Feature request: type stability in internals, specifically at `unlist()` operations
description:
I was experimenting with having S3 classes based on the `vctrs` package as xy coordinates and extending the scales to support these alternative coordinates (link to [specific use case](https://github.com/teunbrand/ggnomics/issues/32) ). However, I ran into the problem that unlist operations in ggplot code drop relevant attributes and recursively flatten the data. This would be preventable if unlist operations on S3 classes preserve type stability.

One of the pieces of code that I'm struggling with, is updating/training limits, which needs to go through the `scale_apply()` function, wherein [data is unlisted](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/660aad2db2b3495ae0d8040915a40d247133ffc0/R/layout.R#L309-L311).

I've asked a [question on stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/59401011/unlist-behaviour-on-vctr-rcrd-class-objects) to try and get around this from the vctrs end that illustrates my struggle with unlist and `vctrs` classes. I'm also aware that the `vctrs` package has its own [syntax](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/395) for unlist operations.

I think that type stability in general would be a good thing, and would allow for a richer set of ggplot extensions that support `vctrs`-based S3 classes. Therefore, I'd like to propose more type stable equivalents of `unlist()` in the ggplot internals.

title: Lines with transparency not showing when margins are 0 (windows only!)
description:
### Problem description
Lines with transparency do not show when the right margin is 0. Changing the margins to a little over 0 fixes the problem and removing the transparency as well. This seems to happen only on windows (does not reproduce on Ubuntu or macOS).

__NB: I want the margins to be 0 because we are embedding these plots in an application.__

### Reprex
``` r
library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(
  time = rep(1:10, 100), 
  val  = rnorm(1000), 
  id   = rep(1:100, each = 10)
)
ggplot(df, aes(x = time, y = val, group = id)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.1) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin())
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11596858/71161746-3b894e80-224a-11ea-8a57-d02e61122340.png)

### How the plot should look
Changing the right margin to a little over 0 fixes this:
```r
ggplot(df, aes(x = time, y = val, group = id)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.1) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, .1, 0, 0))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11596858/71162086-d550fb80-224a-11ea-96e1-59da787dc8b9.png)

title: Add default theme separately from currently active theme
description:
As discussed here:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2-book/issues/172#issuecomment-567048728

In the current code, the currently active theme set with `theme_set()` etc. acts as the fallback if some element is missing from the theme provided with the plot. This is fine, except in cases where an element is missing from the currently active theme, which may happen when extension packages have added their own elements. A solution can be to add a second-level true default that is not intended to be changed by the user but that extension package could add their own elements to.

This is easy to implement, we just need to figure out the API. Do we need a full second set of functions `theme_set()`, `theme_get()`, `theme_update()`, `theme_replace()`? Or should we just provide the equivalent to `theme_replace()`, e.g. `theme_default_replace()`, which gives extension package authors all they need but will be sufficiently obscure that most users may never see it?

title: scale_*_date shows axis labels outside of limits
description:
When using scale_x_date or scale_y_date to bound a graph, the axis shows axis labels outside of the specified limits.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

l <- expand.grid(z, c("a", "b", "c"))
w <- data.frame(x= l[, 1], t = l[, 2])
w$val <- runif(nrow(w))

ggplot(w, aes(x, val)) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = '1 month', limits = c(as.Date('2008/12/1'), as.Date('2015/12/1'))) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))
```
I see four months of extra axis labels on either side of the plot, despite the fact that I'm specifying my limits at 2008/12/1 and 2015/12/1.

title: Feature request: annotation_logticks() tick marks on the outside
description:
Feature request : an option to put tick marks on the outside of an axis. 

The only tick position supported by annotation_logticks is on the inside of the plot. Sometimes it makes sense to have ticks on the outside (or both). 

There is a hack to work around the issue
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54191372/log-scale-minor-tick-marks-on-outside-of-the-axis-line-with-annotation-logticks
But I think it would be best served by msg it an option on the annotation.

title: position_jitterdodge() failed when attribute `fill` is not specified

``` r
library(ggplot2)

                y = rnorm(12),

                   seed = 10)
ggplot(d, aes(x= x, y = y,
```

title: Enable crs transformations of non-sf layers
description:
The recent issue #3653 prompted me to think a little deeper about mixing sf and non-sf layers. Currently, we can mix these layers if the non-sf layers are properly projected.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)

df <- data.frame(
  lat = 35.76667,
  long = -78.63333,
  name = "Raleigh"
)

# works, crs is longlat
ggplot(df, aes(x = long, y = lat)) +
  geom_sf(data = nc, size = 0.1, fill = "white", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = name), hjust = -.1, vjust = 1.1)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/WojXNRY.png)

``` r
# doesn't work, non-sf layers are not transformed
ggplot(df, aes(x = long, y = lat)) +
  geom_sf(data = nc, size = 0.1, fill = "white", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = name), hjust = -.1, vjust = 1.1) +
  coord_sf(crs = 2264)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/xtsmO0e.png)

``` r
# manually transforming coordinates works
df_trans <- data.frame(
  lat = 734165.51156997,
  long = 2108774.28357641,
  name = "Raleigh"
)

ggplot(df_trans, aes(x = long, y = lat)) +
  geom_sf(data = nc, size = 0.1, fill = "white", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = name), hjust = -.1, vjust = 1.1) +
  coord_sf(crs = 2264)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/UrxqijU.png)

<sup>Created on 2019-12-04 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

It would be great (and make life easier in many ways) if non-sf layers could also be transformed by `coord_sf()`. However, this poses a problem: The sf layers carry information about their crs, and therefore `coord_sf()` can figure out if and how they should be transformed. The non-sf layers don't carry that information, and thus whatever `coord_sf()` does will be wrong in some cases. We could add a `crs` argument to all layers, but that seems ugly since it breaks orthogonality between different parts of the API.

The recent [shader experiments](https://github.com/thomasp85/ggfx) by @thomasp85 got me thinking that maybe the right approach is to modify layers, as he does there. What if we added a `with_sf()` function that can take any ordinary layer and turn it into one whose coordinates get transformed by `coord_sf()`? The API would be something like this:

``` r
ggplot(df, aes(x = long, y = lat)) +
  geom_sf(data = nc, size = 0.1, fill = "white", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  with_sf(geom_point()) +
  with_sf(geom_text(aes(label = name), hjust = -.1, vjust = 1.1)) +
  coord_sf(crs = 2264)
```

We could also enable the following:
``` r
ggplot(df, aes(x = long, y = lat)) +
  geom_sf(data = nc, size = 0.1, fill = "white", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  with_sf(
     geom_point(),
     geom_text(aes(label = name), hjust = -.1, vjust = 1.1)
  ) +
  coord_sf(crs = 2264)
```

title: Annotation_map does not work with coord_sf
description:
When using`coord_sf()` to change the projection of a map, the background layer produced by  `annotation_map()` is not getting reprojected.

First, a plot  without changing projection, using the annotation_map layer to give more context to North Carolina
```r
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  annotation_map(map_data("state"),fill="antiquewhite",colour="darkgrey")+
  geom_sf(data = nc)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4990832/70135829-1a8dfe80-168b-11ea-96d1-6734c4480b6b.png)

However, changing the projection looses the annotation layer, but reprojects the geometry layer
```r
ggplot() +
  annotation_map(map_data("state"),fill="antiquewhite",colour="darkgrey")+
  geom_sf(data = nc)+
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(3347))
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4990832/70135882-32658280-168b-11ea-8042-80ee3df9e653.png)

It looks to me like the annotation_layer is not being reprojected.

title: Implement smart merging of guides so inappropriate key glyphs are omitted
description:
Currently, if two layers have non-overlapping values in an aesthetic and different key glyphs, both glyphs are drawn for all data values, as seen here:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = "points")) +
  geom_smooth(aes(color = "regression line"))
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/7t6QCcH.png)

This is suboptimal, because the line glyph is not sensible for the "points" entry and the point glyph is not sensible for the "regression line" entry. The workaround currently is to use `override.aes()`, but it is cumbersome and requires deep knowledge about the default settings for various key glyphs:

``` r

ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = "points")) +
  geom_smooth(aes(color = "regression line")) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        shape = c(19, NA),
        linetype = c(NA, 1),
        fill = c(NA, "grey60")
      )
    )
  )
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/QhyhKqJ.png)

There should be an option, and maybe made the default, to produce the second outcome whenever appropriate.

I suggest using a warning which informs the user that his/her color mapping has been ignored and default color scale is used.

Here a minimal reprex using the standard example in [documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/scale_manual.html): 
```r
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) +
+   geom_point(aes(colour = factor(cyl)))

```

title: legend.justification not preserved when space is limited
description:
## Issue:
When the legend is wider than the plot, the `legend.justification` option in `theme` is ignored.  Here's a quick example where `legend.justification` is left, but the legend is too long, and extends past the plot in both directions (getting cutoff).

``` r
data(iris)
library(ggplot2)
library(magrittr)

p1 <- iris %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Petal.Length, shape = Species, fill = Petal.Width), shape = 21) + 
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.box = "horizontal",
    # legend.background = element_blank(),
    # legend.margin = margin(3, .5, .5, .5, "lines"),
    # legend.key.height = unit(1, "lines")
  ) + 
  geom_point()
p1
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/9dXIsMB.png)

<sup>Created on 2019-11-19 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

## Backstory
In a single plot, having cut-off legends are problematic no matter which direction they go.  When combining plots using patchwork (https://github.com/thomasp85/patchwork), changing the justification allows long legends to extend into the space of adjoining plots.  For example, this allows guides to be manually combined across plots (apparently guide collection is now implemented in patchwork, but it wasn't present earlier.)   It's also useful when the legend spacing differs from the plot spacing (small plot, large legend mixed with a larger plot with a smaller legend) - a situation I run into when use ggplot2 + patchwork to create heavily annotated heat maps.

title: Needle plots
description:
It seems there is no nice way to create needle plots in ggplot2 whereas it is very easy in classic graphics.  `geom_linerange` can work but seems too involved and non-obvious.  A `geom_needle` wrapper around `geom_linerange` would be nice.

```
x <- 1:6
y <- x * c(1, -1)

plot(y ~ x, type = "h")

ggplot(data.frame(x, y), aes(x = x, ymax=pmax(0, y), ymin = pmin(0, y))) + 
  geom_linerange()
```

title: Incorrect documentation for stat_density's trim paramater
description:
The docs currently read:

> This parameter only matters if you are displaying multiple densities in one plot. If FALSE, the default, each density is computed on the full range of the data. If TRUE, each density is computed over the range of that group: this typically means the estimated x values will not line-up, and hence you won't be able to stack density values.

The remark about this only mattering with multiple groups is only true if one does not adjust the limits. Example:

```
r <- rnorm(100)
ggplot() + geom_density(aes(r), trim = FALSE) + xlim(-4, 4),
ggplot() + geom_density(aes(r), trim = TRUE) + xlim(-4, 4)
```

![Rplot01](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15309336/68966000-f4fb8c80-0791-11ea-87c7-71ffd7e3e11a.png)

First encountered [on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58881949/smooth-kernell-density-graph/58882610#58882610).

title: Geom_dotplot dots overlap when 'fill' in 'aes'
description:
When using 'geom_dotplot' whether 'fill' is used in the 'aes' function or not also causes the dots to overlap or not.  This previously appeared in a stackexchange question a few years back but I didn't see that anyone mentioned it was a bug or not.  The behaviour doesn't seem correct to me as I wouldn't expect placing 'fill' in the 'aes' function should affect the layout of the dots.

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38477616/overlapping-points-when-using-fill-aesthetic-in-ggplot2-geom-dotplot-in-r/38479399

I've copied the code from the link above.  I noticed this because I moved 'fill' from outside of the 'aes' into the 'aes' when I decided I wanted the colour to change depending on another attribute.

``` r
library("ggplot2")

n <- 200
x <- data.frame(x = sample(x = letters[1:3], size = n, replace = TRUE),
                y = rnorm(n = n, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                a = sample(x = letters[4:5], size = n, replace = TRUE))

p1 <- ggplot(x, aes(x = x, y = y))
p1 <- p1 + geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")
p2 <- ggplot(x, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = a))
p2 <- p2 + geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")
```

title: plot_env can cause duplicated serialization of ggplot data
description:
Here is an example:

Case 1: saving a ggplot from global
```r
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(1e6))
g <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x)) + geom_density()
saveRDS(g, "/tmp/temp.rds", compress=F)
file.info("/tmp/temp.rds")$size
[1] 8244327
```
Case 2: saving a ggplot from within a function
```r
myplotfun <- function() {
  set.seed(1)
  df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(1e6))
  g <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x)) + geom_density()
  return(g)
}
g <- myplotfun()

saveRDS(g, "/tmp/temp.rds", compress=F)
file.info("/tmp/temp.rds")$size
[1] 24253766
```

In one case, I generate a ggplot from the global environment.  In the second case, I generate the same ggplot but from within my custom plot function.  I then save both these plots to disk and compare the size.  The plot from within the function is 3x the size on disk.  

This is caused by `plot_env`.  If an environment is not a special case (e.g. global), R saves everything within the environment, which could include the original data.frame as well as the ggplot object itself (and therefore, everything in it).

title: position_dodge() doesn't properly dodge segments
description:
See related discussion on [SO.](https://stackoverflow.com/q/58761704/4975218) `position_dodge()` doesn't dodge the `xend` aesthetic and as a consequence segments can't be dodged. In the reprex below, the desired effect is to connect the points of identical color within each group.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1234)

df <- tibble(
    group = rep(letters[1:3], each = 2),
    subgroup = rep(c("A", "B"), 3)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    start = rpois(6, 10),
    end = start + rpois(6, 3)
  )

ggplot(df) +
  geom_point(
    aes(group, start, color = subgroup),
    position = position_dodge(width = 1)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(group, end, color = subgroup),
    position = position_dodge(width = 1)
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = group, xend = group, y = start, yend = end, color = subgroup),
    position = position_dodge(width = 1)
  ) +
  coord_flip()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/cYpd5NJ.png)

<sup>Created on 2019-11-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

title: coord_flip() reverses discrete axis scale direction
description: `coord_flip()` causes what was going left to right on the x-axis to go bottom to top on the now y-axis.  Since we (most of us) read left to right and top down, this behavior is unexpected and unwanted.

title: Faceted histogram displaying NAs when using plotly.
description:
---
I couldn't find an issue (Open or otherwise), so, blatantly pasting [this unanswered question on StackExchange](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51585680/why-does-hover-text-not-work-with-ggplotly-geom-histogram-and-facet-grid), and including a potentially related plotly issue below:

"When using facet_grid() in both rows and columns, with a histogram in ggplotly, the x-axis values turn up as NA in the hover text. This doesn't happen if the faceting is only over rows, only over columns, or if the geom is different e.g. geom_point(). Am I doing something wrong?"

This might be related to [this plotly issue](https://github.com/ropensci/plotly/issues/1526).

Reprex below, also from the StackExchange post.
```r
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
data(iris)


ggplotly(
  ggplot(data = iris,
         aes(x = Petal.Length))+
    geom_histogram()+
    facet_grid(Species~round(Sepal.Length))
)
```
Result:
