title: Ordering of label placement with `geom_text()` depends on whether or not a group aesthetic is set
description:
When creating a stacked bar chart and the `fill` argument is not placed in the initial ggplot call, but in the `aes` of `geom_bar`, the label order of `geom_text` is displayed in reverse order. This behavior can be prevented, when adding `fill` to the `aes` of `geom_text`, however, this produces a warning saying ...

> Ignoring unknown aesthetics: fill

... which is not really correct, since this unknown aesthetics still has some effect on the final plot.

I posted this on [SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58667035/reverse-label-ordering-when-passing-variable-in-geom-baraes-instead-of-ggplo/58674126#58674126) and Claus Wilke found out that the issue is related to grouping. Once the fill variable is added to `geom_text(... group = ...)` labels are displayed in correct order.

I see two possible issues here:

1. Is the reverse label order intended, when calling `fill` in the `aes` of `geom_bar` (and without adding the fill variable to `group` in `geom_text`)? Why is the default labeling in reverse order?
2. Might the warning when providing `fill` to `aes` in `geom_bar` be misleading, since it still has an effect on the plot?

 
A short example:
```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# some toy data
data <- tibble(Category = c("Baseball",
                            "Basketball",
                            "Football",
                            "Hockey"),
               n = c(45,10,25,20)) 

  # fill is provided to the initial ggplot call - labels are in correct order
  ggplot(data, aes (x="", y = n, fill = Category)) +
    geom_bar(width = 1, stat = "identity") +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste(n, "%")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5))

   # fill is provided to geom_bar - labels are in reverse order
  ggplot(data, aes (x="", y = n)) +
    geom_bar(aes(fill = Category), width = 1, stat = "identity") +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste(n, "%")),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5))

  # fill is provided to aes in geom_text - yields warning, but labels are in correct order
  ggplot(data, aes (x="", y = n)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Category), width = 1, stat = "identity") +
  geom_text(aes(fill = Category, label = paste(n, "%")),
          position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5))
  #> Warning: Ignoring unknown aesthetics: fill

  # fill variable is provided to group in geom_text - labels are in correct order
  ggplot(data, aes (x="", y = n)) +
    geom_bar(aes(fill = Category), width = 1, stat = "identity") +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste(n, "%"), group = Category),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5))

```

title: Allow PositionStack to specify the directions on negatives and positives seperately
description:
Context: I need this to finish https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/3529#issuecomment-542493052

`PositionStack` allows to flip the stacking direction by `reverse` parameter, but it forces the data on the positive side and on the negative side have the same direction.

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/528a3740e60520194e3bf4546a5b93e19e37676b/R/position-stack.r#L191-L204

However, it's not a rare case we want to stack them in the opposite direction (i.e. reverse the direction only on the negative side) to draw data properly. `geom_area()` is the very example for this. I wonder if `PositionStack` can accept these.

For the interface, I don't come up with a nice idea yet, but it would be something like:

``` r
geom_area(
  position = position_stack(reverse = c(positive = FALSE, positive = TRUE))
)
```

or

``` r
geom_area(
  position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE, mirrored = TRUE)
)
```

title: Small grammar error in error messages
description:
As error messages are parametrised, some end up having a grammatical error:

```r
theme(axis.line.x = "wrong!")
#> Error in (function (el, elname)  : 
#>   Element axis.line.x must be a element_line object.
```

Should be: *Element axis.line.x must be **an** element_line object*. This could be solved by checking the first character after the ' a ', although it's dependent on the sound, not the vowel itself, and it would go wrong e.g. here:

```r
theme(legend.spacing.x = "wrong!")
#> Error in (function (el, elname)  : 
#>   Element legend.spacing.x must be a unit object.
```
... which is of course already correct.

Maybe then only check for `^(a|e|i|o)`? Or perhaps change to:
```
Element {...} must be an object of type {...}.
```

title: Missing elements in theme definitions
description:
All themes miss some elements in their definitions (i.e., elements are implicitly set to `NULL` rather than explicitly set to `NULL`). I think all themes provided by ggplot2 should explicitly define all elements. This will become more important if we want to allow extensible themes (#2540, #2784), because we'll have to distinguish between elements a theme knows about but wants to be `NULL` and elements a theme doesn't know about that need to be filled in from the theme defaults. Missing element definitions also have led to unexpected problems in the past, e.g. #2724.

Elements that I notice are missing:
- In all themes: some of `panel.grid`, `panel.grid.major`, `panel.grid.minor`, `panel.grid.major.x`, `panel.grid.minor.x`, `panel.grid.major.y`, `panel.grid.minor.y`
- In `theme_void()`: Too many to list, including parts of `axis.*`, `legend.*`, `panel.*`, `strip.*`, `plot.background`.


As an aside, we should recommend as a general practice to external theme developers that they always start with an existing ggplot2 theme and then just modify the parts they want to change, just like we do in most cases:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/6f5ffea70e80ce3aa076fb9da8a6b0ec7ebfbc51/R/theme-defaults.r#L247-L267

title: Incorrect tick positions of the secondary axis
description:
While building a derivative of `facet_wrap`, I stacked several plots, produced from `mtcars` data set, and noticed, that, with `sec.axis` set, top axis ticks of the bottom plot do not **exactly** align with the bottom ticks of the top plot. (See figures below).

![1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8782986/67085951-7c140f80-f1a8-11e9-8045-e6b1eebd1ef4.png)

And a zoomed-in version.

![2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8782986/67085952-7f0f0000-f1a8-11e9-9523-14a0ab64722d.png)

The issue does not seem to be related to any of my modifications and can be easily reproduced in base `ggplot2`. 
In the reprex I build a simple plot with a secondary x axis, then check grobs of each axis and retrieve the `x` coord of `polyLine` grob. The difference, while small, is clearly seen. 

``` r

library(ggplot2, quietly = TRUE, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dplyr, quietly = TRUE, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(grid, quietly = TRUE, warn.conflicts = FALSE)


# Simple plot with secondary, duplicated, x-axis
ggplot(mtcars, aes(hp, mpg)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_continuous(sec.axis = dup_axis()) -> plt

# Converting to gtable to get each grob
plt %>% ggplot_build %>% ggplot_gtable -> tbl
tbl$layout %>% mutate(rowid = 1:n()) -> layout
# Indices of grobs
top_ind <- layout %>% filter(name == "axis-t") %>% pull(rowid)
bot_ind <- layout %>% filter(name == "axis-b") %>% pull(rowid)

# Axis grob is nested, so go deep until we hit the `polyLine` and its `x` coordinates
tbl$grobs[[top_ind]]$children[[2]]$grobs[[2]]$x -> top_tick_pos
# For another axis, slightly different order
tbl$grobs[[bot_ind]]$children[[2]]$grobs[[1]]$x -> bot_tick_pos
# Compare
print(top_tick_pos)
#> [1] 0.199199199199199native 0.199199199199199native 0.52052052052052native 
#> [4] 0.52052052052052native  0.841841841841842native 0.841841841841842native
print(bot_tick_pos)
#> [1] 0.199646643109541native 0.199646643109541native 0.520880179890781native
#> [4] 0.520880179890781native 0.842113716672021native 0.842113716672021native
diff <- convertX(bot_tick_pos, "native", TRUE) - convertX(top_tick_pos, "native", TRUE)

avg_diff <- sqrt(sum(diff^2) / length(diff))
print(avg_diff)
#> [1] 0.0003667319
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This is reproduced in 115c3960d0fd068f1ca4cfe4650c0e0474aabba5.

title: report a bug in ScaleBinned$get_breaks()
description:
hi, @thomasp85 
Firstly, thank you for your hard works to improve ggplot2!

I think there is a small bug in ScaleBinned$get_breaks(), which is in:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/115c3960d0fd068f1ca4cfe4650c0e0474aabba5/R/scale-.r#L991-L993

As I known, end users has no way to set the value of ScaleBinned$n_bins, which has a NULL value by default.
So, when the breaks is a function provided by users, the function's second parameter will always set to be NULL. 
As a consequence, users cannot get meaningful breaks by set breaks as a function in the scales, such as scale_colour_stepsn.  

This is a simple example:
```
df <- data.frame(
    x = runif(100),
    y = runif(100),
    z = rnorm(100)
)

brk <- function(limits, n_bins) {
    if (is.null(n_bins))
        stop("n_bins is always set to be NULL, users cannot implement useful function for breaks.")
    else cat("users can set the value of n_bins, and get meaningful breaks using the values of limits and n_bins.")
}

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = z)) +
    scale_colour_stepsn(colours = terrain.colors(10), breaks = brk)

# Error in f(...) : 
# n_bins is always set to be NULL, users cannot implement useful function for breaks. 
```

I will  opening a pull request for this bug, please consider it, thanks!

title: stat_summary and rlang lambda expressions
description:
While lambda expressions are allowed in `stat_function()` and a few other places, they aren't in `stat_summary()` type functions. Example below. Note that the args `fun.y`, `fun.ymin`, and `fun.ymax` are in the dev version `fun`, `fun.min`, and `fun.max`.

``` r
library("ggplot2")

df <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3),
  y = c(0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.y = mean,
    fun.ymin = function(y) mean(y) - 1,
    fun.ymax = function(y) mean(y) + 1
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Jd8X3Gf.png)

``` r

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.y = mean,
    fun.ymin = ~ mean(.x) - 1,
    fun.ymax = ~ mean(.x) + 1
  )
#> Warning: Computation failed in `stat_summary()`:
#> 'what' must be a function or character string
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/NN58917.png)

title: Downstream packages that subclass position scales need updating
description:
Only two packages subclassing a position scale were identified in the revdeps because they failed for other reasons...position scale subclasses won't error but will instead hide the subclassed position scale (as previously the only correct `guide` value was `"none"` for  a position scale). These packages need to update `guide` property on position scale subclasses to `waiver()`, or axes will stop being displayed after #3356. This will have to be version dependent, as older code does not ignore position aesthetics when building guides. This is the case with [dint](https://github.com/s-fleck/dint/blob/master/R/scale_date_xx.R#L132) and ggforce ([here](https://github.com/thomasp85/ggforce/blob/master/R/scale-unit.R#L54) and [here](https://github.com/thomasp85/ggforce/blob/master/R/scale-unit.R#L91)).

Transformations in position scales must handle `NA` values after #3398 (which allows `NA` values in coordinate system limits), which is a problem for one package ([dint](https://github.com/s-fleck/dint/blob/174e42775848e9baa11fa2d326e3e55d62a39a29/R/zoo-compat.R#L66)).

title: Downstream packages that use `stat_contour()` need to add isoband to Suggests
description:
Just a note from going through [these revdeps](https://github.com/topepo/ggplot2/blob/b73c5852001d2695cfbf814a2e1a31a00e655bfc/revdep/problems.md) that several packages fail as a result of needing the **isoband** package, which is used for `stat_contour()` and friends. This is new after #3439.

Packages that fail are [bayesAB](https://github.com/FrankPortman/bayesAB/issues/new), [fgeo.plot](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.plot/issues/new), and [gganimate](http://github.com/thomasp85/gganimate/issues/new).

title: Internal CoordCartesian updates break downstream packages
description:
In #3356, the `panel_params` generated by `CoordCartesian` were changed so that `panel_params$x` and `panel_params$y` are scale-like objects. Internally we use `panel_params$x.range` and `panel_params$y.range` (the x and y scale limits), so these were kept for backward compatibility. This change broke a number of downstream packages (e.g., #3436 and multiple reverse dependency failures). We should consider adding back the following elements to ease this transition:

- `x.labels`
- `y.labels`
- `x.major.source`
- `y.major.source`
- `x.minor.source`
- `y.minor.source`

Thoughts on this @thomasp85? Also tagging @cpsievert since he was the first one to notice this change.

This is where one would add these parameters back in:

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/9b667b94df789bed4e4fa2ab16c5d428c8282f6c/R/coord-cartesian-.r#L206-L211

title: Limits with NA cause errors when there is no data
description:
The following should create a blank plot without erroring, but does not after #3426. This should probably be fixed in the same PR as #3448.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(x = numeric(0)), aes(x)) + 
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA))
#> Warning in rep(yes, length.out = len): 'x' is NULL so the result will be
#> NULL
#> Error in ans[ypos] <- rep(yes, length.out = len)[ypos]: replacement has length zero
```

The offending code is here (where `self$limits` is not `NULL` and `self$range$range` is `NULL`):

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/10fa0014d6be81a7e641b8c2c3b48e1df1b7e2f5/R/scale-.r#L439-L452

I think that `Scale$get_limits()` needs another case for limits containing `NA` (or `Scale$is_emtpy()` should return `TRUE` for these limits). @thomasp85 any opinion on either of these solutions?

title: Consistently use element_grob() or element_render() instead of textGrob()
description:
There are a few cases where we call `textGrob()` directly instead of `element_grob()` or `element_render()`. Ideally, we should eliminate all of them. Here is a list of cases I'm currently aware of. There may be more. Reprexes will follow below.

* [x] Axis text for non-standard axis position (e.g., x axis on top)
* [ ] Facet labels when using `facet_wrap()` 
* [ ] Facet labels when using `facet_grid()`

(Checkmark means the issue has been addressed.)

title: Theme element calculation fails for derived element classes
description:
The internal function `calc_element()` assumes that parent and child elements always have exactly the same set of member variables. In the general case, this is not going to be the case, in particular if we want to enable new elements such as `element_markdown()` or `element_textbox()`.

Reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

# like element_rect but with a meaningless dummy argument
element_dummyrect <- function(fill = NULL, colour = NULL, dummy = NULL, size = NULL, 
                              linetype = NULL) {
  structure(
    list(
      fill = fill, colour = colour, dummy = dummy, size = size,
      linetype = linetype, inherit.blank = FALSE
    ),
    class = c("element_dummyrect", "element_rect", "element")
  )
}

ggplot2:::calc_element(
  "panel.background",
  theme(
    rect = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = "black", size = 0.5, linetype = 1),
    panel.background = element_dummyrect(dummy = 5))
)
#> Warning in e1[n] <- e2[n]: number of items to replace is not a multiple of
#> replacement length
#> List of 6
#>  $ fill         : chr "white"
#>  $ colour       : chr "black"
#>  $ dummy        : num 0.5
#>  $ size         : num 1
#>  $ linetype     : NULL
#>  $ inherit.blank: chr "white"
#>  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:3] "element_dummyrect" "element_rect" "element"
```

title: strange interaction of geom_raster and scale_{x,y}_continuous
description:
If one applies scale_{x,y}_continuous to a raster plot but sets the x- or y-axis limits to be smaller than the extent of the data grid, the resulting plotting of the raster cells is distorted, with the cells shrunk in the dimension where the limit is set "too" small. 

```
## Setup simple grid.
dat = expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, by = 1), y = seq(-2, 2, by = 1))
dat$val <- (1:nrow(dat))/nrow(dat)

## Case A: This plots fine without scale_{x,y}_continuous.
ggplot() + geom_raster(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = val)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0)

ggplot() + geom_raster(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = val)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-3.5, 3.5)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-3.5,3.5))
```

title: Jitter doesn't match for geom_point() and geom_line() unless data sorted
description:
When attempting to connect jittered points with lines, the lines do not connect to points unless the dataset has been arranged in a specific way first (`group` then `x` in my example). This happens even if either `group` or `x` is a factor (or both). My suspicion is `geom_line()` jitters based on the alphabetical (or factor level) order of `group` then `x`, while `geom_point()` jitters based on the data order.


``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

df <- data.frame("dimension" = rep(LETTERS[4:1], 2),
                 "value" = c(20, 21, 34, 32,
                             20, 21, 36, 29),
                 "time" = c(rep("Second", 4), rep("First", 4)))
df
#>   dimension value   time
#> 1         D    20 Second
#> 2         C    21 Second
#> 3         B    34 Second
#> 4         A    32 Second
#> 5         D    20  First
#> 6         C    21  First
#> 7         B    36  First
#> 8         A    29  First

# The lines do not connect with the points
ggplot(data = df,
       aes(x = dimension, y = value, group = time,
           shape = time, linetype = time)) +
  geom_line(position = position_jitter(width = .3, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .3, height = 0, seed = 1))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Rxbg4sT.png)

``` r


# When dataset arranged by group and then x points connect as expected
df_sorted <-
  df %>%
  arrange(time, dimension)

ggplot(data = df_sorted, 
       aes(x = dimension, y = value, group = time,
           shape = time, linetype = time)) +
  geom_line(position = position_jitter(width = .3, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .3, height = 0, seed = 1))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/YWhE9sr.png)

``` r

# Note you can also get matching points when only passing df_sorted to geom_point()
ggplot(data = df, 
       aes(x = dimension, y = value, group = time,
           shape = time, linetype = time)) +
  geom_line(position = position_jitter(width = .3, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_point(data = df_sorted, 
             position = position_jitter(width = .3, height = 0, seed = 1))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/RnGQtDd.png)

title: Suggestion: improve error message on wrong use of scale_x_datetime
description:
The following code yields an error message 
```
date_issues <- tibble(dates = lubridate::ymd(c("2019-09-19", "2019-09-20", "2019-09-21")), values = 1:3)

ggplot(date_issues, aes(x = dates, y = values)) + 
   geom_line() + 
   scale_x_datetime(date_minor_breaks = "1 day")
```
The error is:
```
Error: Invalid input: time_trans works with objects of class POSIXct only
```

The reason is that we are using the wrong scale function. We should be using `scale_x_date` instead of `scale_x_datetime`. 

A "suggestion flavored" error message would help the user understand and fix the issue. E.g.:

```
Error: Invalid input: time_trans works with objects of class POSIXct only. 
   Did you consider using scale_x_date() instead of scale_x_datetime()?
```

title: na.rm have no effect in geom_col with position_stack
description:
Usually `na.rm = TRUE` will hide the warnings of removing NAs. However when using `position_stack` with `geom_col`, the warning cannot be turned off.

```r
df <- data.frame(x = 1:20, value = c(rep(NA, 10), rep(2, 10)))
# this don't have warnings
ggplot(df, aes(x, value)) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE)

# this have warnings
ggplot(df, aes(x, value)) +
  geom_col(na.rm = TRUE)

```

It seemed that the other usage of `remove_missing` in geom_* take the na.rm parameter, but `position_stack` doesn't take it as parameter thus no way to hide the warning. Maybe `position_stack` was supposed to take cleaned data from `geom_col` too.

title: Don't catch errors in Stat computations
description:
Currently any error from a Stat's `compute_*()` method is caught and converted to a warning. This makes debugging difficult as the backtrace is lost and you cannot `recover()` at the correct location. The reason for the design is (according to @hadley) that `stat_smooth()` may fail in some panels but not all and this should not throw an exception but simply not plot the layer in that panel.

This issue is to discuss whether we should move this responsibility down to each Stat and allow errors to bubble up in the expected way. I am (as may be clear) in favour of letting Stats fail clearly by default, but the change may very well be breaking in unexpected ways that we need to consider.

title: Bug in `geom_vline` when passing an object of class `Date` as `xintercept`
description:
With an existing ggplot object, I want to add an vline for the center of mass for the water year.
```r
      inDF <- GetHydroDF(startDate, endDate)
      plotH <- plotHydrograph_HYYear(inDF)
      if( input$ShowCenterofMass ){
```

I get a very strange error.  It returns returns:

```
Warning: Error in as.Date.numeric: 'origin' must be supplied
```

title: Feature request: compressed TIFF output from ggsave()
description:
Some publications set maximum file sizes. The function ggsave() generates uncompressed TIFF files. Compression can achieve a huge reduction in TIFF file sizes.
Example: ggsave(filename="Fig3.tiff", scale=1, width=80, height=60, units="mm", dpi=300)
  The output file size for this simple black and white geom_boxplot() is 1959 KB.
  I opened this TIFF file in Photoshop and then resaved it with LZW compression.
  The compressed file size is 88 KB.
LZW compression is widely supported and now patent free (see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TIFF and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lempel%E2%80%93Ziv%E2%80%93Welch).
There could be a "compress" argument for ggsave for which the default is appropriate image compression for the particular output. On this point, I wonder if ggsave() is using image compression for PDF and note that image compression for JPEG is not user adjustable.

title: ggsave argument order is counter intuitive
description:
The ggsave argument order is "counter intuitive" (when compared to other functions which write files, e.g., `write_csv`. By that I mean the plot and filename arguments).

It's clear to me that this is because `ggsave` was written long ago, without having `%>%` in mind, and perhaps putting filename first was equivalently reasonable.

I personally keep confusing the two. 

I wonder if we can put some smart validation check in `ggsave` which if encounters a ggplot in the first argument and a string (i.e., path) in the second argument will figure out that arguments were specified in reversed order. Perhaps issue a warning but perform the export.
This will make it more compatible with other functions, and with the %>%, as well as backwards compatible.

title: Documentation for plotting bin proportion in geom_histogram
description:
Showing proportions (instead of counts or density) of a bin in a histogram is a common exercise, but this is not documented.  Most stackoverflow suggestions are either conflicting or [outdated](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11766856/normalizing-y-axis-in-histograms-in-r-ggplot-to-proportion). 

The solution below by @clauswilke  in a now-locked thread seems like the best practice. Could this trick as well as the `width` stat be documented in the `geom_histogram` manual and the ggplot website? 

---


``` r
library(ggplot2)

# instead of plotting the count statistic in geom_histogram, 
# plot the proportion of a bin, which is equivalent to the product of the 
# density and the width statistic
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = stat(density*width))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/07ggGsR.png)

<sup>Created on 2019-09-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

> The solution is to use `aes(y = stat(width*density))`. This converts the density back into a percentage. Reprex follows below.

_Originally posted by @clauswilke in https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2499#issuecomment-448788543_

description:

At least, I want `expand = c(0, 0)` to work so that color bars exactly represents the range of color or fill mappings.

The example below shows that range of color bar is wider than the range specified in `limits` argument even if `expand = c(0, 0)` is specified.

@yutannihilation figured out this is caused by https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/047b528c98a5852d058d77c5e188c9637c88c7f0/R/guide-colorbar.r#L336

``` r
x <- c(0, 1)
ggplot2::qplot(x, x, color = x) + 
  ggplot2::scale_color_gradient(breaks = x, limits = x, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  ggplot2::guides( # Just for the visibility
    color = ggplot2::guide_colorbar(
      barheight = grid::unit(1, "npc") - grid::unit(4, "line"),
      ticks.linewidth = 2
    )
  )
```

new geom suggestion: separate lines for upper and lower intervals
description:
I'm wondering if there's room for a new geom that can produce the following graph

```r
library(tidyverse)

# Example data
df <- tibble(y = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1.5, 1.7, 1.8), 
             upper_y = y + 0.2, 
             lower_y = y - 0.2,
             year = -4:4)

p <- ggplot(df, aes(year, y)) + geom_line()

# geom_errorline would simplify this
p + 
  geom_line(aes(y = upper_y), linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lower_y), linetype = 2)

```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15363607/63652678-e7a1a980-c730-11e9-833a-4a83162ca4fc.png)

So instead of having to use `geom_line` twice, you could instead do

```r
ggplot(df, aes(year, y, ymax = upper_y, ymin = lower_y)) + geom_errorline()

```

and this would fit more neatly into the idea of mapping the upper and lower intervals to the `ymin` and `ymax` aesthetics. 

I imagine there's a way to achieve that same plot with `geom_ribbon` or `geom_area` but I haven't been able to do so so I'm guessing it wouldn't be straightforward even if there is. 

Here is a prototype I wrote a few years ago: [https://github.com/weiyangtham/econothemes](https://github.com/weiyangtham/econothemes)

Thanks!

title: Can ggplot2 have a Stat that simply summarises data by group?
description:
Every time I encounter a question like #3497, I wonder why ggplot2 doesn't have a `Stat` that simply applies a function by group. Though, in terms of the computational efficiency, it's generally better to have a summarised version of the data before entering ggplot2, it would be handy if we can summarise in ggplot2 especially when we generate plots one after another with different groupings.

I believe `StatSummary` *could have* been implemented to be able to summarise data with other groupings than `c("group", "x")` because the code following seems very general one: 

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/b8420241309c8eea00d7086002c01cdf38a50eac/R/stat-summary.r#L163-L169

But, as the current `make_summary_fun()` expects a function that takes a vector, not a data.frame, it would be difficult to expand `StatSummary` to accept a function that summarises both `x` and `y`. So, to satisfy the need, I feel it might be nice to have some simple geom like below.

I don't see reasons why we shouldn't implement such a Stat. Am I missing something...?

``` r
library(ggplot2)

stat_summary_by_group <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL,
                                  geom = "pointrange", position = "identity",
                                  ...,
                                  fun.data = NULL,
                                  na.rm = FALSE,
                                  show.legend = NA,
                                  inherit.aes = TRUE) {
  layer(
    data = data,
    mapping = mapping,
    stat = StatSummaryByGroup,
    geom = geom,
    position = position,
    show.legend = show.legend,
    inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list(
      fun.data = fun.data,
      na.rm = na.rm,
      ...
    )
  )
}

StatSummaryByGroup <- ggproto("StatSummaryByGroup", Stat,
  compute_group = function(data, scales, fun.data = NULL, na.rm = FALSE) {
    summary <- fun.data(data)
    unique <- ggplot2:::dapply(data, c("group"), ggplot2:::uniquecols)
    unique[names(summary)] <- summary
    unique
  }
)

d <- data.frame(x = c(1:5, 3:7), y = 1:10, g = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 5), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
f <- function(d) {
  data.frame(x = min(d$x), xend = max(d$x), y = mean(d$y), yend = mean(d$y))
}

ggplot(d) +
  geom_point(aes(x, y, colour = g)) +
  stat_summary_by_group(fun.data = f, aes(x, y, xend = stat(xend), yend = stat(yend)), geom = "segment") +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(g))
```

title: Confusing behavior when mapping some variables to aes(size) in geom_point and geom_path
description:
I am not sure if this is WAI, but the behavior of the size argument for geom_point and geom_path is quite different if is placed inside or outside of the `aes()` function, and if the variable mapped to size only contains a single unique value.

This behavior makes it difficult to control the size of plots and lines via functions that map variables to the `geom_point(aes(size = ))` and `geom_path(aes(size = )) `

data for reprex:
```
library(tidyverse)

data <- tibble(
  x = c(1, 1, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8, 8),
  y = c(1, 4, 4, 1, 1, 4, 4, 1),
  type = c( "normal",  "normal",  "normal",  "normal",  "bigger", "bigger", "bigger", "bigger" ))
```

Consider the following function, that takes a base point size and a base line size. Both sizes can be scaled by the arguments scalar_point_size and scalar_line_size. 
If the scalars  = 1, the variable mapped inside `aes()` only has one unique value (that value will be equal to the base value).

```r
plot_with_size <-
  function(.data,
           base_point_size,
           scalar_point_size,
           base_line_size,
           scalar_line_size) {
    .data %>%
      mutate(
        point_size = case_when(
          type == "normal" ~ base_point_size,
          type == "bigger" ~ base_point_size * scalar_point_size
        ),
        
        line_size = case_when(
          type == "normal" ~ base_line_size,
          type == "bigger" ~ base_line_size * scalar_line_size
        )
      ) %>%
      ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
      geom_point(aes(size = point_size)) +
      geom_path(aes(size = line_size), color = "red", alpha = 0.5) +
      ggtitle(
        paste(
          "base_point_size =",
          base_point_size,
          "   scalar_point_size =",
          scalar_point_size,
          "   base_line_size =",
          base_line_size,
          "   scalar_line_size =",
          scalar_line_size
        )
      ) +
      theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"))
  }
```

It works as intended when the variables mapped to `aes(size = )` have more than one unique value:
```
data %>%
  plot_with_size(
    base_point_size = 1,
    scalar_point_size = 2,
    base_line_size = 1,
    scalar_line_size = 2
  )
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40394828/63626042-d9a13b00-c601-11e9-9291-5c7ce124f32f.png)

Changing  `scalar_line_size =1` causes the line size argument to only have one unique value. It still works as intended.
```
data %>%
  plot_with_size(
    base_point_size = 1,
    scalar_point_size = 2,
    base_line_size = 1,
    scalar_line_size = 1
  )
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40394828/63626279-ba56dd80-c602-11e9-804b-6bd7e6d0be54.png)

Now comes the confusing part. If we also change `scalar_point_size = 1` the lines in geom_path double in size. Please note that the values mapped to geom_path() are the same as before.
```
data %>%
  plot_with_size(
    base_point_size = 1,
    scalar_point_size = 1,
    base_line_size = 1,
    scalar_line_size = 1
  )
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40394828/63626382-26d1dc80-c603-11e9-9457-f7382a245abe.png)

Is this behavior working as intended? 

Finally, having worked around with various settings and attempts to solve the above I have noticed that the size arguments behave differently wheater they are placed inside or outside of the aes(). Again, I am not sure if this is WAI, but the way it works now is quite confusing to me at least.
Please consider the following plot. The titles contain the settings used to produce them. Code for the plot is below the plot.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40394828/63627099-4f0f0a80-c606-11e9-91cc-ebbdc9a5da77.png)

```
library(patchwork)
base_plot <- data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y))

base_plot+
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_path(size = 1,
            color = "red",
            alpha = 0.5)+
  ggtitle("geom_point(size = 1)+ geom_path(size = 1)")+

base_plot+
  geom_point(aes(size = 1)) +
  geom_path(size = 1,
            color = "red",
            alpha = 0.5)+
  ggtitle("geom_point(aes(size = 1))+ geom_path(size = 1)")+

base_plot+
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_path(aes(size = 1), color = "red", alpha = 0.5)+
  ggtitle("geom_point(size = 1)+ geom_path(aes(size = 1))")+

base_plot+
  geom_point(aes(size = 1)) +
  geom_path(aes(size = 1),
            color = "red",
            alpha = 0.5)+
  ggtitle("geom_point(aes(size = 1))+ geom_path(aes(size = 1))")
```

title: Feature Request - Wouldn't it be cool if ggplot2 recognized `dplyr::group_by()`?
description:
I've got a feature request to give ggplot2 the ability to recognize `dplyr::group_by()`.

```r
    library(tidyverse)
    library(lubridate)
    library(stringr)
    df <- 
      tibble(Date = as.Date(0:364, origin = "2017-07-01"), Value = rnorm(365)) %>% 
      mutate(Year = str_sub(Date, 1, 4), 
             MoFloor = floor_date(Date, unit = "month")) %>% 
      group_by(Year, MoFloor) %>% 
      mutate(MoAvgValue = mean(Value)) %>% 
      ungroup() %>% 
      group_by(Year) %>% 
      mutate(MinMoFloor = min(MoFloor),
             MaxMoFloor = max(MoFloor),
             YearAvgValue = mean(MoAvgValue))
```    

Let's first plot the data frame above.
   
```r 
    ggplot(df, aes(MoFloor, MoAvgValue, group = Year)) + 
      facet_grid(~Year, scale = "free_x", space = "free_x") + 
      geom_point()
```

[![plot1][1]][1]

In my call to the `facet_grid()` function I added the arguments `scale = "free_x"` and `space = "free_x"` to get rid of empty white space on the plots.

When I go ahead and add `geom_segment()`s based on `group_by()`d data, the `scale = "free_x"` and `space = "free_x"` arguments are negated. The empty white space reappears!

```r
    ggplot(df, aes(MoFloor, MoAvgValue, group = Year)) + 
      facet_grid(~Year, scale = "free_x", space = "free_x") + 
      geom_point() + 
      geom_segment(data = df, 
                   aes(x = min(MinMoFloor), 
                       y = YearAvgValue, 
                       xend = max(MaxMoFloor), 
                       yend = YearAvgValue))
```

[![plot2][2]][2]

My `df` data frame is grouped by `Year`. The `geom_segment()` function does not recognize this when I enter (for example) the `x = min(MinMoFloor)` argument. `geom_segment()` is pulling the `min(MinMoFloor)` from the global column, instead of the grouped column. 

I know I could substitute a modified `geom_hline()` function instead of `geom_segment()` for a working solution, but my lines are sometimes diagonal. And sometimes I'll have 50+ of these facet panels in my visualization, so defining the values manually is not practical either.

Thanks for considering this feature.

  [2]: https://i.stack.imgur.com/gETPE.png

title: geom_boxplot using both color and (group or discrete x) aeses
description:
I have described the problem on StackOverflow [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57485779/is-it-possible-to-ggplot-grouped-partial-boxplots-w-o-facets-w-a-single-geom-b) too, where [Calum You](https://stackoverflow.com/users/7028459/calum-you) purposes a workaround for that.

The main problem is related to create a "running grid" of boxplots, without using facets, to track the distributions of some measure (y) in a time-dependent graph (x) on two (or more) characteristics (color) considering a fixed amount of time-points (or all the time points within a given window of time) in each boxplot (cut).

While filtering for a single characteristic, it works well (and maintain the right color!), overall it provides strange results.

There are some issues here between group and color interaction, or the workaround represents the correct approach?

``` r
library(tidyverse)

bar <- tibble(
    time = 1:100,
    group = sample(c("a", "b"), 100, replace = TRUE) %>% as.factor()
) %>% 
    group_by(group) %>% 
    mutate(
        value = rnorm(n()) + 10 * as.integer(group),
        cut = 12.5 * ((time - 1)  %/% 25), # modified this to prevent an extra boxplot
        group_cut = str_c(group, cut)
    ) %>%
    ungroup()


# my natural way of thinking the solution
bar %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = value, color = group)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
    geom_boxplot(aes(x = cut))
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/UhGUOz0.png)

``` r


# using position = "identity"
bar %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = value, color = group)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
    geom_boxplot(aes(x = cut), position = "identity")
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/FBerGPD.png)

``` r


# using group instead of x
bar %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = value, color = group)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
    geom_boxplot(aes(group = cut))
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/mN7qoPG.png)

``` r


# my solution
bar %>%   
ggplot(aes(x = time, y = value, color = group)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
    geom_boxplot(data = filter(bar, group == "a"), aes(group = cut)) +
    geom_boxplot(data = filter(bar, group == "b"), aes(group = cut))
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/vKfN13x.png)

``` r


# workaround by https://stackoverflow.com/users/7028459/calum-you

bar %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y  = value, colour = group)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(group = group_cut), position = "identity")
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula 'y ~ x'
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/BUHjsO5.png)

title: Issue with documentation of stat_summary(_bin) and question about default x-axis position
description:
I recently [tweeted](https://twitter.com/Japhir/status/1158758152113983488) about an issue with `stat_summary` documentation, and here's the issue for it. 

I intended to use `stat_summary_bin()` with custom breaks with gaps in between on the x-axis. I've tried to illustrate below. From the documentation it was not clear whether this was possible/desired, mostly because I didn't understand what kind of function to pass to `binwidth` from the docs. 

Below I'll explain my thinking so that it hopefully highlights the issue with the docs:

I was wondering if I should I try to write a function which is conditional on x-axis values? That sounds like it should be easier to specify with `breaks`. Also, it looks like the fun.data should operate only on the y-value, and doesn't get passed the x-value. I also tried to define a new group variable using `cut` or `findInterval` and set binwidth, but this still draws lines (most right one) that span the outside of the x-axis values. 

So then, when looking at `breaks`, the docs say that they overrules `center` and `boundary`, but neither of those are defined in these docs and don't point to references elsewhere.

In the end I created a new tibble with the summarized values for plotting.

```
data:            ...              . ... ...        ...               .... .......... . ...

desired summary: |*|              |___*___|        |*|               |_________*_________|

actual summary:  |---*---| |---------*--------| |-----*-----| |-----------*--------------|
```

I created below reprex.
- black dashed lines represent the desired breaks
- red dotted l ines highlight the min/max of each of the intervals
- black pointranges show the default method of doing this
- black vertical lines highlight the desired x-axis value to plot this pointrange at
- red pointranges highlight my grouping attempt, which still draws outside the actual x-axis limits.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(tibble)

desired_breaks <- c(0, 40, 90)

dat <- tibble(x = c(1:3, 5:10, 15:23, 25:27, 50:86),
              y = rnorm(length(x), mean = seq(1, 10, length.out = length(x)), sd = 6),
              grp = findInterval(x, vec = desired_breaks))

ggplot(dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  stat_summary_bin(geom = "pointrange", fun.data = "mean_cl_normal",
                   breaks = desired_breaks) +
  stat_summary_bin(aes(group = grp), geom = "pointrange",
                   fun.data = "mean_cl_normal",
                   binwidth = 6,
                   colour = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = desired_breaks, linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(1, 27, 50, 86),
             colour = "red",
             linetype = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c((27 - 1) / 2 + 1, (86 - 50) / 2 + 50))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/yRUYXxi.png)

<sup>Created on 2019-08-11 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This made me think that the default option of plotting these summary values between the specified breaks is actually undesired, since it should probably be drawn in the middle (or median) of the range of x-values. I.e. if you specify breaks like `c(0, 50, 100)` but your data only goes up to 60, your last summary point will be drawn all the way on the right of the data.

Thanks and kind regards

may be related to #3297

title: Jitterdodge and text= aesthetic
description:
The ggplotly package uses the text= aesthetic to control the label that shows up when hovering. Normally this works fine! But I've stumbled upon one case it doesn't: combining with position_jitterdodge, at which point the dodge stops working and it becomes a single-column jitter. ```

```
  geom_point(position=position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.5), alpha=0.5)
```

title: print method for scales does not handle function as limits argument well
description:
I've found a very minor inconvenience when printing scales. When passing a function to the limits arguments in a `scale_*` , the printing method of the scale throws an error. See reprex below.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
g <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length,
                      colour = Petal.Width)) +
  geom_point()

goodprint <- g + scale_colour_continuous(limits = range(iris$Petal.Width))
badprint <- g + scale_colour_continuous(limits = function(lims) {1 * lims})

print(goodprint$scales$scales[[1]])
#> <ScaleContinuous>
#>  Range:  
#>  Limits:  0.1 --  2.5

print(badprint$scales$scales[[1]])
#> <ScaleContinuous>
#>  Range:
#> Error in zero_range(range): x must be length 1 or 2
```

<sup>Created on 2019-08-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

While not really a problem for most applications, it would take only a minor adjustment to the printing function to fix the error. Below you'll find an option for a fix.

```r
scale_print <- function(self, ...) {
  # Same as current
  show_range <- function(x) {
      paste0(formatC(x, digits = 3), collapse = " -- ")
    }
  cat("<", class(self)[[1]], ">\n", sep = "")
  cat(" Range:  ", show_range(self$range$range), "\n", sep = "")
  # Only the following bit is different
  if (is.function(self$limits)) { 
    cat(" Limits: function()\n")
  } else {
    cat(" Limits: ", show_range(self$dimension()), "\n", sep = "")
  }
}

badprint$scales$scales[[1]]$print <- scale_print

print(badprint$scales$scales[[1]])
#> <ScaleContinuous>
#>   Range:  
#>   Limits: function()
```

title: Indexing data.tables and groups defined by strings
description:
I’m using data.table and ggplot and plotting by group (using color = ). When I do this, ggplot creates an index that persists. That is, before I run the ggplot command the data.table does not have an index, and after I run ggplot it does.

This seems to be related to a problem using “color = “ to graph by group when groups are defined by the contents of a string variable. When I do this, sometimes some groups are not graphed, seemingly at random. This can be avoided by changing the group variable to a factor. But, having ggplot create a persistent index seems like it could cause other problems, as well.

title: Continuous fill does not obey fine-grained show.legend settings
description:
If you use fine-grained settings with `show.legend`, the legend for a continuous fill variable is not drawn. E.g. this:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

tribble(
  ~x1, ~y1, ~x2, ~y2, ~id, ~id_int,
    1,   1,   2,   2, "A",       1,
    2,   2,   3,   3, "B",       2
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(xmin = x1, ymin = y1, xmax = x2, ymax = y2, fill = id_int)) +
  # could also do show.legend = c(size = FALSE) here and get the same
  # result; in both cases I would have expected the fill legend to show up
  geom_rect(show.legend = c(size = FALSE, fill = TRUE))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/zQxkVYL.png)

<sup>Created on 2019-07-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I chose `size` here as an unrelated variable, it could be anything. This problem also happens on geoms other than `rect`, so I don't think it's a problem there.

I would expect output that looks like this:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6345019/62009269-47edfd00-b12b-11e9-9fcb-7a479fedbf51.png)

FWIW, with a discrete variable for the fill, it does work as expected:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

tribble(
  ~x1, ~y1, ~x2, ~y2, ~id, ~id_int,
    1,   1,   2,   2, "A",       1,
    2,   2,   3,   3, "B",       2
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(xmin = x1, ymin = y1, xmax = x2, ymax = y2, fill = id)) +
  # could also do show.legend = c(size = FALSE) here and get the correct result
  geom_rect(show.legend = c(size = FALSE, fill = TRUE))
```

title: draw_key_dotplot : more detailed documentation please (ggplot2 v3.2.0)
description:
---

geom_jitter() with small data points (size=1) results in a legend glyph of the same size and shape. 

I'm trying to use key_glyph = draw_key_dotplot(size=5) to increase the glyph size, but ggplot() complains:

Error in match(x, table, nomatch = 0L) : 
  argument "data" is missing, with no default

```r

points <- data.frame( bc = c (1:3), bpc= c(1:3), cluster=c("red", "green", "blue"))

# works great
ggplot() +
  geom_jitter( data=points, aes(x=bc, y=bpc, fill=cluster), shape=21, size=1)

# fails
ggplot() +
  geom_jitter( data=points, aes(x=bc, y=bpc, fill=cluster), shape=21, size=1, 
               key_glyph=draw_key_dotplot(size=5))

```
The draw_key_* documentation in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggplot2/ggplot2.pdf is unhelpful regarding parameters "data" and "params". Please provide some examples as to how these are supposed to be used.

Thanks, keep up the good work.

title: Allow independent color modification of median in boxplot
description:
I'm looking to have control of the color of the box and median independently in `geom_boxplot()`. This could be beneficial for light background as well as for dark background themes. 

Related questions on stackoverflow have used workarounds that seem somewhat convoluted and case by case.
[For example here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/39231388/r-ggplot-change-grouped-boxplot-median-line).

```r
# data
set.seed(1123)
df <- data.frame(matrix(rnorm(100), ncol=2))
names(df) <- c("one", "two")
```

With base graphics, we can have the plot we are looking for 
```r
# base graphics
boxplot(df, medcol="red")
```

However, we don't have such an easy option to do that in `ggplot2`

```r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(reshape2::melt(df),
       aes(variable, value))+
  geom_boxplot(fatten=3)

# But we have that option for outliers!
ggplot(reshape2::melt(df),
       aes(variable, value))+
  geom_boxplot(fatten=3, outlier.color = "red")
```

Having something like `median.colour` would be great to solve this issue.

title: scale_manual throws unexpected error when na.values given and insufficient values provided
description:
In the help documentation for `scale_manual()`, the values portion states: 

> values    "a set of aesthetic values to map data values to. If this is a named vector, then the values will be matched based on the names. If unnamed, values will be matched in order (usually alphabetical) with the limits of the scale. Any data values that don't match will be given na.value."

Given this definition, I was surprised that an error was still thrown in the following situation: 

For discrete scales, regardless of whether the actual values match, if there are too few values provided, the "Insufficient Values" error is thrown, as in the test below:

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/92d27779e210ce16f441eeec26926b8b045a47a8/tests/testthat/test-scale-manual.r#L38

You could provide a sufficient number of (non-matching) values and avoid the error.

```
df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1:3, z = factor(c("a","b", NA), exclude = NULL))
p <- qplot(x, y, data = df, colour = z)

# Case 1: Insufficient values error (as expected)
ggplot_build(p + scale_colour_manual(values = c("a" = "black")))

# Case 2: Insufficient values error (not as expected)
ggplot_build(p + scale_colour_manual(values = c("a" = "black"), na.value="grey"))

# Case 3: plot with "b" points given na.value (as expected)
ggplot_build(p + scale_colour_manual(values = c("a" = "black", "c" = "white"), na.value="grey"))

```

I was expecting an error if `na.value` was not specified (Case 1). 
I was NOT expecting an error if `na.value` WAS specified (Case 2).  

My thinking being that case 2 and case 3 are doing basically the same thing but Case 3 has some arbitrary extra value(s) added simply to match the number of values.  I'm not sure what was intended, but seems to me that if `na.value` is provided, the number of values given shouldn't really matter because "Any data values that don't match will be given na.value."  

Related to #2428

title: `bquote` didn't work with `coord_polar` + `scale_x_continuous`

However, with color defined, a baseline is added which stretches the stretches to include the range of data across all facets. The ideal behavior would be something similar to `geom_density` with `trim = TRUE`.

``` r
set.seed(9416)
data <- tibble(a = rchisq(1000, df = 3),
               b = rchisq(1000, df = 1),
```

title: Funcational limits on non-position discrete scales refer to non-existent field `trans`
description:
Thanks to #3426 we can now use functional limits on discrete position scales. However, when using them on non-position discrete scales, there is an error:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, col = class)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_discrete(limits = rev)
#> Error in self$trans$transform(self$limits(self$trans$inverse(self$range$range))): attempt to apply non-function
```

The issue is that the default implementation of `Scale$get_limits()` refers to `self$trans`, which isn't defined for discrete scales. One way to fix this is to move the default implementation to `ScaleContinuous` and move the implementation in `ScaleDiscretePosition` that was added in #3426 to `ScaleDiscrete`.

title: Feature Request: Define + operator for aes (i.e. uneval) objects
description:
**Problem & Motivation**

Currently you cannot do something like this
`aes(x = am) + aes(y = vs)`

I think that would be a very nifty feature especially in `shiny` settings, where you want to allow the user to dynamically modify a plot like in the following code:

```
library(shiny)
library(ggplot)

dat <- expand.grid(x     = rnorm(20),
                   shape = c("Circle", "Triangle"),
                   color = c("Red", "Blue"),
                   size  = factor(c("Big", "Small"), c("Small", "Big")))

dat$y <- with(dat, -3 * x + 2 * as.numeric(shape) + 8 * as.numeric(color) + 
                as.numeric(size) + rnorm(160, sd = .3))

ui <- fluidPage(checkboxInput("color", "Plot By Color?"),
                checkboxInput("shape", "Plot By Shape?"),
                plotOutput("plot"))

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    base_plot <- ggplot(dat, aes(x, y))
    
    ## Option 1: size can be set properly, but a lot of branching
    if (input$color) {
      if (input$shape) {
        sm_aes <- aes(size = as.numeric(size), color = color, shape = shape)
      } else {
        sm_aes <- aes(size = as.numeric(size), color = color)
      }
    } else {
      if (input$shape) {
        sm_aes <- aes(size = as.numeric(size), shape = shape)
      } else {
       sm_aes <- aes(size = as.numeric(size)) 
      }
    }
    
    base_plot + geom_point(sm_aes) + geom_smooth(method = "lm")
    
    # ## Option 2: aes_string, I need to transform size upfront
    #
    # dat$size_num <- as.numeric(dat$size)
    # color <- if (input$color) "color"
    # shape <- if (input$shape) "shape"
    # sm_aes <- aes_string(size = "size_num", color = color, shape = shape)
    # base_plot %+% dat + geom_point(sm_aes) + geom_smooth(method = "lm")
    
    # ## Option 3: with +.uneval operator
    # 
    # aes_base <- aes(size = as.numeric(size))
    # aes_color <- if (input$color) aes(color = color)
    # aes_shape <- if (input$shape) aes(shape = shape) 
    # base_plot + geom_point(aes_base + aes_color + aes_shape) + geom_smooth(method = "lm")
   
  })
}
shinyApp(ui, server)
```
Maybe I am overlooking any other obvious solution, but option 1 gets messy with all the if branches, option 2 is cumbersome if you want to transform some of your parameters in the `aes` call. Option 3 on the other hand, combines the shortness of option 2 with the convenience of option 1 when it comes to modifying variables in the `aes` call.

I am not sure whether this problem could be efficiently solved with quosures, so if I am overlooking something here, please let me know.

**Potential Implementation**

`uneval` objects seem to be rather straight forward, thus a `+` operator should not to be too difficult:

```
`+.uneval` <- function (e1, e2) {
  goodClass <- c("uneval", "NULL")
  if (!any(goodClass %in% class(e2))) {
    msg <- paste(sQuote("e2"), "must be of class", paste(sQuote(goodClass), 
                                                         collapse = ","))
    stop(msg)
  }
  dup <- names(e1) %in% names(e2)
  if (any(dup)) {
    duplist <- paste(sQuote(names(e1)[dup]), collapse = ", ")
    msg <- sprintf(ngettext(sum(dup), "element %s occurs in both summands - second one gets precedence", 
                            "elements %s occur in both summands - second one gets precedence"), 
                   duplist)
    warning(msg, domain = NA)
  }
  res <- c(e1[!dup], e2)
  class(res) <- "uneval"
  res
}
```

title: Clarify documentation of breaks function in scale_continuous
description:
This is a documentation clarification request (or perhaps it is a bug report). The documentation for `scale_continuous` says that the `breaks` argument can take "a function that takes the limits as input and returns breaks as output". With some experimentation, I determined that the input is the limits after expansion and _not_ what gets passed to the `limits` argument. If this is the intended behavior (reasonable given that having empty bands with no breaks around the data looks weird), it should probably be clear. My attempt to learn how to contribute on GitHub for the last hour did not get far, but here is my recommended wording: "A function that takes the limits (after expansion as specified by expand) as input and returns breaks as output"

To make it obvious what I mean, 

``` r
library(tidyverse)

# Data
dt = tibble(
  x = 1:6,
  y = rnorm(x)
)

# Function that seems to "take the limits as input and return breaks as output"
BreakFunc = function(lim) seq(lim[1], lim[2], 2)

# I expect the plot to have horizontal axis breaks at seq(0, 7, 2) but it does not
ggplot(dt, aes(x=x, y=y))+
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 7), 
    breaks = BreakFunc)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/lZOlef1.png)


``` r
#  Explicitly setting the expand argument gets the expected plot
ggplot(dt, aes(x=x, y=y))+
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 7), 
    breaks = BreakFunc,
    expand = expand_scale(mult = 0, add = 0))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/ZBBcAbE.png)

title: Feature request: enable making copies of trained position scales
description:
To create plots with marginals, it would be helpful if there was a straightforward method to reliably create copies of trained position scales. I'm wondering whether this is possible or can be made possible after @paleolimbot's refactoring of the position scales.

For example, consider this code, which uses the function `cowplot::axis_canvas()`:
``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)

p1 <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)

p1
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/PxeDPqU.png)

``` r

p2 <- axis_canvas(p1, "x", iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_density()

p2 + theme_grey()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/zLMauY1.png)

``` r

p1 %>% insert_xaxis_grob(p2) %>% ggdraw()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/q5K33aH.png)

I'd want to be able to generate the plot `p2` by writing something like the following:
``` r
p2 <- ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_x_copy(p1)
```
or maybe 
``` r
p2 <- ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_x_copy(ggplot_build(p1))
```
The function `scale_x_copy()` would take all information (type, limits, expansion, labels) about the x position scale from the built object of `p1` and then faithfully reproduce it. Importantly, the scale should not change range or other properties based on the data provided in the second plot.

I'd be happy to implement such a scale myself if somebody can give me some hints about how to best go about it.

title: Create a rational api for legends.
description:
# Feature Request

## Issue
Right now, legends are created in an add-hoc way with mysterious non-intuitive sounding layers like `scale_color_manual`. It is very unclear how to create a legend that refers to a specific element.

For instance, if you have 

```
geom_hline(aes(yintercept=10, color='red', linetype='LABEL'), show.legend=T)
```
You don't automatically get a legend. You can do something like

```
scale_linetype_discrete(name='TITLE', values=c('dashed'))
```

and get a legend with title TITLE and a dashed line. But you can't change the color of the line in the legend this way.

## Proposal
I propose a very declarative API as follows:

1. You create legends with a geom `geom_legend`.
2. It has intuitive parameters:
```
geom_legend(title='TITLE', elements=c(el1, el2, el3), <typesetting>, <outlines>, <fills>, ...)
```
3. Other geom elements have a "name" attribute referred to in the legend "elements" attribute.
4. If a "name" is not provided, then the name of the y component of the aes is used.

Using this API, the code below would produce

* A red line from equation 5 + 1.3*x that has squares at the discrete points
* A green line from equation 25 - 0.7*x that has circles at the discrete points
* A black dotted hline at y-interecept 20
* A blue dashed vline at x-intercept 15
* Legend 1
  * titled "Envelopments"
  * red line with square shape with name Vicissitude
  * green line with circle shape with name Mysteriousness
* Legend 2
  * titled Disparities
  * black dotted line with name Discouraged
  * blue dashed line with name Alternative

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

x = c(0,5, 10, 15, 20)

df = data.frame(
  Deliberation = x,
  Vicissitude = 5 + 1.3*x,
  Mysteriousness = 25 - 0.7*x
)

df %>%
  ggplot() +
  ### Data Lines
  geom_line(aes(x=Deliberation, y=Vicissitude, color='red'), name=) +
  geom_point(aes(x=Deliberation, y=Vicissitude, color='red', shape='square')) +
  geom_line(aes(x=Deliberation, y=Mysteriousness, color='green')) +
  geom_point(aes(x=Deliberation, y=Mysteriousness, color='green', shape='circle')) +

  ### Reference guides
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=20, color='black', linetype='dotted'), show.legend=T, name='Discouraged') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept=15, color='blue', linetype='dashed'), show.legend=T, name="Alternative") +

  ### Legends
  geom_legend(title="Envelopements", elements=c('Vicissitude', 'Mysteriousness')) +
  geom_legend(title="Disparities", elements=c("Discouraged", "Alternative"))
```

This would be super easy to remember and control. Someone reading the code should have no trouble understanding what should be graphed. Changing linetypes, colors, or shapes need only be done in one place that makes total sense.

title: Fix for geom_ribbon()
description:
Hello,
Firstly, thank you for providing the world with the ggplot2 package and broader tidyverse ecosystem of packages. It has revolutionised the way people use R and it is the only method I use now when introducing my new students to the language.
I work in climate science and so have a series of requirements for visuals that are perhaps a bit different than data science more broadly. One of these is the necessity to be able to visualise values that are in excess of a given threshold. One would normally use the geom_ribbon() function to accomplish this, but it is my understanding that this function does not have the capability to allow users to choose to fill in the area only above or below one of the given lines (i.e. ymin or ymax). There are multiple posts on stack overflow etc. about this and the work arounds provided do not create very nice figures. Specifically I mean that the corners of the polygons are not satisfactorily filled in. For this reason I went about creating a fix for this issue. The geom I created is called geom_flame() and may be found in my package heatwaveR, which is on CRAN. I have also written the necessary code to allow this geom to work in an interactive plotly environment.
If it would be deemed appropriate I would be happy for my source code to be included in ggplot2 in part or in full, as necessary. Below please find a reprex highlighting the differences between geom_flame() and geom_ribbon(). I did not include a reprex for use in plotly as I don't think that works in GitHub(?).
All the best,
-Robert Schlegel

```r
# Load libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(heatwaveR)

# Detect the marine heatwaves in a time series

  geom_line(aes(y = temp)) +

# Visualise with geom_flame

  geom_flame() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = thresh), colour = "darkgreen")

# Stick them next to each other
cowplot::plot_grid(ribbon_plot, flame_plot, ncol = 1)
```

title: Support nativeRaster in annotation_raster
description:
`annotation_raster` can be quite slow to display a large image. The current implementation converts the numeric image to text (via `grDevices::as.raster`) which must be converted back to numeric values for actual drawing by `grid::rasterGrob`. Supporting `nativeRaster` removes this round-trip conversion and dramatically speeds rendering.

This reprex uses a modified `annotation_raster_native` to demonstrate the improvement. A `ggplot2` implementation could simply skip the `as.raster` call in `annotation_raster` if the incoming raster object inherits from `nativeRaster`. No changes are needed in `GeomRasterAnn` because `grid::rasterGrob`, which it uses, works with `nativeRaster` objects.

```r
library(ggplot2)

# Image from https://github.com/akoyabio/phenoptrExamples/blob/master/inst/extdata/samples/Set12_20-6plex_%5B14146%2C53503%5D_composite_image.jpg
path = "Set12_20-6plex_[14146,53503]_composite_image.jpg"
image = jpeg::readJPEG(path)
dim(image) # 1400 x 1868

# This takes about 4 seconds to display the plot in RStudio on my computer
print(ggplot() + annotation_raster(image,
                                 xmin=0, xmax=1,
                                 ymin=0, ymax=1))

image2 = jpeg::readJPEG(path, native=TRUE)

# annotation_raster without the grDevices::as.raster conversion
annotation_raster_native <- function(raster, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax,
                              interpolate = FALSE) {
  layer(
    data = ggplot2:::dummy_data(),
    mapping = NULL,
    stat = StatIdentity,
    position = PositionIdentity,
    geom = GeomRasterAnn,
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    params = list(
      raster = raster,
      xmin = xmin,
      xmax = xmax,
      ymin = ymin,
      ymax = ymax,
      interpolate = interpolate
    )
  )
}

# This version takes less than two seconds to display.
print(ggplot() + annotation_raster_native(image2,
                                   xmin=0, xmax=1,
                                   ymin=0, ymax=1))
```

title: `geom_density()` for bounded data
description:
Currently `geom_density()` directly uses `density()` to compute kernel density estimation. Due to its nature, it has "extending property": output density can imply that values outside the range of input data are possible (with default "gaussian" kernel). This is a realistic practical setup, but there are cases when this is not true and data is bounded (for example, when only positive values are possible). It can be a good idea to support kernel density estimation on this type of bounded data with new `bounds` argument of `geom_density()`.

In my opinion, one of the methods most easiest to implement, understand, and teach, is "reflection" method. There is one possible description on [this page](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March02/Silverman/Silver2_10.html). Basically, boundary correction is done by doing "standard" kernel density estimation first, and then "reflecting" tails outside of desired interval to be inside. Densities inside and outside of desired interval are added together in "symmetric fashion": `d(x) = d_f(x) + d_f(l - (x-l)) + d_f(r + (r-x))`, where `d_f` is density of input, `d` is density of output, `l` and `r` are left and right edges of desired interval.

I made some quick and dirty changes to ggplot2 for demonstration. `stat_density()` gets `bounds` argument with default value of `c(-Inf, Inf)`. Here are some examples of proposed functionality:

```r
library(tibble)

set.seed(101)

ggplot(tibble(x = runif(100)), aes(x)) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_density(bounds = c(0, 1), color = "blue", ) +
  stat_function(data = tibble(x = c(0, 1)), fun = dunif, color = "red")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/aYGG5Fs.png)

```r
ggplot(tibble(x = rexp(100)), aes(x)) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_density(bounds = c(0, Inf), color = "blue") +
  stat_function(data = tibble(x = c(0, 5)), fun = dexp, color = "red")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/OyzYbJl.png)

title: ggplots are rendered three times on the RStudio graphics device at two different sizes
description:
This is something @thomasp85 noticed at Tidy Dev Day when he was helping Edzer and I with lazy raster rendering. He noticed the `makeContext` method for my custom grob was getting called three times when displaying the plot interactively (using profvis). Two of the three draw calls assume a lower screen resolution. Clicking "Zoom" for any grob results in two additional render calls instead of the expected one (for all grobs), and gtables (but not ggplots) are always rendered twice (even in R Notebooks). I imagine the code to fix this isn't in ggplot2, but I have no idea where that code is.

For context, this all comes out of trying to get (possibly huge) rasters to render in a reasonable amount of time in an interactive session for r-spatial/stars#21. This is the reprex I used to test this below:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)

log_file <- "log.txt"
unlink(log_file)
makeContext.lazyGrob <- function(x) {
  size <- dev.size(units = "px")
  write(sprintf("Drawing %s at %sx%s", x$test, size[1], size[2]), log_file, append = TRUE)
  x
}

GeomPoint2 <- ggproto(
  "GeomPoint2", GeomPoint,
  draw_panel = function(self, data, panel_params, coord, na.rm = FALSE) {
    layer_grob <- ggproto_parent(GeomPoint, self)$draw_panel(data, panel_params, coord)
    gTree(test = "ggplot", children = gList(layer_grob), cl = "lazyGrob")
  }
)

geom_point2 <- function() {
  layer(geom = GeomPoint2, stat = "identity", position = "identity")
}

# log grid drawing
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(gTree(test = "grid", cl = "lazyGrob"))

# log gtable drawing
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(
  gtable::gtable_row(
    "test", 
    grobs = list(gTree(test = "gtable", cl = "lazyGrob")), 
    widths = unit(1, "npc")
  )
)

# log ggplot drawing
ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy)) +
  geom_point2()

# view the log
cat(paste(readLines(log_file), collapse = "\n"))
#> Drawing grid at 504x360
#> Drawing gtable at 504x360
#> Drawing gtable at 504x360
#> Drawing ggplot at 504x360
```

title: key_glyph behavior changes with different geoms
description:
I was playing around with the new `key_glyph` argument today. I ran into some complications when using `draw_key_rect` and `draw_key_path` with different geoms, I think due to my initial misunderstanding of how this argument would work given default aesthetic values.  The behavior doesn't necessarily seem incorrect, but folks may find it confusing.  Maybe this is a place for clarifying documentation?

Solid key boxes is a not-uncommon request on Stack Overflow, and `draw_key_rect` seems like the exact right tool for this.

It works great with `geom_line()` for a problem like [this one](https://stackoverflow.com/a/19457113/2461552).

``` r
df = data.frame(x = rep(1:5, each=3),
                y = 1:15,
                group = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each=5))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color=group) )+
    geom_line(key_glyph = "rect")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Cuv5Dud.png)

But it doesn't work for this [unfilled boxplot example](https://stackoverflow.com/q/48791917/2461552).  This made sense once I looked at the plotting data; since the `fill` defaults to white so does the rectangle glyph fill.

``` r
df2 = data.frame(x = rnorm(10), 
                 y = sample(letters[1:2], 10, TRUE))

ggplot(df2, aes(y, x, color = y) ) +
    geom_boxplot(key_glyph = "rect")
```

title: geom_ribbon expects an unused y-axis variable to be present
description:
Take this example:

```
data <- data.frame(time = 1:10, value = 17 + runif(n = 10) * 4)
ribbon.data <- data.frame(time = data$time, ymin = data$value - 2, ymax = data$value + 2)

ggplot(data, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(data = ribbon.data, aes(x = time, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), alpha = 0.2)
```

It fails with the following error message: `Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : object 'value' not found`

If you arbitrarily define a column named `value` in the `ribbon.data`, it will work without any error. But the value you give to that arbitrary column will affect the Y axis of the output. For example:

```
ggplot(data, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ribbon.data %>% mutate(value = 1),
    aes(x = time, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), alpha = 0.2
  )
```

That will cause the Y-axis to range from 0 to around 26, while this:

```
ggplot(data, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ribbon.data %>% mutate(value = 100),
    aes(x = time, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), alpha = 0.2
  )
```

will cause the Y-axis to range from 0 to 100.

PS: Note that [geom_reboon documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_ribbon.html) never mentions the need for the data passed to it to have matching variables with what goes into the parent plot.

title: geom_sf() examples result in error
Handling of aes() mappings that do not refer to the layer data
description:
There are a number of issues that have been opened expressing surprise at the handling of Layers where `aes()` does not refer to the data and the data is not specified.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:5)) + 
  geom_text(aes(x = 1, y = 1, label = "annotation"))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/MRbR7gz.png)

This plot contains 5 copies of the "annotation" label, since the `geom_text()` layer inherits the plot data, and the aesthetics are recycled to the length of the layer data (if they are length 1). This usually only noticed for partially transparent objects (#2829, #2529, #2790), but has also caused errors in `geom_boxplot()` (#3316).

This is usually caused by slightly spurious ggplot2 usage by users who do not create and map a data frame but instead wire vectors directly into one or more layers directly by `aes()`. The workarounds are:

- Actually create a data frame and map it. This is obviously preferred but can get verbose for something like `geom_boxplot()` with `stat = "identity"`, where even `aes_all(c("ymin", "lower", "middle", "upper", "ymax"))` is pretty verbose.
- Use `annotate()`, although this doesn't work with facets when there are non-position aesthetics with a length != 1 ( https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3305#issuecomment-490919872 ), and doesn't always train the position scales properly for position aesthetics that are not (x|y), (x|y)min, or (x|y)max (#3342).
- For the layer `data`, pass a non-null value for which `ggplot2:::empty()` returns `TRUE` (e.g., `data = data.frame()`). This keeps the layer from inheriting the plot data, since there is no `inherit.data` argument of a plot layer, although it doesn't really make sense.

I think there are some options to discourage this practice and/or make it less verbose to do the right thing.

- Add an `inherit.data` argument that can be set to `FALSE`, such that one can safely and predictably pass vectors into `aes()`.
- Make the `mapping` a function of the data and make a function that returns an automapped data frame. We already sort of do this for `geom_sf()`, where we automatically map the `geometry` column for `data` of class `sf`. Then, one could do something like `geom_text(data = mapped_df(x = 1, y = 1, label = "annotation"))`, which would generate the appropriate mapping.
- Fix `annotate()` so that it works with all position aesthetics and with facets.
- Warn when users supply a mapping that does not refer to data (this was recently vetoed, see #3346)

Here's an example:

```r
df <- data.frame(x = rep(letters[1:2],6),
                 y = sample(100, size = 12),
                 type = rep(c("x","y","z"),4))

df2 <- df[!(df$x == "b" & df$type == "z"),]
df2$type <- factor(df2$type, levels = c("x","y","z"))

ggplot(data = df2) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x=x,y=y, fill=type)) +
```

title: Replacing each .stroke by .pt?
description:
There are two conversion constants in ggplot2: `.pt` converts millimeters to points and `.stroke` converts millimeters to 1/96 inches. According to ggplot2's [documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/graphical-units.html), we use `.pt` to convert millimeters to `lwd` units and `.stroke` to convert millimeters to `fontsize` units. However, the grid documentation says that `fontsize` is given in points, thus we should also use `.pt` to convert to `fontsize` units.

Moreover, there are essentially only four occurrences of `.stroke` in the code base:

```
./R/geom-point.r:130:          fontsize = coords$size * .pt + coords$stroke * .stroke / 2,
./R/geom-point.r:131:          lwd = coords$stroke * .stroke / 2
./R/legend-draw.r:38:      fontsize = (data$size %||% 1.5) * .pt + (data$stroke %||% 0.5) * .stroke / 2,
./R/legend-draw.r:39:      lwd = (data$stroke %||% 0.5) * .stroke / 2
```

All of them appear strange to me. In two cases, we set `lwd`. According to ggplot2's documentation, we should use `.pt` in these cases. The other two cases are also strange, because we add two values that are measured in different units (one is given in points and the other in 1/96 inches).

Perhaps I don’t understand the rationale for `.stroke`, but something appears to be inconsistent. According to the [documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2-specs.html#point), both `size` and `stroke` are given in millimeters. However, as shown above, `stroke` is converted to `lwd` by `.stroke`, and at other places, `size` is converted to `lwd` by `.pt`:

```
./R/geom-ribbon.r:116:        lwd = aes$size * .pt,
./R/geom-segment.r:122:          lwd = coord$size * .pt,
```

Either one of the conversions is incorrect, or `size` and `stroke` cannot be measured in the same unit.

title: Convert guide system to ggproto
description: The guide system is the last remaining major ggplot2 component that has not been converted to ggproto.
