title: Consider adding "static" parameter to geom/stat functions
description:
The current approach to repeating a layer across panels is to not have the layer data contain the variable needed for the faceting. This is an approach also implemented in gganimate when it comes to having layers be static across the animation. While this works intuitively, I feel it often requires some additional dataprep before the plotting code, and sometimes require that layers that otherwise use the same data need to target separate almost identical datasets.

Would it make sense to add a `static` or perhaps `repeat` argument to geom and stat functions to explicitly mark them for being repeated across panels (and frames in the case of gganimate)?

Example API:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Current approach
diamonds_static <- mutate(diamonds, cut = NULL)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = color)) + 
  geom_bar(data = diamonds_static, fill = 'grey70') +
  geom_bar() + 
  facet_wrap(~cut)

# New approach
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = color)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = 'grey70', static = TRUE) +
  geom_bar() + 
  facet_wrap(~cut)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1775316/50890266-25e49580-13fa-11e9-8528-582e451a7704.png)

The "problem" with the current approach is that it requires changes to the data source if we decide to change the faceting variable — not a huge problem, but still a barrier to experimentation.

If the `static` name is too close to the idea of animation, then we can figure out another name for it...

title: Strip aesthetics inconsistency with facet_grid using switch="y"
description:
I have an issue with strip border aesthetics when using `facet_grid(..., switch="y")` in both ggplot2 version `2.2.1` and `3.1.0`. In the example below, border size is different between x and y strip.

```r
df <- data.frame(x=c(1,1,1,1), y=c(1,1,1,1), grp1=c("A","A","B","B"), grp2=c("C","D","C","D"))
ggplot(df) +
	geom_point(aes(x=x,y=y)) +
	facet_grid(grp1~grp2) +
	theme(strip.background=element_rect(colour="black"))
ggplot(df) +
	geom_point(aes(x=x,y=y)) +
	facet_grid(grp1~grp2, switch="y") +
	theme(strip.background=element_rect(colour="black"))
```

The other `element_rect` parameters (fill, linetype, and color) do not display the same behavior and `facet_grid(..., switch="x")` work as expected.

```r
ggplot(df) +
	geom_point(aes(x=x,y=y)) +
	facet_grid(grp1~grp2, switch="x") +
	theme(strip.background=element_rect(colour="black"))
```

In `3.1.0`, I can correct y strip border size independently using `theme(strip.background.y=element_rect(...))` but it's not practical (see below).

```r
ggplot(df) +
	geom_point(aes(x=x,y=y)) +
	facet_grid(grp1~grp2, switch="y") +
	theme(strip.background=element_rect(colour="black")) +
	theme(strip.background.x=element_rect(size=0.5), strip.background.y=element_rect(size=0.25))
```

Also note that strip border has round outside corner with `facet_grid(..., switch="y")`, which is not consistent with other configurations.

Let me know if you have questions.

title: Better error messages for incorrect aesthetic mappings
description:
I encountered some cryptic error messages that pop up in response to fairly normal user mistakes, where the user maps an aesthetic to a data column that doesn't exist. A better error message could help a lot here.

My code example below first shows the desired output and then two incorrect ways in which a user might try to generate it.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

# desired plot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, 1)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = stat(density)), stat = "density") +
  geom_point(position = "jitter")
```

``` r
  geom_point(position = "jitter")
#> Error in is.finite(x): default method not implemented for type 'closure'

# wrong, `fill` aesthetic mapped to data column that doesn't exist
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, 1, fill = density)) +
  geom_tile(stat = "density") +
  geom_point(position = "jitter")
```

title: Should all deprecation notices use warning()?
description:
I wasn't aware of `gg_dep()` until I see https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/3056. During checking the usages of `gg_dep()`, I found there are five ways (!) to show deprecation notices:

* `gg_dep()`
* `message()`
* `warning()`
* `stop()`
* `.Deprecated()`

Though `gg_dep()` seems a good idea, maybe should we consistently use `warning()` (or `rlang::warn()`?) for deprecation notices (except when there's a good reason to use some other way)? One problem of `gg_dep()` is that revdep checks are usually done with the dev version (the current version + `.9000`), which might give the different result with the release version.

``` console
> git grep -P -i '^\s*[^#\s].*deprecated' R
R/aes.r:  warning("aes_auto() is deprecated", call. = FALSE)
R/coord-transform.r:    gg_dep("1.0.1", "`xtrans` arguments is deprecated; please use `x` instead.")
R/coord-transform.r:    gg_dep("1.0.1", "`ytrans` arguments is deprecated; please use `y` instead.")
R/facet-wrap.r:    .Deprecated("strip.position", old = "switch")
R/geom-spoke.r:  message("stat_spoke is deprecated, please use geom_spoke")
R/labeller.r:          warning("Referring to `x` is deprecated, use variable name instead",
R/labeller.r:    .Deprecated(old = "keep.as.numeric")
R/labeller.r:  is_deprecated <- all(c("variable", "value") %in% names(formals(labeller)))
R/labeller.r:  if (is_deprecated) {
R/labeller.r:      "and `value` arguments are now deprecated. See labellers documentation.",
R/layer.r:    warning("`show_guide` has been deprecated. Please use `show.legend` instead.",
R/quick-plot.r:  if (!missing(stat)) warning("`stat` is deprecated", call. = FALSE)
R/quick-plot.r:  if (!missing(position)) warning("`position` is deprecated", call. = FALSE)
R/stat-bin.r:      warning("`drop` is deprecated. Please use `pad` instead.", call. = FALSE)
R/stat-bin.r:      warning("`origin` is deprecated. Please use `boundary` instead.", call. = FALSE)
R/stat-bin.r:      warning("`right` is deprecated. Please use `closed` instead.", call. = FALSE)
R/stat-bin.r:      stop("`width` is deprecated. Do you want `geom_bar()`?", call. = FALSE)
R/theme.r:    warning("`axis.ticks.margin` is deprecated. Please set `margin` property ",
R/theme.r:    warning("`panel.margin` is deprecated. Please use `panel.spacing` property ",
R/theme.r:    warning("`panel.margin.x` is deprecated. Please use `panel.spacing.x` property ",
R/theme.r:    warning("`panel.margin` is deprecated. Please use `panel.spacing` property ",
R/utilities.r:    warning(msg, " (Deprecated; last used in version ", version, ")",
```

title: cut_width should be able to take ... for cut.default
description:
From a question in [community.rstudio.com](https://community.rstudio.com/t/cut-width-labels-false-returns-unused-argument-error/20675) it seems like `cut_width` is the [only one](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/cut_interval.html) of the three functions to not take `...` to pass it to `cut.default`

In particular, `labels` argument can not be used with `cut_width`. Just adding `...` would allow this
```r

  [1]  2  6  9 10  8  7 11  6  6  3 11 11  5  6 10  3  4  8  8 11  2  3  5  2  3  6  8  7  4  6  7 11 10  4 10 11

 [ reached getOption("max.print") -- omitted 900 entries ]
```
or to change labels if the call (could always be done afterward using `forcats`)

I open the issue to reference the question and see if it worth doing. Seems quite easy to be consistent between those three `cut_*` helper in lubridate.

title: type argument in scale_fill_continuous but not in scale_color_continuous
description:
`scale_fill_continuous` has a `type` argument (which can be set to `"viridis"` or `"gradient"`), but not `scale_color_continous`. I don't grasp the reason why.

Since `scale_..._continuous` is a common repeated pattern accross `ggplot2`, I find it strange to force people to move to more exotic functions such as `scale_colour_viridis_c` when they have to use colors – besides the wierdness of the asymetry between `scale_colour_continuous` and `scale_fill_continuous`.

I am not sure what the solution should be, but I'm uncomfortable with the current state. I feel like a `type` argument in `scale_color_continuous` would be a first step.

title: Refactor geom_contour()?
description:
As discussed on Twitter [here](https://twitter.com/thomasp85/status/1076149558281932801) and previously explained in a [blog post by @thomasp85](https://www.data-imaginist.com/2018/what-are-we-plotting-what-are-we-animating/) an argument can be made that `geom_contour()` should take a 2d density map as input and calculate its own contour lines without using a stat. I'm opening this issue so we can discuss pros and cons of various approaches.

I think there is precedent for this kind of refactoring with the refactoring of `geom_bar()`, `geom_histogram()`, and `geom_col()` some time back.

title: geom_tile borders missing notch at top left corners
description:
This is an issue that has been discussed over at Stackoverflow. The original problem can be found [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53767758/geom-tile-border-missing-at-corners). A minimal reprex is included below.

I have the following data frame:

    # Dummy data frame
    df <- expand.grid(x = 1:3, y = 1:3)
    
I would like to plot it as a `geom_tile` using `ggplot2` like so:

    # Tile plot
    ggplot(df) + 
      geom_tile(aes(x = x, y = y), 
                fill = NA, colour = "red", size = 3, width = 0.7, height = 0.7)

which gives, 

![rplot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11167566/50006121-1735ca80-ff83-11e8-8d6c-9101faf1613b.png)

Notice that in the top left corner of each tile the border has a notch missing and that the corner doesn't dovetail nicely like the other corners. The outcome I expected was a square around each tile, perhaps something like this:

![rplot01](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11167566/50006285-a3e08880-ff83-11e8-82e0-8ececb039454.png)

A solution offered [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/53778706/1552004)  by Z. Lin in that Stackoverflow thread suggests that `linejoin` and `lineend` for `geom_tile` are switched to `mitre` and `square`, respectively. Or, that they are at least offered as parameters in the `geom` so that the user can choose for themselves. title: Errorbars are not drawn if they extend outside of limits
description:
ggplot2 version: 3.1.0

---

When I start with a plot with errorbars, it works just fine:

```r
library(ggplot2)

data = data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10, dy = 1:10)

plot = ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = y - dy, ymax = y + dy))
```

![plot-unrestricted](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/976924/49748109-25df6180-fca5-11e8-9ddf-b62976c5635e.png)

But when I restrict the limits of the plot, the errorbars which would extent outside of the plot region vanish:

```
plot2 = plot +
    ylim(0, 10)
```

![plot-restricted](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/976924/49748116-28da5200-fca5-11e8-864c-8618ca1f8421.png)

I would expect to still see the errorbars. We often have plots where some points have really small errors, and when the horizontal cross-bar is smaller than the point marker, one cannot distinguish points with vanishing error and from points with extremely large errors.

For reference, this is how Matplotlib does the same plot:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as pl
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(1, 11)
y = x
dy = x

pl.errorbar(x, y, dy, marker='o', linestyle='none')
pl.ylim(0, 10)
pl.savefig('plot-matplotlib.png')
```

![plot-matplotlib](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/976924/49748435-efeead00-fca5-11e8-9ba7-94d59bb4abcf.png)

I would wish that ggplot does this similarly.

title: sec_axis: minor doc + implementation suggestions
description:
I have used ``sec_axis`` for the first time and it worked great. Two minor comments below.

**Comment 1: Functionality suggestion.**

Consider:

    library(ggplot2)
    ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, hp)) +
        geom_point() +
        scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~. / max(mtcars$hp)))

Suggestion: Allow the scale function to access the variables passed to the ``aes()``, so that this become possible: 

    ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = hp)) +
        geom_point() +
        scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~. / max(y)))

From the end-user perspective, ``+ scale_y_secondary(~./max(y))`` would be even better.  

**Comment 2: Doc improvement suggestion.** 

The following is a quote from the docs:

> This function is used in conjunction with a position scale to create a secondary axis, positioned opposite of the primary axis. All secondary axes must be based on a one-to-one transformation of the primary axes.

With this wording, I expected to be able to do:

    ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, hp)) +
        geom_point() +
        sec_axis() 

So I would suggest changing "in conjunction with" to "inside a"  to make it clear that it's to be used inside. I would also write that it's a function associated with the ``sec.axis`` argument of the position scale or something to that effect.

title: text is misplaced with position_dodge()
description:
In the example below, I would expect all of the text labels to be positioned perfectly on top of the data points. Instead, some of the text labels are not positioned correctly.

I think the issue is due to `position_dodge()`. I'm not sure exactly where to look to find the relevant code.

In the last example, I use ggrepel to help illustrate the problem more clearly. You can see the blue labels `34` and `290` are not pointing to the correct positions. It seems like they're pointing to the "undodged" positions instead of the "dodged" positions.

This issue was originally reported by @raviselker in ggrepel issues: https://github.com/slowkow/ggrepel/issues/122

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
# remotes::install_github("thomasp85/patchwork)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(1337)

df <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(500),
  g1 = factor(sample(c("A", "B"), 500, replace = TRUE)),
  g2 = factor(sample(c("A", "B"), 500, replace = TRUE)),
  rownames = 1:500
)

is_outlier <- function(x) {
  return(x < quantile(x, 0.25) - 1.5 * IQR(x) | x > quantile(x, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR(x))
}

df_outliers <- df %>% group_by(g1, g2) %>% mutate(outlier = is_outlier(x))

p1 <- ggplot(df_outliers, aes(x = g1, y = x, fill = g2)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.3, position = position_dodge(0.5))

p2 <- p1 +
  geom_text(
    data = . %>% filter(outlier),
    mapping = aes(label = rownames),
    position = position_dodge(0.5)
  )

p1 + p2
```

title: Allow ggsave to create directory if path doesn't exist
description:
Motivation: when handed over code, sometimes users have a separate directory for chart outputs that isn't version controlled. That could cause scripts to fail unexpectedly in other environments when the project is pulled, because the charts folder doesn't get created when git pulls it. Example directory structure illustrating problem:
```
my_project (local)
 - charts (not version controlled)
 - scripts (version controlled)

my_project (new environment from a git clone/pull)
 - scripts (version controlled)
```
While there are other solutions to enforce directory structures, I was thinking a relatively painless solution is to allow `ggsave` to have an argument that would allow users to create a path if the path doesn't exist and then export the chart image there. Sounds good?

I can implement this, should be a fairly quick patch :)

title: feature request: `layer_data` returns a tibble
backticks on non-ascii labels
description:
Upgrading to version 3.10 of ggplot2 I encountered a strange behaviour 
with regards to non-ascii (utf-8) characters in labels.
In some cases ggplot will wrap the labels with backticks. In other cases
(with the same character) it will not. I have been examining this and it 
seems that the strange behaviour only occurs when the non-ascii character 
isn't the first one in the string. Thus in the example below when mán is the variable on 
the x axis it gets wrapped but ár does not.

```r
# pseudo data with the same non-ascii letter in two different locations.
> df=data.frame(ár=rep(1991:2000,each=12),mán=rep(1:12,10))
> df$hiti=with(df,ár/2000 + 10* sin(mán/12*2*pi) + rnorm(120))
> library(ggplot2)
> ggplot(data=df,aes(mán,hiti)) + geom_point()
> ggplot(data=df,aes(ár,hiti)) + geom_point()
```

title: Un-releasable memory when using ggplot2 on large data.table?
description:
This is an example code to plot a large `data.table` using `ggplot2`. As displayed at the end of the reprex, even though all pointers to large objects have been removed, some memory cannot be released (even with double `gc()`) compared to baseline memory usage.

```r
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(magrittr)

before.mem.size <- memory.size()

# Simulation of dataset
nrow <- 5e6
ncol <- 60
dt <- do.call(data.table, lapply(seq(ncol), function(i) {return(runif(nrow))}) %>% set_names(paste0("x", seq(ncol))))

# Graph plotting
dummyEnv <- new.env()
with(dummyEnv, {
    fcn <- function(tab) {
        plot <- ggplot(tab, aes(x = x1, y = x2)) + geom_point()
        return(plot)
    }
    lst_plots <- list(
        plot1 = fcn(dt),
        plot2 = fcn(dt[x1 <= 0.7]),
        plot3 = fcn(dt[x3 <= 0.3])
    )
})
with(dummyEnv, rm(list = ls()))
rm(dummyEnv)

# After use, remove and clean up of dataset
rm(dt)
```

title: possible bug in resolution() causes wrong height and width in geom_jitter()
description:
By default, the `height `parameter in `geom_jitter()` is set as
`height=resolution(data$x, zero = FALSE) * 0.4
`
when there is only one unique value in `data$x`, `resolution()` returns 1. If the unique value is, e.g 0.001, height=0.4 is just too big. Therefore, I think `resolution()` should return `abs(unique.value)` when there is only one unique value, so that the `height` can be set correctly.

title: coord_sf() doesn't adjust line size for graticule lines
description:
Line sizes in themes are generally provide in units of mm and converted to grid units by multiplication by `.pt`. However, `coord_sf()` doesn't do that, it uses the value of `size` directly. Reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1, 2, 3))
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()

cowplot::plot_grid(
  p + coord_fixed() + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
    ggtitle("coord_fixed()"),
  p + coord_sf() +
    ggtitle("coord_sf() default"),
  p + coord_sf() + theme(panel.grid = element_line(size = 0.5*.pt)) +
    ggtitle("coord_sf() theme adjusted"),
  nrow = 2
)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/pbhs9MG.png)

<sup>Created on 2018-11-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

The offending lines are here:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/6786969ecb2ad38876ec1df43969467339d7818e/R/sf.R#L576-L582
The fix is simple, but it would affect the visual appearance of a lot of plots out in the wild.

title: Secondary axis doesn't show axis ticks or labels with coord_trans
description:
Exactly the same issue as #2072, which I take it was fixed since it is closed.

The secondary axis ticks and labels do not show up when coord_trans is present, even if using the identity transformation. The axis label ("name" parameter) does still appear.

For example, roughly taking from the examples in sec_axis:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl, mpg)) + geom_point()  +
    scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~.+10, name='MPG + 10'))
```

works as expected, but

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl, mpg)) + geom_point()  +
    scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~.+10, name='MPG + 10')) +
    coord_trans()
```

loses the axis ticks and labels (but keeps the title "MPG + 10").

title: coord_sf() drops axis labels if graticules don't extend all the way to the plot boundary
description:
In ggplot2 3.1.0, `coord_sf()` drops axis labels if graticules don't extend all the way to the plot boundary. This is a regression from 3.0.0. A reprex follows.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

world <- sf::st_as_sf(rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low"))
ggplot(world) + geom_sf() + theme_bw() + coord_sf()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/gU2TQqv.png)

``` r
ggplot(world) + geom_sf() + theme_bw() + coord_sf(expand = FALSE)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/IBrMUns.png)

<sup>Created on 2018-11-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

This bug was introduced by me when I wrote code such as the following, to calculate intersection points between the graticules and the plot boundaries:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/15ddc222d197f1d4fa596ddb930d46f4819d8db0/R/sf.R#L592

I did not consider that the plot range could extend beyond the physical limits of the earth. I'll have to ponder what the options are. One option might be to make the tolerance configurable. (I hardcoded 0.001.) Another option might be to base the tolerance on the expansion factors used for the x and y scales.

title: assigning of parameters in custom geoms depends on computegroup
description:
whether additional parameters in a geom call (outside of aes()) end up in params is dependant on the presence of these parameters in compute_group. This seems to indicate that compute_group is processed before setup_params
I wonder if this is intended behaviour ?

regards, Marco

```r
## GeomTimeline =================================================== =====
GeomTimeline <- ggplot2::ggproto("_class" = "GeomTimeline", "_inherit" = ggplot2::GeomPoint )

## geom_timeline ================================================= =====
geom_timeline <- function(data = NULL, mapping = NULL,
                          stat = "timeline",
                          mindate = -999999,
                          maxdate = 999999,
                          position = "identity", na.rm = FALSE, show.legend = NA, inherit.aes = TRUE, ...) {
        ggplot2::layer( data = data,stat = stat,geom = GeomTimeline,mapping = mapping,
                position = position,show.legend = show.legend,inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
                params = list(  na.rm = na.rm,
                                mindate = mindate,
                                maxdate = maxdate,
                                ... ))}

## StatTimeline =================================================== =====
StatTimeline <- ggplot2::ggproto("_class" =  "StatTimeline","_inherit" = ggplot2::Stat,required_aes = c("x", "y"),
    setup_params = function(data, params) {
      print(params)
      return(params)},

    setup_data = function(data, params) {
             data <- data[data$x >= params$mindate, ]
             data <- data[data$x <= params$maxdate, ]
      return(data) },

    compute_group = function(data,scales,
                               mindate,
                               maxdate,
                              ...) {
            return(data)},

    finish_layer = function(data, scales, params) {
            return(data)
        }
)

datamwe = data.frame(A = c(1,3), B=c(4,2))
library(ggplot2)

# making a plot: working just fine.
ggplot() + geom_timeline(data = datamwe, mapping = aes(x=A,y=B) )

## new version of StatTimeline, identical to the first apart from some compacting, 
##         The only functional difference is 'mindate' and 'maxdate' outcommented in 'compute_group'
StatTimeline <- ggplot2::ggproto("_class" =  "StatTimeline","_inherit" = ggplot2::Stat,required_aes = c("x", "y"),
  setup_params = function(data, params) {print(params) : return(params)},
  setup_data = function(data, params) {data <- data[data$x >= params$mindate, ]
             data <- data[data$x <= params$maxdate, ] : return(data) },
  compute_group = function(data,scales,
                                # mindate,
                                # maxdate,
                              ...) { return(data)},
  finish_layer = function(data, scales, params) {return(data)}
)

## making a plot failed, returning "Warning: Ignoring unknown parameters: mindate, maxdate" 
## because mindate and maxdate are no longer in params
ggplot() + geom_timeline(data = datamwe, mapping = aes(x=A,y=B) )


```

title: Ticks misaligned for sec_axis with some scale transformations and data in 3.1.0
description:
It appears that sec_axis is no longer working correctly with transformed axes. In particular, the secondary axis ticks and labels seem to be misaligned when using `trans = 'sqrt'`:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

data <- data.frame(
  x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100),
  y = seq(0, 4, length.out = 100)
)

ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = 'sqrt', sec.axis = dup_axis())
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/iS963nw.png)

<sup>Created on 2018-11-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

The issue only seems to occur when zero is one of the data points (note the lower limit for `y` is changed to 0.01):

``` r
library(ggplot2)

data <- data.frame(
  x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100),
  y = seq(0.01, 4, length.out = 100)
)

ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = 'sqrt', sec.axis = dup_axis())
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/M4utncE.png)

<sup>Created on 2018-11-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

The issue doesn't show up for `trans = 'log'` or `trans = 'log10'`, probably because they filter zero. I have also tested with a custom cube root transform and it has the same issue as square root.

title: sec_axis formula behaviour
description:
I fail to understand how the transformation formula of `sec_axis` behaves if you have a non-linear transformation (that is, something other than `~a*. + b`). The results become even worse if the primary axis is transformed using `scale_*_*`. Here is a `reprex`:

``` r
 library(ggplot2)

    print(ggplot() +
        geom_point(aes(x = 1:10, y = rep(5, 10))) +
        scale_x_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~log10(.))))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/5MocoAQ.png)

``` r

    packageVersion("ggplot2")
#> [1] '3.1.0.9000'
```

<sup>Created on 2018-11-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>
Now, in the docs (or here, in the comments of [`axis_secondary.R`](../blob/master/R/axis-secondary.R)) there is no mention of any limitation on the transformation formula. One can show that the `~log10(.)` formula can be evaluated using the same technique as shown in [`axis_secondary.R`](../blob/master/R/axis-secondary.R). Here is another `reprex`:

``` r
    library(rlang)
    ff <- ~log10(.)
    eval_tidy(f_rhs(ff), data = list(. = 1:10), env = f_env(ff))
#>  [1] 0.0000000 0.3010300 0.4771213 0.6020600 0.6989700 0.7781513 0.8450980
#>  [8] 0.9030900 0.9542425 1.0000000

    packageVersion("rlang")
#> [1] '0.2.1'
```

<sup>Created on 2018-11-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

The provided formula is a monotonic transformation, as is required by the code. 
You can see that the scale is not logarithmic. Instead, it looks like an equally spaced linear scale between `log10` modified limits. But in that case, supposing you have primary axis with `c(1, 10)` limits, I would expect the secondary to at least have its limits at `log10(c(1, 10)) == c(0, 1)` **and** those `c(0, 1)` breaks aligned with the `c(1, 10)` on the primary axis.
If we dive deep into the plot structure, assuming that the first `reprex` plot is `p`, then if I execute `p$scales$scales[[1]]$secondary.axis$break_info(c(1, 10), p$scales$scales[[1]])`, it gives the proper range and minor/major ticks, equally spaced between 0 and 1, assuming this call does what I think it does. However, the alignment issue on the plot is still there.
At this point, maybe an inverse transformation formula should be allowed to the `sec_axis` in such complicated cases, or the documentation/runtime checks should inform about using non-linear formula.
As a result, to get other than `dup_axis` ticks on the secondary axis, one needs to manually calculate breaks/labels in the scale and apply them explicitly.

As a final argument in favour of such transformations, there are cases in my field, where you want to have two different scales for an axis, which have a 1-to-1 relationship. Examples are: frequencies/periods, frequencies/wavelengths, magnitudes (an astronomical unit proportional to -2.5 log<sub>10</sub>(Flux)) / fluxes, which require `1 / .` and `log(.)` transformations and can be possibly combined with `scale_*_log10`.

title: Unable to add text annotation to geom_sf plot
description:
I would like to use relative positioning (0-1 scale) to add a text annotation to a ggplot object that uses geom_sf.  I've tried two different methods that were mentioned [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/1244), but both seem to fail with different results. 

First attempt, using Hadley's [suggestion](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/1244#issuecomment-128021830) does produce any annotation:
```
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(nc, aes(fill=AREA)) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  annotate("text", -Inf, Inf, label = "Top-left", hjust = 0, vjust = 1)
```
I never see "Top-left" on the plot no matter what values I've tried for hjust or vjust.

Second attempt, using textGrob (via [this comment](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/1244#issuecomment-263666211)):
```
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
nc = st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package="sf"))
ggplot(nc) +geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA))+
	annotation_custom(textGrob(label="xx"))
```
This results in `"Error in grid.Call.graphics(C_setviewport, vp, TRUE): non-finite location and/or size for viewport"`.  I get the same results if I specify x and y locations in textGrob with different units (npc, cm, lines). 

Any help would be most welcome.  Thanks.

(This was originally posted to the sf repo but was posted here at the suggestion of [yutannihilation](https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/879#issuecomment-434853524) who said "I guess coord_sf() forgets to squash Inf within the range, which coord_cartesian() does.")

title: scale_x_discrete with numeric drops axis with no warning
description:
Discrete scales are not designed to work with numeric data, this is clear. However, a careless/naive user could attempt to apply a discrete scale to continuous data. I suggest issuing a warning when a discrete scale is applied to continuous data.  

Use case: I absent-mindedly tried to apply ``scale_x_discrete`` to a continuous scale (the data was intended to be discrete, but was actually numeric) and discovered that the axis was dropped altogether and no warning issued. I hadn't noticed the problem until I used ``expand_scale`` inside the ``scale_x_discrete``. Before that I was able to set limits inside ``scale_x_discrete`` without losing the axis, so alarm bells hadn't sounded.  A warning would save time debugging and/or potentially avoid producing an incorrect plot. 

``` r
library(ggplot2)

# factor/character + scale_x_discrete + expand_scale 
ggplot(mpg, aes(as.factor(hwy), displ)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expand_scale(add = c(5, 5))) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/1CsZQd6.png)

``` r

# num/int + scale_x_discrete + expand_scale : drops the x axis
ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy, displ)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expand_scale(add = c(5, 5))) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Z7d5Bw1.png)

``` r

# num/int + scale_x_continuous + expand_scale
ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy, displ)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expand_scale(add = c(10, 10))) 
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/k0g9Ylj.png)

title: feature request: transforming coordinate system
description:
Hi,

I've got some data that roughly follows some `f(x)`. To now show the *difference* against that function, I'd like to transform the coordinate system, so that the `f(x)` line becomes the horizontal x-axis, and the (previously horizontal) y-grid lines become curves that are labelled on the right and left side of the diagram (like height lines on a map).

I looked at `coord_trans`, but that only allows to give single-parameter functions for x and y transformations; I'd like some way to specify eg. `1-exp(-x)` should become the x-axis line, so the new y-coordinates depend on x as well.
The graph data (points and/or lines) and grid should get transformed as well, of course.


Is that already possible? Would it be enough to pass the x coordinate to the y transformer function as well to use it for coordinate translation?

title: geom_curve with curvature aesthetic
description:
The function geom_curve takes an argument curvature, but this is not accepted as an aesthetic.

The use case I would like to use it for is similar to geom_jitter. Sometimes multiple lines are shown on top of other lines. Using slight random curvatures, it would be possible to see those lines separately.

```r
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

data_points <- tibble(Node = c(1,2,3), X = c(1,2,1.5), Y = c(4,5,6))
data_segments <- tibble(From = c(1,2,3,2), To = c(2,3,1,3), label = c('Line 1: 800', 'Line 2: 1600', 'Line 3: 400', 'Line 2: 2400'))
data <- data_segments %>% 
  left_join(data_points %>% rename(From = Node, X_from = X, Y_from = Y)) %>% 
  left_join(data_points %>% rename(To = Node, X_to = X, Y_to = Y))

p <- ggplot(data) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = X_from, y = Y_from)) + 
  geom_segment(aes(x = X_from, y = Y_from, xend = X_to, yend = Y_to))
ggplotly(p)
```

Two lines (2 and 4) overlap, but this is not visible from the chart.

title: Reference lines break facet_wrap when facets are the product of a function
description:
I want to add some reference lines to a faceted plot. The lines should be the same in every facet. I want to use a custom value not mapped from the data. It works just fine as long as I use plain variables for faceting, but when I mix or alter them, I get an error, which depends on the operation I perform.

I think the problem lies in the fact that the plot wants to compute facets with for the non-mapped layer, but the data doesn't exist. I don't think geom_line has a problem, but rather facet_wrap.


```
## Example 1 ------------------------------
## Works
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 20) +
  facet_wrap(vars(am))

## Doesn't work
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 20) +
  facet_wrap(vars(2 * am)) # <-- there's an operation involved

## Example 2 ------------------------------
## Works
ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.5) +
  facet_wrap(vars(am, vs))

## Doesn't work
ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.5) +
  facet_wrap(vars(paste(am, vs))) # <-- there's an operation involved

## Easiest fix I can think of: move the operation to a mutate
mtcars %>% 
  mutate(facet = paste(am, vs)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(cyl)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.5) +
  facet_wrap(vars(facet))
```

title: using `stat_ydensity` with `geom = "density"`---scaling the density line similar to `geom_violin`
description:
I originally posted this on [SO](https://stackoverflow.com/q/52862039/2375551) thinking it was user error, but it seems that perhaps the functionality I'm looking for has not been implemented in `ggplot2`. I am currently using a modified version of `geom_violin` to achieve the plot below, but it seems overkill to maintain a separate geometry that is so close to existing capabilities in `ggplot2`. 

![sideways density plot](https://i.stack.imgur.com/f6GIp.png)

Essentially, I am looking to plot the left or right outline of a `geom_violin`. I presumed that this would be possible using `stat_ydensity` through the argument `geom = 'density` or perhaps `geom = 'path'` but that seems to not be the case, i.e. the following code will not produce the above plot:
```
ggplot(res.plot, aes(x = time, y = x,group = run)) + theme_bw() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.1) +
  stat_ydensity(aes(group = time), data = res.select, 
    geom = "density", color = "red")
```
![attempt using stat_ydensity](https://i.stack.imgur.com/QH7Kf.png)

I'm guessing that the important difference between how `geom = 'density'` and `geom = 'violin'` are plotted with `stat_ydensity` is that `geom_violin` computes a variable `violinwidth` which is used to scale the violins on the x-axis. I am wondering if something similar could be implemented in `stat_ydensity`/`geom = 'density'` or similar, perhaps by using the argument `width` or some other scaling argument (e.g. a relative width argument `relwidth`).

If it's not feasible to implement this addition, I would like to instead suggest a new argument `sides` for `geom_violin` that allow users to plot either the left, right, or both sides of the violins.

reproducible example datasets:

```
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
# markov chain parameters
mu = 8                           # cm/hr
sigma = 4                        # cm/sqrt(hr)
x0 = 3                           # initial condition
tmax = 200                       # end time
deltat = 10                      # time increment (hrs)
reps = 300                       # number of realizations

random_walk = function() 
  c(0, cumsum(mu*deltat + sigma*rnorm(n, sd = deltat))) + x0

# simulate random walks
n = tmax/deltat
res = cbind.data.frame(seq(0,tmax, by = deltat), replicate(reps, random_walk()))
names(res) = c("time", paste("run", seq(1, ncol(res) - 1)))
# format the data for plotting
res.plot = gather(res, run, x, -time)
# extract specific times to compute marginal densities
res.select = filter(res.plot, time %in% c(50, 150))
```

description:
Hi,

My main motivation is to match an Excel theme that I have been given, which features upwards ticks on the x-axis. I don't want inwards ticks on the y-axis though.

title: Add `space` argument to facet_wrap?
description:
`facet_grid` provides the argument `space` which allows facets to be sized proportionally to their data range. e.g.:
```
ggplot(mtcars) + aes(x = disp, y = qsec) + geom_point() + 
  facet_grid(am~., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y")
```

However, `facet_wrap` does not have the `space` argument, so it is not possible to do e.g.

```
ggplot(mtcars) + aes(x = disp, y = qsec) + geom_point() + 
  facet_wrap(~am, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y")
```
which would be identical to the first plot but with the facet labels **above** the facets, rather than on the facet sides.

Any chance of bringing the `space` argument to `facet_wrap`? 

Alternatively, I wonder if there is a place for something like `facet_row` and `facet_col`. These functions could operate like `facet_grid` but provide simple facet label placement thanks to the single row/column constraint.

title: Feature Request: Warning message and support for non-uniform tile sizes in geom_raster
description:
Feature Request:
(a) add warning in geom_raster() when tiles are NOT all the same size
(b) handle irregularly sized tiles better in geom_raster()

a) sometimes you think that your data are all regularly gridded and then you run geom_raster() and rows appear to be missing from your raster.  In this case, a warning message would be a super helpful alert to the user that they've violated one of the underlying assumptions of geom_raster.

Either in geom-raster.R -> GeomRaster() or in utilities-resolution.R -> resolution(), run a quick check:

```r
if( length( unique( diff( unique(data$x) ) ) ) != 1 ) 
  warning("tiles not all of uniform size in x dimension") 

if( length( unique( diff( unique(data$y) ) ) ) != 1 ) 
  warning("tiles not all of uniform size in y dimension") 

```

b) Special case where entire rows/cols are different height/width.  If there is a way to do this without massively negatively impacting the performance of geom_raster... handle differently sized rows/cols better (e.g., fall back on geom_tile and calculate height/width from the data).  

Pseudo code in GeomRaster(), setup_data() : 

```r

ydiffs <- diff( unique(data$y) )
if( length( unique( ydiffs ) ) != 1 ) {
  warning("tiles not all of uniform size in y dimension") 
  diffvec <- data.frame(y = unique(data$y),
                                       h = c(ydiffs[1], ydiffs))
  h <- diffvec$h[match(data$y, diffvec$y)]
} else {
  h <- resolution(data$y, FALSE)
}

```

title: Enhancement: drop=FALSE should result in inclusion of unused factor levels in BOTH compution and visualization aspects of the analysis.
description:
Suppose someone is interested in including unused factor levels (in a discrete x aes) in the analysis, and thus, she sets drop = FALSE in the scale_x_discrete(). This helps to **visually** include the unused factor levels in the graphs, but it seems that those factors will never be used for any type of computation. If a user shows interest in including unused factor levels in the analysis, then she is probably interested to see their effects in all aspects of the analysis, both computation and visualization aspects.

Here is an example,

```r
myLetters = factor(c("A", "A", "B", "C"), levels = LETTERS)
data1 = data.frame(myLetters)

ggplot(data1, aes(x = myLetters)) + 
stat_count(geom = "point") +
scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE)
```

title: Allow flipping panel.grid theme elements with coord_flip()
description:
Currently it's difficult to create a custom theme that has gridlines only along the primary baseline axis. This is mostly an issue with horizontal bar charts, where you would only want to have vertical gridlines (vs. almost any other plot where you'd only have horizontal gridlines):

``` r
library(ggplot2)

theme_set(theme_bw() + theme(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
))

ggplot(mpg, aes(cut_interval(cty, 5))) + geom_bar()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Z0xh6OR.png)

``` r
ggplot(mpg, aes(class)) + geom_bar() + coord_flip()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/JPVyBei.png)

To match the theme of the first plot, a workaround requires a theme adjustment to exchange `panel.grid.major.x` and `panel.grid.major.y`.

``` r
ggplot(mpg, aes(class)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = calc_element("panel.grid.major.y", theme_get())
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/gV9W8ns.png)

The other coordinate system that changes axis positions (`coord_polar()`) already behaves such that the `panel.grid` elements are applied to the matching aesthetic mappings (i.e. `panel.grid.major.x` always controls gridlines for the variable mapped to the `x` aesthetic). Applying the same logic to `coord_flip()` would fix the above theming issue.

Would this change be feasible? It seems like a simple change, but could break some plot code that's been written around this behaviour. Alternatively there could be an option in `coord_flip()` to control this behaviour, defaulting to the current behaviour for backwards compatibility.

title: `NA` limits in coords
description:
Setting `NA` in limits of `coords` in a similar fashion to `scales` ends up in an error. 

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(cars, aes(speed, dist)) +
   geom_point() +
   coord_cartesian(ylim = c(25, NA))  # emulating scale_y_continuous(limits = c(25, NA))
#> Error in if (zero_range(range)) zero_width else diff(range): missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```


Created on 2018-09-21 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).


I've tinker a bit and found that the error is in this line:
 https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/01155ba2e9394e17066668eace50c13354e03b3a/R/coord-cartesian-.r#L121

Adding this:
`limits <- ifelse(is.na(limits), scale$get_limits(), limits)`
solves the issue in this case. 

``` r
library(ggplot2)

scale_range <- function(scale, limits = NULL, expand = TRUE) {
   expansion <- if (expand) ggplot2:::expand_default(scale) else c(0, 0)
   
   if (is.null(limits)) {
      scale$dimension(expansion)
   } else {
      limits <- ifelse(is.na(limits), scale$get_limits(), limits)
      range <- range(scale$transform(limits))
      scales::expand_range(range, expansion[1], expansion[2])
   } 
}

assignInNamespace("scale_range", scale_range, ns = "ggplot2")

ggplot(cars, aes(speed, dist)) +
   geom_point() +
   coord_cartesian(ylim = c(25, NA))  
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/vsgK4lu.png)

Created on 2018-09-21 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

I'm not versed enough on how `ggplot2` handles coords to know if it's a robust fix across different coords, though.

title: Error using theme_bw() with parameters depending on base_size
description:
I get an error using theme_bw() whenever I insert a base_line_size or base_rect_size that uses the calculation based on base_line_size. E.g.,

The error is:

> Error in structure(list(colour = colour, size = size, linetype = linetype, :
> object 'base_size' not found

This error occurs not only with theme_bw, but with all the other themes I tested.

To get a reproducible error, I ran the simple command:

> test10 <- theme_bw(base_line_size = base_size/11)

This command gives the above error whenever I insert a parameter that depends on base_size. It gives no error if I insert a base_line_size = 0.5. Debugging theme_bw suggests to me that the problem is due to a data_frame problem, but I am not good enough to fix it. The simple work around is, if you have to set base_line_size or base_rect_size, to use an absolute number and not the calculation based on base_size.
Larry Hunsicker

title: aes and aes_string return different plots
description:
I'm working with a [custom geom for split violin plots](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/35717353/split-violin-plot-with-ggplot2) and have noticed that using `aes_string` returns a different plot than `aes`. Given that `aes_string` is supposed to be used when programming with ggplot2, I'm wondering if there's something wrong with the custom geom or if `aes` and `aes_string` are supposed to do different things.

```r
library(grid)
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)
GeomSplitViolin <- ggproto(
  "GeomSplitViolin",
  GeomViolin,
  draw_group = function(self, data, ..., draw_quantiles = NULL) {
    data$xminv <- data$x - data$violinwidth * (data$x - data$xmin)
    data$xmaxv <- data$x + data$violinwidth * (data$xmax - data$x)
    grp <- data[1, 'group']
    print(grp)
    if (grp %% 2 == 1) {
      data$x <- data$xminv
      data.order <- data$y
    } else {
      data$x <- data$xmaxv
      data.order <- -data$y
    }
    newdata <- data[order(data.order), , drop = FALSE]
    newdata <- rbind(
      newdata[1, ],
      newdata,
      newdata[nrow(x = newdata), ],
      newdata[1, ]
    )
    newdata[c(1, nrow(x = newdata) - 1, nrow(x = newdata)), 'x'] <- round(x = newdata[1, 'x'])
    grob <- if (length(x = draw_quantiles) > 0 & !zero_range(x = range(data$y))) {
      stopifnot(all(draw_quantiles >= 0), all(draw_quantiles <= 1))
      quantiles <- ggplot2:::create_quantile_segment_frame(data = data, draw_quantiles = draw_quantiles)
      aesthetics <- data[rep.int(x = 1, times = nrow(x = quantiles)), setdiff(x = names(x = data), y = c("x", "y")), drop = FALSE]
      aesthetics$alpha <- rep.int(x = 1, nrow(x = quantiles))
      both <- cbind(quantiles, aesthetics)
      quantile.grob <- GeomPath$draw_panel(both, ...)
      grobTree(GeomPolygon$draw_panel(newdata, ...), name = quantile.grob)
    }
    else {
      GeomPolygon$draw_panel(newdata, ...)
    }
    grob$name <- grobName(grob = grob, prefix = 'geom_split_violin')
    return(grob)
  }
)
geom_split_violin <- function(
  mapping = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  stat = "ydensity",
  position = "identity",
  ...,
  draw_quantiles = NULL,
  trim = TRUE,
  scale = "area",
  na.rm = FALSE,
  show.legend = NA,
  inherit.aes = TRUE
) {
  return(layer(
    data = data,
    mapping = mapping,
    stat = stat,
    geom = GeomSplitViolin,
    position = position,
    show.legend = show.legend,
    inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list(
      trim = trim,
      scale = scale,
      draw_quantiles = draw_quantiles,
      na.rm = na.rm,
      ...
    )
  ))
}
my_data = data.frame(
    y=c(rnorm(1000), rnorm(1000, 0.5), rnorm(1000, 1), rnorm(1000, 1.5)),
    x=c(rep('a', 2000), rep('b', 2000)),
    m=c(rep('i', 1000), rep('j', 2000), rep('i', 1000))
)
ggplot(data = my_data, mapping = aes(x = x, y = y, fill = m)) + geom_split_violin() + labs(title = 'aes')
ggplot(data = my_data, mapping = aes_string(x = 'x', y = 'y', fill = 'm')) + geom_split_violin() + labs(title = 'aes_string')
```

title: `summarize_layout` does not return final range values
description:
@clauswilke 

Brushing points within shiny apps depends on the output of `ggplot2::summarise_layout(p)` CRAN ggplot2 3.0.0 works as expected.

With changes from https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/2832 , the range values of `CoordTrans` where changed to map back to their original values.  While I agree with the intent, ggplot2::summarise_layout uses the range values to calculate the returned domain value.


``` r
library(ggplot2); 
dat <- data.frame(xvar = c(10^-1, 10^3), yvar = c(2^-2, 2^4))
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(xvar, yvar)) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(expand = c(0 ,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_trans(y = "log2")
p
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/13Dsa8W.png)

> Created on 2018-09-17 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

With v3.0.0 the fully transformed scale values provide: 
```r
ggplot2::summarise_layout(ggplot2::ggplot_build(p))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 10
#>   panel   row   col vars     xmin  xmax  ymin  ymax xscale        yscale       
#>   <fct> <dbl> <dbl> <list>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <list>        <list>       
#> 1 1         1     1 <list …    -1     3    -2     4 <S3: ScaleCo… <S3: ScaleCo…
```

With current github version the fully transformed scale values provide: 
```r
# create `p` again
ggplot2::summarise_layout(ggplot2::ggplot_build(p))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 10
#>   panel   row   col vars     xmin  xmax  ymin  ymax xscale        yscale       
#>   <fct> <dbl> <dbl> <list>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <list>        <list>       
#> 1 1         1     1 <list …    -1     3  0.25    16 <S3: ScaleCo… <S3: ScaleCo…
```

The `ymin` and `ymax` are displaying the original values, not the fully transformed values.


-----------------------------------------------------------

Shiny demo... Try selecting the two points at `x = 150`.  In the dev version, select the very bottom of the plot (around `y = 2`) are at `x = 150` to brush the _transformed data locations_.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(plotOutput("plot", brush = "brush"), tableOutput("table"))
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(mtcars, aes(hp, wt)) + geom_point() +
      coord_trans(y = "log2")
  })
  output$table <- renderTable({
    brushedPoints(mtcars, input$brush)
  })
}
shinyApp(ui, server)
```

title: coord_fixed() option to force equally-spaced breaks
description:
In most cases that call for `coord_fixed()`, it is also helpful to have gridlines that are equally spaced along the horizontal and vertical axes, so that the background grid consists of squares. This can be done manually by choosing the same regular breaks (see below), but

- this is inconvenient, especially when generating many plots at different scales, and
- the internal `break_info()` functions that automatically produce elegant choices of breaks cannot be used.

It seems natural to have an option, e.g. `coord_fixed(breaks = "square")`, that generates elegant breaks that (a) occur at the same frequency on both axes and, perhaps optionally, (b) occur at a subset of the same set of equally-spaced values. The default is compared to (a) and (b) below in a simple example. (The option might be useful even for general cartesian coordinates.)

I had a go at building a new `Coord*()` ggproto, but i quickly realized that it would take a deeper dive into the **ggplot2** internals than i'd prepared for. I'm glad to give it a serious try, and to send a PR if it seems to work, but i wanted to check with the maintainers first to be sure i haven't overlooked something and that the feature makes sense.

Thank you!

``` r
library(ggplot2)

# default breaks form non-square background grid
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, qsec)) + geom_point() + coord_fixed()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/y9GSYbo.png)

``` r

# inelegant way to force a square grid
break_at_2 <- function(limits) {
  seq(ceiling(limits[1]), floor(limits[2]), 2)
}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, qsec)) + geom_point() + coord_fixed() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = break_at_2) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = break_at_2)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/KOadP4O.png)

``` r

# inelegant way to force breaks onto the same sequence
break_by_2 <- function(limits) {
  seq(ceiling(limits[1] / 2) * 2, floor(limits[2] / 2) * 2, 2)
}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, qsec)) + geom_point() + coord_fixed() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = break_by_2) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = break_by_2)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/fIND2S2.png)

title: Should limits be enforced on the calculated geoms?
description:
(This is originally reported on #2879, and I asked on [RStudio Community](https://community.rstudio.com/t/how-can-i-specify-the-limit-of-geom-bar-properly-when-the-x-axis-is-continuous/13709). But, I couldn't find any reasonable answer so far...)

When the x axis is continuous and has limits, `geom_bar()` and `geom_col()` won't automatically consider the width of bars, which means the bars at both ends disappear even if the values are within the range of the limits. I feel this behaviour is counter-intuitive, whereas this won't happen with discrete scales.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(x = 1:3)

# bars at both ends disappear
ggplot(d) +
  geom_bar(aes(x)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limit = c(1, 3))
#> Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values (geom_bar).
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/5a9ZxUf.png)

``` r
# no bars disappear
ggplot(d) +
  geom_bar(aes(factor(x))) +
  scale_x_discrete(limit = c("1", "2", "3"))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/2bdSpSh.png)

Created on 2018-09-10 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

Though I don't come up with how to control whether or not to ignore limits, IIUC about the semantics, `limits` should not be enforced on the computed geoms, but on the values before calculation.

After some investigation, I'm wondering if it's possible to reset `limits` as long as `range` of the scale after computing the widths of the geoms (`compute_geom_1()`) and computing positions (`compute_position()`). More preciesely, `reset_scales()` here:

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/f636f34597e77e9a2a99783aff6233b838490ff3/R/plot-build.r#L68-L78

Though I don't come up with how to implement this yet, does my explanation make sense?

title: Feature request: Argument 'drop' for stat_count() and other similar functions
description:
I suggest to add the argument _drop_ (currently available in the scale_*_discrete functions) also to stat_count() and other similar functions such as stat_summary(), geom_bar(), etc. This helps to provide an option to keep the unused factor levels.

Below please find a simplified example:

```r
myLetters = factor(c("A", "A", "B", "C"), levels = LETTERS)
data1 = data.frame(myLetters)
```

Here, `data1` is a simple data frame that contains a selected set of English letters. The goal is to plot the count of **all 26 English letters** in the above vector.  One natural approach to try is:

```r
ggplot(data1, aes(x = myLetters)) + stat_count() 
```

The output will be:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7562230/45192757-29bf9b80-b1ff-11e8-8ab9-4865e09e4681.png)

But, as mentioned above, I expect to see zero count for all English letters that are not available in the above list. 

I understand that this can be achieved using the following code:
```r
data2 = data.frame(table(myLetters))
ggplot(data2, aes(x = myLetters, y = Freq)) + geom_col() 
```

which results in the (desired) output:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7562230/45192827-8c189c00-b1ff-11e8-9f11-038b2c224dde.png)

But please note that the above alternative approach is easy to implement for the above simplified example. In more complex settings, the argument _drop_ seems to be necessary and the natural solution for this problem.

Also please note that this feature request applies to a variety of other functions such as stat_summary(), geom_bar(), etc.

Thank you for your attention.

title: Need position_stack_line()
description:
`geom_area()` doesn't play well with duplicated `x` values. The docs state:
> `geom_area` is a special case of `geom_ribbon`, where the `ymin` is fixed to 0.

But when there are multiple values of `y` for a given value of `x`, the two are not equivalent. The `geom_ribbon()`  result matches the intuition of "`geom_line()` but with the area under the curve filled in":

``` r
library(tidyverse)
df <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 2, 3), y = 1:4)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/DgsipzA.png)

However, it seems this scenario results in `geom_area()` having the equivalent of `ymin = min(y)` and `ymax = sum(y)` in `geom_ribbon()`.

``` r
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_area()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Qd3ubqt.png)

I'm happy to dig a bit further and see if I can submit a PR for this.

title: geom_area doesn't respond to ymax aesthetic
description:
The documentation for `geom_area()` indicates "For each x value, geom_ribbon displays a y interval defined by ymin and ymax. geom_area is a special case of geom_ribbon, where the ymin is fixed to 0."

When I tried setting `ymax` only, I got an error, and it is actually using the `y` aesthetic instead of `ymax`.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 3.4.4
ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:3), aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = 1)) + geom_area()
#> Error in eval(substitute(list(...)), `_data`, parent.frame()): object 'y' not found

ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:3), aes(x = x, y = 1)) + geom_area()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/UartET2.png)

That suggests that for `geom_area()`, either
* the documentation needs to be updated so that it indicates "`geom_area()` uses the aesthetic `y` instead of `ymax`" or
* the functionality needs to be updated so that `geom_area()` uses `ymax` instead of `y`.

title: Reduce "object 'geometry' not found" error with geom_sf()
description:
Currently, `geom_sf()` works without specifying `geometry` aes only when:

1. the `sf` object has a geometry column named `geometry`
2. the `sf` object is passed directly to `geom_sf()`, not via the plot data

I'm afraid it's a bit confusing that the example of `nc` won't work if we just replace `nc` with another `sf` object.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
attr(nc, "sf_column")
#> [1] "geometry"

# this works
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/a4Et6zO.png)

``` r

nc_gpkg <- sf::st_read(system.file("gpkg/nc.gpkg", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
attr(nc_gpkg, "sf_column")
#> [1] "geom"

# this fails
ggplot(nc_gpkg) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA))
#> Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...): object 'geometry' not found
```

Created on 2018-08-29 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).


I want to let `ggplot(nc_gpkg) + geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA))` simply work. For example, implementing `fortify.sf()` seems to solve our problem quickly.

```r
fortify.sf <- function(model, data, ...) {
  if (! "geometry" %in% colnames(model)) {
    model$geometry <- sf::st_geometry(model)
  }
  model
}
```

But, I'm not fully sure this does the right thing... I feel this is similar kind of problem that we wanted to map grouping variable of `grouped_df` automatically to `group` aes, but couldn't (https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2378). Are there any smarter way to create mappings automatically?

title: geom_dotplot() default y axis is wrong
description:
geom_dotplot() displays a y axis labeled "count" and scaled 0 to 1.  

The y axis currently has no correspondence to the data plotted.   If the range is 0 to 1, then the label should be "frequency" or "relative frequency" or "proportion" AND the height of the stacked dots should scale with ncount.   

A quick temporary fix is to completely remove/suppress the y axis as default.  This is better than defaulting to display a mistake.

title: Unexpected order of text labels when parse=TRUE
description:
## The problem

Text labels can be displayed in an unexpected order if you use `parse = TRUE`:

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

d <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2, 3),
  y = c(1, 0, 1),
  label = c("alpha", "", "gamma")
)

p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) + geom_point(color = "red")

p1 <- p + geom_text(size = 5, parse = FALSE) + labs(title = "Good :)")

p2 <- p + geom_text(size = 5, parse = TRUE) + labs(title = "Bad :(")

ggsave(filename = "issue.png", plot = p1 + p2, width = 4, height = 2)
```

![issue](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/209714/44682017-39c1c900-aa10-11e8-9756-58c1e52603ea.png)

## The culprit: parse() drops empty strings

To my surprise, the `parse()` function silently drops the empty string:

```r
x <- c("alpha", "", "gamma")
x
#> [1] "alpha" ""      "gamma"
length(x)
#> [1] 3

y <- parse(text = x)
y
#> expression(alpha, gamma)
length(y)
#> [1] 2

c(expression(alpha), expression(), expression(gamma))
#> expression(alpha, gamma)
```

Unfortunately, I don't know how to deal with this. Do you have any ideas?

## A workaround

One workaround is to create a second dataframe just for the text labels. That way, you can avoid passing an empty string to the `parse()` function.

```r
d2 <- d[d$label != "",]

p3 <- p + geom_text(size = 5, parse = TRUE, data = d2) + labs(title = "Yay :)")

ggsave(filename = "workaround.png", plot = p1 + p3, width = 4, height = 2)
```

![workaround](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/209714/44682625-e5b7e400-aa11-11e8-9254-04ac2e665b69.png)

## Related issues

@pakidermo5000 originally reported this here: https://github.com/slowkow/ggrepel/issues/114

title: support loess in stat_density2d
description:
The current implementation uses ``kde2d`` which has edge effects for points within the bandwidth of an edge. I believe a 2d loess wouldn't have such a problem. I believe one can calculate the loess using something like `loess(z ~ x + y)`.

To illustrate the edge effects:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(4393)
dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 1000), ] 

# This one just zooms in on the correct plot
p1 <- dsmall %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
    stat_density_2d(geom = "raster", aes(fill = stat(density)), contour = FALSE) + 
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(4.5, 9), expand = FALSE)

# This one recalculates the density after subsetting
p2 <- dsmall %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
    stat_density_2d(geom = "raster", aes(fill = stat(density)), contour = FALSE) + 
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(4.5, 9)) + 
    coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE)

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)
```

title: coord_sf() ignores axis label settings
description:
As mentioned in https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2846#issuecomment-415981057, axis labels cannot be set manually when using `coord_sf()`.

``` r
library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.6.1, GDAL 2.1.3, proj.4 4.9.3
library(ggplot2) 

# graticule labeling via cardinal coordinates (N, S, E, W)
nc <- st_read(system.file("gpkg/nc.gpkg", package="sf"))
#> Reading layer `nc.gpkg' from data source `/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.5/Resources/library/sf/gpkg/nc.gpkg' using driver `GPKG'
#> Simple feature collection with 100 features and 14 fields
#> geometry type:  MULTIPOLYGON
#> dimension:      XY
#> bbox:           xmin: -84.32385 ymin: 33.88199 xmax: -75.45698 ymax: 36.58965
#> epsg (SRID):    4267
#> proj4string:    +proj=longlat +datum=NAD27 +no_defs
ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA), data=nc) + 
  coord_sf() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(34, 34.5, 35.7), # setting breaks manually works
    labels = c("A", "B", "C")   # but labels are ignored
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/o0DiPJV.png)

The reason is that the `setup_panel_params()` function of `coord_sf()` ignores the break info generated by the scales and instead reads and interprets the scales' `breaks` parameters directly: 
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/6500a307780888d5b49aa32d97ea792c07a733c6/R/sf.R#L450-L457
For comparison, `coord_cartesian()` does this:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/6500a307780888d5b49aa32d97ea792c07a733c6/R/coord-cartesian-.r#L102

`coord_sf()` is written the way it is because it needs to let `sf::st_graticule()` make appropriate decisions about where to put graticules and how to label them, with the knowledge of the CRS that is being used. The scales don't have that knowledge and would in general produce bad breaks and labels.

What this means is that if we want to be able to allow manual overriding of labels, we will have to add additional logic to `coord_sf()` / `setup_panel_params()` that essentially mimics the scales' `get_labels()` function:
https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/6500a307780888d5b49aa32d97ea792c07a733c6/R/scale-.r#L289-L309

Also potentially relevant: https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/829

title: Inconsistent Scale Management
description:
I recently upgraded to ggplot2 version 3.0.0, and I was surprised by the change to discrete scales where I was now getting a yellow value (near-invisible on a white background).  As I was looking into how to change the default back to the prior behavior, I noticed inconsistent handling of colour scale types with ggplot2 version 3.

* In `scale_colour_continuous()` a new `type` argument along with an option managed by `getOption("ggplot2.continuous.colour", default="gradient")` determines how the scale is determined.
* `scale_colour_ordinal()` is assigned to `scale_colour_viridis_d()`, but it is not mentioned in the manual.

If global options will be the way that default scales are managed in the future, could a new help page be added for all the options that control ggplot2?  (My preference is that this will be moved away from.)

Can the default function used to control each scale be defined in a single help page to assist with finding  how to change the default behavior?

title: ggplot throws an error when a data is zero row and the lengths of aesthetics are not zero
description:
If a data is zero row and the lengths of aesthetics are not zero, `ggplot` throws an error with an wrong length of the data as follows.

```
Error: Aesthetics must be either length 1 or the same as the data (1): x, y, colour
```

I think the number in the parentheses indicates the length of the data, but it is wrong, since the length is zero.

In addition, this behavior doesn't get along with constant (length-one) aesthetics, while they can be combined with non-zero-row data. I hope `ggplot` tolerates combination of zero-row data and constant aesthetics.

Example (using R 3.5.1 and ggplot2 3.0.0):

```r
library(ggplot2)
d1 <- data.frame(xval = rep(1:5, 4), yval = 1:20)

# The followings are OK
ggplot(d1, aes(xval, yval))
ggplot(d1, aes(xval, yval, colour = "Type 1"))
nrow(d1[0,])
#> [1] 0
ggplot(d1[0,], aes(xval, yval))

# This causes an error
ggplot(d1[0,], aes(xval, yval, colour = "Type 1"))
#> Error: Aesthetics must be either length 1 or the same as the data (1): x, y, colour
```

title: properly formatting a two-line caption in ggplot2
description:
I had raised this issue on StackOverflow (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51976537/properly-formatting-a-two-line-caption-in-ggplot2) but I've gotten 0 responses there. So I am raising this issue on GitHub instead.

I am writing a custom function where I want to add two-line captions to plots. The basic idea is that I want the caption to be formatted properly no matter what the user might choose to enter. I have created a toy example below where I illustrate two problems with the way I've implemented this function right now-

1. When the caption is not `NULL`, the two lines are not aligned to the right.
2. When an expression is entered, the concatenated caption gets completely mangled.

``` r

# needed libraries
library(ggplot2)

# custom function to prepare a caption
caption_maker <- function(caption) {
  # if caption is not null then add line separator
  if (!is.null(caption)) {
    caption <- paste(caption, "; \n", sep = "")
  }

  # prepare the caption with additional info
  caption <- base::substitute(
    expr =
      paste(y,
            "In favor of null: ",
            "log"["e"],
            "(BF"["01"],
            ") = ",
            bf),
    env = base::list(y = caption,
                     bf = 123)
  )

  # return the message
  return(caption)
}

# custom function to add labels to the plot
plot_maker <-
  function(xlab = NULL,
           ylab = NULL,
           title = NULL,
           caption = NULL) {
    caption.text <- caption_maker(caption = caption)

    plot <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point() +
      ggplot2::labs(
        x = xlab,
        y = ylab,
        title = title,
        caption = caption.text
      )

    # return the plot
    return(plot)
  }

# this works just fine
plot_maker(caption = NULL)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/u0Mc1VM.png)

``` r

# this works but the caption is not aligned properly
plot_maker(caption = "This is mtcars dataset")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/jS6yqXD.png)

``` r

# this works but the caption is all mangled
plot_maker(caption =
             expression(paste(italic("Note"), ": This is mtcars dataset")))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/MEJqduo.png)

title: Feature Request: Allow `labs()` to Use Input Data
description:
When creating many figures simultaneously, I often want to create the labels from the data itself automatically.  In my current need, I want to create a title for a figure based on a clinical study title.  In other cases, I want to create the x- and y-axis labels using a combination of a column naming the measurement and its units.

My current method requires external processing prior to `ggplot()`:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
my_data <- data.frame(x=1:4, y=5:8, study=paste("Study", 1:2))
my_data_1 <- my_data %>% filter(study %in% "Study 1")
study_number <- unique(my_data_1$study)
ggplot(my_data_1, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + labs(title=study_number)
```

A (nonworking) example of my thought on how this could be implemented is:

``` r
my_data <- data.frame(x=1:4, y=5:8, study=paste("Study", 1:2))
my_data_1 <- my_data %>% filter(study %in% "Study 1")
ggplot(my_data_1, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + labs(title=aes(title=unique(study)))
```

title: Documentation of `palette` parameter for continuous scales
description:
The documentation is incorrect:

```
continuous_scale            package:ggplot2            R Documentation

Continuous scale constructor.

Description:

     Continuous scale constructor.

Usage:

     continuous_scale(aesthetics, scale_name, palette, name = waiver(),
       breaks = waiver(), minor_breaks = waiver(), labels = waiver(),
       limits = NULL, rescaler = rescale, oob = censor, expand = waiver(),
       na.value = NA_real_, trans = "identity", guide = "legend",
       position = "left", super = ScaleContinuous)
     
Arguments:

aesthetics: The names of the aesthetics that this scale works with

scale_name: The name of the scale

 palette: A palette function that when called with a single integer
          argument (the number of levels in the scale) returns the
          values that they should take
```

This is the expected behavior of `palette` for `discrete_scale`.  Currently `continuous_scale` and `discrete_scale` share the same documentation for this parameter.  PR coming shortly.

Following my Twitter conversation with @dpseidel (https://twitter.com/patilindrajeets/status/1030247641240756224), I am filing an issue. I am trying to create a histogram with both counts and relative frequency (or proportion) data displayed on the y-axes, the former on the left y-axis and the latter on the right. I have managed to write a custom function that does this and it's going to be part of my package. But the function works only when `data = NULL` and not otherwise and I am not sure what's going on.

I have created a toy example here because I didn't want to share the whole function script.

``` r

library(tidyverse)
library(magrittr)
library(ggplot2)

# function body
toy_bar <- function(data = NULL, x) {
  
================ creating data frame ========================

  # preparing a dataframe out of provided inputs
  if (!is.null(data)) {
    # if dataframe is provided
    data <-
      dplyr::select(.data = data,
                    x = !!rlang::enquo(x))

  } else {
    # if vectors are provided
    data <-
      base::cbind.data.frame(x = x)
  }

  # convert to a tibble dataframe
  data %<>%
    tibble::as_data_frame(x = .)

  # denominator for computing proportions later
  total_obs <- nrow(x = data)

================ creating plot =================================

  # constructing the plot
  plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(data = data,
                          mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = x)) +
    # plot counts on y-axis
    ggplot2::stat_bin(
      col = "black",
      alpha = 0.7,
      na.rm = TRUE,
      mapping = ggplot2::aes(y = ..count..,
                             fill = ..count..)
    ) +
    # no color gradient needed for this plot
    ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(name = "count",
                                 low = "white",
                                 high = "white") +
    # adding seconary axis with proportions
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
      sec.axis = ggplot2::sec_axis(
        trans = ~ . / total_obs,
        labels = scales::percent,
        name = "proportion (in %)"
      )
    ) +
    ggplot2::ylab("count") +
    ggplot2::guides(fill = FALSE)

  # return the output
  return(plot)

}

# this works
toy_bar(x = ToothGrowth$len)
#> `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.
```

title: Release a quick ggplot2 3.0.1?
description:
I would like to open a conversation about the feasibility of releasing a bugfix release 3.0.1 relatively soon. If I look at the merged changes so far (https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/NEWS.md), they're mostly things that should have been caught for 3.0.0 but weren't. And in particular, issues #2363 (new graphics device with `ggsave()`) and #2788 (tidy eval for secondary axis) will be frustrating for users of 3.0.0.

I realize how much work it is to prep a release. At the same time, once we start merging code that makes more fundamental changes to the code base, the window of opportunity for a pure bug-fix release is essentially closed. So, a plan to prioritize work might be good. E.g., only merge bug fixes until the end of September, prep a 3.0.1 release then, and start merging more ambitious work after 3.0.1.

I assume we don't want to go to a development model where we're working on a minor and a major release at the same time, in different branches, but that would be an option as well of course.

title: geom_segment() and geom_curve() alpha does not affect transparency
description:
Dear ggplot2-team,

In `geom_segment()` and `geom_curve()`, lowering `alpha` does not appear to affect transparency. This behavior is consistent whether `alpha` is supplied within `aes()` or not. 



Reprex for both cases are below:


**1) `alpha` outside `aes()`**

```r
library(ggplot2)

some_data <- data.frame(xval = 1:10, yval = 1:10)

# parameters
size <- 3
alpha <- 0.2

some_data %>% 
        ggplot(aes(xval, yval)) +
        
        # works as expected
        geom_line(color = "blue", size = size, alpha = alpha) +
        geom_hline(aes(yintercept = yval[5]), size = size, alpha = alpha) +
        geom_vline(aes(xintercept = xval[5]), size = size, alpha = alpha) +

        # alpha setting does not alter transparency 
        geom_segment(aes(x = xval[2], 
                         xend = xval[8],
                         y = yval[8],
                         yend = yval[2]),
                     size = size,
                     alpha = alpha) +
        
        geom_curve(aes(x = xval[2], 
                       xend = xval[8],
                       y = yval[8],
                       yend = yval[2]),
                   size = size,
                   alpha = alpha)
```

![ggplot_alpha_outside](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11796327/44146810-48cabb68-a089-11e8-8a0b-664e87001f97.png)



**2) `alpha` within `aes()`**

```r
library(ggplot2)



some_data <- data.frame(xval = 1:10, yval = 1:10)

# parameters
size <- 3
alpha <- 0.2

some_data %>% 
        ggplot(aes(xval, yval)) +
        
        # works as expected
        geom_line(color = "blue", size = size, alpha = alpha) +
        geom_hline(aes(yintercept = yval[5]), size = size, alpha = alpha) +
        geom_vline(aes(xintercept = xval[5]), size = size, alpha = alpha) +
        
        # alpha setting does not alter transparency 
        geom_segment(aes(x = xval[2], 
                         xend = xval[8],
                         y = yval[8],
                         yend = yval[2],
                         alpha = "less transparent"),
                     size = size) +
        
        geom_curve(aes(x = xval[2], 
                       xend = xval[8],
                       y = yval[8],
                       yend = yval[2],
                       alpha = "more transparent"),
                   size = size) +
        scale_alpha_manual("Alpha", values = c("less transparent" = 0.2,
                                               "more transparent" = 0.6))

```    

![ggplot_aes_inside](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11796327/44146832-58d1f80a-a089-11e8-9467-34b2b6ccae2d.png)

Many thanks for your time!

Cheers,
Alex

P.S.: amazing work, amazing package!
P.P.S.: I hope I didn't overlook anything obvious in the documentation
