title: Separate aesthetic mappings for geoms and for stats
description:
This issue was first brought up in #2570 but it's really a separate issue: In the current ggplot2, mappings for geoms and stats are muddled together. This works great 90% of the time and causes big frustrations the other 10%. The most obvious case is that we need separate stats in a horizontal and vertical context. They are identical except with `x` and `y` flipped. For example, this works:
```r
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = calc(density), color = Species)) + 
  geom_line(stat="density")
```
but this does not:
```r
ggplot(iris, aes(y = Sepal.Length, x = calc(density), color = Species)) +
  geom_line(stat="density")
```
Not very intuitive to the user, in my opinion.

A possible future extension could be to have the option of explicitly naming mappings only for the geom and only for the stat, like so:
```r
ggplot(iris,
       mapping_stat = aes(x = Sepal.Length),
       mapping_geom = aes(y = Sepal.Length, x = calc(density), color = Species)) + 
  geom_line(stat="density")
```
For backwards compatibility and ease of use, the default `mapping` argument could make an educated guess of how the mappings should be split up between the two.

The devils in the details, though, and I'm not sure whether the syntax should be as above, or rather:
```r
ggplot(iris,
       mapping_stat = aes(x = Sepal.Length),
       mapping_geom = aes(y = Sepal.Length, x = density, color = Species)) + 
  geom_line(stat="density")
```
or
```r
ggplot(iris,
       mapping_stat = aes(x = Sepal.Length),
       mapping_geom = aes(y = x, x = density, color = Species)) + 
  geom_line(stat="density")
```
 (I.e., mapping in the geom works directly from the column names provided by the stat.)

Finally, this raises the question whether it should be possible to chain stats together before handing the results to the geom. E.g., first run `stat_density()` to calculate density curves, then chain it to a stat that finds the maximum, and then feed into `geom_point()` to draw a point at the top of the density curve. I think this would be very useful, similar to the pipe operator in dplyr, but I'm not sure what a good user interface would be that gracefully extends the current ggplot2 syntax.

title: Simplify the usage of fortify() in ggplot()
description:
`ggplot.grouped_df()` was implemented in response to #2351. I feet, this is a kind of "fortifying" and at first thought implementing this was enough

```r
fortify.grouped_df <- function(data, ...) {
  data$.group <- dplyr::group_indices(data)
  data
}
```

so that the `ggplot.default()` calls this:

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/4463da6abc9b8ff7a2451686b9685de36933b358/R/plot.r#L80

But, my guess was wrong. Since a `grouped_df` is also a `data.frame`, `ggplot.data.frame()` is actually dispatched, where `fortify()` won't happen.

I wonder if it is possible to remove `ggplot.data.frame()` and change `ggplot.default()` to bellow to let `fortify()` always happen:

``` r
ggplot.default <- function(...) {
  data <- fortify(data)

  # (the current implementation of ggplot.data.frame comes here)
}
```

IMHO, it is a bit beneficial to implement the "fortifying" process as a method of `fortify()` since then the process is more transparent to the users. If this looks ok, I will try to make a PR.

title: font size in legend title theme is not inherited
description:
When setting the title theme via `guide_legend()` the fontsize is not inherited. This causes weird spacing issues because the fontsize is used for spacing calculations if `legend.spacing.x` and `legend.spacing.y` are not set (the default). Reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 3))
ggplot(df, aes(x, x, colour = x)) + geom_point() +
  scale_color_continuous(guide = guide_legend())
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/fgOBWUy.png)

``` r

ggplot(df, aes(x, x, colour = x)) + geom_point() +
  scale_color_continuous(guide = guide_legend(title.theme = element_text()))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/4uF5bER.png)

The fix is to replace this line:
```{r}
title_fontsize <- title.theme$size
```
with this line:
```{r}
title_fontsize <- title.theme$size %||% calc_element("legend.title", theme)$size
```
here: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/4463da6abc9b8ff7a2451686b9685de36933b358/R/guide-colorbar.r#L345
and here: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/4463da6abc9b8ff7a2451686b9685de36933b358/R/guide-legend.r#L348

The subsequent check for `NULL` could be replaced by another `%||%` statement in the same line.

title: Grammar of aesthetics
description:
As the types of plots people make with ggplot get ever more complex, it is becoming increasingly clear that having exactly one aesthetic mapping for each type of aesthetic (color, size, shape, etc.) for the entire plot is too limiting. There are good reasons why one might want, for example, two different color mappings in different layers (e.g., think about a map with a road layer and a city layer) or even in different parts of a geom within a single layer (e.g., the median line in a boxplot could be colored differently from the box itself). Here I want to start collecting some ideas about how this could be accomplished within the current ggplot2 framework. 

There are at least three distinct issues we need to consider:
1. It should be possible to use the same aesthetics with different scales in different layers (see issue https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2492). Ideally, this would happen in a manner that is transparent to the geoms. The geoms don't need to know whether they share aesthetics with other layers or not.

2. It should be possible to invent new aesthetics that don't currently exist in ggplot2, such as `colour.median`, `colour.box`, `colour.whiskers` for different parts of a boxplot (see issue https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2345). This can be done already, but what is not possible is to write a geom such that these alternative aesthetics are optional. For example, for a boxplot, we might want to be able to use `colour` to color everything uniformly, or `colour` + `colour.median`, or `colour` + `colour.whiskers`, etc. In the current codebase, if a geom defines a `colour.median` aesthetic then this aesthetic always has to be set separately from the `colour` aesthetic.

3. It should be possible to create aesthetics that are name-equivalent to other aesthetics. This equivalency currently exists for some aesthetics, such as the different spellings of `color` and `colour`, but it is hardcoded: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/b4796db28f20e3247e53b3a065c8f47a7fff741e/R/aes.r#L10-L23 If I invent a new aesthetic `colour.line` I cannot easily make it equivalent to `color.line` to accommodate both possible spellings.

I think that these three items can be addressed with three additions to the grammar, `aes_equal()`, `aes_distinct()`, and `aes_inherit()`.

## 1. `aes_equal()`

Usage:
```{r}
aes_equal(color = colour)
```

This means any instance of `color` in any geom, stat, scale, etc. is replaced by `colour` before any calculations are done. It's as if you had typed `colour` instead of `color` throughout the code.

Example:
```{r}
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, fill.colour = Species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7) + aes_equal(fill.colour = fill)
```
would be equivalent to:
```{r}
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7)
```

## 2. `aes_distinct()`

Usage:
```{r}
aes_distinct(colour2 = colour)
```

This means that `colour2` is treated as its own aesthetic all throughout the statistical transformations and scale training, but right before it is handed to a geom it is renamed into `colour`. This would allow different scales for different layers.

Example:
```{r}
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point(aes(color1 = Petal.Length), shape = '+') +
  geom_point(aes(color2 = Petal.Width), shape = 'x') +
  aes_distinct(color1 = colour, color2 = colour)
```
would draw a + and an x at each point position, each colored by a different data column.

## 3. `aes_inherit()`

Usage:
```{r}
aes_inherit(fill = colour)
```

This means that the `fill` aesthetic automatically mirrors the `colour` aesthetic, unless it is explicitly defined. In other words, if no variable is explicitly mapped onto `fill` then the mapping to `colour` is copied over to the mapping to `fill`.

Example:
```{r}
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, colour = Species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7) + aes_inherit(fill = colour)
```
would be equivalent to:
```{r}
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, colour = Species, fill = Species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7)
```

description:
Working on gganimate I came upon a little problem. For GeomPolygon and related geoms the alpha value is set to `NA` rather than 1, which is in practice the same. This results in bad transitions as transitioning into NA is ill-defined.

I could hack around this in tweenr/gganimate, but wondered whether you would be interested in a fix here instead.

title: qplot() ignores xlab and ylab arguments
description:
For example:
```r
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- rnorm(100, mean=x, sd=1/4)

qplot(x, y, xlab="x label", ylab="y label")
```
yields:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22243578/39480231-910a9a3a-4d35-11e8-904d-72dc86b810f6.png)
instead of:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22243578/39480273-b41b50fa-4d35-11e8-9e72-86e5083347d1.png)

A pair of minor changes to https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/R/quick-plot.r will resolve this issue.  At [line 86](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/2495ba23ee34ecd57330a3e8af1f9d089a5f3374/R/quick-plot.r#L86)
```r
xlab <- rlang::quo_name(exprs$x)
```
to 
```r
if(missing(xlab)) xlab <- rlang::quo_name(exprs$x)
```
and at [lines 88-91](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/2495ba23ee34ecd57330a3e8af1f9d089a5f3374/R/quick-plot.r#L86-L91):
```r
if (rlang::quo_is_null(exprs$y)) {
        ylab <- "NULL"
    }
    else {
        ylab <- rlang::quo_name(exprs$y)
    }
```
to
```
if(missing(ylab)) {
  if (rlang::quo_is_null(exprs$y)) {
          ylab <- "NULL"
      }
      else {
          ylab <- rlang::quo_name(exprs$y)
      }
}
```

title: Relative positioning of `annotate` -- extend the documentation
description:
I think the documentation of `ggplot2::annotate` should be extended with explanation of how to use `hjust` and `vjust` to position the output **relatively** to the plot boundaries.
At least one example should be added as well. 

-----
Background:

In the usual scenario where I use `ggplot2::annotate` I do not want to position the text at the exact XY location. I rather care about something like "top-right-corner". I strongly believe this is the case for most users. 
The documentation of `ggplot2::annotate` however is very much focused on the XY positioning, including a bunch of examples. 

According to [this answer on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/a/27777562/3494126) it's actually quite easy to position the text relatively to the plot box. 
The usage should also be obvious to an advanced ggplot user. However, I still think it belongs into the documentation. I am not sure how exactly `hjust` and `vjust` work here, so I cannot provide examples myself.

title: No default angle in element_text when using label.theme and title.theme in guide_legend leads to error when setting other parameters
description:
When using `guide = guide_legend(...)` to change non-`angle` parameters of `label.theme` or `title.theme`, an error is generated due to non-`NULL` value for `angle`.


Here are examples trying to set `face`, without setting `angle`:

``` r
library(ggplot2)                                                                                                                                                       
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                                                                               
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                         
scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(label.theme = element_text(face = "italic")))                                                                                
#> Error in element_grob.element_text(element = label.theme, label = label, : Text element requires non-NULL value for 'angle'.
                                                                                                                                                                       
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                                                                               
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                         
scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(title.theme = element_text(face = "italic")))                                                                                
#> Error in element_grob.element_text(guide$title.theme %||% calc_element("legend.title", : Text element requires non-NULL value for 'angle'.
```

(`reprex` inserts an 'empty plot placeholder' here, despite the code above errors...)
![](https://i.imgur.com/uPzwuEC.png)

Trying to set `size`, `hjust` or `vjust` without setting `angle` leads to the same error.


To change any non-`angle` parameters, we need to set `angle` as well. E.g.:

``` r
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                                                                               
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                         
scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(label.theme = element_text(face = "italic", angle = 0)))                                                                     
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Ur6kZLm.png)

----

In contrast, there is no need to explicitly set any of the other `NULL` arguments in `element_text` when setting `angle` only:

``` r
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                                                                               
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                         
scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(                                                                                                                             
label.theme = element_text(angle = -5)))                                                                                                                               
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/njLYTVF.png)

``` r
                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                       
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                                                                               
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                         
scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(                                                                                                                             
title.theme = element_text(angle = 5)))                                                                                                                                
```

title: Enable User Defined Theme Elements
description:
This issue is at the suggestion of Hadley, based on the following: 

https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/2305

I am the author of the [ggtern](http://ggtern.com) package, which requires a whole bunch (50+) of new theme elements outside of the standard ggplot2 themes defined in the non-exported `.element_tree` object.

In this issue I will speak of my experience with ggtern, however, it is possible that any extension author may face the same problem.

The complexity of ggtern (and its sensitivity to changes within ggplot2) can be HUGELY reduced if there was a mechanism for extension authors such as myself to be able to create their own theme elements, and add them to the `.element_tree`. The solution I had proposed within the above link (via use of R6 class) had resolved this, with no impinging effect or risk to existing ggplot2 functionality.

Because I cannot add new theme elements, this means that I need to duplicate the `.element_tree` within the ggtern package, and add my new theme elements / hierarchies. This in turn means that many of the plot construction routines also needs to be held as a duplicate inside the ggtern library, leading to fragilities and vulnerabilities to changes within base ggplot2, which happens almost every year. I am trying to remove these fragilities.

To me it seems very logical for extension authors to be able to create their own theme elements. At the moment there is no way to do this to my knowledge other than the method used in ggtern, which is far from ideal. The theme element tree offered by ggplot2 is quite substantial, but by no means is it exhaustive, as has been demonstrated in ggtern, requiring dozens more for it to function properly.

title: Feature request: make clipping configurable
description: I frequently would like to be able to draw things that fall outside of the plot panel. This is currently not possible, as clipping is strictly enforced and not configurable. I think it would be nice if this could be switched on or off. First, as motivation, an example where it would be useful. Then my proposal of how it could be implemented. Consider this plot: ```{r} mt_named <- data.frame(mtcars, name = row.names(mtcars)) p <- ggplot(mt_named, aes(mpg, reorder(name, mpg))) + geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#0072B2") + geom_text(aes(x = mpg + .5, label = name), hjust = 0, size = 3) + scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, breaks = NULL, expand = c(0, 1)) + theme_bw() + theme(panel.border = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.line.x = element_line(), plot.margin = margin(6, 45, 6, 6)) p ``` The top-most text label is cut off because it extends beyond the plot area. To make it fit, I could extend the axis range, but that would extend the axis line as well. It looks more elegant to switch of clipping and have the text label extend outside of the plot area: ```{r} g <- ggplotGrob(p) index <- grep("panel", g$layout$name) g$layout$clip[index] = "off" grid::grid.newpage() grid::grid.draw(g) ``` I would like to propose to address this by making clipping a feature of the coordinate system. For example, the above plot could be generated by something like this: ```{r} p + coord_cartesian(clip = "off") ``` This feature requires very minimal changes to the coord code and the facet layouting code. I'll see if I can put together a pull request implementing this.

title: Close Contours Correctly for `geom='polygon'` in stat_contour
description:
Currently contours that end at the edges of the domain are not closed as one would expect, e.g.:

```r
library(reshape2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(melt(t(volcano)), aes(x=Var1, y=Var2, z=value, fill=..level..)) +
  stat_contour(geom='polygon')
```
Produces:
![screen shot 2018-04-26 at 8 37 40 am](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6105908/39306085-244fcc82-492d-11e8-8636-c69676219fa1.png)

Closed issue #1066 is related.

@eliocamp has a [potential fix](https://github.com/eliocamp/metR/blob/master/R/stat_contour_fill.R#L36) that involves expanding the grid to create a margin of sorts and setting all the values there to the mean of the z values so that the contours will close naturally.

@mdsumner has a [work-around using using `countourPolys::fcountour`](https://github.com/hypertidy/contourPolys) which if I understand correctly computes all the sub-polygons required to get the full contour working, and plots them all.  I haven't actually run this so I may be misunderstanding.  Scaling is likely an issue, and there is the issue that we're faking a large polygon with lots of little ones.

Ideally we would actually modify the contour function so that it internally closes the contour, but that is likely a fair bit more difficult to do.  

Another option suggested by @hadley in #1066 is to patch up the output of `contourLines` rather than tricking `countourLines` to close the contours by expanding the range.  This seems slightly cleaner, but I'm not sure the final result is actually any better than @eliocamp's solution and is more work relative to where we are today.

title: geom_label hjust/vjust pulls text out of box
description:
## Problem description

For two plots on an automatic report, we try to add labels with standard quality information (like RMSE) to the upper left corner. We use `geom_label` to display the multi-line text with a box around it.

The label with `x = -Inf, y = Inf` is aligned in the upper left corner without any space between the border of the plot and the border of the box (see `plot_functional`).

We try to use the `hjust` and `vjust` parameters of `geom_label` to introduce a spacing between the box border and the plot border (e.g. y-axis).

### Expected behavior
The box created by `geom_label` is horizontally and vertically adjusted according to the `hjust` and `vjust` parameter **and** the text within the `geom_label` box is properly aligned within the box according to the box border.

### Observed behavior
The box created by `geom_label` is horizontally and vertically adjusted according to the `hjust` and `vjust` parameter **but** the text is dragged out of the `geom_label` box and isn't properly aligned according to the box border (or text begin).

*See section 'Plots of the reproduction code'*


## Code for problem reproduction
Executed with `ggplot2` from the current CRAN release and the master branch from this repository.

```r
library(ggplot2)

# Prepare data with only two points to span a plot (with min and max)
data <- data.frame(x = c(1, 100), y = c(1, 100))

# Plot only the two given points
plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()

# Add label in upper left corner, with different hjust and vjust values (to align distance to upper left corner)
plot_functional  <- plot + geom_label(x = -Inf, y = Inf, aes(label = "ABC\nABCDEF\nAB"), hjust =  0, vjust = 1)
plot_error_hjust <- plot + geom_label(x = -Inf, y = Inf, aes(label = "ABC\nABCDEF\nAB"), hjust = -2, vjust = 1)
plot_error_vjust <- plot + geom_label(x = -Inf, y = Inf, aes(label = "ABC\nABCDEF\nAB"), hjust =  0, vjust = 7)
plot_error_both  <- plot + geom_label(x = -Inf, y = Inf, aes(label = "ABC\nABCDEF\nAB"), hjust = -2, vjust = 7)

# Print them
print(plot_functional)
print(plot_error_hjust)
print(plot_error_vjust)
print(plot_error_both)
```

## Plots of the reproduction code
**Output: `plot_functional`**
Plot the box in the upper left corner.
The text is left aligned in the box and the box is correctly displayed in the upper left corner.

![plot_functional](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7292949/39236465-4018d436-4879-11e8-87c0-81ae9570b48b.png)

**Output: `plot_hjust`**
Plot the box in the upper left corner and apply a bigger `hjust`.
The text is dragged out of the box and isn't correctly aligned at the line beginning.

![plot_hjust](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7292949/39236490-45b5bd64-4879-11e8-9cbe-24a27cbd657b.png)

**Output: `plot_vjust`**
Plot the box in the upper left corner and apply a bigger `vjust`.
The text is dragged in top direction and not correctly aligned in the box anymore.

![plot_vjust](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7292949/39236496-48757e90-4879-11e8-9724-c9da8a7a9ace.png)

**Output: `plot_both`**
Plot the box in the upper left corner and apply a bigger `hjust` **and** `vjust`.
The text is dragged out of the box. It looks like the previous effects superposition each other.

![plot_both](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7292949/39236445-379afd16-4879-11e8-947c-fe4fdba386ea.png)

title: Export generics
description:
From Kurt Hornik:

---

You may have seen that from R 3.5.0 onwards searching for S3 methods
uses the registry after hitting topenv and before the search path, and
there is also a way of not using the search path at all, which can be
achieved by setting R_S3_METHOD_LOOKUP_BASEENV_AFTER_GLOBALENV_=true in
the environment.  The Debian regular checks are currently performed with
this setting.

This shows S3 method lookup problems in about 250 CRAN packages, mostly
simply due to packages failing to register S3 methods when they could
and should.  However, there are also cases when this is not possible:
R-exts says in "Registering S3 methods",

  To ensure that these methods are available the packages defining the
  methods should ensure that the generics are imported and register the
  methods using 'S3method' directives.

which of course needs that the generics are *exported*.

Now, apparently several packages see the need to provide S3 methods for
the generics

  guide_train 
  scale_type

which ggplot2 provides but does not export: my current list is

  colorplaner/NAMESPACE:export(guide_train.colorplane)
  ggraph/NAMESPACE:export(guide_train.edge_colourbar)
  ggraph/NAMESPACE:export(guide_train.edge_direction)
  phylopath/NAMESPACE:export(guide_train.edge_colourbar)

  ggforce/NAMESPACE:export(scale_type.units)
  ggmosaic/NAMESPACE:export(scale_type.product)
  ggmosaic/NAMESPACE:export(scale_type.productlist)
  ggraph/NAMESPACE:export(scale_type.geometry)

Would it be possible for ggplot2 to export these generics, so that the
above exports could be turned into proper S3 method registrations?

title: Possible to get coef to behave in geom_boxplot like range behaves in boxplot?
description:
The `coef` argument in `geom_boxplot` doesn't behave like the `range` argument like `boxplot`. It seems that these two arguments are meant to be the same thing. I would like the whiskers to extend to the extremes of the distribution. With base `boxplot` setting `range=0` will do this, but `range` won't work with `geom_boxplot`. Setting `coef` to 0 in `geom_boxplot` gets you no whiskers at all. One could set `coef` to an absurdly large number to achieve the goal, but if the IQR is 0, then it won't work. I see in the `geom_boxplot` example the other workaround is to populate the 5 cardinal values of the boxplot, but that's a lot for what seems like a simple goal.

```r
d <- diamonds[ sample(nrow(diamonds), 1000), ] %>% select(carat, cut)
garbage <- tibble(cut="garbage", carat=c(rep(0, 195), 1, 1.2, 2.3, 2.4, 3))
d_garbage <- rbind(d, garbage)

p <- ggplot(d_garbage, aes(x = cut, y = carat))
p + geom_boxplot()
p + geom_boxplot(range=0) #Warning: Ignoring unknown parameters: range
p + geom_boxplot(coef=0) #No whiskers
p + geom_boxplot(coef=10000) #Whiskers extend to extremes for everything but "garbage"

boxplot(d_garbage$carat ~ d_garbage$cut) #Output similar to p + geom_boxplot()
boxplot(d_garbage$carat ~ d_garbage$cut, range=0) #Desired output
```

title: Allow `fun` in stat_summary_2d to return `data.frame`
description:
I'm working with very dense timeseries (indeed very dense series of images), where I want to plot the spatial/temporal variability of certain parameters in a 2D histogram-like object. Since I have too many points, I do not want to simply use `geom_raster` or `geom_tile`, but I'd like to bin them into larger units first.  
Of course, this is possible with `stat_summary_2d`; however I'd like to have more flexibility in controlling how the statistics are mapped to the aesthetics.  
As an,  example, I will be using a dataset from `gstat`. Here I'm plotting the mean PM10 concentration measured by several stations versus  time and station altitude, where I bin the time in units of 30 days:
``` r
library(gstat)
library(sp)
library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date
library(tidyverse)

data("DE_RB_2005")

msd <- function(x)
{
  data.frame(mean=mean(x), sd=sd(x))
}

#Re-add dates to STFDF object
DE_RB_2005.df <- as.data.frame(DE_RB_2005) %>% mutate(time=ymd(time))

#Binning units
bins <- c(7, 100)

p.base <- ggplot(DE_RB_2005.df, aes(x = time, y = station_altitude, z = PM10))

#This works
p1 <-  p.base + geom_raster(stat = "summary_2d",aes(fill = ..value..), binwidth = bins)

p1
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/Dhfx0dD.png)

And clearly this first approach works.  
Now, suppose that `stat_summary2d` would accept a function such as `msd`, which takes a numerical vector and returns a dataframe; where the "secret double dot variables" `..mean` and `..sd..` would be pulled from the dataframe returned when `msd` is called for each bin. This would be useful to simultaneously display several pieces of information about the distribution of PM10 inside each bin, by mapping these variables to different aesthetic:
``` r
 
#This does not work, would require fun to accept data.frame as output
p2 <- p.base + geom_raster(stat="summary_2d", fun=msd, aes(fill =..mean.., alpha=..sd..))

p2
#> Warning: Computation failed in `stat_summary2d()`:
#> replacement has 1302 rows, data has 651
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/8YE6m5T.png)

This does not work, I presume the error message means that the returned dataframe is somehow flattened by appending both columns together. 
Would it be possible/easy to change the behavior of `stat_summary_2d` to accept a dataframe as an output and to map the columns to double dot variables?

The "orthogonal" operations would be very useful as well, allowing to select multiple variables for `z` and having `fun` applied to each of the variables, similarly to `dplyr::summarise_all`:
``` r

#This is crazy and definetly does not work
p3 <- ggplot(DE_RB_2005.df, aes(x = time, y = station_altitude, z = c("PM10", "annual_mean_PM10"))) + geom_raster(stat = "summary_2d", fun = msd, aes(fill =..value_PM10.., alpha=..value_annual_mean_PM10..))

p3
#> Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...): object '..value_PM10..' not found
```
Clearly this does not work at the moment, I suppose it would require tidy evaluation or something of that sort.

title: Exported function ggplot2::exprs conflicts with Bioconductor Biobase::exprs
description:
The recent export of `exprs` poses a real problem when used in combination with `Biobase`, which is basically systematically loaded when using any package from Bioconductor. I suspect this will affect many users (i.e. almost any body working in the field of Bioinformatics). It is equivalent to shadowing a fundamental function in the `base`, on which any analysis or package code rely.
Given how long `Biobase::exprs` has been around and the trouble this can pose to the R community, it would be great to consider renaming this function.

The export by the `rlang` package is actually also a problem, although it may have had a lesser impact because it is less often imported and loaded, and can be selectively imported.

title: `position = "jitter"` and `position = position_jitter()` have different behavior
description: I noticed today that `position = "jitter"` is not the same as `position = position_jitter()`, and the behavior described in the documentation for `position = position_jitter()` cannot be obtained for `position = "jitter"`. The underlying issue is a ggproto behavior that has caught me off guard many times (see below). First the reprex. We start with a simple plot with jitter: ```{r} df <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 1, 2), y = c(1, 1, 2, 2)) set.seed(1234) ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(position = "jitter") ``` The following code produces different jitter: ```{r} set.seed(1234) ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(position = position_jitter()) ``` However, this reproduces the jitter from the first example: ```{r} set.seed(1234) ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(seed = NULL)) ``` The problem is that `position = "jitter"` does not use the default arguments defined in `position_jitter()`, and therefore `seed` is set to `NULL`, not to `NA`, when we use `position = "jitter"`. This same problem happens generally with ggproto, e.g. when we call a geom with `geom_*()` vs. `geom = "*"`, and it has bitten me many times in different scenarios. There are two ways to fix this particular problem: 1. The simple way: Don't set `seed = NA` as default in `position_jitter()`. 2. The complicated way: Fix the ggproto behavior so the default arguments apply when objects are specified by their name.

title: Better pipe support
description:
ggplot uses addition between the different elements. I see the argument against using a the pipe operator, especially because ggplot does not use function composition. However, I find piping into ggplot a  a bit awkward, and I propose that a kind of sum function is added that makes piping cleaner. The piping is especially awkward when the return value is piped further on.



In the examples below I use print as a placeholder function, this could be a function that handled saving the plot.

    plotting_function <- print

Example using plain ggplot. Note the ugly parentheses needed because of the precedence of pipe over plus operators.

    # Parentheses needed. Ends after ggtitle()
    (mtcars %>% 
        ggplot() +
            aes(x=hp, y=mpg) +
            geom_point() +
            geom_smooth() +
            ggtitle('Fantastic Plot')) %>%
        plotting_function()


Example implementation:

    ggplot_sum <- function(data, ...){
        p <- ggplot(data)
        args = list(...)
        for (arg in args){
            p <- p + arg
        }
        return (p)
    }

Which allow you to nicely group the ggplotting

    mtcars %>% 
        ggplot_sum(
            aes(x=hp, y=mpg),
            geom_point(),
            geom_smooth(),
            ggtitle('Fantastic Plot')) %>%
        plotting_function()

I think it is a good call to not include the pipe operator as rejected in #2326, but I still think the interaction with the tidyverse could be improved. An alternative to the above is to use `add` from `magrittr`

    mtcars %>% 
        ggplot() %>%
        add(aes(x=hp, y=mpg)) %>%
        add(geom_point()) %>%
        add(geom_smooth()) %>%
        add(ggtitle('Fantastic Plot')) %>%
        plotting_function()

I think the `ggplot_sum` is much cleaner and I like how it groups plotting elements together.

title: Polygons with holes
description:
Is stat_density2d behaving like it should? It seems to me that it is not making holes into existing polygons when the same value region is inside another.  The thing is that these areas show up as denser colors when you have alpha enabled. Yet the value of each of the shapes is the same and with fully opaque they do fill completely.

![rplot02](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/18376200/37932563-78c5e1e6-3151-11e8-98fc-cb5c199137bc.png)

**Image 1**: Image with holes is probably how it should work, image on the right (without holes) is how it works.

Is this intentional or is this a limitation of the engine? Because seems to me that the engine itself can make compound paths and thus should be easy to use even odd rule to make them holes. If not one could just connect the shapes with a sliver, although i would avoid that.

The way i have fixed these images is just make every color region a compound path and then set the rule to even odd. But seems quite misleading and should be easily addressable.

description:

I'll include an example of the book "Text Mining With R: a Tidy Approach" by Julia Silge and David Robinson so you can see where it fails.

title: Percentage-y-scales with ..density.. in geom_histogram() works in facets with natural numbers, but not with (downscaled) decimal numbers
description:
I have a problem with percentage y-axes for histograms in facet-pots (using the scales-package). Everything worked just fine when I used the original scale, but it failed when I rescaled the items in an interval between 0 and 1.

Here's my example data:

```r
# ----- Facet Plot ------
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)
library(reshape2)

# Trial 1 ----
set.seed(1234)
id <- c(1:40)

# Create five items with values between 0 and 5
x1 <- runif(n = 40, min = 0, max = 5) %>% round()
x2 <- runif(n = 40, min = 0, max = 5) %>% round()
x3 <- runif(n = 40, min = 0, max = 5) %>% round()
x4 <- runif(n = 40, min = 0, max = 5) %>% round()
x5 <- runif(n = 40, min = 0, max = 5) %>% round()

# Make data
data <- cbind(id, x1, x2, x3, x4, x5) %>% as.data.frame()

# Make Index
data %<>% mutate(x6 = (x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5)/5)
```

Now I wanted to make a facet-plot, showing the histograms of each of the items and its respective percentage on the y-axis. Therefore I used **aes(y = ..density..)** (as I found out on [Stack Overlow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9614720/obtaining-percent-scales-reflective-of-individual-facets-with-ggplot2?rq=1) for the histograms and everything works perfectly fine. This was exactly the plot I needed:

```r
# Long format data frame for facet plot
long.data <- melt(data, id.vars = "id")
head(long.data)

# And make the plot:
ggplot(data = long.data, aes(value)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 6,
                 aes(y = ..density..)) +
  facet_wrap(~variable) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  theme_bw()

# Everything is just fine: The continuous x-scale and a percentage-y-scale.
```
![01-facets](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/31796340/37893463-651bffd4-30db-11e8-97a8-8c79f4f2870b.jpeg)


But then, I had to re-scale the items to the interval between 0 and 1 for different models and analyses:

```r
# Trial 2 ----

data %<>% mutate(x1_resc = x1/6,
                 x2_resc = x2/6,
                 x3_resc = x3/6,
                 x4_resc = x4/6,
                 x5_resc = x5/6,
                 x6_resc = (x1_resc + x2_resc + x3_resc + x4_resc + x5_resc)/5)
```

As I ran the code again (the ggplot-code is identical to the one above), the y-axes of the histograms changed. Instead of the respective percentages, the axes show now percentage values between 0 and 200%. 

```r
# Long format
long.data <- melt(data[, c(1, 8:13)], id.vars = "id")
head(long.data)

# And the plot
ggplot(data = long.data, aes(value)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 6,
                 aes(y = ..density..)) +
  facet_wrap(~variable) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  theme_bw()
```
![02-facets](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/31796340/37893469-68351bf6-30db-11e8-8910-573ca18f351f.jpeg)

I can work with multiple workarounds (e.g. upscaling my items in the long-format and re-labelling the x-axis of the first plot), but I still hope this is an issue worth noticing.

```r
  geom_smooth(method = "gam")

ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
```

title: No errors when size and color are not constant over the line and linetype is dotted / dashed
description:
The code below
`
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_line(aes(mpg, wt, colour = factor(cyl),
                linetype = factor(am), size = gear))
` 
produces the following error: 
`
Error: geom_path: If you are using dotted or dashed lines, colour, size and linetype must be constant over the line
`

However, this code works without throwing the error message: 

`
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_line(aes(mpg, wt, colour = factor(cyl),
                linetype = factor(am), size = factor(gear)))
`

even though the color and size are not constant over the line. As well as those snippets: 

`
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_line(aes(mpg, wt, colour = factor(cyl), size = factor(gear)), linetype = 2)

ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_line(aes(mpg, wt, colour = factor(cyl)), linetype = 2)

ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_line(aes(mpg, wt, size = factor(cyl)), linetype = 2)
`

It seems that either 1) the error message is wrong and should change "constant" to "discrete" because the error is thrown only in case continuous variables or 2) just a bug.

title: Facetting and preserve = 'single' produces ever narrower bars.
description:
This may be similar to #2290

When using `position_dodge(preserve='single')` to maintain the width of bars in a `geom_bar`, applying facetting results in the bars getting their 'single' width from the number of bars for each x value as a whole, rather than within the facet. 

Applying `preserve='total'` simply results in bars being wider than desired.

Hopefully the example below makes things clear.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)
player <- c('Player1', 'Player1', 'Player2', 'Player2', 'Player3', 'Player3', 'Player4')
bool_val <- c('TRUE', 'FALSE', 'TRUE', 'FALSE', 'TRUE', 'FALSE', 'TRUE')
var1 <- c(1.5, 1.9, 2.7, 2.8, 3.0, 1.4, 1.7)
var2 <- c(1, 2, 3, 1.5, 1.2, 2.4, 2.2)
var3 <- c(1.7, 0.2, 1.3, 2.5, 2.2, 2.2, 3)

df <- data.frame(player, bool_val, var1, var2, var3)

long_df <- melt(df, id.vars=c('player', 'bool_val'))

ggplot(long_df, aes(x=variable, y=value, fill=bool_val)) + geom_bar(stat='identity', position=position_dodge2(preserve='total')) + facet_grid(player~., scales='free_x')
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/0LLVANe.png)

``` r

ggplot(long_df, aes(x=variable, y=value, fill=bool_val)) + geom_bar(stat='identity', position=position_dodge2(preserve='single')) + facet_grid(player~., scales='free_x')
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/xB0eZSM.png)

title: Error occurs when changing facet labels in facet_grid and add geom_vline at the same time
description:
An error suggesting that one column cannot be found when the facet labels are changed in `facet_grid`, while that column does exist.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

df <- data.frame(weeks = rep(-3:3, each = 2),
                 is_manual = rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), times = 7),
                 value = c(rnorm(7, 10), rnorm(7, 20)))

# This works
ggplot(df %>% mutate(is_manual = ifelse(is_manual, "Manual", "Uploaded")),
       aes(x = weeks, y = value)) + geom_line() +
  facet_grid(is_manual ~ .) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = 2)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/mv93bm9.png)

``` r

# But this generates an error listed below
ggplot(df, aes(x = weeks, y = value)) + geom_line() +
  facet_grid(ifelse(is_manual, "Manual", "Uploaded") ~ .) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = 2)
#> Error in ifelse(is_manual, "Manual", "Uploaded"): object 'is_manual' not found
```

The last chunk of codes returns an error:

> Error in ifelse(is_manual, "Manual", "Uploaded"): object 'is_manual' not found

, but it can actually be found in the data frame. Once the `geom_vline` line is deleted, the code works fine.

For more detailed demonstration and trials that I've done, please check [my question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49355839/error-occurs-when-changing-facet-labels-in-facet-grid-and-add-geom-vline-at-the) on Stack Overflow.

title: geom_hex ignores size aesthetic/parameter
description:
geom_hex defines a size default of 0.5, which by analogy with other filled geoms I would expect to control line weight (e.g. geom_bin2d, see bottom).

But it never gets passed to `hexGrob` so there is no change in the output size.

There's also an interesting inconsistency which may or may not be issue-worthy: geom_hex claims size as an aesthetic (in docs), whereas geom_bin2d does not, and for geom_bin2d size does indeed not work as an a aesthetic, only as a parameter, it seems.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price))

# This doesn't work as expected
p + geom_hex(size = 0.1, color = "red")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/4vzHcmx.png)

``` r
p + geom_hex(size = 2, color = "red")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/B5sAJPm.png)

``` r
p + geom_hex(aes(size = cut), color = "red")
#> Warning: Using size for a discrete variable is not advised.
```

``` r

# This does work as expected
p + geom_bin2d(size = 0.1, color = "red")
```

title: A possible geom_table
description:
I am the author and maintainer of 'ggpmisc'. In the Bitbucket version of 'ggpmisc' at "aphalo/ggpmisc" I have defined a `geom_table` that uses almost the same syntax as `ggplot2::geom_text` but accepts tibbles mapped to `label`. The code relies on package 'gtable' for much of actual work.

For this to work tibbles need to be handled by 'ggplot2' as such all the way through to geoms. This is the case for 'ggplot2' 2.2.1.9000. This has been working as far back as May 2017, but I think it was made possible by a commit even earlier in 2017.

So, I have two questions:
1) Is this something you would like to add to 'ggplot2'? (would add a dependency on 'gtable').
2) If it seems preferable to keep `geom_table` in 'ggpmisc', do you have any idea of when 'ggplot2' 2.2.2 will make it to CRAN? (this is related to deciding on whether to delay the next update to 'ggpmisc' until the release of 'ggplot2' 2.2.2 or create a branch without this geom for CRAN.

A example follows:
```
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpmisc)

tb <- tibble("alpha" = c("x[2]~\"=\"~a^2", "sqrt(y)"), 
             "beta" = c("x[2]~\"=\"~b^2", "sqrt(1/y)"))
my.tb <- tibble(x = 0, y = 0, tb = list(tb))
ggplot(my.tb, aes(x, y, label = tb)) +
  geom_table(parse = TRUE)
```

title: The cross effect in legend when use geom_hline and geom_vline in the same plot.
description:
That problem was very discussed in issue [geom\_vline messes up geom\_line legend, if show\_guide = TRUE](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/1267), but a similar problem still happen, as was mentioned by [rdcominer](https://github.com/rdcomineor) in this [comment](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/1267#issuecomment-187116698), when both hline and vline are in the same plot. _**The legend of that plot, regarding hline and vline will be overlapping.**_

Here's are the examples:

``` r
library(ggplot2)                                                                                                                                                                               
df <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2), y = c(1, 2), z = c("a", "b"))                                                                                                                                    
threshold <- data.frame(x = c(1.2, 1.5), name = c("bar", "foo"))                                                                                                                               
```
Both legends are shown (vline and hline) which procude the cross effect

``` r
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = z)) +                                                                                                                                                            
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                                                 
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1.25, linetype = "dotted"), colour= 'red', data = threshold) +                                                                                                     
geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 1.75, linetype = "1F"), colour= 'blue', data = threshold) +                                                                                                        
scale_linetype_manual(name = "Thresholds",values = c(2,2))                                                                                                                                     
```
![unnamed-chunk-2-1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1872321/37482519-5a458788-2852-11e8-8c1a-bfffb499fe13.png)

I tried to use show.legend = FALSE in one of them, to see what happens, but ggplot2 preserve the pattern of another one in both legends.

Then the next example, show us only geom\_vline legend which preserves the vline pattern in legends

``` r
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = z)) +                                                                                                                                                            
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                                                 
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1.25, linetype = "dotted"), colour= 'red', data = threshold) +                                                                                                     
geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 1.75, linetype = "1F"), colour= 'blue', 
                     data = threshold, show.legend = FALSE) +                                                                                   
scale_linetype_manual(name = "Thresholds",values = c(2,2))                                                                                                                                     
```
![unnamed-chunk-3-1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1872321/37482542-65e7c8ee-2852-11e8-9f49-d577df8a907b.png)

The next one, the only geom\_hline legend is shown which preserve the hline pattern in legends

``` r
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = z)) +                                                                                                                                                            
geom_point() +                                                                                                                                                                                 
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1.25, linetype = "dotted"), colour= 'red', 
                    data = threshold,show.legend = FALSE) +                                                                                 
geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 1.75, linetype = "1F"), colour= 'blue', data = threshold) +                                                                                                        
scale_linetype_manual(name = "Thresholds",values = c(2,2))                                                                                                                                     
```
![unnamed-chunk-4-1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1872321/37482548-6d7bfae4-2852-11e8-932d-b2f6d00f445a.png)

-----

If is possible, would be nice to allow both hline and vline in the same plot, with a horizontal line in hline legend, and a vertical line in vline legend.

title: Giving boundary might produce incorrect histogram
description:
In the following cases the plotted histogram has the first to bins incorrectly merged into one.
```R
qplot(c(1,1,1,2,2,3), binwidth=1, boundary=0)
qplot(c(1,1,1,2,2,3), binwidth=1, center=0.5)
```
The expected behaviour should be similar to the output of
```R
qplot(c(1,1,1,2,2,3), binwidth=1, boundary=1e-16)
```

Surprisingly, the following behaves correctly (only adding `xlim` w.r.t. the first example)
```R
qplot(c(1,1,1,2,2,3), binwidth=1, boundary=0) + xlim(0,3)
```
Note: I'm using master (39e4a3b) to test.

title: position_dodge2() should handle both point and interval geoms
description:
Displaying raw data together with box plots can be useful.

If using both 'x' and 'fill' aesthetic geom_boxplot() handles NA's elegantly through the new position_dodge2(), but unfortunately geom_point() with a matching 'colour' aesthetic is misaligned with the boxes both when using position_dodge() and position_dodge2().

This problem only occurs when handling NA's, and position_dodge() and position_dodge2() gets it wrong in different ways:

```r
library('tidyverse')

dat <- data.frame("value" = rnorm(n=30, mean=2, sd=0.5),
                  "group" = LETTERS[1:3],
                  "x" = factor(1:2))

dat$value[dat$group=="A"&dat$x=="1"] <- NA

ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=value)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=group), alpha=0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour=group), position=position_dodge(width=0.75), size=3, alpha=0.5)

ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=value)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=group), alpha=0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour=group), position=position_dodge2(width=0.75), size=3, alpha=0.5)

```

title: hjust inconsistent in strip.text: text is still self-centered
description:
This may be the same underlying issue as #1892 but I don't think the explanation there covers this consequence:

![Example](https://i.imgur.com/5oanmU5.png)

```r
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(strip.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))

# hjust correctly aligns the text block
p + facet_wrap(~ am, labeller = as_labeller(c(
    `0` = "This is manual. Or is it auto?",
    `1` = "This is auto. Or is it manual?"
  )))

# but it doesn't align the text itself, visible when there's a line break
p + facet_wrap(~ am, labeller = as_labeller(c(
    `0` = "This is manual.\nOr is it auto?",
    `1` = "This is auto. Or is it manual?"
  )))

# Unlike other themed elements
p + xlab(paste0(
    "This is probably the number of cylinders, and you have to wonder\n",
    "if anyone ever made a car with an odd number of cylinders"
  )) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
}
```

title: Scaling of plot depends on letter shapes in titles
description:
When trying to create two different graphs with identical dimensions, I stumbled across this problem.

# Expected behaviour
Scaling of a graph should not depend on which letters are used in main or axis titles.

# Actual behaviour
Using g, j, p, q, or y in a title leads to different vertical scaling of the graph.

# Suspected cause
The space calculation is probably not based on the font baseline but rather on the absolute letter size. I guess this is a general issue with element_text().

```r
# y-scaling should look exactly the same, but doesn't.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point() + ggtitle("Title with an h")
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point() + ggtitle("Title with a g")
```

title: facet_grid uses unexpected environment to evaluate I(.) (AsIs) -- trouble with ad-hoc faceting
description:
I'm trying to facet by an ad-hoc column like so:

```
library(ggplot2)
NN = 100
DF = data.frame(x = rnorm(NN), grp1 = runif(NN) > .3, grp2 = runif(NN))
ggplot() + 
  geom_density(data = DF, aes(x = x, group = grp1)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ I(grp2 > .6))
# Error in structure(x, class = unique(c("AsIs", oldClass(x)))) : 
#   object 'grp2' not found

# compare to (works as expected, only difference is
#   grp2_break was ad-hoc above, explicitly
#   defined here)
DF$grp2_break = DF$grp2 > .6
ggplot() + 
  geom_density(data = DF, aes(x = x, group = grp1)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ grp2_break)
```

That is, my code fails saying `grp2` not found. But it seems to still have `DF` in scope (i.e., it's not that I've suddenly introduced a new column), as seen in the latter snippet where we add the ad-hoc column, which works as expected.

My current workaround is to call `DF` directly, but this is unworkable if the `data` input is dynamic/subsetted/any case where a direct call to `DF` is impossible:

```
ggplot() + 
  geom_density(data = DF, aes(x = x, group = grp1)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ I(DF$grp2 > .6))
```

Is this expected behavior? It should be documented if so, since this differs from the expected `formula` functionality.

------

FWIW this came up when I was trying to facet the hours of the day into a 4x6 grid; the way I thought to do this is `facet_grid(I(hour %% 4) ~ I(hour %/%4))`. Neither of those quantities makes sense to store as a new variable, they're simply dummies to trick `facet_grid` into giving me what I want. It doesn't solve the issue presented above (which rears its head in other forms as well), but I'm open to other suggestions to accomplish this as well.

title: stat_contour's breaks parameter is undocumented
description:
When trying to use `geom_contour` to draw lines at specific levels à la `contour(..., levels = ...)`, I discovered [this SO answer](https://stackoverflow.com/a/19658236/4497050) which documents that `geom_contour` can be passed a `breaks` parameter to specify particular _z_ values where contour lines should be drawn.

Weirdly, this behavior is not documented in `?geom_contour`, `?geom_density_2d`, `?layer`, or `?ggplot2:::StatContour`, and taking a cursory look at the source, I'm not sure where the `breaks` parameter is picked up. Given the behavior is important enough to merit a parameter in `contour`, seems like it should be in the docs.

I can make a PR if you like, but the problem is that I'm not exactly sure _how_ this behavior should be documented, as I'm not sure what `breaks` is a parameter of. An example wouldn't be too hard to add, though.

Reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

v <- ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, z = density)) 

v + geom_contour()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/6O8WuRl.png)

``` r
v + geom_contour(breaks = c(0.002, 0.02))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/yedk4HS.png)

title: Error thrown for legend creation with multiple calls of geom_sf, when using show.legend
description:
I am trying to graph several geographic datasets together using the `ggplot2` and the new (and awesome) simple features mapping packages `geom_sf`. I'm receiving an error when trying to get the legend to show up in a particular way, and `traceback()` indicates that the issues is due to `ggplot2`. Posts on both Stack Overflow and the `sf` git development site suggested I post here.

Here is a minimum reproducible example, with the error `Error: length(rows) == 1 is not TRUE`. This example is due to user Gilles at Stack Overflow and replicates the issue I initially posted about (see links at bottom).
 
    library(sf)
    #> Linking to GEOS 3.5.1, GDAL 2.1.3, proj.4 4.9.2, lwgeom 2.3.2 r15302
    library(ggplot2)

    # Create a ploygon object (with 3 polygons)
    poly1 <- cbind(lon=c(5, 6, 7, 5), 
                   lat=c(52, 53, 51, 52))
    poly <- st_sf(st_sfc(list(st_polygon(list(poly1)), 
                              st_polygon(list(poly1 - 1)), 
                              st_polygon(list(poly1 + 1)))))
    poly$treatment <- factor(c("Omitted", "Control", "Treated"))
    
    # create two line objects 
    line1 <- st_sf(st_sfc(list(st_linestring(cbind(lon = c(5.5, 4.5), lat = c(53.5, 54.5))))))
    line2 <- st_sf(st_sfc(list(st_linestring(cbind(lon = c(5, 7.5), lat = c(53, 52))))))

    ggplot() + 
        geom_sf(data= line1, aes(color="A"), show.legend = "line") +
        geom_sf(data = poly, aes(fill = treatment))
    #> Error: length(rows) == 1 is not TRUE

Running `traceback()` indicates that the issues lies within `ggplot2`. If  `show.legend` is omitted, no error is thrown, and a graph is created, but the legend is incorrect -- it is a box outlined in the correctly colored line, rather then just the line:

    ggplot() + 
      geom_sf(data= line1, aes(color="A")) +
      geom_sf(data = poly, aes(fill = treatment))

![mapwrong](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30906872/36496050-1eda4138-1705-11e8-9943-cf2f489c21e7.png)

Links +[Stack Overflow Post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48873972/ggplot-and-geom-sf-and-error-lengthrows-1-is-not-true) +[sf git](https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/643#issuecomment-367008590)

title: enhancement request: geom_flat_violin.R
description:
This is not an issue, but an enhancement request for the development version. Any possibility that next release of `ggplot2` will have David Robinson's awesome `geom_flat_violin` function in it?

@name geom\_flat\_violin
@author David Robinson
@note Author’s note: Somewhat hackish solution to:
https://twitter.com/EamonCaddigan/status/646759751242620928. This function
is based mostly on copy/pasting from ggplot2::geom\_violin function

``` r
library(tidyverse)
#devtools::install_github(repo = "IndrajeetPatil/ggstatsplot")
library(ggstatsplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)


"%||%" <- function(a, b) {
  if (!is.null(a))
    a
  else
    b
}

#=========================== function definition ===========================

geom_flat_violin <-
  function(mapping = NULL,
           data = NULL,
           stat = "ydensity",
           position = "dodge",
           trim = TRUE,
           scale = "area",
           show.legend = NA,
           inherit.aes = TRUE,
           ...) {
    ggplot2::layer(
      data = data,
      mapping = mapping,
      stat = stat,
      geom = GeomFlatViolin,
      position = position,
      show.legend = show.legend,
      inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
      params = list(trim = trim,
                    scale = scale,
                    ...)
    )
  }
```

@rdname ggplot2-ggproto
@format NULL
@usage NULL
@export

``` r
GeomFlatViolin <-
  ggproto(
    "GeomFlatViolin",
    Geom,
    setup_data = function(data, params) {
      data$width <- data$width %||%
        params$width %||% (resolution(data$x, FALSE) * 0.9)
      
      # ymin, ymax, xmin, and xmax define the bounding rectangle for each group
      data %>%
        dplyr::group_by(.data = ., group) %>%
        dplyr::mutate(
          .data = .,
          ymin = min(y),
          ymax = max(y),
          xmin = x,
          xmax = x + width / 2
        )
    },
    
    draw_group = function(data, panel_scales, coord)
    {
      # Find the points for the line to go all the way around
      data <- base::transform(data,
                              xminv = x,
                              xmaxv = x + violinwidth * (xmax - x))
      
      # Make sure it's sorted properly to draw the outline
      newdata <-
        base::rbind(
          dplyr::arrange(.data = base::transform(data, x = xminv), y),
          dplyr::arrange(.data = base::transform(data, x = xmaxv), -y)
        )
      
      # Close the polygon: set first and last point the same
      # Needed for coord_polar and such
      newdata <- rbind(newdata, newdata[1,])
      
      ggplot2:::ggname("geom_flat_violin",
                       GeomPolygon$draw_panel(newdata, panel_scales, coord))
    },
    
    draw_key = draw_key_polygon,
    
    default_aes = ggplot2::aes(
      weight = 1,
      colour = "grey20",
      fill = "white",
      size = 0.5,
      alpha = NA,
      linetype = "solid"
    ),
    
    required_aes = c("x", "y")
  )

#============ Example ========================

# trying out only the geom_flat_violin function
ggplot2::ggplot(data = iris, mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length)) +
  geom_flat_violin()
```

Error: Found object ("histogram") is not a geom, says update_geom_defaults()
description:
I was trying to set the default aesthetics for a `geom_histogram()`, so I naturally typed:

```r
library("ggplot2")
update_geom_defaults("histogram", list(fill = "tomato"))

# Error: Found object is not a geom.
```

But then I guessed that `geom_histogram()` must be shorthand for `geom_bar(stat = "bin")`, and that worked fine. 

```r
update_geom_defaults("bar", list(fill = "tomato"))
qplot(data = diamonds, x = price, geom = "histogram")
```

Maybe "histogram" can be recognised by `update_geom_defaults()` to save future ggplotonauts some confusion? Perhaps warn that it's actually `geom_bar` being edited?

title: Secondary axis tick behaviour
description:
---
Secondary axis tick labels (values) are calculated properly, but tick positions are significantly off and seem to suffer either from poor interpolation or from issues with floating point operations.
The  `x` variable values cover range of the actual data which produced this issue for the first time.

```r
library(tidyverse)
x = 10 ^ (seq(-27, -23, length.out = 100) + runif(100, 0, 1))
t = 1:100

p = tibble(x, t) %>%
        ggplot(aes(t, x)) +
        geom_point() +
        scale_y_log10(sec.axis = sec_axis(~log10(.*100)))

print(p)

```
One should expect that right y axis ticks perfectly align with grid lines, but label values are 100 larger (e.g. 1e-25 on the left corresponds to 1e-23 on the right precisely).
However, the output looks like this:

![1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8782986/35855863-0ad919a8-0b3d-11e8-8c16-b98794644a9c.png)

Two labels even overlap - I guess it is the 1e-23 and 1e-24.
Also, right axis tick positions do not align well with lines drawn by e.g. `annotate(geom="segment", x = 95, xend = 100, y = 10^(-26:-24), yend = 10^(-26 : -24))` suggesting tick positions on the right are really off.

title: No default angle in element_text when using label.theme and title.theme in guide_legend -> Error when setting other parameters
description:
When using `guide = guide_legend(...)` to change non-`angle` parameters of `label.theme` or `title.theme`, an error is generated due to non-`NULL` value for `angle`:

>Error in element_grob.element_text(element = label.theme, label = label, : Text element requires non-NULL value for 'angle'.

Here are examples trying to set `face`, without setting `angle`:

    ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                   
      geom_point() +                                                                                             
      scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(label.theme = element_text(face = "italic")))                                                              
                                                                                                           
    ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                   
        geom_point() +                                                                                             
        scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(title.theme = element_text(face = "italic")))                                                              

Trying to set `size`, `hjust` or `vjust` without setting `angle` leads to the same error.

To change any non-`angle` parameters, we need to set `angle` as well. E.g.:

    label.theme = element_text(face = "italic", angle = 0)))


In contrast, there is no need to explicitly set any of the other `NULL` arguments in `element_text` when setting `angle` only:

    ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                   
       geom_point() +                                                                                             
       scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(                                                                 
       label.theme = element_text(angle = -5)))                                                                   

                                                                                                           
    ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +                                   
       geom_point() +                                                                                             
       scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(                                                                 
       title.theme = element_text(angle = 5)))                                                                    

----

Thus, it would be nice if there was a sensible default `angle` value (`0`) when setting other legend parameters.

title: `solid` and non-`solid` shapes in scale_shape: nonsensical shapes and inconsistent removal of points
description:
`scale_shape` has the `solid` argument:

> `solid`: Should the shapes be solid, `TRUE`, or hollow, `FALSE`?

Although "solid" and "hollow" are not clearly defined in the help text, I believe that most people have a general idea about how the respective shapes would look like. At the very least, one would expect shapes corresponding to `TRUE` and `FALSE` to differ. However, this is not the case.

In addition, `scale_shape` has a rule for when an aesthetic is "difficult to discriminate", with a corresponding _removal_ of points, which is _inconsistent_ with other aesthetics.

Here's an example with three plots: (a) `solid = TRUE`, (b) `solid = FALSE`, and (c) an example of points which I would percieve as "hollow". 

``` r
                                                                   
d <- data.frame(x = factor(1:10), y = 1)                           
library(ggplot2)                                                   
library(cowplot)                                                   
                                                                   
                                                                   
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, shape = x)) +                     
geom_point(size = 8) +                                             
scale_shape_discrete(solid = TRUE,                                 
guide = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +                                  
annotate(geom = "text", x = 1, y = 1.2,                            
label = 'solid = TRUE, "non-hollow"', hjust = 0) +                 
ylim(0.8, 1.2)                                                     
                                                                   
d$shape <- ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]][ , "shape"]                   
solid <- p + geom_text(data = d, aes(y = y + 0.1, label = shape))  
                                                                   
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, shape = x)) +                     
geom_point(size = 8) +                                             
scale_shape_discrete(solid = FALSE,                                
guide = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +                                  
annotate(geom = "text", x = 1, y = 1.2,                            
label = 'solid = FALSE, "hollow"', hjust = 0) +                    
ylim(0.8, 1.2)                                                     
                                                                   
d$shape <- ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]][ , "shape"]                   
hollow <- p + geom_text(data = d, aes(y = y + 0.1, label = shape)) 
                                                                   
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, shape = x, fill = x)) +           
geom_point(size = 6) +                                             
scale_shape_manual(values = c(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 21:25),               
guide = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +                                  
annotate(geom = "text", x = 1, y = 1.2,                            
label = "Hollow?", hjust = 0) +                    
ylim(0.8, 1.2)                                                     
                                                                   
d$shape <- ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]][ , "shape"]                   
hollow2 <- p + geom_text(data = d, aes(y = y + 0.1, label = shape))
                                                                   
p <- plot_grid(solid, hollow, hollow2, nrow = 3, align = "v")      
save_plot("solid.png", p, base_height = 7)                         
```
![solid](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3583910/35782175-b520736a-09f4-11e8-9e54-9679ac09b0c7.png)

-----

# The problems:
1. In the '`solid = TRUE`, "non-hollow"' points (a), `pch` 3, 7, and 8 don't seem very "solid"
2. In the '`solid = FALSE`, "hollow"' points (b), `pch` 3, and 8 don't seem very "hollow"
3. `pch` 3, 7 and 8 appear in _both_ `solid = TRUE` and `solid = FALSE`. I consider this a bug. Why have an argument where `TRUE` and `FALSE` alternatives don't differ?
4. The code for both plot (a) and (b) generates warnings, and removes points:

> Warning messages:
1: The shape palette can deal with a maximum of 6 discrete values
because more than 6 becomes difficult to discriminate; you have 10.
Consider specifying shapes manually if you must have them. 

...which in turn leads to:
> 2: Removed 4 rows containing missing values (geom_point). 

This is inconsistent with the behaviour of other `aes`sthetics. Compare with e.g. `color`/`fill`/`alpha`, where you can map to "as many values you want", with an indistinguishable appearance as a result, _without_ warning or removal of points (see below). If anything, a warning would suffice for the shapes. On the other hand, if you start producing warnings for all cases of poor visualisation, where to stop? 
    
    d <- data.frame(x = factor(1:100), y = 1)
    ggplot(data = d, aes(x = x, y = y, color = x)) + geom_point()

![rplot02](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3583910/35736145-3da20aa2-0827-11e8-8f55-785c7bf62773.png)

---------

Thanks a lot for your tremendous work with the package!

title: Feature request: discrete color scales that don't fail with too few colors
description:
When you make a chart that uses many discrete colors, you never have to worry about the number of colors if you use the default colors.
```r
require(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(x=letters[1:26],y=runif(26)),aes(x=x,y=y,fill=x))+geom_col()
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3317138/35529808-075f5352-04e7-11e8-9c48-3015147ebd4c.png)

If you want to use your own colors (for instance, if you have company colors), it's easy to use a scale_manual to set the colors

```r
company_colors <-c("#E50000", "#008A8A", "#AF0076", "#E56800", "#1717A0", "#E5AC00", "#00B700")

ggplot(data.frame(x=letters[1:7],y=runif(7)),aes(x=x,y=y,fill=x)) +
geom_col() +
scale_fill_manual(values=company_colors)
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3317138/35529873-30a62ed4-04e7-11e8-97b2-963531eca37c.png)

However, when you use this method you'll run into trouble if your number of needed colors is greater than the length of your color vector. This can be especially problematic because you generally want to just say "always use my company colors so I don't worry about it."

```r
ggplot(data.frame(x=letters[1:26],y=runif(26)),aes(x=x,y=y,fill=x)) +
geom_col() +
scale_fill_manual(values=company_colors)
Error: Insufficient values in manual scale. 26 needed but only 7 provided.
```

One solution to this is to create a function that makes a desired length vector of colors based on your existing ones:
```r
make_color_vector <- function(desired_length,base_colors){
  if(desired_length <= length(base_colors)){
    base_colors[1:n]
  } else {
    ramp_to_colors <- function(color,amount){
      if(amount > 1){
        current_color <- color
        return_colors <- c()
        for(a in 1:(amount)){
          return_colors <- c(return_colors,current_color)
          current_color <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(c(current_color,"#222222"))(4)[2]
        }
        return_colors
      } else {
        color
      }
    }
    iterations <- ceiling(desired_length/length(base_colors))
    as.vector(do.call(rbind,lapply(base_colors,function(x) ramp_to_colors(x,iterations))))[1:desired_length]
  }
}

ggplot(data.frame(x=letters[1:26],y=runif(26)),aes(x=x,y=y,fill=x)) +
geom_col() +
scale_fill_manual(values = make_color_vector(26, company_colors))
```

But the downside to this is you still need to keep track of how many colors you need.

__This seems like something that could be added to ggplot2 without breaking anything!__ One solution would be to let scale_fill_manual take a function which takes an integer as an input and returned the desired number of colors (rather than just a vector of colors). This feels similar to how some of the labels and breaks parameters work for scales. You could include the "make_color_vector" function within ggplot2 itself, or leave other people to make their own. Improving this functionality seems like it would help other packages downstream (like [ggthemr](https://github.com/cttobin/ggthemr), which sets default themes but breaks if your custom theme doesn't have enough colors).

I'm happy to help write the code to do this, but unfortunately I'm struggling to figure out where in the ggplot2 code base I would make these changes.

Thank you!

title: Strange behaviour of geom_smooth and splines::ns
description:
The following example produces two different smooths where I believe they should be the same.
 (This is a simulation based on a rather larger real data set)

The only difference in the geom_smooth is the use of splines::ns versus ns

If using R 3.4.3 on windows and ggplot2 version 2.2.1


```r
require(splines)
require(ggplot2)

set.seed(12345)
dat = data.frame(claim=rbinom(1000,1,0.5))
mns = c(3.4,3.6)
sds = c(0.24, 0.35)
dat$wind = exp(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean=mns[dat$claim+1], sd=sds[dat$claim+1]))
dat = dat[order(dat$wind),]

ggplot(dat, aes(wind,claim))+geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "glm",
              method.args = list(family = binomial), 
              formula = y ~ splines::ns(x, df=5))+
  geom_smooth(method = "glm",
              method.args = list(family = binomial), 
              formula = y ~ ns(x, df=5))
```
