title: ggsave is not rendering alpha in device=png output files
description:
`ggsave` is not rendering `alpha=` of the `ggplot` object as expected in the png files: 
png file obtained from `ggsave` contains non-alpha objects only. i.e. `geom_lines` are rendered by default theme color (black in the case of theme_void() ) , where png files output from rstudio --> export --> save as Image or rstudio--> export --> copy to clipboard render the alpha as expected i.e light gray lines.

```r
gg<-ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length,group=Species)) + geom_density(size=.1,alpha=.1) + theme_void()
ggsave(gg, filename = "gg.png", device = "png", width = 1, height = 1)
```

title: Feature Request: facet_grid strip Widths (and Heights) Span Appropriate Panels
description:
When `facet_grid` has more than one column or row in order of facets that the value covers, it would be helpful to have the strip cover all appropriate columns so that the data are more logically grouped.

In the example below, it would help if the "1" spanned the first two columns of facets and the "2" spanned the last two columns.  That way, the data would be visually grouped more clearly.

The feature should apply to both rows and columns of facets and only look within a group.  E.g. if the A=2, B=3 column didn't exist in the example below, then the strip labels should look something like:

```
[   1   ] [2]
[3]   [4] [4]
```

Not like the below (or maybe there is an option to enable the below behavior, but it isn't the default):

```
[   1   ] [2]
[3] [   4   ]
```

``` r
library(ggplot2)
d <- expand.grid(A = 1:2, B = 3:4)
d$C <- 1:nrow(d)
d$D <- nrow(d):1

ggplot(d, aes(x = C, y = D)) + facet_grid(~A + B) + geom_point()
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/ikadyNK.png)
```

title: geom_bar with position = "fill",  y-axis label is count, but value is a proportion
description:
This example is from [r4ds chapter 3.8: Position Adjustments](http://r4ds.had.co.nz/data-visualisation.html#position-adjustments)

---
## Observed behavior:
When geom_bar is called with aesthetic mappings for two categorical variables AND a position value of "fill", the actual statistic represented visually by the height of a plot element on the y axis is a proportion (the cumulative proportion of b.a in a), but the y axis is labeled "count". 

To describe this using the actual example from the r4ds chapter: in the diamonds data set, when plotting a bar chart of cut grouped by clarity, if we use the position = "fill" value, the actual statistic on the y axis is the proportion of a given cut level that is comprised of each clarity level. The y axis is labeled "count".

## Expected behavior:
The y-axis would be labeled "proportion", or "cumulative proportion of clarity in cut"

## reprex
```r
library(ggplot2)
# directly from the book:
ggplot(data = diamonds) + 
  geom_bar(mapping = aes(x = cut, fill = clarity), position = "fill")
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3392948/35311862-0ebe9a42-0076-11e8-870c-f23b6261613d.png)

## Comment
Presumably behind the scenes position = "fill" tells geom_bar to calculate the proportion (clarity.cut/ cut) for each value of cut, and to do that it uses the count statistic, but the actual value represented by the cumulative height of the different color bars is not a count.

title: qplot(x) stored in a variable gets modified when modifying x
description:
When passing a vector (e.g. *x*) to `qplot()` (to produce e.g. a histogram) and storing the plot into a variable (e.g. *p1*), if the variable *x* is modified the plot *p1* gets also modified. This does not happen if the data is passed as a `data.frame()`

```r
# Generate random vector.
x <- rnorm(100, mean = 0)
p1 <- qplot(x)
p1

# Modify variable x (either of these options replicate the behavior).
x <- rnorm(100, mean = 10)
x <- x + 10
# Now p1 plots a histogram centered at 10, the data in p1 has been modified.
p1

# This however works as expected:
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100, mean = 0))
p1 <- qplot(x, data = d)
p1

d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100, mean = 10))
# Modifying d does not cause p1 to be modified.
p1
```

title: ggplot fails with duration objects.
description:
Trying to print a `ggplot` object created using a `tibble` with a `duration` object inside yields the same error.

```r
df <- tibble::tibble(                                                       
  a = 1:10,                                                                   
  b = lubridate::as.duration(1:10)                                            
)                                                                           
                                                                            
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(x = a, y = b)) + ggplot2::geom_point()
p                                                                           
#> Error: Incompatible duration classes (Duration, integer). Please coerce with `as.duration`.
```

Initially, I thought this might be caused by the bug at https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/issues/88, due to the same error message. Indeed, we encounter the same error message if `df` is `print`ed, and this *is* caused by the `pillar` issue.

However, trying to print a `ggplot` object created using a `data.frame` with a `duration` object inside still yields the error, even though we're not using `tibble`s anymore.

``` r
df <- data.frame(                                                           
  a = 1:10,                                                                   
  b = lubridate::as.duration(1:10)                                            
)                                                                           
                                                                            
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(x = a, y = b)) + ggplot2::geom_point()
p                                                                           
#> Error: Incompatible duration classes (Duration, integer). Please coerce with `as.duration`.
```

Given that `ggplot2` depends on `tibble`, this is still likely caused by https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/issues/88, even though we're not actually printing tibbles here. Perhaps the `data.frame` is being coerced to a `tibble`?

title: Inconsistency between generated pdf and png files
description:
I have observed an inconsistency between the generated pdf and png files in the plot below.
In the plot I insert an annotate object with the type 'label'; where the width of the black line around the label is set to zero.
This works fine when exporting to a png file.
But when I export the plot to a pdf file, the black line is still present.

```
library(tidyverse)
#> ── Attaching packages ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse 1.2.1 ──
#> ✔ ggplot2 2.2.1     ✔ purrr   0.2.4
#> ✔ tibble  1.4.1     ✔ dplyr   0.7.4
#> ✔ tidyr   0.7.2     ✔ stringr 1.2.0

#> ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
p <- tibble() %>%
  ggplot() + 
  annotate('label', x = 1, y = 0, 
           label='is there a border around this label?',

title: Default width inconsistent between geom_boxplot and others
description:
The default width of geom_boxplot seems to be 0.75*(resolution), whereas for stat_identity it is 0.9*(resolution). This causes unexpected behavior when using stat = "identity" in geom_boxplot, because the default width is changed. The default width of boxplots seems to be undocumented, or at least I could not find it anywhere.

This took me an annoyingly long time to figure out, and I think it'd be great if these values could be made consistent to aid in user-friendliness. Barring that, documenting the width calculation in the doc for geom_boxplot would also be very helpful.

```r
library(tidyverse)

# Example data
ncat1 <- 2
ncat2 <- 3
a <- data.frame(cat1 = factor(rep(1:ncat1, each = ncat2*100)), 
                cat2 = factor(rep(rep(1:ncat2, each = 100), ncat1)), 
                val = rnorm(ncat1*ncat2*100))
abox <- a %>% 
  group_by(cat1, cat2) %>% 
  summarise(ymin = min(val),
            lower = quantile(val, .25),
            middle = median(val),
            upper = quantile(val, .75),
            ymax = max(val),
            mean = mean(val))

# Plot boxplots and means with default boxplot stat and dodge width = 0.75
a %>% 
  ggplot(aes(cat1, val)) + 
    geom_boxplot(aes(fill = cat2)) + 
    geom_point(data = abox, aes(group = cat2, y = mean), 
               position = position_dodge(width = .75),
               color = 'blue', 
             size = 3)

# Plot boxplots and means with identity stat, having whiskers cover entire range of data, 
# and with dodge width = 0.75 (points misaligned)
abox %>% 
  ggplot(aes(cat1)) + 
    geom_boxplot(aes(fill = cat2, 
                     ymin = ymin, 
                     lower = lower,
                     middle = middle,
                     upper = upper,
                     ymax = ymax),
                 stat = 'identity') + 
    geom_point(aes(group = cat2, y = mean), 
               position = position_dodge(width = .75),
               color = 'blue', 
               size = 3)
```

title: Inconsistency in handling of characters in geom_point and geom_smooth
description:
I recently had a data set where a numeric column was coded as character. Since this produces a meaningful result with geom_point, I was surprised that with geom_smooth there were no data shown.


```
library(ggplot2)
d = data.frame(x = sample(1:100,10, TRUE), y = as.character(sample(1:100, 10, TRUE )))

# Works (would be ok if it gave an error message, though)
ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y = y)) + geom_point()
# Fails  without error, but without output.  Suprisingly, given the above
ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y = y)) + geom_smooth()

# Clearly works as expected
ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y = as.numeric(y))) + geom_smooth()

```

title: The colorbar guide (guide_colourbar) converts units into cm and then uses them as mm
description: The colorbar guide (`guide_colourbar`) converts units into cm and then uses them as mm. Reproducible example: ``` library(ggplot2) p1 <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length, color = Petal.Width)) + geom_point() + scale_color_distiller(name = "gap width = 1cm") + theme(legend.spacing.x = grid::unit(1, "cm"), legend.position = "top") p2 <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length, color = Petal.Width)) + geom_point() + scale_color_distiller(name = "gap width = 10cm") + theme(legend.spacing.x = grid::unit(10, "cm"), legend.position = "top") p3 <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length, color = Petal.Width)) + geom_point() + scale_color_distiller(name = "gap width = 50cm") + theme(legend.spacing.x = grid::unit(50, "cm"), legend.position = "top") cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, p3, nrow = 1) ``` The problem exists for both `legend.spacing.x` and `legend.spacing.y` but cannot be shown for `legend.spacing.y` because of issue #2260, which has not yet been fixed for `guide_colourbar`. The relevant lines in the code are [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/3fb3fb00555bab5b270b3467a1ddd90341a62886/R/guide-colorbar.r#L301) (convert `legend.spacing.x` and `legend.spacing.y` into cm) and [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/3fb3fb00555bab5b270b3467a1ddd90341a62886/R/guide-colorbar.r#L434) (use all widths and heights as mm values.)

title: The colorbar guide (guide_colourbar) incorrectly uses a vertical unit in a horizontal setting
description: The colorbar guide (`guide_colourbar`) incorrectly uses a vertical unit in a horizontal setting. The simplest way to see this issue is the following experiment: Increase the height of the colorbar title and observe that the guide ticks are moving to the right at the same time. ``` library(ggplot2) p1 <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length, color = Petal.Width)) + geom_point() + scale_color_distiller(name = "Petal Width") p2 <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length, color = Petal.Width)) + geom_point() + scale_color_distiller(name = "Petal\nWidth") p3 <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length, color = Petal.Width)) + geom_point() + scale_color_distiller(name = "Petal\n\nWidth") cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, p3, nrow = 1) ``` The problem is caused by [this line](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/3fb3fb00555bab5b270b3467a1ddd90341a62886/R/guide-colorbar.r#L378) and/or [this line.](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/3fb3fb00555bab5b270b3467a1ddd90341a62886/R/guide-colorbar.r#L384) The variable `vgap` is being used as a width. The correct variable here would be `hgap`. See e.g. [this line,](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/3fb3fb00555bab5b270b3467a1ddd90341a62886/R/guide-colorbar.r#L410) which is correct.

The example developed by @baptiste and titled "Align two plots on a page" no longer works with current versions of the R packages and R. The line `g <- rbind(g1, g2, size="first") # stack the two plots` now results in `Error in rbind_gtable(x, y, size = size) : ncol(x) == ncol(y) is not TRUE`. I have

```
other attached packages:
[1] gtable_0.2.0  ggplot2_2.2.1
```

and am running R Under development (unstable) (2018-01-07 r74096).

title: geom_dotplot binwidth Parameter Can Change Plot Range
description:
Choosing different values of `binwidth` changes the numeric range of the plot. `binwidth` is not documented as having an effect on the plot boundaries and I wouldn't intuitively expect it to, so I think it's a bug. Try:

```
plotData <- data.frame(measurement = c(2.76, 16.60, 1.12, 13.81),
                       class = factor(c("Bad", "Bad", "Good", "Good")))
ggplot(plotData, aes(x = class, y = measurement)) +
       geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center", position = "dodge", aes(colour = class), binwidth = 1)
```

Now, remove the `binwidth = 1` setting. The 0 position on the y-axis vanishes.

title: Error in UseMethod("rescale") prevents ggplot from creating object
description:
I am having trouble graphing with ggplot2 after updating RStudio to version 1.1.383 from 0.98.053. Previously I used ggplot2 exhaustively without problems.

Each time I receive the following error:

Error in UseMethod("rescale") : 
  no applicable method for 'rescale' applied to an object of class "c('double', 'numeric')"

This error is produced even with the most simplified example, and even when forcing the scales library to load first. The most recent version of ggplot2 has been installed from CRAN.

Any help is greatly appreciated!

```r
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(10), y = rnorm(10))
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y =y)) + geom_point()
```

title: Error in installing dev version of ggplot2
description:
**Brief description of the problem**
When trying to install the development version of ggplot2 using devtools package in RStudio, an error occurs like below
    _Error : 'enexprs' is not an exported object from 'namespace:rlang'
          Error : unable to load R code in package ‘ggplot2’
          ERROR: lazy loading failed for package ‘ggplot2’_

It used to get installed successfully with the earlier versions but recently started having problems in the installation. To recreate the problem, remove the existing version of ggplot2 from RStudio and download the latest release using the reprex below.

```r
devtools::install_github("tidyverse/ggplot2")
```

title: space reserved for facet strip text does not respect strip text length/size
description:
The strip text is not allocated enough space to prevent it from being cut. Used an example from @karawoo when working on strip.text angle issues.

``` r
df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:3,
  y = 1:3,
  g = c("b", "bbbb", "bbbbbbbbbohnogettingcut")
)
library(ggplot2)
base <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(g ~ .) 
base +
  theme(
    strip.text.y = element_text(size=24))
```

title: Controlling graticule appearance  with geom_sf
description:
The control of the appearance (color, linewidth, linetype...) of the graticule produced with geom_sf  is quite counter-intuitive and something seems to be wrong.

For the examples below I used the latest ggplot2 version from github reinstalled today (2.2.1.9000) and sf 0.5-4 (with R version 3.4.3 - Ubuntu 16.04.3 LTS).
This issue was initially posted on the [sf github repository](https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/610#issuecomment-356028830)

I expected to be able to control for example the color and linetype of the graticule with panel.grid but these commands seem to be ignored
```r
library(ggplot)
library(sf)
nc = st_read(system.file("gpkg/nc.gpkg", package = "sf")) 

ggplot() + 
    geom_sf(data = nc) + 
    theme(panel.grid = element_line(color = "red", linetype = 2))
```
![rplot001](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4679586/34680588-d1278334-f499-11e7-8bec-f8ed84b375d8.png)


It works as expected with `panel.grid.major` (but I would expect that panel.grid.major will inherit from panel.grid)

```r
ggplot() + 
    geom_sf(data = nc) + 
    theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "red", linetype = 2))
```
![rplot001](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4679586/34680627-e7fc0e4a-f499-11e7-8392-3c4eeefa2758.png)


If you want to change only -say- the x grid color with panel.grid.major.x both x and y are changed : 

```r
ggplot() + 
    geom_sf(data = nc) + 
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "red", linetype = 2))
```
![rplot001](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4679586/34680669-044fc8b6-f49a-11e7-9adf-52e5e126a975.png)


If you want to change both x and y in different ways nothing happens : 

```r
ggplot() + 
    geom_sf(data = nc) + 
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "red", linetype = 2),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "blue", linetype = 3))
```

![rplot001](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4679586/34680738-268b7880-f49a-11e7-87c2-8e2ecb1e935a.png)

Each example works as intended when I use another geom : 

```r
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(10), y = rnorm(10))
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x,y)) + geom_point()
p + theme(panel.grid = element_line(color = "red",  linetype = 2))
p + theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "red",  linetype = 2))
p + theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "red",  linetype = 2))
p + theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "red", linetype = 2),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "blue", linetype = 3))
```

By the way, if I'm not wrong, a few weeks ago (30 november) the default color of the graticule was also much lighter and less conspicuous (better to my taste)

title: Feature request: percentage labels for pie chart with ggplot2
description:
Hi, 

Apologies in advance for a long-winded mail. I have been trying to make a pie chart in `ggplot2` with a custom function to get percentage labels, but it doesn't seem to work and I'm not sure how to modify it to get it to work. Here is the code I am using-

```
## custom function to write results from chi-square test into subtitle for the plot
# x stands for the chi-square object
# effect is the text label that needs to be entered to denote which interaction effect is being investigated in 
# the chi-square test presented...if not entered, the default will be "Chi-square test"

chi_subtitle <- function(x, effect = NULL) {
  
  # if effect label hasn't been specified, use this default
  if (is.null(effect)) effect <- "Chi-square test"
  
  base::substitute(
    paste(y, " : ", italic(chi)^2,"(", df, ") = ", estimate, ", ", 
          italic("p")," = ", pvalue, ", Cramer's ", italic(V), " = ", phicoeff),
    list(y = effect,
         estimate = specify_decimal(as.data.frame(x$chiSq)[2], 3),
         df = specify_decimal(as.data.frame(x$chiSq)[3], 0),
         pvalue = specify_decimal(as.data.frame(x$chiSq)[4], 3),
         phicoeff = specify_decimal(as.data.frame(x$nom)[4], 3))
  )
  
}

## ggpie with percentages

# df$main should contain observations of interest
# df$condition can optionally be used to facet wrap
# labels should be a character vector of the same length as group_by(df, main) or
# group_by(df, condition, main) if facet wrapping

pie_chart <- function(data, main, labels = NULL, condition = NULL, stat_title = NULL) {
  
  # convert the data into percentages. group by conditional variable if needed
  df <- dplyr::group_by_(data, .dots = c(condition, main)) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(counts = n()) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(perc = counts / sum(counts)) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(desc(perc)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(label_pos = sum(perc) - cumsum(perc) + perc / 2,
                  #label_pos = cumsum(perc) - 0.65*perc, 
                  perc_text = paste0(round(perc * 100), "%"))
  # label_pos is a tricky variable to define...the one here will work fine in most, but not all, cases
  # if it doesn't work, try toying with the formula for the label_pos to get the desired result
  
  # reorder the category factor levels to order the legend
  df[[main]] <- factor(df[[main]], levels = unique(df[[main]]))
  
  # if labels haven't been specified, use what's already there
  if (is.null(labels)) labels <- as.character(df[[main]])
  
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(data = df, aes_string(x = factor(1), y = "perc", fill = main)) +
    
    # make stacked bar chart with black border
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black", width = 2) +
    
    # add the percents to the interior of the chart
    #geom_text(aes(x = 1.10, y = label_pos, label = perc_text), size = 5) +
    geom_label(aes(x = 1.10, y = label_pos, label = perc_text), fontface = 'bold', color = 'black', size = 5, 
               show.legend = FALSE, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    
    # convert to polar coordinates
    coord_polar(theta = "y") +
    
    # formatting
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
    scale_fill_discrete(name = "", labels = unique(labels)) +
    theme_grey() +
    theme(panel.grid  = element_blank(), 
          axis.ticks = element_blank(),  
          axis.title = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_blank(), 
          axis.text.y = element_blank(),
          strip.text.x = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
          strip.text.y = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"), 
          strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 14),
          legend.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
          legend.title.align = 0.5,
          legend.text.align = 0.5,
          legend.direction = 'horizontal', 
          legend.position = 'bottom',
          legend.key = element_rect(size = 5),
          legend.key.size = unit(1.5, 'lines'),
          legend.margin = margin(5,5,5,5),
          legend.box.margin = margin(5,5,5,5),
          panel.border = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = NA, size = 1),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "black", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
          plot.title = element_text(color = "black", size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = NA))) + # remove black diagonal line from legend
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2")
  
  # facet wrap if that's happening
  if (!is.null(condition)) {
    
    # create a dataframe on which chi-square tests will be carried out in case there is "condition" variable present
    df2 <- data %>% dplyr::select(condition, main)
    colnames(df2) <- c("col1", "col2")
    p <- p + facet_wrap(condition, labeller = "label_both") 
    p <- p + labs(subtitle = chi_subtitle(jmv::contTables(df2, rows = 'col1', cols = 'col2', phiCra = TRUE), 
                                          effect = stat_title))
  }
  
  return(p)
  
}

```

This is the output I get- 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11330453/34445576-adbb92e0-eca2-11e7-8bb1-0643a57a1319.png)

As you can see, it works fine for some conditions, but not for other. Changing the equation for the position labels (`label_pos = sum(perc) - cumsum(perc) + perc / 2`) inevitably messes up one of the conditions. So I was wondering if the next release of ggplot2 would possibly contain functionality to handle percentages labels for a pie chart. 

Thanks!

P.S. The exact function call was-
```
choice_pie <- plyr::dlply(fmri_md, .(question), function(data)
  pie_chart(data, main = "choice", labels = NULL, condition = "dilemma", stat_title = "dilemma x choice") +
    labs(title = paste("Question:", as.character(data$question))) + 
    guides(fill = guide_legend(title = "Choice")))
```

title: Feauture request: Custom ribbon for geom_abline
description:
Hi,

in psychology there is a simple method for assessing clinical significance. Therefore the pre treatment score of an instrument (e.g. questionnaire) for every patient is plotted against the post treatment score. In the example below, all points that fall below the center diagonal show an improvement. But the instrument used has an error of measurement, indicated by the surrounding diagonals.

The workaround for this is a little annoying so it would be extremely helpful to create a custom ribbon for a `geom_abline` with manual specifications for `ymin` and `ymax`. Thus the area of interest would be shaded and could have a legend entry.

```r
library(ggplot2)

# Some example data, scores on a questionnaire per patient before and after treatment
pre.x <- rnorm(70, mean = 24, sd = 4)
post.x <- rnorm(70, mean = 12, sd = 4)
clinical.data <- data.frame(pre.x, post.x)

# This tells us that changes from pre to post within 3.2 points
# fall into the error of measurement of that questionnaire
error.measurement <- 3.2

# Plot
clinical.significance.plot <- ggplot(clinical.data, aes(x = pre.x, y = post.x)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = -error.measurement) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = +error.measurement) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,40), ylim = c(0,40))
clinical.significance.plot
```

title: String with "." considered as float
grouped_df should not require a ".group" variable for data on the other layers
description:
Due to the change in response to #2351, a grouped_df now creates a variable called `.group`. This may be problematic because ggplot2 treats the first layer so special as all the following layers are required to contain all mapped variables except when another mapping is specified individually. Here is an example:

``` r
reprex::reprex_info()
#> Created by the reprex package v0.1.1.9000 on 2017-12-22

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:10,
  y = 1:10,
  type = rep(c("a", "b"), 5),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) %>%
  group_by(type)

df_labels <- data.frame(
  x = 1,
  y = 2,
  text = "foo!"
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = type)) +
  geom_label(data = df_labels, aes(label = text))
#> Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...): object '.group' not found

ggplot(ungroup(df), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = type)) +
  geom_label(data = df_labels, aes(label = text))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/GHZwsYn.png)

Though I'm not sure this is just a bug, I'm afraid #2351 needs a bit more considerations (better error messages, at least).

title: Add support for integer64 variable types
description:
Results collected from databases can, including aggregations, could return an `integer64` variable type which does not seem to be supported by `aes()`.  The workaround is to coerce `as.numeric()` prior to plotting.

<details>

Code that collects the data:
```r
> by_month <- flights %>%
+     group_by(month) %>%
+     tally() %>%
+     collect() 
> 
> head(by_month)
# A tibble: 6 x 2
  month               n
  <dbl> <S3: integer64>
1    10          556205
2     4          598126
3    12          544958
4     5          606293
5     2          569236
6     7          627931
```

The plot that is attempted followed by the error's text:
```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(by_month) +
  geom_line(aes(x = month, y = n)) 
```

`Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type integer64. Defaulting to continuous.`

</details>

title: Current development version breaks compatibility with scale() output, e.g. in qq-plots
description:
Supplying `scale()`- standardised values to e.g. the `sample` aesthetic for the use of qq-plots does work in the current CRAN version, however, it does not work anymore with the current GitHub version.  
I looked through the `NEWS.md` to find any mention of a possible breaking change, but could not find anything that seemed to indicate that this change is intended.

Previous behavior:
```
# install.packages("ggplot2")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(sample = scale(mpg))) +
  geom_qq()
```

Works fine.

Behavior with current GitHub version:

```
# devtools::install_github("tidyverse/ggplot2")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(sample = scale(mpg))) +
  geom_qq()

# Error: Column `sample` must be a 1d atomic vector or a list
```

I'm aware that `scale` returns a 1d-matrix instead of an atomic vector, so I know I can circumvent this issue by using `as.numeric(scale(mpg))`, but this is simply a case of not wanting to change old code if I don't have to.

Tested versions of ggplot:

- CRAN: ` ggplot2      * 2.2.1      2016-12-30 CRAN (R 3.4.0) `
- GitHub: `ggplot2      * 2.2.1.9000 2017-12-18 Github (tidyverse/ggplot2@bfff1d8)`

title: very long geom_bar computation time with iso-8859-1 encoded character in aes fill
description:
While reading in an `ISO-8859-1` encoded csv file, I noticed a strange behaviour when plotting certain columns as a bar plot. `geom_bar` enters an infinte loop (or at least takes unreasonaby long to compute) if the column used for `fill` in `aes_string` ends with a special character (German Umlaut).

Takes forever:
```r
library(ggplot2)
data <- data.frame(
  a = "a",
  b = iconv("Some_prefix_ä", "utf8", "iso-8859-1")
)
ggplot(data) +
  geom_bar(aes_string("a", fill = "b"))
```

Works as expected:
```r
library(ggplot2)
data <- data.frame(
  a = "a",

title: Feature request: stat_function for each row
description:
**The problem:** If you want to plot a function for multiple sets of args you currently have to add a `stat_function(fun=func, args=list(arg1=1, arg2=3))` for each set of args, resulting in many layers and convoluted code. In my case, I would like to visualize MCMC samples, plotting ~200 curves for each of seven different groups (colored by group), so it would result in ~1400 layers. Others have taken this approach and [found it to be very slow](https://stackoverflow.com/a/19847207/1297830).

**Solutions?** It would be nice if `stat_function` could work like `geom_point` which adds an element for each row in the data and optionally format it using other variables in the data. It could work like this:
```R
# Three sets of arguments to dnorm
df_args = data.frame(mean=c(1,3,5), sd=c(1,2,3))
g = ggplot2::ggplot(df_args, aes(x))  # aes does not do anything in this example

# Plot curves from data
g + stat_function(fun=dnorm)  # Should recognize that "mean" and "sd" are defined and use them
g + stat_function(fun=dnorm, args=list(mean=mean, sd=sd))  # Explicit mapping. Useful if colnames do not match argument names

# Plotting curves not defined by data:
g + stat_function(data=list(mean=c(6,7), sd=1,1), fun=dnorm)  # Multiple curves
g + stat_function(fun=dnorm, args=list(mean=1, sd=2)  # A single curve
```

I guess many find it intuitive that `stat_function` should work in this way since people repeatedly have [inquered on Stack Overflow how to do this](https://www.google.dk/search?q=stat_function+ggplot+multiple&oq=stat_function+ggplot+multiple).I currently resort to [this tidyverse solution](https://stackoverflow.com/a/43133823/1297830), just using `geom_line` for pre-computed pairs of `x` and y=`func(x)` values.

I really appreciate ggplot2. Thanks a lot!

title: Supplement scale_*_manual documentation with user-created function example
description:
I recently discovered you can create a _re-usable_ custom color scale by wrapping it in a function - see this SO [post](https://stackoverflow.com/a/43440604/5170276). The post also clarifies that named vectors can be used.

The current [documentation](http://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/scale_manual.html) for the `scale_*_manual` functions would be improved by adding an example that illustrates these strategies:
``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

scale_my_custom_colours <- function(aesthetic, ...) {
  ggplot2:::manual_scale(
    aesthetic,
    ...,
    values = setNames(
      c("green", "blue", "red", "orange"),
      LETTERS[1:4]
    ),
    drop = FALSE
  )
}

df1 <- data.frame(
  Value = c(40, 20, 10, 60),
  Type = c("A", "B", "C", "D")
)

df2 <- data.frame(
  Value = c(30, 45),
  Type = c("A", "D")
)

df3 <- data.frame(
  X = c(10, 20, 30, 40),
  Y = c(40, 20, 10, 60),
  Type = c("A", "B", "C", "D")
)
g1 <-
  ggplot(df1, aes(x = Type, y = Value, fill = Type)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_my_custom_colours("fill")

g2 <-
  ggplot(df2, aes(x = Type, y = Value, fill = Type)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_my_custom_colours("fill")

g3 <-
  ggplot(df3, aes(x = X, y = Y, colour = Type)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_my_custom_colours("colour") # "color" doesn't work

grid.arrange(g1, g2, g3, ncol = 1)
```

title: Update NSE to rlang so quosures work
description:
Hi! It would be really useful if we could write:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

plot_stuff <- function(data, x, y){
    x <- enquo(x)
    y <- enquo(y)
    
    ggplot(data, aes(x = !!x, y = !!y)) + geom_point()
}
```
instead of
```r
plot_stuff <- function(data, x, y){
    ggplot(data, aes_(substitute(x), substitute(y))) + geom_point()
}

plot_stuff(data.frame(foo = 1:10, bar = 1:10), foo, bar)
```
which becomes particularly important if the function also uses quosure-enabled parts of the tidyverse in it as well, as mixing NSE systems gets more than a little confusing for users.

A look at `aes.r` shows that it defines its own NSE system with `match.call` and an S3 class called `uneval`. Refactoring the code to create the `uneval` object with rlang would pretty much only require altering `aes.R`, assuming the structure of that object remains a list of atomic expressions. As a side benefit, `aes_`, `aes_q`, and `aes_string` would all become unnecessary, though it seems wise not to deprecate `aes_string`.

title: Better support for custom color and fill aesthetics?
description: Hello, I'm wondering whether it would be possible to better support custom color and fill aesthetics. What I mean are cases where maybe we want two separate color mappings in the same geom, e.g. `line_color` and `point_color`. With the current ggplot2, if I create such aesthetics, I can't take advantage of any of the existing color scales. But with a few small changes, I think this would be possible. First, to demonstrate that this is a real situation, some example code from ggridges: ```r cols = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73") cols_dark = c('#C18511', '#289ACF', '#0D8561') ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Species, fill = Species)) + geom_density_ridges(aes(point_color = Species), alpha = .2, jittered_points = TRUE) + scale_fill_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") + scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0.01, 0)) + ggplot2:::manual_scale("point_color", values = cols_dark, guide = "none") + theme_ridges(grid = FALSE, center = TRUE) ``` In this example, everything needs to be drawn at once in one geom, because the filled areas and solid lines can overlap the points. But, I want to be able to specify line colors and point colors separately, and the point colors should also be different from the fill colors. The only way I see to solve the problem is to add a `point_color` aesthetic. My code example brings up one immediate and easy to fix issue: ggplot2 doesn't export `manual_scale`, but it's what is needed here to make this example work without too much effort. Second, it would be helpful if the various existing color scales took an optional `aesthetics` argument that can be used to override the aesthetics in the function name. While this may sound a bit strange, the resulting code would be quite legible and look reasonable. For example, using the default hue color scale for fill and also applying it to the points might look like this: ```r ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Species, fill = Species)) + geom_density_ridges(aes(point_color = Species), alpha = .2, jittered_points = TRUE) + scale_color_hue(aesthetics = "point_color") + scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0.01, 0)) + theme_ridges(grid = FALSE, center = TRUE) ``` So, in summary, I'm making the following requests: 1. Export `manual_scale` 2. Add optional `aesthetics` parameter to all existing color scales I'd be happy to work on a pull request if you're willing to consider these changes.

title: Colourbar does not have all colors of the scale.
description:
For some data it is possible for the colourbar to cover a fraction of the colourspace smaller than that covered by the data. It can be confusing when the guide for a continuous scale does span the full *mapped* space of an aesthetic.

Actually, this bug is probably triggered every time there is a colourbar, but in most cases it is small and imperceptible. With colourmaps like `viridis`, the cases where it is obvious should only go up.

In the reprex below, I had to do some contriving (`nbin=7`) to reveal it. 

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(faithful, aes(x = eruptions, y = waiting)) +
  geom_point()  +
  stat_density_2d(aes(fill=..level..), geom='polygon') +
  xlim(0.5, 6) +
  ylim(40, 110) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  guides(fill=guide_colorbar(nbin=7))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/9NkqiQ0.png)

The root of the issue is `pretty` does not guarantee that the breaks it computes are close enough to the limits that the difference is not perceptible when mapped to a colour. 

A simple but partial solution is to increase the default `guide$nbin` parameter. This would give `pretty` enough wiggle room to work with and reduce incidences of the bug.

A better solution is recognising that the "raster" colourbar does not need to be generated using 'pretty' breaks, a `seq(.limits[1], .limits[2], length=guide$nbin)` can do. For this solution the current value of `nbin` need not change except for the craziest of colourmaps.

title: doc improvement for filled symbols + suggestion to add warning
description:
I came across this issue using ``geom_boxplot``, but it's very general. Some symbols accept a fill, some don't.  (see for example: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15819762/plot-functions-with-filled-point-symbols-and-legend) Advanced ``R`` users know this. It's not a ``ggplot2`` issue. **However, I would like to suggest some improvements to the ``ggplot`` documentation and perhaps even some added feature.** 

Case in point (pun intended):  In ``geom_boxplot``, ``outlier.fill`` works only with "fillable" symbols This is not explicit in the ``geom_boxplot``documentation. In fact, the doc does little more than naming the options. The ``outlier.stroke`` option is one of the more mysterious ones. 

In addition to improving the doc (see below a sentence that could be inserted), I would suggest implementing a warning if a user tries to mix ``fill`` with a ``non-fillable`` symbol, e.g. (proof of concept)

    if(outlier.shape %in% c(21, 22, 23, 24, 25) & !(is.null((outlier.fill)))) 
        print("outlier.fill is designed to work with outlier.shape values in c(21, 22, 23, 24, 25) only. If other values of outlier.shape are supplied, outlier.fill defaults to NULL")

title: Actual result of ..ndensity.. does not match the documentation
description:
In `help(stat_bin)`, it defines `..ncount..` as "count, scaled to maximum of 1" and `..ndensity..` as "density, scaled to maximum of 1".  From this I would expect that:

`..ncount..` is `..count.. / max(..count..)`

and that

`..ndensity..` is `..density.. / max(..density..)` 

However, the latter is not the case.  Instead, `..ndensity..` appears to be `..count.. / max(..density..)`

If this is a bug, it looks like it could be fixed with a one line change to R/bin.R (which I'd be happy to submit as a pull request if you want).  But if this is the intended behavior, perhaps the documentation could be made more clear.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

standard_normal <- data.frame(X = rnorm(1E5, 0, 1))

# ..ndensity.. is ..count.. / max(..density..)
# which is not "density, scaled to a maximum of 1"
ggplot(standard_normal, aes(x = X)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(y = ..ndensity..), binwidth = 0.2, center = 0, size = 1.5, color = 'black') +

title: geom_histogram: boundary default + minor issue + doc improvement
description:
__1__.  

In ``geom_histogram`` is the default ``boundary`` value sensible?

Has this been the subject of some discussions? There are, presumably, so many use cases that it must be difficult to find a common ground. However, in the case of a continuous distribution defined on a numeric interval, e.g. the uniform distribution on ``[0, 1]`` the default behaviour is probably __not__ the most desirable. A more suitable histogram may be drawn by setting the option ``boundary=0`` or ``boundary=1``. 

Is there a case for setting ``boundary=0`` as a default? This looks like what ``hist(df$x)`` does. 

However, there is a minor issue when doing this: the base of the bins extends beyond where it is supposed to. Not sure if this is a minor bug or a by-product of my misusing the boundary option. 

See screenshot: just above the value ``1.0`` the horizontal line extends too far.

![rplot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6339274/32346036-f208a1a0-c046-11e7-920c-0d9ae12b2ba5.png)

Still, better than the default, where the first and last bins are "wrong":

![rplot01](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6339274/32346107-3b36a12e-c047-11e7-9cb9-fca9a98b8f0a.png)


Moreover, Is there a case for allowing users to set ``boundary = c(a,b)``, that is a left-right vector of values, to cater for situations where the data is restricted to ``[a,b]``, e.g. with the uniform distribution below?

    ## data
    set.seed(1)
    df = data.frame(x = runif(100000, min = 0, max = 1))

    ## default histogram
    ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x)) + 
        geom_histogram(color = "black", fill = "white")

    ## basic ggplot structure:
    p <- ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x)) + 
        scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2))

    ## play around with boundary

    # default histogram very similar to this:
    p + geom_histogram(boundary = 0.5,
        color = "blue", fill = "white") 

    # boundary = 0 leaves training line on rhs
    p + geom_histogram(boundary = 0,
        color = "blue", fill = "white") 

    # boundary = 1 leaves training line on lhs
    p + geom_histogram(boundary = 1,
        color = "blue", fill = "white") 

    ## feature suggestion: boundary = c(0, 1)

    ## play around with bins or binwidth to try to fix problem

    bins = 10
    binwidth = (max(df$x)-min(df$x))/bins
    p + geom_histogram(binwidth = binwidth, boundary = 0,
        color = "blue", fill = "white") 

    p + geom_histogram(bins = bins, boundary = 0,
        color = "blue", fill = "white") 


In addition:

  __2.__ The documentation for ``geom_histogram`` here 
http://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html

refers to a ``width`` argument which, if I'm not mistaken, is now obsolete:

> 
boundary | A boundary between two bins. As with center, things are shifted when boundary is outside the range of the data. For example, to center on integers, use width = 1 and boundary = 0.5, even if 0.5 is outside the range of the data.  At most one of center and boundary may be specified.

Using ``width = 1``, as suggested, throws in an error.

title: typo in documentation
make list() behave as NULL
description:
To me it feels counter intuitive that `NULL` is a no-op while `list()` results in a modified object. Of course the rendered plots do not differ. In the  current definition of function `add_ggplot()` the test for returning `p` unchanged uses `is.null(object)`, one could use `length(object) == 0` instead, but maybe it is just me that is surprised, and there is a good reason behind treating `NULL` and `list()` differently.

``` r
library(ggplot2)

myplot <- ggplot(data = mtcars,
                 aes(x=disp, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point()

identical(myplot, myplot + NULL)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(myplot, myplot + list())
#> [1] FALSE
```

title: feature request: increase_fontsize()
description:
I'm requesting a function (e.g. `increase_fontsize()` or `bigger_text()`) that can be used interactively to quickly increase the font size of a graph. This could be extended for programmatic usage (explored below).

### Motivation

The motivating issue is when you plot your first graph and want to play with the font sizes and make the text bigger. I imagine that the most-often used way to do this is:
```
d <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price)) + 
   geom_point()

## works well, but not quick for the coder
d + theme( axis.title = element_text(size = 12))
```
This could be made a lot quicker. (How does one even know that the default theme size is 11 without [S/O ](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11955229/how-to-change-the-default-font-size-in-ggplot2)?)

Perhaps better for quick workflow would be:
```
## make all titles, legends, axis text, etc one unit bigger
d + increase_fontsize()
```

### Implementation

The `increase_fontsize()` function would take in the values of the text sizes supplied by `d` and increase the font sizes by 1. I think this would be doable with `theme_set()` or `theme_update()`. Sorry, I'm not a ggplot2 wiz, so I can't say I have a solution for this right now.

### Optional arguments

Here's some examples of how this function could be made even more useful:
```
## make all titles, legends, axis text, etc 2 units bigger
d + increase_fontsize(by= 2)

## increase only the size of the titles
d + increase_fontsize(what = `titles`)
```

### Extension to programmatic usage

It is not necessarily the goal of the grammar of graphics to supply a hacky workaround for quick coding like I'm suggesting. But I think there's a good chance that this could be extended with the use of a second function that can be used to re-implement this programmatically. I'm calling this function `return_theme()`:

``` 
> d + increase_fontsize() + return_theme()
#
# function(){
#   theme(
#     axis.text.x = element_text(size=12),
#     axis.text.y = element_text(size=12),
#     legend.title = element_text(size = 12),
#     legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
#     ...[etc]...
#     axis.title.x = element_text(size=12),
#     axis.title.y = element_text(size=12)
#   ) 
# }
```

In this example, `return_theme()` is like `xtable()` in that it returns textual output. the user should copy-paste this output into a script and save it for later use. (NB: `return_theme()` could instead be a closure which returns a customized `theme()` function, but I don't know if this is as applicable for programmatic usage)

#### Possible new workflow?

Now, with these proposed functions, the user can initially find a "pretty good" text size by specifying relative sizes with `increase_fontsize()`. Then, once the user feels pretty good, they can output those settings with `return_theme()` and save it as a new function `my_theme()`. Of course, the thematic options in the guts of `my_theme()` could be adjusted at a later time if desired. 

As an example:

``` 
p1 <- d + increase_fontsize(by = 2) + 
    increase_fontsize(by = 2, what = "titles") + 
    increase_fontsize(by = 1, what = "axes") +
    increase_fontsize(by = 4, what = "caption")

p1 

## Looks good, so save the theme for later use

p1 + return_theme()
```

I would imagine that there are other great ways to make it easier for the user to quickly find the settings they're looking for, change them, and repeat programmatically. Perhaps this is food for thought? Thanks for reading!

title: Feature request: allow function as argument value in `scale_*(limits=)`
description:
Request is to allow `limits` arg in e.g. `scale_x_continuous` to accept a function which takes the default limits and returns new limits, in parallel with the same functionality in `breaks` and `labels`.

At present it seems like the two options are (1) specify literal limits, which is inflexible (2) calculate the preferred limits outside of the ggplot statement, but that is messy and can result in redoing calculations already happening inside ggplot (e.g. for position="stack").

It looks like this may be a one line change in scale-.r's `get_limits`, but I don't know my way around well enough to be sure.

Motivating example follows.

``` r
library(ggplot2)


p <- ggplot(mtcars) + geom_point(aes(cyl,mpg))

p # But suppose we don't like the default y-axis breaks...
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/ADmOIcM.png)

``` r

# ...we have a general mechanism in breaks= to modify them with a function...
breaker <- function(by) {
  function(limits) {
    low <- floor(limits[1]/by)*by
    high <- ceiling(limits[2]/by)*by
    seq(low, high, by)
  }
}

# ...but it doesn't override the limits so we get an (IMHO) ugly y axis where
# the data exceeds the range of the tick marks...
p + scale_y_continuous(breaks = breaker(10))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/RYICyku.png)

``` r

# In principle we can function-ise the limits in the same way
limiter <- function(by) {
  function(limits) {
    low <- floor(limits[1]/by)*by
    high <- ceiling(limits[2]/by)*by
    c(low, high)
  }
}

# But for now the best we can do is manually override the limits
p + scale_y_continuous(breaks = breaker(10), limits = limiter(10)(range(mtcars$mpg)))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/EpPQvLF.png)

``` r

# Feature request: if limits arg is a function, pass it the existing limits automatically
p + scale_y_continuous(breaks = breaker(10), limits = limiter(10))
#> Warning in is.na(self$limits): is.na() applied to non-(list or vector) of
#> type 'closure'
#> Error in rep(yes, length.out = length(ans)): attempt to replicate an object of type 'closure'
```

title: Feature request: simple geom_boxplot
description:
I introduced a simple boxplot to students today and had to restrict myself to plain R boxplots, because the ``ggplot2`` syntax I know is IMHO too roundabout. 

The simplest boxplot appears to be something like this:

    x = 1:15
    df <- data.frame(x = x)
     ggplot(data = df, aes(x = factor(""), y = x)) +
     geom_boxplot() + 
     theme_minimal() + xlab(NULL)  #  simplify

By contrast, a decent boxplot in plain R can be obtained with:

    boxplot(x)

Questions: 

  **1. Is there a simple way to obtain a simple geom_boxplot()?**
  **2. May I suggest adding a "minimal boxplot" feature, if it is not currently available?**

Perhaps analogous to ``qplot`` something like ``qboxplot`` that would have the following syntax

    qboxplot(x, data = df)

Or allowing to set ``aes(x=x)`` without having to set an ``x`` value, and automagically removing the unwanted theme elements, e.g.:

    ggplot(data = df, aes(y = x)) + geom_boxplot(stat = "identityx")

(I know ``stat="identity"`` is already in use, so not sure if it can be recycled easily like that)

title: No legend with trans = log10 for certain fill/color values

1 1 4 0.31 0.30
2 1 3 0.42 0.10
3 1 2 0.71 0.15
4 1 1 0.59 0.18
5 2 4 0.32 0.18
6 2 3 0.45 0.34
7 2 2 0.64 0.26", 
  header = TRUE)


library(ggplot2)


# fill = z1
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = z1)) + geom_point(pch = 21, size = 10)

# no legend generated
p + scale_fill_continuous(trans = "log10")

title: Boxplot is too narrow when used with facetting
description:
Boxplot is too narrow when used with faceting, and this issue never appears in 2.2.1 release.
I encountered this issue with a dataset similar to below:
```
va <- c(rnorm(10, 1, 1))
vb <- c(rnorm(10, 3, 1))
vc <- c(rnorm(10, 2, 1))
vd <- c(rnorm(10, 3, 1))

                 factor1 = rep(c('A', 'B'), each = 20,times=4),
                 factor2 = rep(c('A', 'B', 'A', 'B'), each = 10, times = 4),
                 factor3 = rep(c(LETTERS[1:4]), each = 40),
                 value = rep(c(va, vb, vc, vd), times = 4)
                 )

```
The plot below is with a discrete x-axis and a continuous y-axis:
```
ggplot(tf, aes(factor1, value)) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor2)) +
    facet_wrap(~factor3, ncol = 2) +

    geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor2)) +
    facet_grid(.~factor3) +

I don't know if it is a bug, or something internal changed from the 2.2.1 release. My original code works fine on release version, but has this issue on the dev version.

title: legend titles for continuous scales need more padding
description:
I see that there has been recent work on the spacing around the legend title in #1881 and #2215. This has fixed the issue for categorical legends but things are still awfully squashed for continuous legends. [Here](https://twitter.com/drob/status/917739357083176960) is an example from the wild, and here is a small reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg, 
                   size = as.factor(cyl), color = qsec)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_gray(base_size = 20)

title: ggtitle height varies with descending letters
description:
Hi there,

I just noticed that the height of a ggplot2 main title depends on the letters used. library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(ggplot() + ggtitle("arrr"),
             ggplot() + ggtitle("brrr"),
             ggplot() + ggtitle("prrr"),
             nrow = 1)
```

Thanks in advance!

title: Additive constant in `expand=` behaves unexpectedly on discrete axes in facets with one group
description:
This issue occurs when using a discrete axis on in a faceted plot with free scales and free space, and one of the panels only has a single break on the axis. I would expect that the physical space taken up by each tick is the same (it is), but also that the `expand = ` argument would behave independently of the number of ticks on the axis (it does not). This means that the physical space outside the ticks increases for panels with multiple ticks, but it is not changing for panels with only one tick.

---



```r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)

iris %>% 
  mutate(S2 = fct_collapse(Species, "not versicolor" = c("setosa", "virginica"))) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(Species, Sepal.Length)) + 
  geom_boxplot(width = 1) +
  facet_grid(~S2, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0.6))

# Note the default `expand = c(0, 0.6)`

```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13338560/31157286-c3643f5c-a887-11e7-8f67-81f3d61e8bd7.png)


Here the boxes touch the edges of the panel in the **versicolor** facet, but there is an expansion gap in the **not versicolor** facet. This seems to not be expected behavior, since the space for 0.6 of an extra tick should be there in both panels.

If you try to increase the additive constant to add an expansion gap in the **versicolor facet**, no gap is created:

```
iris %>% 
  mutate(S2 = fct_collapse(Species, "not versicolor" = c("setosa", "virginica"))) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(Species, Sepal.Length)) + 
  geom_boxplot(width = 1) +
  facet_grid(~S2, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 2))

# Note additive constant increased from 0.6 to 2

```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13338560/31157325-18c2fc0e-a888-11e7-8c0a-babf9c76da52.png)

Space for a full discrete break was added on each side of the **not versicolor** facet, but no space was added to the sides of the **versicolor** facet, so the edges of the box still touch the edge of the panel.

title: geom_path should support intermediate arrows
description:
`geom_path()` supports the arrow argument, but this only adds an arrow to the end of the path.

```r
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(660124238)
plotDF <- data.frame(x = runif(6), y = runif(6))
ggplot(plotDF, aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_path(arrow = arrow())
```

If this geom supported intermediate arrows, it would be trivial to use ggplot2 to create [connected scatterplots](https://eagereyes.org/papers/the-connected-scatterplot-for-presenting-paired-time-series). It's currently possible--but cumbersome--to create connected scatterplots with `geom_segment()`.

```r
ggplot(plotDF, aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_segment(aes(xend = dplyr::lead(x), yend = dplyr::lead(y)),
               arrow = arrow())
```

If folks agree that this change is worth making, I'm not sure if it would be cleaner to implement this by passing a vector of arrow objects to the geom's arrow argument, or through changes to the arrow function.

title: stat_count does not work with line
description:
When I make an empirical probability mass functions (pmf), I like to use linerange with ymin=0 and ymax equal to the value of the empirical pmf. stat_count works well but I cannot use linerange with it without using kind of weird hack.


```r
library(ggplot2)
# works and gives a bar chart
ggplot(mtcars,aes(x=gear))+stat_count()

# throws an error
ggplot(mtcars,aes(x=gear))+stat_count(aes(ymax=..prop..,ymin=0),geom="linerange")
# Error: stat_count() must not be used with a y aesthetic.

# this works because it does not populate the ymin variable
ggplot(mtcars,aes(x=gear))+stat_count(aes(ymax=..prop..,ymin=..prop..-..prop..),geom="linerange")
```

The reason that it fails is because when I set `ymin=0` in `aes`, the data variable has a column with name `ymin` and `is.null(data$y)` returns true which results in the error. The hack involves setting `ymin=..prop..-..prop..` in the `aes` call.

title: Plotting and saving slow with geom_label
description:
### Description

We use ggplot2 in an internal application.
Therefore multiple lines and labels are needed in one plot.
The application allows to save the plot as png.
The addition of one label with `geom_label()` is increasing the needed time to plot and save the graphic.

### Expected Behavior

There should be an small time difference between processing a plot with and without `geom_label()`.

### Actual Behavior

`geom_label()` slows down the plotting process significantly.
Even with only one label.


### Minimal Example

```r

library(ggplot2)

s <- seq(0, 300, 0.25)

df <- data.frame(
    x = s,
    y = sin(s)
)

time_plot_without_label <- system.time({
    plot_without_label <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_line()
    print(plot_without_label)
    ggsave(filename = "plot_without_label.png", plot = plot_without_label)
})

time_plot_with_label <- system.time({
    plot_with_label <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_line() + geom_label(x = 1, y = 0, label = "test")
    print(plot_with_label)
    ggsave(filename = "plot_with_label.png", plot = plot_with_label)
})

print("Used time without label")
print(time_plot_without_label)

print("Used time with label")
print(time_plot_with_label)


```

title: Adding message for overwriting a coordinate system
description:
When one supplies multiple scales for the same aesthetic, a message is printed that notifies the user. When multiple coordinate systems are supplied, however, the last one is used without notification. This is sometimes confusion for new users, that e.g. expect `coord_trans` to work with other `coord_` functions. Could a message be added?

This gives a nice message:
```r
qplot(1:2, 1:2) + ylim(0, 2) + ylim(0, 3)
# Scale for 'y' is already present. Adding another scale for 'y', which will replace the existing scale.
```
But this doesn't:
```r
qplot(1:2) + coord_trans(y = 'log10') + coord_polar()
```
Unfortunately, it's not obvious to me where a replacement could be detected, as there is no `coord_list` like there is `scales_list`. I could prepare a PR, but I'd need some pointers.

title: stri_unescape_unicode() with labels - Unicode characters problem
description:
There is a problem with subscripts, superscripts and maybe more Unicode characters added to: axis labels, titels, etc. using `stri_unescape_unicode()`.

When the default *sans* font (TT Arial) is used subscripts are change to rectangles. Also the *mono* font (TT Courier New) does not work correctly, here problem is even bigger, becuase also superscrips are not working. However, when the font was changed to *serif* (TT Times New Roman) everything works fine - as it is seen on second image.

---
**Example of buggy code:**
``` r

library(ggplot2)
library(stringi) #stri_unescape_unicode()

data(mpg, package="ggplot2")

y_label <- "\\u2082\\U2082\\u2083\\U2083\\U0042"

plot <- ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy)) + geom_point() +
        labs(x = stri_unescape_unicode(gsub("\\U", "\\u", "\\u0041\\u2082\\U2082\\u2082\\U2076\\u2078", fixed = T)),
             y = stri_unescape_unicode(gsub("\\U", "\\u", y_label, fixed = T)) )

print(plot) # rectangles instead of subscripts
```
![](https://i.imgur.com/KAWQ78P.png)

``` r

plot <- plot + theme(text=element_text(family="serif"))
print(plot) # ok
```
![](https://i.imgur.com/EqtYY0i.png)

``` r

plot <- plot + theme(text=element_text(family="mono"))
print(plot) # rectangles instead of substripts & superscripts
```
![](https://i.imgur.com/DcaTRCw.png)


---

**Additional info:**
 * ggplot package version:	 2.2.1

title: legend.spacing.y error "only one operand may be a unit"
description:
This problem was first reported to us at stan-dev/bayesplot#106 for a user using a dev version of ggplot2 (tidyverse/ggplot2@c592e32). I troubleshooted the problem and came up with the following minimal example.

```r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(iris) + 
  aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, color = Species) + 
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.spacing.y = unit(1, "cm"))
#> Error in Ops.unit(theme$legend.spacing.y %||% 0.5, unit(title_height,  : 
#>  only one operand may be a unit
```

Adding ` theme(legend.spacing.x = unit(1, "cm"))` to the plot instead does not yield an error though.

title: Problems with plot area scaling in serial print
description:
Hi,

I just did a serial print of ggplot2 graphics and noted that depending on the letters used in the headline the plot area is scaled differently. If the title contains characters that drop below the baseline (e.g. "g" or "y") the plot area will begin a few points lower than with a title like "abc". For a serial print this is a somewhat undesired behaviour as this is easily noted when scroling through a set of slides with these serial plots on it.



```r
X <- data_frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
p1 <- ggplot(X, aes(x = x, y = y)) + ggtitle("abc")
p2 <- ggplot(X, aes(x = x, y = y)) + ggtitle("abcefg")

p1
p2 ## <- plot area begins a few points lower than in p1
```

title: unwanted reordering of facets
description:
When using the method below to add an "all" facet to a facet_wrapped plot, the facets are reordered alphabetically and do not appear in the same order as the levels of the wrapping variable.

It would be good if there was some way to control the order of the facets in this situation (for example, one may prefer to have the "all" facet appear first.

```r
library(ggplot2)

p <- qplot(displ, hwy, data = transform(mpg, cyl = as.character(cyl)))
cyl6 <- subset(mpg, cyl == 6)
p + geom_point(data = transform(cyl6, cyl = "7"), colour = "red") +
  geom_point(data = transform(mpg, cyl = "all"), colour = "blue") +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl)

```
The method above was from : https://stackoverflow.com/questions/18933575/easily-add-an-all-facet-to-facet-wrap-in-ggplot2

Error in grid.Call(C_textBounds, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  : 
  polygon edge not found

I spent some time to create a reproducible error and even learned to use the reprex package. But I didn't actually post the issue. Then I opened my lap top this morning and ran the reprex example again. No error. I couldn't think of any reason why it started working, but it worked so I went on about my business. After several hours of work I hit the same error again, under somewhat different circumstances. Given the earlier inconsistency, I tried running the same call multiple times and did not get the error when the same call was repeated. 

I think there is a problem, but I have only a nebulous idea of what the problem is. So I will put my non-reproduced reproducible error code below and maybe I won't be the only person who gets an intermittent "polygon edge not found" error. I realize this is not a terribly helpful issue report.

First, here is a copy of my console showing several variations of a geom_sf() call. I was varying the size parameter because I thought that triggered the error in this case. But if you look closely you can see that I make the identical call to geom_sf() and get an error in one instance and no error in another )with the same parameters (size = 0.1).

title: Same position_dodge2() for different width geom_bar() and geom_errorbar() doesn't match
description:
When using the same `position_dodge2()` with a `geom_bar()` and a `geom_errorbar()` that have different widths, the `geom_errorbar()` does not line up correctly with the `geom_bar()` like the first `position_dodge()` does. Not a major issue because increasing `padding` in the `position_dodge2()` of `geom_errorbar()`  produces the desired behavior. It makes sense that it is behaving this way because of the way everything is collapsed toward the middle, so please close this if it was expected behavior. 

```r
library(ggplot2)
packageVersion("ggplot2")
# [1] ‘2.2.1.9000’

df <- data.frame(
    trt = factor(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2)),
    resp = c(1, 5, 3, 4, 5),
    group = factor(c(1, 2, 1, 2, 3)),
    upper = c(1.1, 5.3, 3.3, 4.2, 5.5),
    lower = c(0.8, 4.6, 2.4, 3.6, 4.4)
)

dodge2 <- position_dodge2(width = 0.9)

p <- ggplot(df, aes(trt, resp, fill = group, ymin = lower, ymax = upper))

# Using the same position_dodge2() with different width geom_bar() and geom_errorbar()
p +
    geom_col(position = dodge2) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), position = dodge2, width = 0.5)
```
![conflict](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16431187/29733615-44e91cd8-89ab-11e7-8b44-4294f3df7d78.png)

```r
# Increased padding with same width geom_bar() and geom_errorbar()
p +
    geom_col(position = dodge2) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), position = position_dodge2(width = 0.9, padding = .6))
```
![padded](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16431187/29733634-53b41b32-89ab-11e7-81d6-1bd8ba578596.png)

title: Dev versions of ggmosaic and ggplot2 clash - why?
description:
See explanation, reprex, and session info at haleyjeppson/ggmosaic#11. `ggmosaic` does something bad, breaking ggplot2 internals. The only clue is the fact that `"as.tibble.list"` is getting printed via `cat`, which only appears in [this file](https://github.com/haleyjeppson/ggmosaic/blob/32bd2297cebb6a6b93243440c488e39481ccd6a9/R/scale-product.R#L84), and that unloading `tibble` is the only way to get ggplot functional again.

While this is primarily a ggmosaic/tibble issue, the fact that ggplot2 is breakable in this way might be useful to know and guard against.

title: Errors with element_text when setting axis.text.x/y after theme_void()
description:
Using `ggplot` version 2.2.1, R 3.4.1, I note the following behavior which did not occur in previous versions. After theming a plot with `theme_void`, `element_text` requires certain arguments (at least `angle` and `debug`) when setting `axis.text.x` and `axis.text.y` but not `axis.text`.

```r
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(data.frame(), aes(x = 0, y = 0))

# Works
p + 
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 5)
  )

# Works
p + 
  theme(
    axis.text.y= element_text(size = 5)
  )

# Fails
p +  
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    axis.text.y= element_text(size = 5)
  )
# > Error in element_grob.element_text(el, ...) : 
#  Text element requires non-NULL value for 'angle'.

# Fails
p +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    axis.text.y= element_text(size = 5, angle = 0)
  )

# > Error in if (debug) { : argument is of length zero

# Works
p  +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    axis.text.y= element_text(size = 5, angle = 0, debug = FALSE)
  )


```

title: Geoms and scales: default settings in theme
description:
This idea has been floated around multiple times but I'll raise it again. Currently, themes do not affect the geom properties, such as point and line colour, etc. Scales, in particular colour and fill, suffer the same issue. 

Users who wish to use a specific theme – theme_dark() is a striking example – end up having to change the geom and/or scale defaults. A consistent yet original look, such as a company's brand, may require to set default colour schemes for discrete and continuous scales. 

These two steps currently require adding multiple manual parameters to each plot, or fiddling around with the awkward combination of `set_geom_defaults()` and `scale_colour_discrete <- scale_colour_brewer`.

The suggestion made here is to consider default aesthetics an integral part of the grammar – they're not mapped to data (unless they are), but should be _consistent_ with the overall look of the theme. Themes have gained in consistency with `rel()` and inheritance, but at the moment setting a dark background will make points invisible: not a great default behaviour.

Lattice, as well as Julia's Gadfly, seem to have followed this line of thought to include geom defaults in the theme description. Beamer themes define default colour schemes to be inherited by slide elements.

A proof-of principle, setting point colours to default to the plot title's colour (an existing theme element, for simplicity), was [implemented here](https://github.com/baptiste/ggplot2/commit/03ead2bc00739560719b62822b8fc6a6ac22aa8a). (Note: the use of complex numbers is just for curiosity – it would correspond to something like `waiver()` in the standard ggplot2 way of dealing with values that are to be resolved just before rendering.

title: Proposal: theme-altering shortcuts
description:
I love the thought that's gone into making `theme()` work so well - the inheritance, the structure, it's all really sophisticated and mature. 

I also forget how to change common things most of the time. I don't think I'm alone in having to look up how to rotate the `x` axis labels. Part of the reason for this is that the structure works against ease of use (we're supposed to be making it easier for the human, right?). RStudio will help a little way in auto-completing, but I still need to know that 

    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))

is what I am aiming for. No doubt this is a hurdle to adoption for new users.

My proposal: a (likely quite long) list of shortcuts (in the style of the `magrittr` aliases listed under `?magrittr::extract`) to easily achieve 'common' recipes. In the case of the above example, a starting point might be

```
theme_label_x_vertical <- function(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5) {
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = angle, vjust = vjust))
}
```

This is certainly a) near trivial, and b) easily implemented in another package, but I would like to suggest that having this native in `ggplot2` would be of the most benefit. This would:

 - be available to the auto-complete system (with the right naming patterns)
 - have sensible argument defaults, but ones that can be specified if desired
 - be easier to recall
 - be available to be inspected in the console (not a method) to see exactly what it does.

Food for thought if nothing else. If it's not suitable for `ggplot2` then I'll put together an extension package.

title: geom_errorbar linetype overrides line types in legend
description:
The problem occurs with multi-layer line graphs, in which the color and linetype are both
mapped to the same factor. If you plot without specifying a line type for the error bars
the legend correctly displays the combination of color and line type, but
the error bars are plotted using the line types, which doesn't look good.
Setting a solid linetype for the error bars makes them plot correctly, but then all of the line types
in the legend are solid, even though the plot still uses different line types. 

An example data set:

data <- data.frame(Day = rep(c(0,1,2,3,4), 4), mean = c(-0.06, 0.19, 0.38, 0.54, 0.67, 0.00, 0.18, 0.37, 0.51, 0.37, 0.00, 0.20, 0.42, 0.69, 1.17, 0.00, 0.08, 0.35, 0.44, -0.37),
                   combined = as.factor(c(rep("A",5), rep("B",5), rep("C",5), rep("D",5))))

data$lower <- data$mean - 0.1
data$upper <- data$mean + 0.1
                   

This first example doesn't set a line type for the error bars, 
which causes the error bars to use the line types of the lines. Dotted lines in error bars aren't desirable.

ggplot(data, aes(x = Day, y = mean, color = combined, linetype = combined)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2) +
  theme_bw()

Setting the line type for the error bars makes them plot with solid lines, but then this
overrides the line types in the legend.

ggplot(data, aes(x = Day, y = mean, color = combined, linetype = combined)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, linetype = 1) +
  theme_bw()

The desired behavior is to have solid error bars, but legend entries that show the correct
line types. This can be achieved by overriding the line types with a guides() statement, like so:

ggplot(data, aes(x = Day, y = mean, color = combined, linetype = combined)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, linetype = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  guides(linetype = guide_legend(override.aes = list(linetype = c(1,2,3,4))))

However, this should be unnecessary - line types of the error bars shouldn't 
override the line type of the lines.

title: scale_color_gradient2 doesn't entirely respect limits argument
description:
If `midpoint` is not half-way between the two values in `limits`, then the gradient scale extends beyond the limit that is closer to `midpoint` but the guide stops where `limits` specifies.  Especially in conjunction with `na.value`, this can mislead the reader.

In this plot the color scale goes below what the guide displays, and values below 2 are not indicated as `NA`.

```r
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width) ) +
  geom_point(data = iris, aes(color = Petal.Length), size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = iris %>% filter(Petal.Length < 2), size = 4, shape = 5, color = "red") +
  geom_point(data = iris %>% filter(Petal.Length > 6), size = 4, shape = 0, color = "red") +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = muted("green"), high = muted("navy"), 
                        mid = "gray80",
                        midpoint = 3, limits = c(2, 6), 
                        na.value = "orange")
```

If we change `midpoint` to `3`, then the scale truly runs from 2 to 6 and values below 2 are 
flagged.

```r
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width) ) +
  geom_point(data = iris, aes(color = Petal.Length), size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = iris %>% filter(Petal.Length < 2), size = 4, shape = 5, color = "red") +
  geom_point(data = iris %>% filter(Petal.Length > 6), size = 4, shape = 0, color = "red") +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = muted("green"), high = muted("blue"), 
                        mid = "gray80",
                        midpoint = 4, limits = c(2, 6), 
                        na.value = "orange")
```

title: geom_area is orders of magnitude slower than geom_ribbon
description:
Depending on the data, `geom_area` can be orders of magnitude slower than `geom_ribbon`, despite being ostensibly equivalent.

This seems especially glaring when the data has long “runs” of equal y values. Here’s a reprex where it’s 15x slower. By making the runs longer, this factor can be increased:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(342415)
n = 1000

rle = data.frame(
    Lengths = sample.int(100, n, replace = TRUE),
    Values = runif(n, 1, 100)
)

data = data.frame(
    x = seq_len(sum(rle$Lengths)),
    y = rep(rle$Values, rle$Lengths)
)

p = ggplot(data, aes(x, y, ymax = y))

system.time(plot(p + geom_ribbon(ymin = 0)))
```

![](http://i.imgur.com/DlET7jn.png)

    #>   0.997   0.051   1.065

    system.time(plot(p + geom_area()))

title: Modify fun.data in stat_summary for multiple imputed data
description:
I am interested in using stat_summary with datasets that comprise separate runs of a multiple imputation algorithm. It seems like this should work great given stat_summary's use of the fun.data option, but currently stat_summary is set up to only pass a numeric vector to the fun.data function. In order to calculate the correct means and standard errors, however, it is necessary to also pass an ID variable representing the imputations because standard errors have to differentiate between the within-imputation and between-imputation variance.

I am obviously willing to write the function, but I am looking for some advice on what I would have to do to get this to work with fun.data. Is it possible to pass in the index via a column attribute in the data frame without modifying any ggplot2 code? Or would it require some kind of patch?

title: Mapping shape or size aesthetics is not propagated to legend in geom_sf
description:
I looked around and wasn't able to find other documented instances of this. 

```r
library(sf)

devtools::install_github("tidyverse/ggplot2") ##most recent version of dev ggplot2
library(ggplot2)

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)

## Create some point data to plot
points_sf <- data.frame(
  Latitude = c(35.7596, 35.7796), 
  Longitude = c(-79.0193, -78.6382),
  Site = c("X1","X2")
) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4267)

## Looks good on this plot; aesthetic not replicated in legend
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_sf(data = points_sf, aes(shape = Site))

## Same here 
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_sf(data = points_sf, aes(size = Site))
```
Even when some element is mapped to the legend like with `colour`, the empty box is unexpected:
```r
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_sf(data = points_sf, aes(colour = Site))
```
Typically `ggplot2` would add appropriate points to the legend like this:
```r
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Species))
```
I am highlighting this because it seems like this is an instance where `geom_sf` doesn't function like a `ggplot2` user would expect it to do so.
