title: Wrong error message with NA name in scale_linetype_manual, inconsistent with scale_color_manual
description:
When NAs are included as a name with the scale_linetype_manual, an incorrect error occurs:

```
Error in grid.Call.graphics(C_lines, x$x, x$y, index, x$arrow) :
  invalid hex digit in 'color' or 'lty'
```

The error says that the linetype or color given is invalid even when all colors and linetypes are in fact valid. The problem is with an NA in the names of the value vector given to the scale_linetype_manual function.

However, the same vector of names with colors (with color identifiers rather than linetype identifiers) does not produce an error (although the line does not get drawn either).

It seems as if an NA value is given a specific linetype, then the line should be drawn. Even if you disagree, the error message given should point the user at the correct problem, an NA in the names, and not send them down a rabbit hole trying to diagnose a non-problem.

Here is some code that demonstrates both the inconsistent behavior and the error

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(data.table)
library(RColorBrewer)


# Setup
line_types = c('solid', 'dotted', 'longdash')
color_group = 'Paired' # 'Dark2'...
IS_POOL = c(NA_character_, letters) # pool of names to label lines
IPTS = 6 # how many lines to plot
IS = IS_POOL[1:IPTS]
DENPTS = 20 # the number of points used to draw the density
BUG_FIX = F

if (BUG_FIX) {
    IS[is.na(IS)] = "NA"
}

dt = data.table(index=rep(1:IPTS, each=DENPTS),
                 x=rep(seq(-4,4, length.out=DENPTS), times=IPTS))
dt[, i := IS[index]]
setkey(dt, i, x)
dt[, `:=`(mean=rnorm(1), var=runif(1, 0.5, 2)), by=.(i)]
dt[, density := dnorm(x, mean, var)]


# set up line and color sequences
colors = brewer.pal(ceiling(length(IS) / length(line_types)), color_group)
colorrep = rep(colors, each=length(line_types))[1:length(IS)]
names(colorrep) = IS
linerep = rep(line_types, times=length(colors))[1:length(IS)]
names(linerep) = IS

# this works fine
plt = ggplot(dt) + geom_line(aes(x=x, y=density, color=i, linetype=i))
plt

#  this works fine, despite the NA in colorrep
plt = plt + scale_color_manual(values=colorrep)
plt

# this fails with, even though linerep and colorrep names are setup identically
# Error in grid.Call.graphics(C_lines, x$x, x$y, index, x$arrow) :
#   invalid hex digit in 'color' or 'lty'
plt + scale_linetype_manual(values=linerep)
```

title: geom_dotplot "count" axis is meaningless
description:
`geom_dotplot` produces a "count" scale which is meaningless; it just ranges from 0 to 1.

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(hp)) + geom_dotplot(binwidth = 10)
```

![dotplot1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/128019/28145245-909a986c-6725-11e7-9f5f-850bafbe04cc.png)

If rendering to a taller device, the rendered geometry stays the same but the y scale expands:

![dotplot2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/128019/28145281-df2804ba-6725-11e7-91ea-fda03a66af46.png)

This makes sense from the standpoint that we are rendering circular points whose diameter is determined by the `bindwidth` argument. But it's unfortunate that the y scale has no intrinsic meaning. It's inconsistent with histograms, where "count" means the number of items in a bin:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(hp)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 10)
```

![histogram](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/128019/28145333-5fdcea12-6726-11e7-864d-68344ba34d76.png)

Couldn't the "count" scale for dotplots be used to mean how many dots are in a given column?

title: stat_bin2d with drop=FALSE still drops some 0-count cells
description:
The `drop` parameter in stat_bin2d does not appear to work as advertised: docs state that "if [drop is] TRUE removes all cells with 0 counts." Given this, my expected behavior when `drop = FALSE` was something akin to the bottom plot. Instead, `drop = FALSE` results in the second plot, which does keep 0-count cells in x- or y-bins with some values but omits them in bins with no values.

Is this expected behavior? Or should bin indices that don't appear at all in the data be added back into the output of [`ulevels`](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/8778b48b37d8b7e41c0f4f213031fb47810e70aa/R/facet-grid-.r#L402) applied to bin indices in [`tapply_df`](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/b05c6c1f61a52311809ffda775eb258b07518dab/R/stat-summary-2d.r#L119)?


``` r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

data(iris)

iris %>%
  ggplot(aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)) + stat_bin2d(aes(fill=..count..), drop=TRUE)
```

![](http://i.imgur.com/KrMmVtC.png)

``` r

iris %>%
  ggplot(aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)) + stat_bin2d(aes(fill=..count..), drop=FALSE)
```

![](http://i.imgur.com/akcg9rh.png)

``` r

iris %>% 
  mutate(
    bin_x = cut(Petal.Length, breaks = 30),

  ) %>% 
  count(bin_x, bin_y) %>%
```

title: Add model II regression with lmodel2 to stat_smooth
description:
In ggplot2 it is very easy for me to plot a standard linear regression with lm, also with loess, glm etc.

```r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm")
```

However, I would like to just as easily be able to do model II regression when both x and y variables are noisy, like this:

```r
library(lmodel2)
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lmodel2")
```

This doesn't work. As the wiki says, "Calculation is performed by the (currently undocumented) predictdf generic and its methods."

If predictdf could be implemented for lmodel2, that would be great. Alternatively, if you were able to document predictdf and how to write a predictdf method, I would do that in a fork and put in a pull request. And it would be easy for others to add methods in the future.

Thanks,
Edward

title: `geom_sf()` return values of latitude and longitude for data in a projected coordinate system

title: Setting 'fill' for data label on stacked geom_bar inverts order of labels
description:
First: Hadley, you are truly amazing. To me, you are the personification of data science. I'm a PhD student (antimicrobial resistance analysis, really cool) and I'm always citating your packages that I use in papers (mostly `ggplot2`, `dplyr` and `readr`). Thanks for making the life of this microbiologist so much easier!

Now the bug: 
When using `fill` on a label in conjunction with a stacked plot, the order of labels get inverted.

```r
# create a nice table
tbl2 <-
structure(list(x = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 6L, 1L, 2L, 
3L, 4L, 5L, 6L), .Label = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"), class = "factor"), 
    y2 = c("type 1", "type 1", "type 1", "type 1", "type 1", 
    "type 1", "type 2", "type 2", "type 2", "type 2", "type 2", 
    "type 2"), y = c(210, 131, 149, 215, 325, 203, 239, 103, 
    172, 195, 189, 157)), .Names = c("x", "y2", "y"), row.names = c(NA, 
-12L), class = "data.frame")

# create a nice stacked plot
p <- ggplot(data = tbl2, 
            aes(x = x, 
                y = y, 
                fill = y2)) + 
  geom_bar(width = 0.65,
           stat = 'identity',
           position = 'stack')
              
# Win 10 x64
# R version 3.4.0 (2017-04-21)
# RStudion version 1.0.143, desktop
# ggplot2 version 2.2.1
```

Now watch 😉 

This code:
```r
p + geom_label(aes(label = y),
               position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
               size = 2.75,
               colour = 'white')
```
Gives the expected result (although the coloured legend boxes contain a small white `a`) :
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7526559/28087035-5c8c9132-6681-11e7-9e60-63e783609d8c.png)

Whereas this code:
```r
p + geom_label(aes(label = y),
               position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
               size = 2.75,
               colour = 'white',
               # only difference: add fill
               fill = 'black')
```
Inverts the order, and plots the labels on the other bar:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7526559/28087143-b8cb0bfe-6681-11e7-961e-9033a3d05c56.png)

The alignment is also inverted, as you can see.

title: `include.lowest` missing in function arguments of cut_interval et.al.
description:
The documentation for `cut_interval` reads

``` r
...   other arguments passed on to base::cut
```

One of the arguments of base::cut is `include.lowest`, but using it with `cut_interval`/`cut_number`/`cut_width` results in an error.

``` r
table(ggplot2::cut_interval(runif(1000), 10, include.lowest = FALSE))
#> Error in cut.default(x, breaks(x, "width", n, length), include.lowest = TRUE, :  formal argument "include.lowest" matched by multiple actual arguments
```

So either `include.lowest = TRUE` should be included in the main function arguments of `cut_interval` *et.al.*, e.g. `cut_number(x, n = NULL, include.lowest = TRUE, ...)` This is to be preferred IMHO since it makes it's use transparent. Or the documentation should be transparent about `include.lowest` not being allowed.

BTW: Shouldn't these functions rather be part of `scales`, since both these functions and scales are about transforming variables?

title: Single colour specification, e.g. aes(..), colour = "black", overrides legend appearance
description:
Even if you specify just a single fill to have a coloured border, the legend will show all fills as having that border. Please find the reprex and the plot output below. R 3.4.0 (64-bit), RStudio 1.0.143, ggplot2 2.2.1.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

txhm <- add_column(txhousing, dttm = date_decimal(txhousing$date, tz = "UTC"))

normal.plot <- txhm %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=dttm)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = listings, fill = "listings")) +
  geom_col(aes(y = sales, fill = "sales"))
normal.plot

blank.plot <- txhm %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=dttm)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = listings, fill = "listings")) +
  geom_col(aes(y = sales, fill = "sales"), colour = "black")
blank.plot
```

title: Width changes in geom_col may render the plot invisible
description:
If two time series are plotted as overlapping bar charts, with timeline in the `datetime` format, any changes to width (incl. `width = 0.9`) will render the data invisible. Please find a reproducible example, and plot examples from it, below. RStudio 1.0.143, R 3.4.0. (64-bit), ggplot2 2.2.1.

With date as `double` (as seen in `date` column of `txhousing` dataset) the code works as intended.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

txhm <- add_column(txhousing, dttm = date_decimal(txhousing$date, tz = "UTC"))

normal.plot <- txhm %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=dttm)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = listings, fill = "listings")) +
  geom_col(aes(y = sales, fill = "sales"))
normal.plot

blank.plot <- txhm %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=dttm)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = listings, fill = "listings"), width=1) +
  geom_col(aes(y = sales, fill = "sales"), width=1)
blank.plot
```

title: labs() doesn't inherit the dataframe
description:
I find myself wanting to include summary statistics for the dataframe in the caption, but labs() doesn't inherit the dataframe. Here's an illustrative (albeit meaningless) example. 

An illustration of the mean:
```r
diamonds %>%
  group_by(carat) %>%
  summarize(ncolor = length(unique(color))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ncolor)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(ncolor)))
```

But calculating the mean fails within labs():
```r
diamonds %>%
  group_by(carat) %>%
  summarize(ncolor = length(unique(color))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ncolor)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(ncolor))) +
  labs(caption = paste0("Average Number of Colors for a Carat Amt  = "), mean(ncolor))
```

As this shows, geoms inherit the dataframe, making calculations of summary statistics from inherited variables possible, but labs() does not.

title: geom_curve curvature argument as an aesthetic rather than as an argument
description:
Currently geom_curve accepts an argument of curvature which is static within that function call. 
e.g: geom_curve(aes(... ) curvature=0.5)

It is also possible to imagine curvature as an aesthetic - thus something which could vary within a function call, e.g.

geom_curve(aes(x=Xvar, y=Yvar, xend=X2var, yend=Y2var, curvature=alive))

in this example were alive=0 for a record, this would yield a straight line between(Xvar, Yvar) and ( X2var, Y2var), and where alive=1 the line would be curved.

title: scale_x_date passes NAs to the label function
description:
When using `scale_x_date(..., label = fun)`  it can be that NAs are passed to `fun` which adds undesirable complexity to the definition of the function.

See this example:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/44616530/prevent-showing-the-year-several-times-unnecessarily-with-time-series/44751923#44751923

where this line had to be added to avoid errors even though the NAs do not actually correspond to breaks:

    b[is.na(b)] <- Sys.Date()

Any date could have been used in place of `Sys.Date()` since it seems that the date itself is not actually used if the passed break is NA.

title: Plotting bad sf data can make R crash
description:
Providing bad data to `geom_sf` can lead ggplot to crash the current R session.  

The problem is something related to using different projections in the layers (which I realize is improper, but probably shouldn't crash R). It's also somewhat specific to the projections I've chosen; using Lambert azimuthal equal-area (`+proj=laea`) instead of Robinson (`+proj=robin`) doesn't cause a crash.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

robin_crs <- "+proj=robin +lon_0=0 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +ellps=WGS84 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs"
india_crs <- "+init=epsg:24383"  # India-centered Lambert conformal conic projection

bad_point <-  st_as_sf(data.frame(longitude = 0, latitude = 92),  # bad latitude
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = st_crs("+init=epsg:4267"))

plt <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_transform(bad_point, crs = india_crs)) +
  geom_sf(data = st_transform(bad_point, crs = robin_crs))
ggplot_build(plt)  # force calculation here (print would work too)

```
Other details: I'm using the latest development version of ggplot2, 2.2.1.9000, commit f1bef79. This crash happens inside and outside RStudio. It's not a caught segfault; it's an immediate crash. Adding `coord_sf()` doesn't help.

Would you like me to contribute a failing test for this?

title: Is it possible to add reverse= to position_dodge()?
description:
Currently position_stack() has the reverse parameter to change the order of stacking, but this feature is not available in position_dodge().

One would need to reverse the order of dodging in a group bar chart when it is a horizontal bar chart with the vertical axis starts from the top to the bottom.

title: geom_area() cannot change stacking order (v 2.2.1)
description:
In ggplot2 version 2.2.1 stacking order of geom_area() does not change, and code has broken backward compatibility with previous package syntax without any warnings etc.

Consider the following examples

```r
dx <- data.frame(x=rep(1:8,3),y=rep(c(2,3,2,4,3,5,3,2),3),z=c(rep("bread",8),rep("butter",8),rep("fish",8)))
ggplot() + geom_area(data=dx, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=z))
```
Used to create graph with stacking order top to bottom = fish, butter, bread. And the following code on rearranging the factor levels would change the stacking order top to bottom to bread, butter, fish.

```r
dx <- data.frame(x=rep(1:8,3),y=rep(c(2,3,2,4,3,5,3,2),3),z=c(rep("bread",8),rep("butter",8),rep("fish",8)))
dx$z <- factor(dx$z, levels = rev(levels(dx$z)))
ggplot() + geom_area(data=dx, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=z))
```

Reference: 
1- Several Stack overflow questions including [this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38306081/r-order-of-stacked-areas-with-ggplot-geom-area)
2- R Graphics cookbook, Winston Chang, First Edition, Chapter 4, section 4.7

title: Embedded fonts in PDF output
description:
Not sure if this is the correct place to report this, but thought I should mention it.

In many publication venues it is required that all PDF files have the fonts being used embedded in the PDF files themselves.

AFAIK the PDF files output from `ggsave` do not have their fonts embedded, requiring us to perform [an extra step](https://tex.stackexchange.com/a/109460) to ensure every figure (and consequently the final paper) has its fonts embedded in the file.

Is the PDF output part of  gpplot, or this is a more general problem with R graphics output?

title: geom_point border and fill portions of the point overlap
description:
---
Using ggplot2 with R3.3.3 on windows.

The border and the fill areas of a point are overlapping. I understand from other issue posts that stroke should not be affected by alpha, but on points, it is. When the point has an alpha of .5 and the stroke is set rather large (say 15), you see an overlap of the border and the point. I am plotting points like this (with alpha = .5 to show density) and since the overlap is happening, the overlap section of the point is much darker than the rest of the point. This is not aesthetically pleasing.

The code below produces 2 points of the same size fill area. They appear (by my crude screen measures) to be the same size (fill area) as they should, but it appears that the fill area on the point with stroke = 15 has been drawn larger and is assuming that the border will mask the difference. With alpha = .5, this doesn't happen.

So, either the point border should not be impacted by alpha or, preferably, the point border and fill should not overlap.

```r
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(0, 1)), aes(x = x, y = 0)) +
  geom_point(size=15,
             fill = "red",
             colour = "black",
             shape = 21,
             stroke = c(0, 15),
             alpha = .5) +
  scale_size_identity()
![rplot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19614636/26906752-13f62d9a-4bbd-11e7-900a-eda613c7942a.png)
```

title: Double coordinate transformations for geoms that draw with other geoms
description:
When a `geom` queries the coordinate range and uses the result to create data that is then plotted by another `geom`, there is potentially a double transformation. i.e. `coord.range()` yields results in coordinate space and if followed by `coord.transform()`, the data may get transformed two times. Affects `coords` that transform the limits in `coord$setup_panel_params` and also do transforms in `coord$transform`. This includes `coord_trans` and `coord_sf`.

Affected geoms include `geom_abline`, `geom_hline` and `geom_hline`.

**reprex**
``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x=1:6, y=10^(1:6))
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept=3, color='red') +
  coord_trans(y='log10')
```
![](http://i.imgur.com/XAf6Y4t.png)

The red line (at x=3) should be top to bottom.

title: qplot gives warnings for unknown parameters when following example code qplot
description:
qplot has the ... argument to pass aesthetics into each layer. If I follow the example code from http://ggplot2.org/book/qplot.pdf , ggplot2 version 2.2.1 throws a warning about unknown parameters.

This problem occurs when different layers are constructed by eg using multiple geoms, and using the dots argument to pass extra arguments to those. The arguments are used correctly, but nevertheless a warning is thrown.

```r
set.seed(1410) # Make the sample reproducible
dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]
qplot(carat, price, data = dsmall, geom = c("point", "smooth"),
      span = 0.2)
```
Throws a warning but gives a correct plot. The warning can be emulated by explicitly writing this out as:

```r
ggplot(dsmall, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point(span = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(span = 0.2)
```

The help page says that ... should be *aesthetics* passed into each layer, but it clearly passes any extra argument to all layers constructed, not just aesthetics. So the help page could use an update as well.

title: Round the weighted survival estimates in the risk table
description:
I was trying to reproduce the plot in p. 311 of Berglund, Heeringa, and West's Applied Survey Data Analysis. The data is available online at their website, which I linked [here](http://www.isr.umich.edu/src/smp/asda/ASDA%20Analysis%20Examples%20Data%20Sets%20Stata%20and%20SAS%20Format.zip). How can I round off the survival estimates in the risk table? Can we have something like `risk.table.decimal.place` which defaults to a whole number?

title: geom_density with groups of 1 or 2 elements
description:
Hello,

I am struggling with `geom_density` when groups consist on fewer than 3 elements. 
For a group of 1 element, the density plot consists on a single line of length 1. For a group of 2 elements, this is a rectangle of height 0.5.
Since this does not depends on the _y_ scale, the interpretation of the area under the curves breaks down. This problem becomes obvious when changing coordinates on the _x_ axis (_eg_ unit conversion).

This reproducible example illustrates my point.
This is the density of the measurements of `Speed`, for the 5 experiments. Each consists on 20 runs.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(MASS)

michelson %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Speed, fill = Expt)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)
```
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/10049355/25946761/ce5a35ae-364c-11e7-95f9-5af4138e1add.png)

The density of the measurements, for the 5 experiments when we re-normalize the speed. As expected, the only changes are in the axis texts.

```r
michelson %>%
  mutate(Speed = Speed / mean(Speed)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Speed, fill = Expt)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)
```
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/10049355/25946798/ee373aac-364c-11e7-8216-0bbc8bfff12e.png)

The problem arises when the groups are small,
so we modify the data for the last group to consist on only two runs.
```r
michelson_modif <- michelson
michelson_modif$Expt[83:100] <- 2

michelson_modif %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Speed, fill = Expt)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)
```

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/10049355/25946983/b396509e-364d-11e7-980a-7e60c3546585.png)


```r
michelson_modif %>%
  mutate(Speed = Speed / mean(Speed)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Speed, fill = Expt)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)

```
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/10049355/25946991/c3c0481c-364d-11e7-99eb-a7e590754a6b.png)

The two graphs are no longer similar.

Do I miss something here? Is it possible to force the behaviour of `geom_density` to be similar (_ie_ smooth curves) for all the groups, regardless of the number of elements in them?

Thanks a lot!

title: geom_tile() + coord_map() is extremely slow.
description:
Using a projected coordinate system and `geom_tile()` takes ~100 times longer than without one.  

``` r
library(ggplot2)

lat <- seq(-87.159, -2, by = 3.7)
lon <- seq(0, 360, by = 3.75)
month <- 1:12

gdata <- expand.grid(lat = lat, lon = lon, month = month)
gdata$z <- rnorm(nrow(gdata))

g <- ggplot(gdata, aes(lon, lat)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = z)) +
    facet_wrap(~month, ncol = 4) 

benchplot(g)
#>        step user.self sys.self elapsed
#> 1 construct     0.000    0.000   0.000
#> 2     build     0.776    0.016   0.793
#> 3    render     1.552    0.052   1.607
```

title: facet_wrap() doesn't play well with expressions in facets.
description:
`facet_wrap()` doesn't get along with faceting by function. It works sometimes, but not always and also the error messages are not informative. For example, it breaks if I add annotations. This is a minimal example of what I'm talking about:
``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(stringi)

dates <- as.Date(c("2015-01-01", "2016-03-01"))
df <- expand.grid(x = 1:10, date = dates)
df$y <- rnorm(nrow(df))
df$yearnum <- year(df$date)

g1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_line()
g2 <- g1 + annotate(geom = "text", x = 5, y = 0, label = "test") 


g1 + facet_wrap(~year(date))    # works
```

![](http://i.imgur.com/lHebUhX.png)

``` r
g2 + facet_wrap(~year(date))    # error
#> Error in as.POSIXlt.default(x, tz = tz(x)): do not know how to convert 'x' to class "POSIXlt"
g2 + facet_wrap(~yearnum)    # works fine
```

![](http://i.imgur.com/fnf2yWU.png)

Is not only a problem with date

``` r
g1 + facet_wrap(~sqrt(yearnum))    # works
```

``` r

```

You get the same behaviour if you use geoms

``` r
df2 <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = rnorm(10))

```

![](http://i.imgur.com/Zb8N7U9.png)

``` r

#> Error in as.POSIXlt.default(x, tz = tz(x)): do not know how to convert 'x' to class "POSIXlt"
```

title: coord_proj() is superior to coord_map() and could be included in the default ggplot
description:
`coord_proj()` from package `ggalt` is a superior way of projecting map data in `ggplot2` compared to `coord_map()`. [The function](https://github.com/hrbrmstr/ggalt/blob/master/R/coord_proj.r) uses industry-standard CRS codes and the under the hood calculation uses the yet again industry-standard (and pretty awesome) PROJ.4 library. The advantage of using standard CRS codes instead of the definitely non-standard values from `mapproj` allows for better automation and less manual fiddling for finding which values correspond to which CRS parameters.

A more detailed reasoning (not mine, but from the author of `ggalt`) can be found [here](https://rud.is/b/2015/07/24/a-path-towards-easier-map-projection-machinations-with-ggplot2/).

I believe a kind of `coord_proj()` could be included directly in the default `ggplot2` as a superior alternative to `coord_map()`.

EDIT: I see that `coord_sf()` already works quite a bit better then `coord_map()` from this point of view, at least. Can you implement the same nice working lines and labels into `coord_proj()`?

title: scale_identity doesn't play well with guide = "legend"
description: To get a legend guide when using `scale_identity` we need to specify `guide = "legend"`. In addition, "you'll typically* also need to supply `breaks` and `labels`" (`?scale_identity`). However, when trying to get legends for `color`, `fill`, `shape`, `size` and `alpha`, when using `scale_identity`, a correct legend is obtained only for `color`. All other aesthetics generate either an incorrect legend (`fill`) or an error (`shape`, `size` and `alpha`). Some data: ``` r df <- data.frame(x = 1:2, y = 1, color = c("red", "blue"), fill = c("blue", "red"), shape = 21, size = c(20, 10), alpha = c(0.8, 0.4)) ``` Then try to get legends, without and with specification of `labels` and `breaks`. Legends for `color` and `fill`: ``` r library(ggplot2) ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = color, fill = fill, shape = shape, size = size, alpha = alpha)) + geom_point(stroke = 5) + scale_color_identity(guide = "legend") + scale_fill_identity(guide = "legend") + scale_shape_identity() + scale_size_identity() + scale_alpha_identity() ``` ![](http://i.imgur.com/Eyzney6.png) ``` r ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = color, fill = fill, shape = shape, size = size, alpha = alpha)) + geom_point(stroke = 5) + scale_color_identity(guide = "legend") + scale_fill_identity(guide = "legend", labels = df$fill, breaks = df$fill) + scale_shape_identity() + scale_size_identity() + scale_alpha_identity() ``` ![](http://i.imgur.com/wzM71wp.png) The plot itself looks OK for all aesthetics. The legend for `color` is OK, but the `fill` legend only displays black points. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Legend for `shape` errors (`Error: Continuous value supplied to discrete scale`) ``` r ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, shape = shape)) + geom_point() + scale_shape_identity(guide = "legend") #> Error: Continuous value supplied to discrete scale ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, shape = shape)) + geom_point() + scale_shape_identity(guide = "legend", labels = df$shape, breaks = df$shape) #> Error: Continuous value supplied to discrete scale ``` ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Legends for `size` and `alpha` error (`Error in !self$na.translate : invalid argument type`) ``` r ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, size = size)) + geom_point() + scale_size_identity(guide = "legend") #> Error in !self$na.translate: invalid argument type ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, size = size)) + geom_point() + scale_size_identity(guide = "legend", labels = df$size, breaks = df$size) #> Error in !self$na.translate: invalid argument type ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, alpha = alpha)) + geom_point() + scale_alpha_identity(guide = "legend") #> Error in !self$na.translate: invalid argument type ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, alpha = alpha)) + geom_point() + scale_alpha_identity(guide = "legend", labels = df$alpha, breaks = df$alpha) #> Error in !self$na.translate: invalid argument type ``` ------------------------------------------------------------------------ By accident, I also mapped `alpha` while specifying a `size` legend, resulting in an `alpha` legend: ``` ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, alpha = alpha)) + geom_point() + scale_size_identity(guide = "legend") ``` -------- \* It's unclear what 'typically' means here. At least in my examples, including or excluding `labels` and `breaks` makes no difference.

description:
The geom_tile and geom_raster functions are fantastic for plotting maps.  However, it is not uncommon to want to compare maps with different resolutions on the same plot, ie as different facets.  Whilst it is easy to build a data.frame containing the relevant data and structure, it seems that the geom_tile and geom_raster functions do not handle this correctly. They try valiantly, but don't quite manage it...

![lai ta 2090-2100 allruns biomesexample v0 0](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/6500068/24956991/70bfc57c-1f8a-11e7-89db-210cdffc6f6e.png)

There is half a workaround, using interpolate does fill in the white spaces, but it comes out so blurry that it hurts my eye to look at it.  It is definitely not suitable for a report, publication etc...

As far as I can see, it might be possible to correctly handle different resolutions in different panels.  One would need to include the recalculation of ymin, ymax, xmin and xmax, (or equivalent) in the facetting command, perhaps following a fresh call to resolution() for each facet (perhaps at the finish_data stage).  The details are highly speculative, I just looked at the ggplot2 source code for the first time today.

Could this be feasible?  It would be a really great for many geo-scientists and statisticians!

title: With discrete_scale( ... drop=FALSE), add an option to drop unused levels in legend
description: This is related to issue #1433 . When some levels in color factor variable are not used, adding `drop=FALSE` can keep the color mapping. This is useful when there are different subset of data from same levels set. ``` df <- data.frame( x = c(0,1,0,1,0,1), y = c(0,1,1,2,2,3), f = factor(c(1,1,2,2,3,3)) ) ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = f)) + geom_line() ggplot(subset(df, f != "1"), aes(x, y, colour = f)) + geom_line() + scale_colour_hue(drop = FALSE) ``` ![ggplot_drop_level](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/25039897/24808021/679b140c-1b88-11e7-8465-e7c852701429.png) In above plot it make sense to keep the unused levels in legend. However in my Shiny app I have a dataset of locations and time. A histogram grouped the time into 14 bins, and I colored the points in scatter plot with same color in the bin of time, this way it's easier to visualize the time distribution of points in the scatterplot. Note I'm maintaining the color mapping manually now, so the screenshot above didn't have the unused levels. If all 14 levels and colors were reported in the legend of scatter plot, it will be too overwhelming and misleading. **What I wish to have is to add an option for legend, which will drop the unused levels in guide.** I keep the colors synchronized in many plots, tables, and I'm maintaining color mapping manually for all of them. If we can have this option, most of the color sync code can be simplified a lot. All the screen shots are to show the usage. The above code is a working example already.

title: scale_reverse() prevents expanded minor grid lines
description:
When using `scale_reverse()` while expanding the axis limit to a value close to the upper minor break necessary, this minor grid line is omitted.
Removing `scale_reverse()` produces all of the grid lines expected.
Using `expand_limits()` instead of `coord_cartesian()` only solves the problem for a few cases.

```r
library(ggplot2)

limit_ok <- c(8, 10, 12, 8.1, 8.2, 9.9) # a few limit values for which grid lines are ok 
limit_not_ok <- c(9, 11, 9.1, 10.9) # a few limit values for which the upper minor grid line after the data is omitted 

test_limit <- sample(limit_not_ok, 1) # sample one value among the few examples

ggplot(
  data = iris,
  aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length)
) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0, test_limit) 
  ) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  annotate("text", x = 7.5, y = 2, label = test_limit )
```

title: theme_void() does not remove grids
description:
When using a custom grid, `theme_void` does not remove it. Here is a simple example illustrating it:

```r
library(ggplot2)
qplot(1:10, (1:10)^2)                   # Basic plot
theme_update(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "red",
    size = 0.5))                        # I want major grid in red
qplot(1:10, (1:10)^2)                   # Works OK
qplot(1:10, (1:10)^2) + theme_void()    # Grid still here
```

Given that `theme_void` is supposed to be a completely empty theme, I think `theme_void` should redefine all elements to `element_blank()`, including `panel.grid.major` and `panel.grid.minor`, and probably others (I believe it is somehow related to #2058, in the sense that `theme_void` should redefine more elements than it currently does).

title: aes(colour="myname") doesn't like "myname" in UTF-8
description:
---

Brief description of the problem

This program explores the relation between correlation coefficients and regression coefficients for various combinations of correlations between the variables.

The correct output is three curves (red, blue, green), with a horizontal line of the same colour that intercepts the curve at the Y-axis.
The incorrect output has the horizontal line in a colour that does not match.

The issues appears to be caused by
  geom_line(aes(colour=...))
not liking the colour names being UTF-8 (versus ANSI) strings.  But that's the extent of my expertise.  Maybe this is even a limitation that is documented somewhere, but I searched around 
Please briefly describe your problem and what output you expect. If you have a question, please don't use this form, but instead ask on the mailing list <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/ggplot2> or stackoverflow <http://stackoverflow.com>.

Please include a minimal reprex. The goal of a reprex is to make it as easy as possible for me to recreate your problem so that I can fix it. If you've never heard of a reprex before, start by reading <https://github.com/jennybc/reprex#what-is-a-reprex>, and follow the advice further down the page. Do NOT include session info unless it's explicitly asked for, or you've used `reprex::reprex(..., si = TRUE)` to hide it away.  



```r
# Written by Nick Brown (nick.brown@free.fr), March 2017.

# Possible bug in ggplot2?
# Correct output: three curves (red, blue, green), with a horizontal line of the same colour
#  that intercepts the curve at the Y-axis.
# Incorrect output: horizontal line colour does not match.
# Note that UTF-8 encoding is required.

rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))

library("ggplot2")

rYX1 <- 0.17         # first predictor-outcome correlation
rYX2 <- 0.08         # second predictor-outcome correlation
rmin <- -0.85        # lowest negative predictor-predictor correlation to include
rmax <- 0.92         # highest positive predictor-predictor correlation to include
detail <- 200        # number of points; increase for slightly smoother curves
col.X1 <- "#0000FF"
col.X2 <- "#00FF00"
col.Rsq <- "#FF0000"

baseRsq <- -99.0
prevRsq <- 0.0

crX1X2 <- c()
cbeta1 <- c()
cbeta2 <- c()
cRsq <- c()

r12min <- round(rmin * detail)
r12max <- round(rmax * detail)
for (r12 in r12min:r12max) {
  rX1X2 <- r12 / detail
  denom <- 1 - (rX1X2 ^ 2)
  beta1 <- (rYX1 - (rYX2 * rX1X2)) / denom
  beta2 <- (rYX2 - (rYX1 * rX1X2)) / denom
  Rsq <- (rYX1 * beta1) + (rYX2 * beta2)

  if (r12 == 0) {
    baseRsq <- Rsq         # remember R-squared when rX1X2 is zero, so we can detect it again later
  }

  crX1X2 <- c(crX1X2, rX1X2)      # Please don't write to tell me this is inefficient
  cbeta1 <- c(cbeta1, beta1)
  cbeta2 <- c(cbeta2, beta2)
  cRsq <- c(cRsq, Rsq)

  prevRsq <- Rsq
}

my.breaks <- c("b1", "b2", "Rsq")
# >>>>>>>>>> To produce the "bug", uncomment the next line <<<<<<<<<<
#my.breaks <- c("β1", "β2", "R²")
# Note: if you don't see two occurrences of the Greek letter beta, and one of the "squared" symbol,
# in the above line, then something has gone wrong with the encoding at some point.

df <- as.data.frame(cbind(crX1X2, cbeta1, cbeta2, cRsq))
names(df) <- c("rX1X2", "beta1", "beta2", "Rsq")

gg <- ggplot(df, aes(x=rX1X2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=(seq(-0.5, 1.0, 1) / 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name="betas and Rsq", breaks=(seq(-1.0, 1.0, 2) / 10)) +
  geom_line(aes(y=beta1, colour=my.breaks[1])) +
  geom_line(aes(y=beta2, colour=my.breaks[2])) +
  geom_line(aes(y=Rsq, colour=my.breaks[3])) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    paste("rYX1=", rYX1, "  \n", "rYX2=", rYX2, sep=""),
    breaks=my.breaks,
# A workaround is to use the ANSI version of  "my.breaks" and add a labels clause here, e.g.:
#    labels=c("β1", "β2", "R²"),
    values=c(col.X1, col.X2, col.Rsq)
  ) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=rYX1), colour=col.X1) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=rYX2), colour=col.X2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=baseRsq), colour=col.Rsq) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=0.0)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept=0.0))

gg

```

title: position_dodge(perserve="single") shifts everything left
description:
The new `preserve` parameter of `position_dodge` is awesome (#1935, I think), but when applied to `stat_count` or `stat_boxplot` (maybe more), with missing levels that aren't the final one, it shifts groups to the left to fill the empty level:

``` r
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(x = rep(letters[1:3], each = 3), 
                 fill = factor(c(2,2,3, 1:3, 3,3,3)))

ggplot(df, aes(x, fill = fill)) + 
    geom_bar(position = position_dodge(preserve = 'single'))
```
![plot with left-shifted bars](http://i.imgur.com/w948wmq.png)

``` r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(vs), mpg, fill = factor(cyl, c(8,6,4)))) + 
    geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(preserve = 'single'))
```
![boxplot example](http://i.imgur.com/hbPrBqw.png)

While that behavior makes sense given that these stats previously didn't care about empty groups didn't need drawing or spacing, I suspect most users would expect bars to keep their group position à la `geom_col`/`stat_identity` (which has 0s to keep things in place):

``` r
ggplot(data.frame(table(df)), aes(x, Freq, fill = fill)) + 
    geom_col(position = 'dodge'))
```
![plot with normally-arranged bars](http://i.imgur.com/mUylAaz.png)

Is this desired behavior or a bug?

title: the xlim/ylim ranges in stat_binhex are sometimes exclusive instead of inclusive
description:
I've been loving ggplot and the hexogonal plots for quite a while, but recently I looked back at a scatterplot of my data and noticed a line close to the x-axis of my chart, that wasn't there in the hexogonal plot of it.

Some trails led me to the insight that the ylim and xlim ranges can have quite an unpredictable impact on which data is plotted. Similarly the size and ratio of the plot.

I understand that the size and ratio has an effect on the size of the hexagons, yet it shouldn't change the limits.

Here are some examples of the confusion:

```R
set.seed(42)
dt4 = data.frame(
  x = c(rep(1, 100), rnorm(10000, mean = 10, sd = 2), rep(18,100)),
  y = c(rep(2, 100), rnorm(10000, mean = 10, sd = 2), rep(19,100))
)
```

some random data with two points in the corners

```R
hex_base = ggplot(dt4, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_hex() +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours=c("grey90","black"))

png(filename = "/tmp/nolimits.png", width=600, height=480)
hex_base
dev.off()
```

the base ggplot figure, which looks like this:

![nolimits](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376469/74d16768-fd2c-11e6-9da8-ec224b6f60bc.png)


```R
png(filename = "/tmp/withxlim.png", width=600, height=480)
hex_base + xlim(1,18)
dev.off()
```

Changing the xlim to still fit the data, we loose the bottom left point:

![withxlim](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376549/cd71219c-fd2c-11e6-9c4c-96ddaf500af8.png)
 
Okay, maybe the xlim is not inclusive as we would expect.

```R
png(filename = "/tmp/withxlim2.png", width=600, height=480)
hex_base +
  xlim(0,18)
dev.off()
```

now we loose the top right point:

![withxlim2](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376578/ea7448d2-fd2c-11e6-8c1a-1edd702d695b.png)


let's look at ylim.

```R
png(filename = "/tmp/withylim.png", width=600, height=480)
hex_base +
  ylim(2,19) 
dev.off()
```

okay as expected, both points still showup:

![withylim](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376612/0a85706a-fd2d-11e6-82d3-4da6c419db79.png)


what you most likely use:


```R
png(filename = "/tmp/withxylim.png", width=600, height=480)
hex_base +
  xlim(1,18) +
  ylim(2,19) 
dev.off()
```

again, the left bottom point drops out:

![withxylim](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376633/252982f8-fd2d-11e6-8464-b23498bfbab8.png)


```R
png(filename = "/tmp/withxylim2.png", width=600, height=480)
hex_base +
  xlim(0,18) +
  ylim(2,19) 
dev.off()
```

and again, we switch to dropping the right top point.
![withxylim2](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376676/578ef5b6-fd2d-11e6-8269-cd6c5b1defab.png)

with different random data set's i've seen the exact opposite, the `ylim` is dropping points around the edges. and it can't always be solved by making the ranges wider.


Now for reference, let's look at the underlying function `hexbin`:

```R
png(filename="/tmp/manual.png", width=600, height=480)
hexbinplot(y~x,dt4, xlim=c(1,18))
dev.off()
```
okay, that's a very  literal limit, but at least it's consistent.

![manual2](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376739/936b8b1c-fd2d-11e6-804d-aa4cbfc4ed2f.png)


another work around is to use subset.

```R
png(filename="/tmp/manual.png", width=600, height=480)
hexbinplot(y~x,subset(dt4, x >= 1 & x <= 18 & y >= 2 & y <= 19))
dev.off()
```

![manual](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/179603/23376784/c68ab784-fd2d-11e6-827a-c4113886a5e3.png)


I hope this is not a too long/wordy issue, but I think this is at the very least  confusing behaviour.

title: Docs for discrete_scale inaccurate
description:
In the documentation for `?discrete_scale`, the `labels` parameter is documented as
	
> `NULL` for no labels, `waiver()` for default labels (labels the same as breaks), a character vector the same length as breaks, or a named character vector whose names are used to match replacement the labels for matching breaks.

However, in `?scale_x_discrete`, the final example shows a very important alternative: passing a function as a formatter:

```r
# Use abbreviate as a formatter to reduce long names
ggplot(mpg, aes(reorder(manufacturer, displ), cty)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = abbreviate)
```

and thus should probably be documented more like `continuous_scale`'s `labels` parameter:

> One of:
> - NULL for no labels
> - waiver() for the default labels computed by the transformation object
> - A character vector giving labels (must be same length as breaks)
> - A function that takes the breaks as input and returns labels as output

I'm happy to assemble a quick PR if you like, but will everything get redone in the course of dealing with #1750 anyway?

title: Proportion in geom_bar() with no fill
description:
I'm not sure if this a bug in the code or a lack of clarity in the documentation.

The documentation of geom_bar() indicates that there are two calculated values "count"  and "prop".   However, when making a bar plot with just one variable it seems to not be possible to use `..prop..` unless you use a workaround to create a single stacked bar with the variable as fill. 

This is what I expected to be able to use:  
`ggplot(mpg, aes(x=class)) + geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop..))`

to create a plot like this:  

`ggplot(mpg, aes(x=class)) + geom_bar(aes(y = (..count..)/sum(..count..)))`

I believe that when there is no fill, the prop calculation is using the n for each attribute as the denominator rather than the n for all of x. Hence the proportions are always 1.00.   

Examples 4, 6 and 8 below are the only ones with correct proportions. 

```r
# 1. Basic bar
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=class)) + geom_bar()
# 2. Explicitly request count
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=class)) + geom_bar(aes(y = ..count..))
# 3. Explicitly request prop
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=class)) + geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop..))
# 4. Calculate prop, what we are aiming for
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=class)) + geom_bar(aes(y = (..count..)/sum(..count..)))
# 5. Pretend that there is an x factor and the y is the fill stacked
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=factor(0))) + geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop.., fill=class))
# 6. Pretend there is an x factor, y is fill, position fill, correct calculations
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=factor(0))) + geom_bar(aes(fill=class), position ="fill")
# 7. Pretend that there is an x factor and y is the fill dodge
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=factor(0))) + geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop.., fill=class), position ="dodge")
# 8. Aes with fill, but request prop
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=factor(0))) + geom_bar(aes(fill=class, y = ..prop..))

```
I've seen this kind of plot requested on Stackoverflow so I know I'm not the only one who ever needs it, but I think that just clarifying the documentation would be good.  I'm happy to work on a PR if that would be helpful.

I do think that probably in principle, the stack _is_ the preferred visualization when showing percents that add up to 100.

title: `geom_bar` inconsistently handling date values
description:
Description
===========

There are unexpected plot results when specifying the fill aesthetic in `geom_bar` when the `x` aesthetic is a Date or POSIXct value. Below I have listed examples using Date and POSIXct objects, respectively. Similar data represented with these two classes results in rather different plots, see below.

Date Examples
=============

The following examples use Date objects produced with `make_date()`.

1 month with 2 fill values
--------------------------

In this example January fill values are TRUE and FALSE, February and March fill values are only FALSE.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

d1 <- data.frame(
  dates = rep(make_date(year = 2017, month = 1:3), each = 2),
  highlight = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
)

# this unexpectedly changes the width of one of January's bars
ggplot(d1, aes(x = dates)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = highlight))
```

    ## Warning: position_stack requires non-overlapping x intervals

![unnamed-chunk-1-1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3228369/22983239/85c7973e-f36f-11e6-9678-979aa5a9da1a.png)

1 month with distinct fill value
--------------------------------

In this example January fill values are only TRUE, both February and March are only FALSE.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

d2 <- data.frame(
  dates = make_date(year = 2017, month = 1:3),
  highlight = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
)

# only one bar for January, but as above it is thin
ggplot(d2, aes(x = dates)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = highlight))
```

![unnamed-chunk-2-1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3228369/22983226/7f9afcde-f36f-11e6-9013-0d726fe40db1.png)

3+ fill values
--------------

This example introduces a third fill value to the highlight column.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

d3 <- data.frame(
  dates = make_date(year = 2017, month = 1:3),
  highlight = c(1, 2, 3)
)

# all bars are now equally thin, additional breaks added to x-axis
ggplot(d3, aes(x = dates)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = factor(highlight)))
```

![unnamed-chunk-3-1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3228369/22983219/79dfa8f8-f36f-11e6-9096-281dbf9f3a29.png)

POSIXct Examples
================

The following examples use POSIXct objects produced with `make_datetime()`.

1 month with distinct fill value
--------------------------------

In this example, when January fill is only FALSE, February and March are only TRUE, the January bar does not show. The bar may be too thin to see.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

d4 <- data.frame(
  datetimes = make_datetime(year = 2017, month = 1:3),
  highlight = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
)

# January bar is no longer thin, instead missing 
ggplot(d4, aes(x = datetimes)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = highlight))
```

![unnamed-chunk-4-1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3228369/22983215/72d436aa-f36f-11e6-910a-77da404f6447.png)

3+ fill values
--------------

Similar the 3+ fill value example above, however in this example the bars are not equally thin, they are all missing.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

d5 <- data.frame(
  datetimes = make_datetime(year = 2017, month = 1:3),
  highlight = c(1, 2, 3)
)

# no bars
ggplot(d5, aes(x = datetimes)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = factor(highlight)))
```

![unnamed-chunk-5-1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3228369/22983198/6403b560-f36f-11e6-904f-eaacd4e36319.png)

Conclusion
==========

The `geom_bar` fill aesthetic is not properly handling Date and POSIXct objects. I am not weighing in yet on whether bars ought to be thin or wide, rather I am hoping to iron out `geom_bar` so Date and POSIXct values are handled consistently. I hope I have not misunderstood how `geom_bar` is intended to handle date values.

I will look under the hood to try and identify the problem. For now I am not sure of a work around.

title: Control expression atop lineheight with ggplot theme element text lineheight
description:
Is it possible to override the minimum lineheight of plotmath expressions that use atop for line breaks?
```
library(ggplot2)
# Multi line expression
qplot(x = 1, y = 1, xlab = expression(atop("line1", ~line^2)))

# Adjust line height to no avail
qplot(x = 1, y = 1, xlab = expression(atop("line1", ~line^2))) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(lineheight = 0.5, debug = TRUE))

# Insert extra line break with \n allows control of that line height
qplot(x = 1, y = 1, xlab = expression(atop("line1\n", ~line^2))) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(lineheight = 0.5, debug = TRUE))

# But we can't control the line break created by atop
qplot(x = 1, y = 1, xlab = expression(atop("line1\n", ~line^2))) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(lineheight = 0.00001, debug = TRUE))

# Removing atop causes other issues with centering...
qplot(x = 1, y = 1, xlab = expression("line1\n" ~line^2)) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(lineheight = 1, debug = TRUE))
```

I've tried searching everywhere and the only solution I could find was reverting to base graphics and mtext or maybe using arrangeGrob. Is there an easier solution that could be built in to ggplot?

title: geom_smooth behaves like geom_path
description:
I noticed that `geom_smooth` behaves like `geom_path` rather than `geom_line`. For example,

```
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(transform(mtcars, 
                 pred.mpg = predict(lm(mpg ~ poly(hp, 2), 
                                       data = mtcars), 
                                    interval = "confidence"))) + 
  geom_smooth(aes(x = hp,
                  y = pred.mpg.fit, 
                  ymin = pred.mpg.lwr, 
                  ymax = pred.mpg.upr), 
              stat = "identity")
```

produces
![smooth_example](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/321235/22558177/cab9539e-e93a-11e6-8738-3364e1467fd4.png)

Whereas ordering by the x-axis variable produces the desired result:

```
ggplot(transform(mtcars, 
                 pred.mpg = predict(lm(mpg ~ poly(hp, 2), 
                                       data = mtcars), 
                                    interval = "confidence"))[order(mtcars$hp), ]) + 
  geom_smooth(aes(x = hp,
                  y = pred.mpg.fit, 
                  ymin = pred.mpg.lwr, 
                  ymax = pred.mpg.upr), 
              stat = "identity")
```
![smooth_example2](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/321235/22558263/12bcc69e-e93b-11e6-9c4a-382a8b90298e.png)

I looked at the `geom_smooth` code, but I don't understand why it behaves this way. It looks like `GeomSmooth` calls `GeomLine`, and `GeomLine` does 

```{r}
  setup_data = function(data, params) {
    data[order(data$PANEL, data$group, data$x), ]
  }
```
so I would have thought ordering the data myself would make no difference.

title: Ensure travis tests across multiple R versions
Issues with extending ggplot2 in a package
description:
# Tips for Adding ggplot2 Functions to an R Package

1. In the vignette [Extending ggplot2](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggplot2/vignettes/extending-ggplot2.html), under the definition of the function `stat_chull`, you will see the text:

> (Note that if you are writing this in your own package, you will either need to call `ggplot2::layer()` explicitly, or import the `layer()` function into your package namespace.)

An important bit of information that is not present in the vignette is that if you are writing your own package, you need to call `ggplot2::ggproto` and `ggplot2::Stat` explicitly in the definition of the function `StatChull`.  Also in both your `stat` and `Stat` functions, you will need to call any other ggplot2 functions explicitly that you use, for example, `ggplot2::unit`.


2. When you use `package.skeleton` to start creating your new package, any `Stat` functions you have created will be placed under the **data** folder with the extension _.rda_ instead of under the **R** folder with the extension _.R_.  This is because once a `Stat `function has been created in an R workspace, R considers it a data object instead of a function.  If you just leave things as is, then when you build your package you will get the message that you need to create a help file for the `Stat` data objects that were created, and R will expect you to use the form of the help file that is appropriate for a data object.  To remedy this situation, after you have run `package.skeleton`, delete the `Stat `data objects under the **data** folder, and place the ACSII files that contain the `Stat `function definitions under the **R** directory.  These files should have the name _Statname_.R; for example, the file containing the definition of the function `StatChull `given as an example in the vignette should have the name StatChull.R.


3. You may want to export your `Stat `functions (i.e., using the `export `function in the NAMESPACE file) so that they are visible to the user.  If you do export them, you will have to create help files for them.  If you just want the user to be able to see them so that advanced users can easily see the code but you do not want users in general to know about them and you do not want to write help files for them, you can include the `Stat `functions in the help file _packagename_-internal.Rd, where _packagename_ is the name of your package.

title: Unify the type required by geoms/layers when POSIXct values used
description:
I stumbled into a possible bug, or at least what I thought was odd behavior. Here's a reproducible example:

```
## create the data
dat <- data.frame(date = paste0(2016, "-0", 1:9, "-01"),
                  val = 1:9)
dat$date <- as.POSIXct(dat$date)

## a simple base plot which I'll add to
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = date, y = val)) + geom_point()

## I tried to add a vertical line at a date and figured that I needed
## to match the class of the x variable used in the base plot,
## but it fails, complaining about being POSIXct
p + geom_vline(xintercept = as.POSIXct("2016-05-01"))

## I found a stackoverflow post[1] that suggested using as.numeric(), which works
p + geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(as.POSIXct("2016-05-01")))

## I happened to *also* want to add some text, and given the success
## of the above line, I assumed all additions needed as.numeric(as.POSIXct())
## so this seemed logical but it fails
p + annotate("text", x = as.numeric(as.POSIXct("2016-05-01")),
             y = 6, label = "test")

## instead, it appears that annotate() wants POSIXct after all
p + annotate("text", x = as.POSIXct("2016-05-01"), y = 6,
             label = "test")
```

Is this a bug? It would seem nice if layers expected a unified class for the coordinate specifications, or at least this is what I expected. I don't think it matters too much what it is, per se, as long as `ggplot2` is clear about what it should be. In other words:

- regardless of the `aes(x = blah)` in the base layer, all additional coordinate specifications need to be in their `numeric` form; or:
- the definition of `aes(x = blah)` fundamentally changes how all subsequent layers should be defined and the coordinates need to be the same class as `x`

Does that make sense? Thanks for considering or clarifying my thinking if I'm not understanding what's going on in this example!

---

[1] http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5388832/how-to-get-a-vertical-geom-vline-to-an-x-axis-of-class-date

title: coord_flip() seems to lose coord_cartesian() specifications when geom_bar() is present.
description:
The simple graphs that show the behavior may seem silly so I am outlining a use case here.

Use case:

I was building a presentation with a facet-wrap where the units of each facet were different (say classifier measures such as accuracy, AUC, deviance, and so on ).  So I thought the best was to express that was to make sure there was a sale on each facetted element.  The only way I know how to do that is to set the facet_scale to some variation of "free".  I also wanted the presentation with bars left to right, and the way I know how to do that is a coord_flip().


The issue:

I noticed the desired/expected coord_cartesian() effect is lost after the coord_flip() if there is a geom_bar() in the plot.  scale_*_continuous() seems to work (not sure if it does in all cases), and removing the geom_bar() (leaving only the geom_point()) also seems to work.  Below are some simplified graphs (which obviously are not themselves convincing use cases, which is why I explained by use case above).

Examples (with expected behavior, and differing observed behavior):

```
library("ggplot2")

#> packageVersion('ggplot2')
#[1] '2.2.0'

d <- data.frame(x=0.5,
                y=0.7,
                g=c('a','b'), 
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Example graph that works.
# Expected behavior limits are obeyed:
# plot 1 face_wrap(scale='free') obeys 
# coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(0,1))
# obeys limits as expected.
ggplot(data=d,mapping=aes(x=x,y=y)) +
  geom_point() + geom_bar(stat='identity') + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(0,1)) +
  facet_wrap(~g, scale='free')

# Very similar graph (differs only in coord_flip()) that
# has unexpected behavior.
# Expected behavior limits are obeyed:
# plot 1 face_wrap(scale='free') obeys 
# coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(0,1)).
# Observe: graph extent does not obey limits.
ggplot(data=d,mapping=aes(x=x,y=y)) +
  geom_point() + geom_bar(stat='identity') + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(0,1)) +
  facet_wrap(~g, scale='free') + 
  coord_flip()


# graph pair that works
ggplot(data=d,mapping=aes(x=x,y=y)) +
  geom_point() + geom_bar(stat='identity') +  
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~g, scale='free')
# related graph that also works.
ggplot(data=d,mapping=aes(x=x,y=y)) +
  geom_point() + geom_bar(stat='identity') + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~g, scale='free') +
  coord_flip()
```

title: aspect() for sf is assuming longitude/latitude
description:
It's not appropriate to use the cosine-latitude-hack for projections that aren't in angular units, and currently we have to use `coord_sf()` manually to fix it.  

Here's an example where the defaults give catastrophic results (map is flipped). (I haven't explored enough to know if this will behave with sensible defaults given other work that's going in. )


The following code gives a "y-flipped" map in ff80b239

```R
library(ggplot2)
library(maptools)
library(sf)

data(wrld_simpl)

m <- st_transform(st_as_sf(subset(wrld_simpl, NAME %in% c("Australia", "New Zealand"))), 
                  "+proj=laea +y_0=1.3e6 +lon_0=155 +lat_0=-30 +ellps=WGS84 +no_defs")

ggplot(m) + geom_sf(aes(geometry = geometry)) 

## tell it not to do that
ggplot(m) + geom_sf(aes(geometry = geometry)) + coord_sf(lat_lon = FALSE)
```

Personally I think the cosine hack does more harm than good  (providing a kind of expectation that working with angular coordinates in a planar context is "fine"), it's really from a legacy age when projecting was computationally expensive and inaccessible. 

I'm confused about why it's a default, but then maybe I'm picking at this too early.

title: Change way themes are added
description:
I've created a `textboxGrob` that allows for automatic wrapping of text etc. I'm trying to create an `element_textbox` as a subclass of `element_text` to allow people to use it for titles etc, but there are some problems in how themes are added that makes it impossible to subclass elements.

Specifically the class of the added elements are dropped if the element is already present, since `add_theme` is merely modifying the slots of the original element rather than using the added element as the base.

Will you be willing to consider a PR that flipped this behaviour so that `add_theme` would use the added element as base and modify the `NULL` slots of this?

title: Non-x/y coordinate systems
description:
For sf, we want`aes(geometry = geometry)`, but currently there's no way for the coordinate system to get this information and generate the x and y positions from it.  To fix this, I think, the generation of x and y scales needs to be made primarily the responsibility of the coordinate system: we need to call `coord$train()` once for each layer with the full data, and allow it to generate the `x` and `y` scales however it likes.

Other coordinate systems this would facilitate:

* graph layout as coordinate system
* product plots
* projections from higher dimensions

title: ggplot2::waiver throws a warning on r-devel
description:
The recent R commit r71841 deprecates what `ggplot2::waiver` does. In the development version of R,
```
ggplot2::waiver()
```
yields

> Warning message:
In structure(NULL, class = "waiver") :
  Calling 'structure(NULL, *)' is deprecated, as NULL cannot have attributes.
  Consider 'structure(list(), *)' instead.

This is leading to some largely spurious test failures in other packages that use `testthat::expect_silent()` but end up calling something in ggplot2 that calls `waiver` internally.

title: Add option for range ticks (tick labels between tick marks)
description:
Achieving this with built-in methods is [pretty hacky](http://stackoverflow.com/a/22221898/247482), and a more generic way on top of ggplot2 still involves combining a special scale and a special theme, none of which make sense in isolation. (the scale has every second tick labeled, and the theme hides the dummy ticks and grid lines.)

Idk how to do this best, as it deviates from the 1:1 relationship between ticks and tick labels – range ticks are associated with the value range between tick marks.

I think the formatting function would get passed either the middle between the tick positions or the previous and next tick position. e.g. for ticks spaced 1, the formatting function would either be passed `(0.5)` or `(0, 1)` for the tick label between the values 0 and 1.

title: Change stacking behaviour in ggplot2 2.2.0 geom_bar collide with unchanged behaviour of geom_text
description:
According to the blog https://blog.rstudio.org/2016/11/14/ggplot2-2-2-0/ (and my own observations) the stacking behaviour of geom_bar has been reversed such that the order of items is the same as in the legend.

In some scenarios stacked bar charts (geom_bar) are combined with stacked text labels (geom_text). Because geom_text seems not to be changed accordingly, the charts are wrongly formatted now.

Please change this. I suggest one of the following:

1. revert to the old behaviour of geom_bar
2. add an option to geom_bar to reverse the order (default is behaviour from 2.1.0: reverse = false)
3. the new geom_col function may use the new ordering (default: reverse = true)
4. Alternatively a less invasive change would be to reverse the order of the legend.
5. If 1-3 or 4 are not an option please change geom_text accordingly.

Thank you for your support!

title: layer quietly renames certain parameters
description:
Motivated by exercise 2 under section "Creating a new stat" of the "Extending ggplot2" vignette.
> 2. Modify the final version of StatDensityCommon to allow the user to specify the min and max parameters. You’ll need to modify both the layer function and the compute_group() method.

### case 1 (no warning generated)

Parameters named col, color, pch, cex, lty, lwd, srt, adj, bg, fg, min, or max (see `ggplot2:::.base_to_ggplot`) are renamed without warning when passed to layer(). Values do get passed to methods such as `setup_params()`, but as the renamed names. See the following example,

```R
library(ggplot2)

# create an example Stat which passes along data without
# modification, but outputs information to the console
StatExample <- ggproto(
  'StatExample', Stat,

  setup_params = function(data, params) {
    cat('\n`params` includes:\n')
    print(params)
    params
  },

  # here is where we use ymin, ymax, and fill instead of min, max, and bg
  # to work around the internal renaming
  compute_group = function(data, scales, ymin, ymax, fill, extra) {
    data
  }
)

# create a new stat function
stat_example <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL, geom = 'point',
                      position = 'identity', na.rm = FALSE, show.legend = NA,
                      inherit.aes = TRUE, min = 'min arg', max = 'max arg',
                      bg = 'dodgerblue', extra = 'still extra', ...) {
  layer(
    stat = StatExample, mapping = mapping, data = data, geom = geom,
    position = position, show.legend = show.legend, inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list(na.rm = na.rm, min = min, max = max, bg = bg, extra = extra,
                  ...)
  )
}

d <- data.frame(
  x = 1:5,
  y = 1:5
)

# runs without error, but we knew to name the arguments
# ymin, ymax, and fill, see console output below
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  stat_example()
```

console output,
```
> d <- data.frame(
+     x = 1:5,
+     y = 1:5
+   )
> ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
+     stat_example()

`params` includes:
$na.rm
[1] FALSE

$ymin
[1] "min arg"

$ymax
[1] "max arg"

$fill
[1] "dodgerblue"

$extra
[1] "still extra"
```

### proposal 1

I am unsure what to propose as a solution. But, I would like to propose an update to the ggproto vignette. I suggest adding a note of caution to the ggproto vignette about using "min" or "max" as parameter names in `stat_density_common()`. Especially if no change is made, the reader will know to work around the problem by using different parameter names in `stat_density_common()` or use the prediction gimmick from above in the `StatDensityCommon` methods.

### case 2 (warning generated)

In addition to the above bug, there is an interesting case when *not* predicting the internal renaming i.e. in the `compute_group()` method use "min" or "max" instead of "ymin" or "ymax". See the following example,

```R
library(ggplot2)

# recreate the Stat from above, but with a small, key change
StatExample <- ggproto(
  'StatExample', Stat,

  setup_params = function(data, params) {
    cat('\n`params` includes:\n')
    print(params)
    params
  },

  # this time use min, max, and bg instead of ymin, ymax,
  # or fill as we did above
  compute_group = function(data, scales, min, max, bg, extra) {
    
    # min, max, and bg will all be missing, see console output below
    if (missing(min) && missing(max) && missing(bg)) {
      cat('In `compute_group`, missing arguments min, max, and bg')
    }
    data
  }
)

# create the stat function
stat_example <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL, geom = 'point',
                      position = 'identity', na.rm = FALSE, show.legend = NA,
                      inherit.aes = TRUE, min = 'min arg', max = 'max arg',
                      bg = 'dodgerblue', extra = 'still extra', ...) {
  layer(
    stat = StatExample, mapping = mapping, data = data, geom = geom,
    position = position, show.legend = show.legend, inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list(na.rm = na.rm, min = min, max = max, bg = bg, extra = extra,
                  ...)
  )
}

d <- data.frame(
  x = 1:5,
  y = 1:5
)

# runs without error again, but produces a somewhat confusing warning
# see console output below
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  stat_example()
```

console output,
```
> d <- data.frame(
+     x = 1:5,
+     y = 1:5
+   )
> ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
+     stat_example()
Warning: Ignoring unknown parameters: ymin, ymax

`params` includes:
$na.rm
[1] FALSE

$extra
[1] "still extra"

In `compute_group`, missing arguments min, max, and bg
```

### ~proposal 2

In this case `params` does not include the problematically named values and I believe lines [136 and following](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/cb3bdde0e0ba65be3042083092eb397057af8e3f/R/stat-.r#L136-L145) may be responsible for this. As a result the arguments are missing within `compute_group()`. Additionally, in this case a warning is raised, but the warning cryptically only mentions "ymin" and "ymax" and not "fill". This "proposal" is more of a heads up.

title: axis order for factor disordered by adding geoms with different subsets of the data
description:
When adding geoms to a ggplot with different subsets of the original data the order of the axis changes from factor level order to alphabetical order.

Here a minimal working example:
```
dat <- data.frame(cat = factor(rep(c('a', 'b', 'c'), times = 2), 
                               levels = c('c', 'b', 'a')))
dat$value <- c(1, 2:3, c(-2, -1, -2))

# plot with correct order of the x-axis
ggplot(dat, aes(y = value, x = cat)) +
  geom_bar(data = dat[dat$value > 0, ], 
           stat = "identity") +
  geom_bar(data = dat[dat$value < 0, ],
           stat = "identity")

# deleting first row of dat
dat <- dat[-1, ]
# plot with disordered x-axis
ggplot(dat, aes(y = value, x = cat)) +
    geom_bar(data = dat[dat$value > 0, ], 
             stat = "identity") +
    geom_bar(data = dat[dat$value < 0, ],
             stat = "identity")
```

title: geom_smooth() warning about ymin/ymax
Draw order ignores group factor levels
description:
When plotting data with different groups, I had expected that the draw order of said groups to follow the factor levels. However, the draw order seems to be entirely dictated by the order of points in the data frame:

A basic example:

```
df <- data.frame(x=1:3, y=1:3, g=factor(c("a", "b", "c")))

# Resize plot window so that points overlap. The draw order is point "a", "b", "c".
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, col=g)) + geom_point(size=5) + xlim(-30, 30) + ylim(-30, 30)

# We want to change the order of the factor levels so that the group 
# we care about is shown at the top layer:
df$g <- factor(df$g, levels=c("c", "b", "a"))

# Plot is drawn in the order as shown before:
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, col=g)) + geom_point(size=5) + xlim(-30, 30) + ylim(-30, 30)

# The draw order instead depends entirely on the order of points in the data frame:
ggplot(df[3:1,], aes(x=x, y=y, col=g)) + geom_point(size=5) + xlim(-30, 30) + ylim(-30, 30)
```

title: Secondary date/datetime axis (to show an alternative tz, for example)
description:
I'm trying to add a secondary axis to a datetime axis so the audience has a reference for the times in another timezone, but it appears`sec.axis` has not been implemented for date/datetime scales (yet).

Example:

```R
df <- data.frame(
  x = as.POSIXct(c(
    "2016-11-30 00:00:00",
    "2016-11-30 06:00:00",
    "2016-11-30 12:00:00",
    "2016-11-30 18:00:00",
    "2016-12-01 00:00:00"
  ), tz = "UTC"),
  y = c(0, -1, 0, 1, 0)
)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_datetime("UTC", date_breaks = "2 hours", date_labels = "%I%p",
                   sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . - lubridate::hours(8), name = "PST"))
```

which I envision yielding:

![tz](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1807519/20765740/83f4c206-b6e8-11e6-83fa-208cea62524a.png)

which I faked via:

```R
format_hour <- function(x, ...) {
  x[x < 0 & !is.na(x)] <- 24 + x[x < 0 & !is.na(x)]
  return(paste0(sprintf("%02.0f", ifelse(x %% 12 == 0, 12, x %% 12)), ifelse(x < 12, "AM", "PM")))
}
df$x2 <- lubridate::hour(df$x)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x2, y = y)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous("UTC", breaks = seq(0, 23, 2), labels = format_hour,
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . - 8, "PST", breaks = seq(0-8, 23-8, 2), labels = format_hour))
```

title: Inconsistency in required aesthetics between errorbar and errorbarh
description:
In [the geom_errorbar code](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/R/geom-errorbar.r),
the required aesthetics are
`required_aes = c("x", "ymin", "ymax"),`

However, in [the geom_errorbarh code](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/master/R/geom-errorbarh.r),
the required aesthetics are
`required_aes = c("x", "xmin", "xmax", "y"),`

In other words, the `x` aesthetic is required for both plots, but the `y` aesthetic is required only for `errorbarh`.

I believe the correct answer would be to drop the `x` requirement from `errorbarh`

```
library(ggplot2)
```
