title: scale_fill* doesn't see NaN as NA
description:
Had some weirdness in my plots and eventually tracked it down. the `<na.value>` parameter in the various scale_fill\* scales doesn't recognize `<NaN>` and instead fills them white.

Example:

``` R
# four points, top ones are NA and NaN
df <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2, 1, 2),
  y = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
  z = c(1, 2, NA, NaN)
)

# ggplot sees top left as NA and colors red,
# but the NaN on top right colors white (which
# is invisible if the background is white)
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = z), size = 50) +
  scale_colour_gradient(na.value = "red")
```

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1226866/12231673/eed212b4-b81e-11e5-9f56-ab868689167b.png)

I don't _think_ this is the desired behavior.

It's also difficult to debug why this is happening because many R functions will  put `<NaN>` where a user might expect `<NA>`.  For example `<mean(c(NA, NA), na.rm = TRUE)>` returns `<NaN>`. I ran into this when doing some ddply on a large dataset. The problem was difficult to isolate because `<all.equal()>` can't always tell `<NA>` from `<NaN>`:

``` R
all.equal(
  a <- mean(c(NA, 10), na.rm = FALSE),
  b <- mean(c(NA, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

returns `<TRUE>`.

Also, while the View() function in Rgui will show `<NaN>` the View function in R-Studio will replace it with `<NA>`. The `<write.csv()>` function will also convert `<NaN>` to `<NA>`.

title: setting default scale for aesthetics in a new stat_ function
description:
I created a new `stat_topo()` requiring `x`, `y`, and `val` aesthetics, plotting a simple `geom_raster` of interpolated `val` mapped to `fill`.

```
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(akima)

cpt_grp <- function(data, scales) {
  #interpolate data in 2D
  itrp <- akima::interp(data$x,data$y,data$val,linear=F,extrap=T)
  out <- expand.grid(x=itrp$x, y=itrp$y,KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = F)%>%
    mutate(fill=as.vector(itrp$z))
  # str(out)
  return(out)
}

StatTopo <- ggproto("StatTopo", Stat,
                    compute_group = cpt_grp,
                    required_aes = c("x","y","val")
)

stat_topo <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL, geom = "raster",
                       position = "identity", na.rm = FALSE, show.legend = NA, 
                       inherit.aes = TRUE, ...) {
  layer(
    stat = StatTopo, data = data, mapping = mapping, geom = geom, 
    position = position, show.legend = show.legend, inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list(na.rm = na.rm, ...)
  )
}

set.seed(1)
nchan <- 30
d <- data.frame(val = rnorm(nchan), # some random values to be mapped to fill color
         x = 1:nchan*cos(1:nchan), # the x and y position of the points to interpolate
         y = 1:nchan*sin(1:nchan))
plot(d$x,d$y)

ggplot(d,aes(x=x,y=y,val=val)) +
  stat_topo() +
  geom_point()
```

When I run this, I get the following error:

```
Error: numerical color values must be >= 0, found -1
```

I understand that this is because somehow the values I pass to the `fill` aesthetic are interpreted as color values. If the `fill` values are all positive it works but the scale is discrete by default.

If I enter this: 

```
ggplot(d,aes(x=x,y=y,val=val)) +
  stat_topo() +
  scale_fill_continuous() +
  geom_point()
```

I get what I wanted: the expected raster with a continuous color scale, as I want the `stat_` to do by default...

A puzzling behavior is the following:

```
dd <- cpt_grp(d)
ggplot(dd,aes(x=x,y=y,fill=fill)) +
    geom_raster()
```

Which does what I expect, setting a continuous color scale...

So I guess the question is: 
How can I prevent ggplot from setting a discrete scale here, and ideally set a default scale within the call to my new `stat_` function. Can I do this in `setup_params`?

title: geom_bar fill order not maintained with stat='identity'
description:
Before v2.0.0 I ordered the `fill` of `geom_bar()` using the `order` aesthetic in addition to making the column used as `fill` a `factor` with the `levels` ordered as desired, and it worked (even though doing both was probably redundant). However, in `ggplot2` v2.0.0 the `order` aesthetic is deprecated. Now code that used to work produces out of order `fill`s.

Below is code (using `data(mpg)`) and corresponding plots that seem to indicate that ordering the `levels` of the `factor` works in the case of `stat='bin'`, but not in the case of `stat='identity'`. It's worth noting that the legend is correctly ordered, but the fill is not (which, based on Stack Exchange questions pre-v2.0.0, was solved with the `order` aesthetic).

It's entirely possible that I've missed something and that this isn't actually a bug, but I've tried everything I can think of to remedy the misordering of `fill`, and can't figure it out.

The `scale_fill_brewer()` and `theme()` statements are extraneous with respect to the bug, but it made the graphs easier for me to read and to notice the fill was out of order.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
data(mpg)

##############
# Example 1

  # Simple geom_bar with manufacturer on the x with class as fill
  # Ordering is alphabetical by ggplot2 default
  # Everything is fine here
  g = ggplot(mpg, aes(manufacturer))
  g = g + geom_bar(aes(fill = class)) + scale_fill_brewer() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

``` r

  # Change the order of manufacturer to reverse, and class as in the df
```

title: With coord_flip(), the default behavior should be to invert the old x-scale with Factors
description:
Dear ggplot2 developers,

First of all, thanks a lot for your contribution for this wonderful packages. I think it taught a lot of people around the world the way of creating graphics and its grammar. 

I would like to make suggestion with `coord_flip()`: when the original variable on the x-scale is a factor, then it would be beneficial to inverse the order on the new y scale. I know there are tricks to force the ordering on ggplot2, but I think, this could be an easy improvement. 

Thanks a lot for your time!

title: New error about continuous/discrete x comes up with geom_histogram() in ggplot2 2.0

``` r

 Factor w/ 3 levels "Fri","Sat","Sun": 1 1 1 2 2 3
```

Any tips on what I'm doing wrong or what's going wrong? I tried looking at earlier issues and at `?geom_histogram`.

``` R
# now with half height legend keys
t1 <- t + theme(legend.key.height = 0.5 * t$legend.key.size )
g + t1
```

Now, with ggplo2 v.2.0.0 I get the error message:

``` R
> Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : Unknown input
```

It seems that theme() does no longer accept objects of class unit.arithmetic. 
WORKAROUND:

``` R
t2 <- t + theme(legend.key.height = unit(0.5 * as.numeric(t$legend.key.size),
                                         attr(t$legend.key.size, "unit")))
g + t2
```

May be I'm have missed a point.
Best regards,
Uwe

title: position_nudge defaults do not nudge
description:
The defaults of position nudge are `x = 0`, `y = 0`, which means that calling `position_nudge()` does not actually nudge anything:

```
df <- data.frame(
  x = c(1,3,2,5),
  y = c("a","c","d","c")
)

# no nudge
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = y), position = position_nudge())

# no nudge (if it worked)
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = y), position = "nudge")
```

(At the moment the second code doesn't seem to work for other reasons, #1428).

I urge you to set the defaults to `x = 0.1`, and `y = 0.1`, so the `position = "nudge"` syntax will become a simple way to do something useful. Also, I'd prefer to work once to not nudge after I call position nudge, e.g. `position = position_nudge(x = 0)`, than to work twice each time I want to nudge (first by calling nudge then by setting a nudge, e.g. `position = position_nudge(x = 0.1)`. This would be similar to how `position_jitter` will jitter even if you do not set width and height.

title: `position_nudge` doesn't work when called as `position = "nudge"`
description:
Here's the example from `?position_nudge`, which works.

```
df <- data.frame(
  x = c(1,3,2,5),
  y = c("a","c","d","c")
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = y))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = y), position = position_nudge(y = -0.1))
```

But the code breaks when you call `position = "nudge"`, as you might do with other positions. 

```
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = y), position = "nudge")
```

There's no warning message, the text layer just disappears.

This is bad for me because I'd prefer to be able to teach beginners all five position adjustments without having to teach them the `position = position_nudge()` syntax. The second syntax is a bit overwhelming for someone new to R since it contains a function inside an argument. (We begin new R students with `ggplot2` because visualizations are cool.)

title: nrow and ncol are not swapped correctly for vertical facetting
description:
There's a bug in facet-wrap.r on lines 89-90 that is not apparent unless you use an nrow other than what it defaults to when nrow is NULL. For example, try:

```
mpg2 <- subset(mpg, cyl != 5 & drv %in% c("4", "f") & class != "2seater")
base <- ggplot(mpg2, aes(displ, hwy)) + 
  geom_blank() + 
  xlab(NULL) + 
  ylab(NULL)
base + facet_wrap(~class, nrow = 2, dir = "v")
```

you should get a figure with 2 rows. Instead the figure has 3 rows. Inspecting the plot shows that nrow and ncol both have a value of NULL.

Likewise when you run

```
base + facet_wrap(~class, ncol = 2, dir = "v")
```

both nrow and ncol are 2 when it should be nrow == 2 and ncol == NULL.

The problem is that the swap code always results in nrow and ncol being equal or both being NULL, depending on which argument is defined:

```
# swap
nrow <- sanitise_dim(ncol)
ncol <- sanitise_dim(nrow)  # nrow here is not what you thought it was!
```

You'll have to create a dummy variable to swap them, e.g.:

```
# swap
nrow_swap <- ncol
ncol_swap <- nrow
nrow <- sanitise_dim(nrow_swap)
ncol <- sanitise_dim(ncol_swap)
```

I mentioned this in hadley/ggplot2#1279 but I should have started a new issue instead.

title: Best practices for supporting both the latest stable and the development versions of ggplot2 in R package?
description:
Hello,

I have now updated my [cowplot](https://github.com/wilkelab/cowplot) package so it works with both the latest stable and the development versions of ggplot2. This works fine in principle, but I don't see how I can upload the package to CRAN, because `R CMD check` complains about various errors in the code when the latest stable version of ggplot2 is installed. For example:

```
* checking R code for possible problems ... NOTE
theme_cowplot: possible error in element_text(family = font_family,
  face = "plain", colour = "black", size = font_size, hjust = 0.5,
  vjust = 0.5, angle = 0, lineheight = 0.9, margin = ggplot2::margin(),
  debug = FALSE): unused arguments (margin = ggplot2::margin(), debug =
  FALSE)
```

To support both versions of ggplot2, I'm using code-paths such as:

```
if (utils::packageVersion("ggplot2")<="1.0.1"){
  # code for current stable version
}
else{
 # code for development version
}
```

The respective code paths execute without error depending on which version of ggplot2 is installed, but `R CMD check` doesn't understand that. Is there a solution for this issue, or should I wait until the new ggplot2 has been released? Or is there a better way to write code conditional on the installed package version?

I suspect I can't be the only one who has this issue, but I haven't seen it mentioned anywhere yet.

title: "u" required in "colour" when using `override.aes()`
description:
I asked and answered [this question](http://stackoverflow.com/q/33703417/903061) on Stack Overflow for why my `guide_legend(override.aes = list(color = NA))` wasn't removing the colored line from a fill legend. The answer was that "color" needs the "u" in this case: `colour = NA` works just fine.

I suggest that this should either be changed to accept both spellings OR documented in `?guide_legend`.

**MWE:**

``` r
set.seed(47)
data = data.frame(year = rep(2000:2004, 3), value = runif(15), group = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 5))

p = ggplot(data, aes(x = year, y = value, fill = group)) +
    geom_area(position = position_fill(), color = "white") +
    scale_fill_grey()

# legend with color lines
p + guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(color = NA)))

# legend without color lines 
p + guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = NA)))
```

title: speed of ggplot
description:
ggplot2 is a well documented and has abundant community supports, which is why I decided to write the new visualization package [ggcyto](https://github.com/RGLab/ggcyto) for flow cytometry data to replace the existing  R package [flowViz](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/flowViz.html) that was based on [lattice](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lattice/index.html) since its syntax and interface makes it difficult to use nowadays.

However, the internal usage of `data.frame` and `plyr` of `ggplot` makes `ggcyto` package spend almost twice as much time as `flowViz` to plot any two dimensional scatter plot (after binned).

I looked into `ggvis` as a possible solution but it seems to lack some key features such as facetting, hexbin. 

I wonder if there is any plan for improving the speed of `ggplot` by taking advantage of `dplyr` or `data.table`?

title: Facet Grid Error if First Plot Layer Data Frame is Empty
description:
An obscure error message is printed if the data frame of the first layer has no rows.

```
empty <- diamonds[0, ]
plot <- ggplot(empty, aes(color, depth)) + geom_boxplot()
plot <- plot + geom_bar(data = diamonds[1:100, ], aes_string("color", "depth"), stat = "identity")
plot + facet_grid(. ~ clarity)
```

Which results in `Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : subscript out of bounds`.

The bug is **not** present in version 1.0.1. It occurs when using version 1.0.1.9003.

title: Feature Request: Option to Modify Legend Wrapping Behaviour
description:
If a legend is wrapped into more than one row, the legend's elements are ordered into columns. It'd be nice to have an option to allow it to order the elements into rows.

For example,

```
qplot(data = mtcars, x = factor(cyl), y = mpg, colour = factor(hp)) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

I'd like 52, 62, 65, ... to appear in the first row, from left to right.

title: outlier.colour in geom_boxplot
description:
It would be great if it was possible to make outliers automatically inherit the colours of the boxplot as an alternative to the default: outlier.colour = "black".

"hadley commented on 3 Dec 2011
I'd suggest that when outlier.colour = NULL it defaults to the same colour as the boxes."
(https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/146)

This issue seems to have been raised and closed before (https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/146 ) and posts on stackoverflow (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/15273148/coloring-boxplot-outlier-points-in-ggplot2/16035956#16035956) indicate that there has been a solution to set outlier.color=NULL. 

``` r
library(ggplot2)
point_size=10
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl), y=mpg, col=factor(cyl))) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.size = point_size)
```

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/4373417/10925327/c4b54a6c-82d8-11e5-8933-14164cd9e444.png)

Gives black outliers.

and

``` r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl), y=mpg, col=factor(cyl))) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.size = point_size,outlier.colour = NULL)
```

title: Create GeomCustom that uses a list-column of grobs
description:
[I thought I'd raised this before, but can't find it anywhere so maybe I didn't.]

Currently `annotation_custom` and `annotation_raster` don't allow specifying a particular facet, they're always drawn on each facet, but that's often not the desirable behaviour. See [this recent example](http://stackoverflow.com/q/32807665/471093)

For the raster, one can always use a new `geom_raster` layer as a workaround, but there's no layer equivalent for `annotation_custom`, so one is left with no option but post-processing the plot.

I believe there's an easy fix (see my answer in that same thread), but I'm not very up-to-date with the inner workings of ggplot2.

title: Double vision on facet grid graph
In facet_wrap, multiple geom_text layers not commutative under new R
description:
I recently re-ran an old script that uses ggplot2 to create boxplots and found that, without having changed anything in the code, the output is different. Unfortunately, I can't recall the initial version of R or ggplot2 that I had working, but I do have a clear, reproducible example of it not working:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
library(reshape2)

options(stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

# Generating synthetic data here
tpl <- c('1st', '2nd', '3rd', '4th', '5th')
dat <- data.frame(foo=as.factor(sample(tpl, 1000, replace=TRUE)),
  bar=as.factor(sample(tpl, 1000, replace=TRUE)),
  effect=runif(1000, 0.1, 0.7))

# Just doing a cross-tabulation
ctab <- melt(table(subset(dat, select=c('foo', 'bar'))), id.vars='foo')
ctab$y <- rep(0.8, dim(ctab)[1])

# Just conducting ANOVA tests here
tests <- c()
for (q in levels(dat$bar)) {
  test <- aov(effect ~ foo, data=subset(dat, bar == q))
  tests <- c(tests, sprintf('p-value: ~%.4f', summary(test)[[1]][['Pr(>F)']][[1]]))
}
tests <- data.frame(p.value=tests, bar=levels(dat$bar),
                    x=rep(1, 5), y=rep(0, 5))

ggplot(dat, mapping=aes(y=effect)) +
  geom_boxplot(mapping=aes(x=foo)) +
  geom_text(data=tests, aes(x=x, y=y, label=p.value), hjust=0.1, vjust=0.1) +
  geom_text(data=ctab, aes(x=foo, y=y, label=value), vjust=0.7) +
  xlab('2000 Census White Pop. Proportion Quintile') +
  ylab('Vegetation Cover Proportion') +
  labs(title='Vegetation Cover by 2000 Census Tract, Pop. Density Quintiles') +
  facet_wrap(~ bar) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(text=element_text(size=16),
        plot.margin=unit(c(0.5, 0.2, 0.5, 0), 'cm'),
        panel.grid.major.y=element_line(color='gray'),
        panel.grid.major.x=element_blank())
```

**The problem is in the `ggplot` `geom_text` layers.** As it is (above), I get 10 facets instead of 5; there are only 5 levels to the faceting variable (`bar`) so I don't know why I see 10 facets, **particularly as the extraneous facets are completely empty** (see image).

![rplot](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1211103/10854748/0848c6fa-7f14-11e5-92db-fc6d2335d0d8.png)

**If I transpose (reorder) the two `geom_text` layers I get the correct result: 5 facets, not 10.** This switch is seen in the code below:

``` r
ggplot(dat, mapping=aes(y=effect)) +
  geom_boxplot(mapping=aes(x=foo)) +
  geom_text(data=ctab, aes(x=foo, y=y, label=value), vjust=0.7) +
  geom_text(data=tests, aes(x=x, y=y, label=p.value), hjust=0.1, vjust=0.1) +
  xlab('2000 Census White Pop. Proportion Quintile') +
  ylab('Vegetation Cover Proportion') +
  labs(title='Vegetation Cover by 2000 Census Tract, Pop. Density Quintiles') +
  facet_wrap(~ bar) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(text=element_text(size=16),
        plot.margin=unit(c(0.5, 0.2, 0.5, 0), 'cm'),
        panel.grid.major.y=element_line(color='gray'),
        panel.grid.major.x=element_blank())
```

This problem arises in `R version 3.2.2 (2015-08-14)`, Platform: `x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)`, Running under: `Ubuntu 14.04.3 LTS` with ggplot2 version 1.0.1.

This problem does **NOT** arise in `R version 3.2.0 (2015-04-16)`, Platform: `x86_64-apple-darwin13.4.0 (64-bit)`, Running under: `OS X 10.10.5 (Yosemite)`, **also with ggplot version 1.0.1.** I also did not have this problem on Ubuntu Linux before upgrading R (and ggplot); I can't imagine its specific to the platform.

**So, I guess the operative question is what changed in R since 3.2.0 to cause these layers to no longer commute?**

As context, I am using ggplot2 to produce multiple boxplots--quintiles of a Census variable within quintiles of another Census variable compared to the mean proportion of vegetation cover in a Census tract. The `geom_text` layers display the counts in each boxplot and the p-values.

title: Missing values and facets
description:
Plots with facets don't seem to like missing values very much.

``` r
df = rbind(
  data.frame(z = "A", x = 1:3, y = 1:3),
  data.frame(z = "B", x = 2:4, y = c(1, 2, NA)),
  data.frame(z = "C", x = 5:7, y = c(NA, NA, NA))
)
```

This works, but it does not show any values of `x` in the facet for "C":

``` r
ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "grey66") +
  facet_grid(. ~ z, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x")
```

![rplot](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/322533/10807281/3f050a3c-7dde-11e5-9e55-2bc2edcee639.png)

Also, `x` is in fact an interval variable, not a continuous one.

Let's try coercing `x` to a factor to solve both issues at once:

``` r
ggplot(data = df, aes(x = factor(x), y = y, group = family)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "grey66") +
  facet_grid(. ~ family, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x")
```

This used to work, but it now fails:

```
Error in if (zero_range(from) || zero_range(to)) { : 
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
In addition: Warning message:
Removed 4 rows containing missing values (position_stack). 
```

Yet it works if we subtitute zeros to the missing values:

``` r
ggplot(data = df, aes(x = factor(x), y = ifelse(is.na(y), 0, y))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "grey66") +
  facet_grid(. ~ z, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x")
```

description:

```
m <- read.csv(textConnection(t))
m$Response <- factor(m$Response, levels=1:7, ordered=TRUE)
ggplot() + 
    aes(x=Group, fill=Response, order=Response) + 
    geom_bar(data=m, aes(y=pct_freq), position="stack", stat="identity") + 
    facet_grid(. ~ disp, space="free") + 
    coord_flip())
```

![geombarfacet_prob](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5226494/10800342/c9af7df4-7d87-11e5-8c87-13f4b142a339.jpg)

It has been pointed out to me that the most likely reason it behaves like this is that without the `coord_flip()`, the plots are the same height and this property is being kept. If this is actually the "expected behavior" rather then a bug, it might be useful to add a `geom_bar_horiz`.

In trying to help me find a work around, @mattantaliss sent me the following code based on the accepted answer to http://stackoverflow.com/questions/12560858/using-coord-flip-with-facet-wrapscales-free-y-in-ggplot2-seems-to-give-u
This makes the size of 'b' behave the way I was expecting, but has a side effect of messing up the bars in 'a', and also requires `scales="free"` to be set (which I don't want).

```
library(ggplot2)
library(proto)

geom_bar_horz <- function (mapping = NULL, data = NULL, stat = "bin", position = "stack", ...) {
  GeomBar_horz$new(mapping = mapping, data = data, stat = stat, position = position, ...)
}

GeomBar_horz <- proto(ggplot2:::Geom, {
  objname <- "bar_horz"

  default_stat <- function(.) StatBin
  default_pos <- function(.) PositionStack
  default_aes <- function(.) aes(colour=NA, fill="grey20", size=0.5, linetype=1, weight = 1, alpha = NA)

  required_aes <- c("y")

  reparameterise <- function(., df, params) {
    df$width <- df$width %||%
      params$width %||% (resolution(df$x, FALSE) * 0.9)
    OUT <- transform(df,
                     xmin = pmin(x, 0), xmax = pmax(x, 0),
                     ymin = y - .45, ymax = y + .45, width = NULL
    )
    return(OUT)
  }

  draw_groups <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ...) {
    GeomRect$draw_groups(data, scales, coordinates, ...)
  }
  guide_geom <- function(.) "polygon"
})

t <- "Group,Response,Freq,pct_freq,disp

low,4,40,0.151515152,b
```

title: geom_dotplot method "dotdensity" fails with NA values, "histodot" removes without warning.
description:
``` r
library(ggplot2)

mtcars2 <- mtcars
mtcars2[1, "disp"] <- NA

# Complete data works fine
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = as.factor(gear), y = disp)) + 
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")
# Missing value produces a warning and an empty plot
ggplot(mtcars2, aes(x = as.factor(gear), y = disp)) + 
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")
# Method "histodot" removes NA's (without a warning!)
ggplot(mtcars2, aes(x = as.factor(gear), y = disp)) + 
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center", method = "histodot")
```

In either case, this is not documented behavior, as the default of `na.rm = FALSE` should remove missing values with a warning.

I'm on Windows 10, using R v3.2.2 with the 1.1.0 pre-release of ggplot2 (1.0.1.9003).

title: How to get vertical lines in legend key using ggplot2 for geom_pointrange() type graphic
description:
#### As outlined on [SO](http://stackoverflow.com/q/33319235/2727349):

For ggplot2 graphics that have a symbol for a point estimate and a vertical line representing a range about that estimate (95% confidence interval, Inter-quartile Range, Minimum and Maximum, etc) I cannot get the legend key to show the symbol with a **vertical** line.  Since `geom_pointrange()` only has arguments for `ymin` and `ymax`, I would think the intended (default) functionality of `geom_pointrange(show_guide=T)`  would be to have vertical lines (I say default because I understand that with `coord_flip` one could make horizontal lines in the plot).  I also understand that having vertical lines in the legend key when the legend position is right or left will have the vertical lines "run together"...but for legends in the top or bottom having a vertical line through the symbol means that the key will match what appears in the plot.

Yet the approaches I've tried still put horizontal lines in the legend key:

```
## set up
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(123)
ru <- 2*runif(10) - 1
dt <- data.frame(x   = 1:10, 
                 y   = rep(5,10)+ru, 
                 ylo = rep(1,10)+ru, 
                 yhi = rep(9,10)+ru,
                 s   = rep(c("A","B"),each=5),
                 f   = rep(c("facet1", "facet2"), each=5))
```

Default `show_guide=T` for `geom_pointrange` yields desired plot but has horizontal lines in legend key where vertical is desired (so as to match the plot):

```
ggplot(data=dt)+
  geom_pointrange(aes(x     = x, 
                      y     = y, 
                      ymin  = ylo, 
                      ymax  = yhi, 
                      shape = s), 
                  size=1.1,
                  show_guide=T)+
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

[![enter image description here](http://i.stack.imgur.com/RkJ46.png)](http://i.stack.imgur.com/RkJ46.png)

An attempt with `geom_point` and `geom_segment` together yields desired plot but has horizontal lines in legend key where vertical is desired (so as to match the plot):

```
ggplot(data=dt)+
  geom_point(aes(    x = x, 
                     y = y, 
                 shape = s), 
             size=3,
             show_guide=T)+
  geom_segment(aes(   x = x, 
                   xend = x, 
                      y = ylo, 
                   yend = yhi), 
               show_guide=T)+
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

[![enter image description here](http://i.stack.imgur.com/MEbQM.png)](http://i.stack.imgur.com/MEbQM.png)

An attempt with `geom_point` and `geom_vline` together yields **desired legend key** but does not respect the `ymin` and `ymax` values in the plot:

```
ggplot(data=dt)+
  geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, shape=s), show_guide=T, size=3)+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept=x, ymin=ylo, ymax=yhi ), show_guide=T)+
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

[![enter image description here](http://i.stack.imgur.com/6uP6u.png)](http://i.stack.imgur.com/6uP6u.png)

How do I get the legend key of the 3rd graph but the plot of one of the first two?

Attempted answers on (as outlined on SO):

[1.  Using geom_point(show_guide=T) + geom_segment(show_guide=F) + geom_vline(show_guide=T) where vline is plotted out of range of data and then coord_cartesian() excludes the vline.](http://stackoverflow.com/a/33319236/2727349)

My solution involves plotting a vertical line with `geom_vline(show_guide=T)` for an x-value that is out of the bounds of the displayed x-axis along with plotting `geom_segment(show_guide=F)`:

```
ggplot(data=dt)+
  geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, shape=s), show_guide=T, size=3)+
  geom_segment(aes(x=x, xend=x, y=ylo, yend=yhi), show_guide=F)+
  geom_vline(xintercept=-1, show_guide=T)+
  theme(legend.position="bottom")+
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0.5,10.5))
```

[![enter image description here](http://i.stack.imgur.com/SiAKN.png)](http://i.stack.imgur.com/SiAKN.png)

[2.  Using grid and gtable:](http://stackoverflow.com/a/33323334/2727349)

```
library(grid)
library(gtable)

gg <-     
ggplot(data=dt)+
  geom_pointrange(aes(x     = x, 
                      y     = y, 
                      ymin  = ylo, 
                      ymax  = yhi, 
                      shape = s), 
                  size=1.1,
                  show_guide=T)+
  theme(legend.position="bottom")

gb <- ggplot_build(gg)
gt <- ggplot_gtable(gb)

seg <- grep("segments", names(gt$grobs[[8]]$grobs[[1]]$grobs[[4]]$children))
gt$grobs[[8]]$grobs[[1]]$grobs[[4]]$children[[seg]]$x0 <- unit(0.5, "npc")
gt$grobs[[8]]$grobs[[1]]$grobs[[4]]$children[[seg]]$x1 <- unit(0.5, "npc")
```

title: geom_violin not respecting facet_grid's scale='free*'
description:
geom_violin won't use free scales with facet_grid.  It works for boxplot, but not violin.  Tested with ggplot2_1.0.1.9003.  Here is an example.  

```
library(ggplot2)

dat <- 
  data.frame(statistic = rep(c("stat1", "stat2"), each = 100),
             scenario  = rep(rep(c("scenario1", "scenario2"), each = 50),
                             times = 2),
             group     = rep(rep(c("control", "treatment"), each = 25), 
                             times = 4),
             value     = c(rnorm(100, 0.5, 0.25), rexp(100, 0.5)))

ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = value, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(statistic ~ scenario, scales = "free")

ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = value, fill = group)) +
  geom_violin() +
  facet_grid(statistic ~ scenario, scales = "free")
```

title: Update plot's data with pipes
description:
There's currently no easy way to update a data frame in a pipeline.

The data frame pipeline needs to be on the RHS, which does not feel natural, and wrapped in parentheses:

``` r
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = hp)) + geom_point()

p %+% (mtcars %>%
  mutate(wt = wt + 10) %>%
  slice(1:10))
```

So how about adding an updating function?

``` r
ggupdate <- function(data, plot) {
  plot %+% data
}

mtcars %>%
  mutate(wt = wt + 10) %>%
```

title: Use alpha for lines of geom_density(), geom_bar(), and so on
description:
Hi, thanks for this great package!

I saw many people (including me) are confused at the behavior of `alpha` when used in Geoms which draw areas or rects (e.g. `geom_desity()`). So, let me ask if this is your design decision or not.

When I draw a chart with `alpha`, I expect that the whole layer, the line and fill, will become transparent. But the line stays clear red.

``` r
ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat)) +
    geom_density(fill = "red", colour = "red", alpha = 0.1)
```

![plot3](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1978793/10501293/cf987d82-731a-11e5-8ade-a8a462af878b.png)

I expect the one like this.

![plot1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1978793/10501292/cb700022-731a-11e5-8c30-db8ff67ff6d0.png)

I know we can draw the latter chart by using `colour=alpha("red", 0.1)`, but I believe `alpha` is a transparency param for **the entire layer**, not only for the line or the fill. For me, this is a matter of semantics. Are there any reason not to use `alpha` for `colour`?

The possible implementation is very simple. We just need to change those two lines to `col = alpha(aes$colour, aes$alpha)`:

https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/bbc1b5ad3c0f55e8809d4fe1a9bd2783eb9fa29c/R/geom-rect.r#L55
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/bbc1b5ad3c0f55e8809d4fe1a9bd2783eb9fa29c/R/geom-ribbon.r#L95

If this looks good to you, I'm happy to submit PR :smile:

title: plot background on pdf
description:
Running the code below, adapted from ggsave documentation, graphics that show up within Rstudio look as expected, but pdf files all have grey background in plotting area, which is unexpected for theme_bw.  Besides the plot background, other aspects of bw theme (e.g. black labels on axes) show up in pdf file.  The problem remains whether pdf() or ggsave is used to create pdf files.  No where in documentation does it suggest that this should be normal behavior.  I was surprised that I could find no mention of this problem elsewhere online.
Mark

require(ggplot2)
qplot(rating, data=movies, geom="histogram") #displays default theme on screen
qplot(rating, data=movies, geom="histogram")+theme_bw() # Shows bw theme on screen
pdf("ratings2.pdf")
qplot(rating, data=movies, geom="histogram") # pdf shows default theme
qplot(rating, data=movies, geom="histogram")+theme_bw() # pdf shows default theme plot background and black rather than grey labels
qplot(rating, data=movies, geom="histogram")+theme(panel.background=element_rect(fill="White")) # pdf shows default theme

title: geom_errorbar width incorrect when grouped and position dodged
description:
Reproducible simplified example:

``` R
library(ggplot2)
dat <- data.frame(category = c(rep("a", 3), rep("b", 6)),
                  item = c(1:9),
                  value = c(2.9,3.3,3.2,5.4,5.6,7,6.2,6,6.7),
                  error = c(0.1,0.12,0.09,0.3,0.32,0.33,0.45,0.26,0.24))

pos <- position_dodge(width=0.25)
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=category,
                     y=value,
                     ymin = value - error,
                     ymax = value + error, 
                     group = item)) +
  geom_point(size=2, position=pos, stat="identity") +
  geom_errorbar(position=pos, aes(width=0.5), show_guide=FALSE) 
```

![ggplot_error_bar_2](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/7646415/10004774/85f59e5e-6081-11e5-828a-ce0b155a78a1.png)

The value for the width of the error bars is being divided by the number of items grouped at the x position. Category 'b' has twice as many items as 'a' and its error bars are half the width.

I can work around the issue by making a column with value equal to the number of grouped values, and multiply width by that:

``` R
dat <- data.frame(category = c(rep("a", 3), rep("b", 6)),
                  item = c(1:9),
                  value = c(2.9,3.3,3.2,5.4,5.6,7,6.2,6,6.7),
                  error = c(0.1,0.12,0.09,0.3,0.32,0.33,0.45,0.26,0.24),
                  number =c(3,3,3,6,6,6,6,6,6))

pos <- position_dodge(width=0.25)
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=category,
                     y=value,
                     ymin = value - error,
                     ymax = value + error, 
                     group = item)) +
  geom_point(size=2, position=pos, stat="identity") +
  geom_errorbar(position=pos, aes(width=number*0.5), show_guide=FALSE) 
```

This gives a warning, but the plot is correct:

![ggplot_error_bar_3](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/7646415/10004804/be55c7f6-6081-11e5-8b8b-066310144048.png)

> Warning message:
> position_dodge requires non-overlapping x intervals

However, this is a bit more work and can cause possible bugs (count wrong, the value changes later, etc.)

The same behaviour happens if I take the width=0.5 out of aes(), but it needs to be in aes() if I want to use the width=number*0.5 workaround.

If I remove group=item from the first aes() the error bar widths are ok, but the points and the error bars do not dodge.

For reference I am using R 3.2.1 and ggplot2 1.0.1

title: default position for geom_histogram()
description:
The default behavior of `geom_histogram(position = "stack")` may be a bit unexpected (alternatively, I would love to hear the reasoning behind the choice). I would expect, when plotting a histogram of `n` levels, to have `n` "self contained" histograms, overlapping for better or worse. On the other hand, doing `geom_density` plots the data "as expected" which is conceptually very similar to `geom_histogram`. My suggestion would be to consider changing the default position in `geom_histogram` to `position = "identity"`.

``` r
xy <- data.frame(pop = sample(letters[1:2], 100, replace = TRUE), value = c(rnorm(50, mean = 5), rnorm(50, mean = 10)))

library(ggplot2)

# overlapping histograms
ggplot(xy, aes(x = value, fill = pop)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", position = "identity", alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1")

# stacked histogram, not very histogram-y anymore
ggplot(xy, aes(x = value, fill = pop)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1")

# density graphs do overlap
ggplot(xy, aes(x = value, fill = pop)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1")
```

title: integer type has "continuous values" according to scale_color_discrete.
description:
This minimal reproducible example builds on that of the [similar bug for scale_shape_identity](https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/402#issuecomment-139673899) which was previously resolved (so the example may seem more than minimal, but I'm referencing a precedent bug with a solution - why I also commented there)

``` r
R version 3.2.2 (2015-08-14) -- "Fire Safety"
library(ggplot2)
df2 <- data.frame(x = 1:5 , y = 1:25, z = 1:25)
s <- ggplot(df2, aes(x = x, y = y))
s + geom_point(aes(shape = z), size = 4) + scale_shape_identity()
s + geom_point(aes(shape = z, color=z), size = 4) + scale_shape_identity() + scale_color_discrete() 
# Error: Continuous value supplied to discrete scale
```

Note there's no error for scale_shape_identity. But there is for scale_color_discrete. Integer is a discrete variable, not a continuous variable, which creates cognitive dissonance for the person trying to interpret this error. Seems like integer type should be treated like an ordered factor, but that may not be the best solution internally... 
Thanks!

title: Legend key borders can become too large when rescaled
description: Using ggplot2 1.0.1.9003, the border around legend keys is now inherited from the size of the border in the plot. This poses a problem when legend keys are scaled down—the border does not scale correspondingly. Here's an example: ``` library(ggplot2) # Example data from ggplot::geom_map documentation ids <- factor(c("1.1", "2.1", "1.2", "2.2", "1.3", "2.3")) values <- data.frame( id = ids, value = c(3, 3.1, 3.1, 3.2, 3.15, 3.5) ) positions <- data.frame( id = rep(ids, each = 4), x = c(2, 1, 1.1, 2.2, 1, 0, 0.3, 1.1, 2.2, 1.1, 1.2, 2.5, 1.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.2, 2.5, 1.2, 1.3, 2.7, 1.2, 0.5, 0.6, 1.3), y = c(-0.5, 0, 1, 0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5, 1, 0.5, 1, 2.1, 1.7, 1, 1.5, 2.2, 2.1, 1.7, 2.1, 3.2, 2.8, 2.1, 2.2, 3.3, 3.2) ) # Thick border set outside of aes() makes legend keys borders gigantic p <- ggplot(values, aes(map_id = id, fill = id)) + geom_map(map = positions, size = 2, colour = "black") + expand_limits(positions) p ``` ``` # Shrinking the legend.key.size down makes the legend keys unusable p + theme(legend.key.size=unit(0.65, "lines")) ``` ``` # This is also the case when using guide_legend() p + guides(fill = guide_legend(keywidth = 0.65, keyheight = 0.65)) ``` ``` # Current workaround is to use override.aes inside guide_legend() p + theme(legend.key.size=unit(0.65, "lines")) + scale_fill_discrete(guide = guide_legend(override.aes=list(size = 0.3))) ``` ``` # Alternatively... p + guides(fill = guide_legend(keywidth = 0.65, keyheight = 0.65, override.aes=list(size = 0.3))) ```

title: ggplot2 breaks Hmisc installation
description:
I can't tell if ggplot2 or Hmisc are at fault, but am posting here so others are aware of the problem and a workaround.

Installing the development ggplot2 breaks subsequent installation of Hmisc:

``` R
> devtools::install_github("hadley/ggplot2")
> install.packages("Hmisc")
** R
** inst
** preparing package for lazy loading
Warning: replacing previous import by ‘ggplot2::unit’ when loading ‘Hmisc’
Warning: replacing previous import by ‘ggplot2::arrow’ when loading ‘Hmisc’
Warning: replacing previous import by ‘scales::alpha’ when loading ‘Hmisc’
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : could not find function "eval"
Error : unable to load R code in package ‘Hmisc’
ERROR: lazy loading failed for package ‘Hmisc’
```

As a workaround, revert to ggplot2 release, install Hmisc, then install ggplot2 dev. Warning messages appear when loading Hmisc, but everything works:

``` R
> install.packages("ggplot2")
> install.packages("Hmisc")
> devtools::install_github("hadley/ggplot2")
> require("Hmisc")
Warning messages:
1: replacing previous import by ‘ggplot2::unit’ when loading ‘Hmisc’ 
2: replacing previous import by ‘ggplot2::arrow’ when loading ‘Hmisc’ 
3: replacing previous import by ‘scales::alpha’ when loading ‘Hmisc’ 
```

As previously discussed ([ggthemes #35](https://github.com/jrnold/ggthemes/issues/35)) the warning messages arise because Hmisc's NAMESPACE imports grid, ggplot2, and scales, causing `unit`, `arrow`, and `alpha` to be imported twice:

``` R
import(methods)
import(stats)
import(survival)
import(Formula)
import(grid)
import(lattice)
import(ggplot2)
import(proto)
import(scales)
```

Arguably, Hmisc should change how it imports its namespace. However, given that there are probably a number of packages importing ggplot2 along with grid or scales, these warning messages might spook users.

I don't know what causes`Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : could not find function "eval"` during lazy loading, but it looks like the community is aware of the issue: [ggthemes #36](https://github.com/jrnold/ggthemes/issues/36) and [ggmap #65](https://github.com/dkahle/ggmap/issues/65)

title: stat_binhex() not rendering when using  coord_map() to project coordinates
description: I'm posting this here in the possible chance that it's just a small fix, or a completely obvious snafu that I've missed...It _seems_ like the error would originate from ggplot2. On the other hand, `stat_binhex()` seems to require the hexbin package, so I initially [posted the issue there](https://github.com/edzer/hexbin/issues/1#issuecomment-139127132). The maintainer believes the error is in ggplot2. I haven't taken the time to look through both codebases but will hopefully have time later this week. But since I already wrote out the bug report...might as well paste it here. Original text: When using ggplot2's `coord_map()` to project a geospatial plot, the `stat_binhex()` method doesn't appear to accommodate the projection when rendering the plot. I thought that this might be just an issue with statbinning in general, but `stat_density2d()` and `stat_bin2d()` seem to work without problem. I'm currently using: - R version 3.2.1 - ggplot2_1.0.1 - hexbin_1.27.1 Full [sessionInfo at the bottom of this post](#sessioninfo) ### Data downloading and prep code Here's the code to get some (public) data for example purposes: **Note:** This script creates a local directory named ./data ``` R dir.create('./data') library(ggplot2) library(rgdal) library(hexbin) theme_set(theme_bw()) # Downloads map to ./data m_fname <- "./data/cb_2014_us_state_20m.zip" download.file("http://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2014/shp/cb_2014_us_state_20m.zip", m_fname) unzip(m_fname, exdir = "./data/shp") us_map <- readOGR("./data/shp/cb_2014_us_state_20m.shp", "cb_2014_us_state_20m") # just keep lower 48 us_map <- subset(us_map, !(us_map$STUSPS %in% c('AK', 'HI', 'AS', 'DC', 'GU', 'MP', 'PR', 'VI'))) # Download earthquake data q_fname <- "./data/all_week.csv" download.file("http://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/all_week.csv", q_fname) quakes <-read.csv(q_fname, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) ######################## # Data filtering # make the sp data frame xsp <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(data = quakes, coords = quakes[,c("longitude", "latitude")]) xsp@proj4string <- us_map@proj4string # filter out non-us quakes us_quakes <- as.data.frame(xsp[us_map,]) p_map <- ggplot(data = us_quakes, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude)) + geom_polygon(data = us_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group), fill = NA, color = "#888888", size = 0.3) ``` ### Default projection hex-binned map: ``` R p_map + stat_binhex(bins = 30, color = "white") + scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("pink", "red")) + coord_equal() ``` ![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/121520/9773717/c408caf0-56f8-11e5-8a14-01423cde9a2e.png) ### Albers-projected, rect-binned map: ``` R p_map + stat_bin2d(bins = 30, color = "white") + scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("pink", "red")) + coord_map("albers", lat0 = 39, lat1 = 42) ``` ![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/121520/9773721/d133f56a-56f8-11e5-9168-98cf377812f2.png) ### Albers-projected, density map: ``` R p_map + stat_density2d() + coord_map("albers", lat0 = 39, lat1 = 42) ``` ![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/121520/9773740/eb823a08-56f8-11e5-8558-d9c40df61b37.png) ### Albers-projected, hexbinned map ``` R p_map + stat_binhex(bins = 30, color = "orange") + scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("pink", "red")) + coord_map("albers", lat0 = 39, lat1 = 42) ``` ![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/121520/9773756/03dd80f8-56f9-11e5-8872-3d0816b431eb.png) Note that I set the `color` to `orange` so that you might make out the dots that each hexbin reduces to (if you squint). ### Not using coord_map() FWIW, I can get a properly hexbinned map by not using `coord_map()`...but if `stat_bin2d()` works without the following workaround, I figured maybe there was a bug in `hexbin`: ``` R albers_crs <- CRS("+proj=laea +lat_0=45 +lon_0=-100 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +a=6370997 +b=6370997 +units=m +no_defs") # Apply Albers projection to earthquakes data # note: `us_quakes` is a data frame and needs to be re-spatialized ysp <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(data = us_quakes, coords = us_quakes[,c("longitude", "latitude")]) ysp@proj4string <- us_map@proj4string albers_quakes <- as.data.frame(spTransform(ysp, albers_crs)) # Apply the Albers projection to usc_map albers_map <- spTransform(us_map, albers_crs) # Note: We have to use longitude.2` and `latitude.2` in the aesthetic # due to the way SpatialPointsDataFrame constructor avoids naming collisions ggplot(data = albers_quakes, aes(x = longitude.2, y = latitude.2)) + geom_polygon(data = albers_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group), fill = NA, color = "#888888", size = 0.3) + stat_binhex(bins = 30, color = "white") + scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("pink", "red")) ``` ![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/121520/9774018/c1ac2eee-56fa-11e5-97f1-e5e4cfc8ad9d.png) #### My full sessionInfo() ``` R version 3.2.1 (2015-06-18) Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin14.4.0 (64-bit) Running under: OS X 10.10.5 (Yosemite) locale: [1] en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/C/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8 attached base packages: [1] stats graphics grDevices utils datasets methods base other attached packages: [1] hexbin_1.27.1 rgdal_1.0-6 sp_1.1-1 ggplot2_1.0.1 loaded via a namespace (and not attached): [1] Rcpp_0.12.0 lattice_0.20-31 digest_0.6.8 MASS_7.3-40 grid_3.2.1 plyr_1.8.3 [7] gtable_0.1.2 magrittr_1.5 scales_0.3.0 stringi_0.5-5 reshape2_1.4.1 proto_0.3-10 [13] tools_3.2.1 stringr_1.0.0 munsell_0.4.2 colorspace_1.2-6 ```

title: stat = "identity" in geom_smooth errors out on unknown parameters
description:
Example 1 (from the book draft, pg. 61): 

```
library(ggplot2) # 1.0.1.9003 2015-09-09 Github (hadley/ggplot2@9c7fb3e) 
y <- c(18, 11, 16)
df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = y, se = c(1.2, 0.5, 1.0))

base <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, ymin = y - se, ymax = y + se))
base + geom_smooth(stat = "identity")
##Error: Unknown parameters: method, formula, se
```

The example [here](http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.3.1/geom_smooth.html) also returns the same error.

`find_subclass("Stat", "identity")$parameters()` returns `character(0)`. It looks like the `StatIdentity` class doesn't have the parameters it's supposed to:

```
StatIdentity$parameters()
##character(0)

StatSmooth$parameters()
## [1] "method"      "formula"     "se"          "n"           "span"       
## [6] "fullrange"   "xseq"        "level"       "method.args" "na.rm"  
```

Manually kludging it in during the call to `layer()` (I did it during `debugonce()`) works:

```
geom_params <- params[intersect(names(params), geom$parameters())]
stat_params <- params[intersect(names(params), stat$parameters())]
# Manually sub in parameters
all <- c(geom$parameters(), c("method", "formula", "se"), geom$aesthetics()) 
extra <- setdiff(names(params), all)
```

I'm not particularly savvy on the internals of ggplot2, but I hope this is useful!

title: Non-interactive calls to ggsave() can have irritating side effects
description:
Posting an issue sort of on behalf of @cscheid because I am so thrilled at the prospect of this getting fixed! (Please correct me if I'm mangling your problem, @cscheid.)

Calls to `ggsave()` that don't specify device width and height cause a graphics device to be opened and consulted for dimensions. In non-interactive settings, this can have irritating side effects, such as leaving an (empty or corrupt) `Rplots.pdf` file behind.

Reprex: put these commands in `foo.R`:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=cyl,y=mpg)) + geom_point()
ggsave("cars.png", p)
```

and run `Rscript foo.R`. This produces `cars.png` AND `Rplots.pdf`, at least on my Mac.

Other places people where people have vented about this: stackoverflow thread [How to stop R from creating empty Rplots.pdf file when using ggsave and Rscript](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17348359/how-to-stop-r-from-creating-empty-rplots-pdf-file-when-using-ggsave-and-rscript), ggplot2 board thread [ggsave always opens a graphics window on Mac OS](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/ggplot2/ZGevTRMz9iE/xz8PjlR4KMEJ)

title: Documentation error on %+replace% ?
description:
The ggplot2 documentation for +.gg {ggplot2} (the addition operator) reads as follows:

The + operator completely replaces elements with elements from e2.

In contrast, the %+replace% operator does not replace the entire element; it only updates element properties which are present (not NULL) in the second object.

And, yet, when one runs the examples in the documentation that purport to illustrate this point, it appears to me that precisely the opposite is true. That is, the + operator really amounts to inheritance, the result inherits from the LHS side of the + but changes only that found on the RHS. Whereas the %+replace% operator basically kills off the LHS side by NULLing out anything for which there is no value on the RHS.

So my questions are: 1) am I misunderstanding what is going on? 2) is there an error in the documentation 3) assuming I understand the role of %+replace% correctly, why would one ever use it?

title: dev version 1.0.1.9003 has some breaking changes
description:
I have a package that [adds marginal plots to ggplot2 scatterplots](https://github.com/daattali/ggExtra), and I'm seeing many breaking changes when updating to the latest version. Only the first two seem like actual "bugs" from your point of view, but the rest are behaviour changes that are frustrating enough that I wanted to see if you could give them some attention :)
## geom_bar() looks completely different

The following code produces very different plots in 1.0.1 vs 1.0.1.9003

```
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt)) + geom_bar()
```

Old version:

![rplot](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/952340/9618855/fb447ef0-50be-11e5-8085-a14c202f64fa.png)

New version:

![rplot](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/952340/9618866/093f152e-50bf-11e5-9390-2f107fd0f980.png)
## Providing a binwidth to geom_bar doesn't work anymore

Previously this worked

```
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt)) + geom_bar(binwidth = 5)
```

The new version throws an error

```
Error: Unknown parameters: binwidth
```

I did see the NEWS said there was a change to do with geom_bar having its own stat_bar, but I didn't think this is the same issue

The NEWS also mentions that  "It's now obvious that you can set the `binwidth` parameter for ...", but that doesn't tell me why it no longer works for a layer that used to work.
## Providing unused params to a layer throws an error

This is documented in the NEWS, but it'd be nice to be able to suppress these error messages. A simple example could be: If I have a function that takes in the name of a layer and accepts a list of arguments to pass to the layer, and it just uses a default list of arguments, previously it was easy enough to just say "call whatever layer you want, and use this list of arguments". But now this throws an error and you'd have to check which layer exactly is used and filter all the arguments.  Maybe I'm alone on this one, but if I'm getting errors from it, I assume there are others who will also all of a sudden get errors when updating.
## Possible to suppress "warning" messages?

It looks like the scales were completely changed internally, and this (or some other change) is causing my code to now produce a message every time

```
Scale for 'x' is already present. Adding another scale for 'x', which will replace the existing scale.
```

Previously the "stat:bin: binwidth default to ..." message used to appear all the time without an easy way of suppressing it.  I think it's be great if there was a way to suppress these types of messages directly from ggplot2, maybe with a global option or something like that, because it's a bit annoying to keep seeing these messages appear, and I'm not sure when exactly they get printed.

Again, this may be just an issue for me.

title: legend for `geom_line` colour disappears when `alpha` < 1.0

Issue exists with ggplot2 1.0.1 and 1.0.1.9003.
I'm using R 3.2.1

This example works as expected

``` r
ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(x = qsec,
           y = mpg,
           colour = factor(am))) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point()
```

It also works when I set `alpha = 1.0`

``` r
ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(x = qsec,
           y = mpg,
           colour = factor(am))) + 
  geom_line(alpha = 1.0)
```

But as soon as I change `alpha` to any value less than 1.0, look at the change in the legend.

``` r
ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(x = qsec,
           y = mpg,
           colour = factor(am))) + 
  geom_line(alpha = .99) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .99)
```

It seems to affect only `geom_line`.  I've looked at `geom_point` and `geom_text`, and neither of those appear to be affected.

title: geom_jitter inconsistency

I found that the result of geom_jitter varies depending on what is printed beforehand:

``` R
library(ggplot2)
dat <- data.frame(a = rep(1:100, 2), b = sqrt(rep(1:100, 2)))

p <- ggplot(dat, aes(a, b)) + 
  geom_jitter(shape = 1)


p_linear <- p +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 10))

p_sqrt <- p +
  scale_x_sqrt(limits = c(0, 100)) + 
  scale_y_sqrt(limits = c(0, 10))

print(p_linear)
dev.off()

png("plot_sqrt.png")
print(p_sqrt)
dev.off()
```

``` R
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(a, b)) + 
  geom_jitter(shape = 1)

p_linear <- p +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 10))


p_sqrt <- p +
  scale_x_sqrt(limits = c(0, 100)) + 
  scale_y_sqrt(limits = c(0, 10))
```


One of the two must be wrong, or I missed an important part of how ggplot works (absolutely possible as well). In my opinion, the first plot is the correct behavior.

title: ggplot2 can't pass ... to fortify
description:
`ggtree` is designed by extending `ggplot2` and implemented several `fortify` methods for tree objects.

I compile `ggtree` with newest version of `ggplot2`, it throw the following error:

```
Error: processing vignette 'ggtree.Rmd' failed with diagnostics:
Unknown parameters: time_scale, yscale_mapping
```

This is due to I pass these two parameters to `ggplot` via `...`, and these two parameters were defined in the parameter list of `fortify` method. 

It works fine with release version of ggplot2 but throw error with newest one.

For `ggtree`, the issue can be solved by passing these two parameters explicitly via `ggplot`, but I think `...` is a good mechanism and hope it's supported.

title: Flawed `label_bquote()` implementation
description:
I think the approach of referring to names in `label_bquote()` is flawed :(

With formulaes of the type `var1 ~ var2`, the labels are not sent simultaneously to the labeller but in turn. They are only sent together with `. ~ var1 + var2`. So this doesn't work:

``` r
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point()
p + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs, labeller = label_bquote(alpha ^ .(cyl)))
## Error: object 'cyl' not found
```

We need to find another way. My first implementation created aliases `x`, `y` and `z` for the labels so that bquote would take expressions like `.(x) ^ .(y)`. This is a bit more general but this would still not work in case the number of facetted variables is not the same in both dimensions. Maybe the only way is to go back to a single `x` alias.

Or, we could add an attribute to the labels data frames specifying from which facetting side the variables come from: columns or rows. `facet_wrap()` would send `cols` labels. Then `label_bquote()` could take `cols_expr` and `rows_expr` arguments, and when one of them is missing we fall back on `label_value()`. It actually makes more sense to allow different formulaes in each dimension.

I'm away this weekend so I'll fix this next week

title: Better handling of geom and stat params
description:
Would be nice to have consistent way of discovering parameters so that layer can warn early if you have parameters that don't exist in the geom/stat.

Probably the easiest way would be to provide a character vector that lists the names of the parameters. This will require some manual book-keeping, but you should notice quickly during testing if you've forgotten to add a param.

Then should be able to eliminate use of `...` in many of the individual methods. (Will still need it in the default `compute_panel()` because it passes onto `compute_group()`

title: span parameter won't work in geom_smooth

title: labels=NULL in discrete scale generates a warning

# Summary

A warning is generated when the `labels` argument is set to `NULL` in a discrete scale
# Reproducible example

``` r
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl))) +
    geom_bar()

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl))) +
```

title: environment Parameter to Geoms Silently Ignored
description:
Although the geoms accept `environment` without complaint, they don't use it, which means local variables can't be used, such as in the `switch` statements in the example code. This problem was described a long time ago on the mailing list. Could there be a satisfactory solution before the next version of **ggplot2**? The least that the geoms could do is print a message to the user that the `environment` is being ignored, so the user knows that it is happening.

This problem is limiting, as shown in this runnable, short example : 

```
f <- function()
{
  Xvar <- "comp"
  oneData <- data.frame(algorithm = LETTERS[1:3], computer = factor(c("IBM", "MAC", "Tablet")),  error = runif(3))
 otherData <- data.frame(algorithm = rep(LETTERS[1:3], 3), computer = rep(c("X", "Y", "Z"), 3),  error = runif(9))
  fillColour <- "comp"

  g = ggplot() + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
                 scale_fill_manual(values = scales::hue_pal()(6)) +
                 scale_colour_manual(values = scales::hue_pal()(6)) + theme(legend.position = "none")

  g = g + geom_bar(data = oneData, stat = "identity", aes(x = switch(Xvar, algo = algorithm, comp = computer), y = error, fill = switch(fillColour, algo = algorithm, comp = computer)), environment = environment()) +
          geom_boxplot(data = otherData, aes(x = switch(Xvar, algo = algorithm, comp = computer), y = error, fill = switch(fillColour, algo = algorithm, comp = computer)), environment = environment())
  print(g) # Error message. object 'Xvar' not found

  # Setting environment does work in ggplot function, however.
  h = ggplot(data = oneData, aes(x = switch(Xvar, algo = algorithm, comp = computer), y = error), environment = environment()) + geom_point()
  print(h)
}

f()
```

I suppose the user could make all necessary variables global with `<<-` and delete them at the end of the function, although that's bad practice.

With version 1.0.1.

title: geom_vline messes up geom_line legend, if show_guide = TRUE
description:
Let's say I have some line graph via `geom_line` and would like to add some `geom_vline`s as thresholds.
Let's further say that I have _several_ such `geom_vline`s and would therefore require a **legend**.

Here's the **base layer** plot:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
data(mpg)

# base plot
g <- ggplot()
g <- g + geom_line(data = mpg, mapping = aes(y = cty, x = year, color = manufacturer), stat = "summary", fun.y = mean)
g
```

So far, so good:

![baseplot](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/9293911/416f952a-443c-11e5-9f9a-1d9c6cb79799.png)

---

Now let's try and add the threshold **via `geom_hline` with a custom legend**:

``` r
# add threshold via geom_hline()
g + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 2004, linetype = "Funny Law"), show_guide = TRUE) + scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Funny Law" = "dashed"))  # screws up all geom_line legends
```

Not so great, the base-layer legends are all screwed up:

![geomhline](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/9293919/7983362e-443c-11e5-8ee2-606355392693.png)

---

Ok, let's see whether we can make this work **via `geom_linerange()` with separate dataframes**:

``` r
thresholds <- data.frame(threshold = "Funny Law", year = 2004, ymin = 0, ymax = 35)
g + geom_linerange(data = thresholds, mapping = aes(x = year, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, linetype = threshold))  # works ok
```

Works ok, except that the `geom_linerange` doesn't fill the entire y-height of the plot, but ok:

![linerange](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/9293925/cc48354e-443c-11e5-80a8-d096266de376.png)

---

Then wouldn't we expect the same approach to work **via `geom_vline()` with a separate dataframe?**

``` r
# add threshold via geom_hline() WITH separate data
g + geom_vline(data = thresholds, mapping = aes(xintercept = year, linetype = threshold), show_guide = TRUE)  # screws up all geom_line legends
```

Nope, the same problem with screwed up legends returns:

![vlinesep](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/9293937/fe9b8e24-443c-11e5-98ad-835162344b35.png)

---

Bug or my mistake?

---

May be related:
- http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5027016/missing-legend-with-ggplot2-and-geom-line
- http://stackoverflow.com/questions/30807890/add-geom-hline-legend-without-screwing-up-geom-line-legend

title: Add examples to geom_text: text together with geom_bar
description:
In `?geom_text` all examples concern scatterplot-oid plots, with or without points. There are no examples of `geom_text` together with `geom_bar`. Given the large number of questions on SO of how to position `geom_text` in relation to dodged or stacked bars I believe this gap in the help text should be filled. Here is a suggestion with some toy data and code which may be a start for additional examples.

Some data:

```
df <- data.frame(x = factor(c(1, 1, 2, 2)), y = c(1, 3, 2, 1), grp = c("a", "b", "a", "b"))
```

`position = "dodge"` only set for `geom_bar` obviously doesn't work [a common "error" in SO questions]

```
ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = grp, label = y)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
    geom_text() 
```

Then set `position = "dodge"` for both `geom_bar` and `geom_text` [a highly sensible attempt, and why it doesn't work is not very intuitive]

```
ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = grp, label = y)) +
   geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
   geom_text(position = "dodge")
```

The solution:

```
dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.7)

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = grp, label = y)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = dodge) +
  geom_text(position = dodge, vjust = -0.3) # *
```

(\* why do we need to use a  _negative_ `vjust` to move the text in a _positive_ direction (up)?)

---

The `dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.7)` trick is described in `?geom_errorbar`, but I must say that I don't quite understand the explanation for its use:

```
# Because the bars and errorbars have different widths
# we need to specify how wide the objects we are dodging are
```

Is it really about the width of the `geom`s? Consider some long labels and try to dodge them with `"dodge"` only. Same lack of dodging of the text:

```
df$lab = c("loooooooong", "tadaaaaaaaa", "o la laaaaaaa", "yeeeeeeees")

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = grp, label = lab)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
    geom_text(position = "dodge")
```

title: Adding creating your own theme section to extension vignette
description:
Draft from book below

---
## Creating your own theme

Instead of modifying an existing theme piecemeal, you might want to start from scratch and create your own unique theme.
If you want to create your complete theme, you'll need to understand a bit more about the structure of themes.
### Global settings

There are four elements that affect the global appearance of the plot.

Element      | Theme function    | Description
-------------|--------------------------------------------
line         | `element_line()`  | all line elements
rect         | `element_rect()`  | all rectangular elements
text         | `element_text()`  | all text
title        | `element_text()`  | all text in title elements (plot, axes & legend)

These set default properties that are inherited by more specific settings. These are most useful for setting an overall "background" colour and overall font settings (e.g. family and size).

`r columns(2, 1, 2/3)`

``` r axis-line-ex
df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3)
base <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()

base + theme(text = element_text(colour = "pink"))
```

It's also possible to use `rel()` to specify a relative size.

Inheritance

Complete vs. incomplete.

`%+replace%`
### Complete vs incomplete

It is useful to understand the difference between complete and incomplete theme objects. A _complete_ theme object is one produced by calling a theme function with the attribute `complete = TRUE`. 

Theme functions `theme_grey()` and `theme_bw()` are examples of complete theme functions. Calls to `theme()` produce _incomplete_ theme objects, since they represent (local) modifications to a theme object rather than returning a complete theme object per se. When adding an incomplete theme to a complete one, the result is a complete theme. 

Complete and incomplete themes behave somewhat differently when added to a ggplot object:
- Adding an incomplete theme augments the current theme object, replacing only 
  those properties of elements defined in the call to `theme()`. In particular, 
  any NULL element properties specified in `theme()`.
- Adding a complete theme wipes away the existing theme and applies. 

To deal with this problem, the concept of a complete theme (object) was introduced in the new theming system. In particular, `theme_grey` and `theme_bw` are both complete theme functions and return complete theme objects when called. When added to a plot, a complete theme object overrides the current default theme and in fact _replaces_ it. This idea is implemented by endowing a theme function with the attribute `"complete"`: its value is `TRUE` for complete themes and `FALSE` for incomplete themes. Examples are shown in the next section.
### Modifying a theme function

There is a second type of inheritance in themes

``` r
theme_grey()$legend.key

new_theme <- theme_grey() + theme(legend.key = element_rect(colour = "red"))
new_theme$legend.key

new_theme <- theme_grey() %+replace% theme(legend.key = element_rect(colour = "red"))
new_theme$legend.key
```

title: Write vignette about grid
description:
Text removed from book below

---

If you want to arrange multiple plots on a single page, you'll need to learn a little bit of grid, the underlying graphics system used by ggplot. The key concept you'll need to learn about is a viewport: a rectangular subregion of the display. The default viewport takes up the entire plotting region, and by customising the viewport you can arrange a set of plots in just about any way you can imagine. \index{Layout} \index{Publication!multiple plots on the same page}

To begin, let's create three plots that we can experiment with. When arranging multiple plots on a page, it will usually be easiest to create them, assign them to variables and then plot them. This makes it easier to experiment with plot placement independent of content. The plots created by the code below are shown in Figure \ref{fig:layout}.

`r columns(3)`

``` r layout
a <- ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) + geom_line()
b <- ggplot(economics, aes(uempmed, unemploy)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(se = FALSE) 
c <- ggplot(economics, aes(uempmed, unemploy)) + geom_point()
a
b
c
```
### Subplots

One common layout is to have a small subplot drawn on top of the main plot.  To achieve this effect, we first plot the main plot, and then draw the subplot in a smaller viewport.  Viewports are created with (surprise!) the `viewport()` function, with parameters `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` to control the size and position of the viewport. By default, the measurements are given in 'npc' units, which range from 0 to 1. The location (0, 0) is the bottom left, (1, 1) the top right and (0.5, 0.5) the centre of viewport.  If these relative units don't work for your needs, you can also use absolute units, like `unit(2, "cm")` or `unit(1, "inch")`. \index{Sub-figures} \index{Subplots}

``` r viewports
library(grid)
# A viewport that takes up the entire plot device
vp1 <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)
vp1 <- viewport()

# A viewport that takes up half the width and half the height, 
# located in the middle of the plot.
vp2 <- viewport(width = 0.5, height = 0.5, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)
vp2 <- viewport(width = 0.5, height = 0.5)

# A viewport that is 2cm x 3cm located in the center
vp3 <- viewport(width = unit(2, "cm"), height = unit(3, "cm"))
```

By default, the x and y parameters control the location of the centre of the viewport. When positioning the plot in other locations, you may need to use the `just` parameter to control which corner of the plot you are positioning.  The following code gives some examples.

``` r viewport2
# A viewport in the top right
vp4 <- viewport(x = 1, y = 1, just = c("right", "top"))
# Bottom left
vp5 <- viewport(x = 0, y = 0, just = c("right", "bottom"))
```

To draw the plot in our new viewport, we use the `vp` argument of the `print()` method.  This method is normally called automatically whenever you evaluate something on the command line, but because we want to customise the viewport, we need to call it ourselves. The result of this is shown in Figure \ref{fig:subplot-1}.

``` r polish, results='hide'
pdf("figures/polishing-subplot-1.pdf", width = 4, height = 4)
subvp <- viewport(width = 0.4, height = 0.4, x = 0.75, y = 0.35)
b
print(c, vp = subvp)
dev.off()
```

This gives us what we want, but we need to make a few tweaks to the appearance: the text should be smaller, we want to remove the axis labels and shrink the plot margins. The result is shown in Figure \ref{fig:subplot-2}.

``` r polish2, results='hide'
csmall <- c + 
  theme_gray(9) + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + 
  theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1/4, 0, 0, 0), "lines"))

pdf("figures/polishing-subplot-2.pdf", width = 4, height = 4)
b
print(csmall, vp = subvp)
dev.off()
```

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \subfigure[Figure with subplot.]{
    \includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{figures/polishing-subplot-1}
    \label{fig:subplot-1}
  }%
  \subfigure[Subplot tweaked for better display.]{
    \includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{figures/polishing-subplot-2}
    \label{fig:subplot-2}
  }
  \caption{Two examples of a figure with subplot. It will usually be necessary to tweak the theme settings of the subplot for optimum display.}
  \label{fig:subplot}
\end{figure}

Note we need to use `pdf()` (or `png()` etc.) to save the plots to disk because `ggsave()` only saves a single plot.
### Rectangular grids

A more complicated scenario is when you want to arrange a number of plots in a rectangular grid. Of course you could create a series of viewports and use what you've learned above, but doing all the calculations by hand is cumbersome. A better approach is to use `grid.layout()`, which sets up a regular grid of viewports with arbitrary heights and widths. You still need to create each viewport, but instead of explicitly specifying the position and size, you can specify the row and column of the layout.

The following example shows how this work.  We first create the layout, here a 2 by 2 grid, then assign it to a viewport and push that viewport on to the plotting device.  Now we are ready to draw each plot into its own position on the grid.  We create a small function to save some typing, and then draw each plot in the desired place on the grid.  You can supply a vector of rows or columns to span a plot over multiple cells.  The results are shown in Figure \ref{fig:layout-2}.

`r columns(1)`

``` r layout-2
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2, 2)))

vplayout <- function(x, y) 
  viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
print(a, vp = vplayout(1, 1:2))
print(b, vp = vplayout(2, 1))
print(c, vp = vplayout(2, 2))
```

By default `grid.layout()` makes each cell the same size, but you can use the `widths` and `heights` arguments to make them different sizes.  See the documentation for `grid.layout()` for more examples.

title: Clean up axis expansion
description:
- Currently it's difficult to follow the code that computes axis expansion. The code (and default values) are spread out over both coordinate systems and scales.
- We need to distinguish between setting the limits of a coordinate system exactly and approximately (e.g. expanded and not expanded). It's not exactly clear what the correct behaviour. It looks like the old `wise` parameter used to control expansion, but was removed, with the claim that expansion was now the default behaviour.
- Given that the behaviour has clearly changed over the last few years, and I don't remember any complaints about it, it's probably not a heavily used feature so we can change it to do the "right" thing.
- I would prefer to keep the `expand` parameter in one place (the scale), but I think there is some interaction with the coord, because the default expansion varies based on the coordinate system. Maybe the coordinate system could have a boolean expand flag, with the details controlled in the scale.

title: Printing a proto2 method should display method contents
description:
Presently, proto2 methods print out like this:

```
> GeomBar$reparameterise
function (...) 
res(self = self, ...)
<environment: 0xa1a0db0>
attr(,"class")
[1] "proto2_method"
```

This is just the wrapper function added by the `$` method, and isn't very helpful for debugging. It would be better to print out the content of the called function, like this does:

```
> environment(GeomBar$reparameterise)$res
function(self, df, params) {
      df$width <- df$width %||%
        params$width %||% (resolution(df$x, FALSE) * 0.9)
      transform(df,
        ymin = pmin(y, 0), ymax = pmax(y, 0),
        xmin = x - width / 2, xmax = x + width / 2, width = NULL
      )
    }
<environment: namespace:ggplot2>
```

Additionally, the print method make it clear that this is a method, and is wrapped up in another function.

title: Extra padding is added between facet labels on vertical axis and plot when using also facets on horizontal axis
description:
Using the `facet_grid` option of `switch = "y"` for vertical facets and also using facets on the horizontal axis, I get some padding between the labels on the vertical axis and the plot. This padding is not present if I only plot the vertical facets.

See plots for illustration:

 **vertical facets only**
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1554520/8777254/3626f852-2ef7-11e5-9da4-49845ede28b6.png)

**vertical & horizontal facets**
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1554520/8777279/62fd96a6-2ef7-11e5-9b5b-2daec14ab7d1.png)

The code for both is identical (except for the facet definition) and will attach it below. I have attempted all the options I could find, to get rid of the padding, with no success. Therefore, I believe this might be a bug, since it would make sense to be able to have no padding between the facet labels and the plot (esp. since there is none if there are no "horizontal" facets).

Using ggplot2 version 1.0.1.9002.

See code bellow: 

```
library(ggplot2)
data("iris")

# add another column to data to facet by in the second example
iris2 <- iris
iris2$Species2 <- rep(c("one","two","three"), 50)

# plot with facet on vertical axis
ggplot(data=iris2, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width )) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(Species ~ . , switch = "y") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "cm"),
        axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "cm"),
        axis.line.y = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_blank(),
        panel.margin = unit(0, "cm"),
        strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 180),
        strip.switch.pad.grid = unit(0, "cm")
  )

# plot with facets on both axis
ggplot(data=iris2, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width )) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(Species ~ Species2 , switch = "y") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "cm"),
        axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "cm"),
        axis.line.y = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_blank(),
        panel.margin = unit(0, "cm"),
        strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 180),
        strip.switch.pad.grid = unit(0, "cm")
        )


```
