title: Log scales should have more values labeled on their axes
description:
The vast majority of the time I use a log scale in ggplot, by default it ends up with only 2 values labelled on the axis. This is problematic because with only two values, it is not immediately obvious that the scale is non-linear. I would say that 3 is the absolute minimum number of values that should be allowed on the scale, to make the non-linearity clear. And I think that as long as room is available, every order of magnitude should be labelled, since orders of magnitude are the basic unit that one thinks about when working on a log scale. I'm attaching a plot that demonstrates both problems (the actual content of the plot is unimportant):

![Under-labeled log scales](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/228145/8680016/5cd3ee6c-2a13-11e5-99ad-751d2c8053e6.png)

title: `annotation_raster` isn't working when data is not specified in the base layer?
description:
Refer to: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/31396095/why-doesnt-annotation-raster-work?noredirect=1#comment50768233_31396095

The question is copied as below:

---

In the documentation, there's one example showing the usage of `annotation_raster` as below.

```
ggplot(aes(x=mpg, y=wt), data=mtcars) +
  annotation_raster('red', -Inf, Inf, -Inf, Inf) +
  geom_point()
```

This works fine, however, when I move the data and aes into the layer, suddenly it doesn't work anymore:

```
ggplot() +
  annotation_raster('red', -Inf, Inf, -Inf, Inf) +
  geom_point(aes(x=mpg, y=wt), data=mtcars)  # doesn't work
```

This is perplexing because to me these two seem semantically identical.

Is there a reason why the second line won't work and is there a way to use `annotation_raster` without specifying data and aes early in the base layer?

title: problems with devtools::check() and suggested usage idioms
description:
Hi.  I followed the suggested usage idiom, and check() complains

My plot code (taken from the ggplot2 documentation), but fixed to used fully qualified package names as suggested by devtools (which btw is pretty awkward for plyr::.  ):

```
domore <- function(df){
    ## Compute sample mean and standard deviation in each group
    ds <- plyr::ddply(df, plyr::.(gp), plyr::summarise, mean = mean(y), sd = sd(y))

    ## Declare the data frame and common aesthetics.
    ## The summary data frame ds is used to plot
    ## larger red points in a second geom_point() layer.
    ## If the data = argument is not specified, it uses the
    ## declared data frame from ggplot(); ditto for the aesthetics.
    q <- ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(x = gp, y = y)) +
        ggplot2::geom_point() +
        ggplot2::geom_point(data = ds, ggplot2::aes(y = mean),
                           colour = 'red', size = 3)
    print(q)
    q
}
```

`devtools::check()` spits out the following warnings:

```
domore: no visible binding for global variable ‘gp’
domore: no visible binding for global variable ‘y’
```

Is it the same thing to do df$gp, df$y then ds$mean in the second?  And anyway, how to you guys get around the Rcheck notes?

title: Errors in geom_tile examples
description:
# Summary

Certain examples in `geom_tile` throw errors and do not plot anything
# Reproducible example

Running `example("geom_tile")` will show the error, but the specific lines which cause the error are

``` r
cars <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(y=factor(cyl), x=mpg))
cars + geom_point()
cars + stat_bin(aes(fill=..count..), geom="tile", binwidth=3, position="identity")
cars + stat_bin(aes(fill=..density..), geom="tile", binwidth=3, position="identity")
```

Which give

``` r
> cars <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(y=factor(cyl), x=mpg))
> cars + geom_point()
> cars + stat_bin(aes(fill=..count..), geom="tile", binwidth=3, position="identity")
Error : Mapping a variable to y and also using stat="bin".
  With stat="bin", it will attempt to set the y value to the count of cases in each group.
  This can result in unexpected behavior and will not be allowed in a future version of ggplot2.
  If you want y to represent counts of cases, use stat="bin" and don't map a variable to y.
  If you want y to represent values in the data, use stat="identity".
  See ?geom_bar for examples. (Defunct; last used in version 0.9.2)
> cars + stat_bin(aes(fill=..density..), geom="tile", binwidth=3, position="identity")
Error : Mapping a variable to y and also using stat="bin".
  With stat="bin", it will attempt to set the y value to the count of cases in each group.
  This can result in unexpected behavior and will not be allowed in a future version of ggplot2.
  If you want y to represent counts of cases, use stat="bin" and don't map a variable to y.
  If you want y to represent values in the data, use stat="identity".
  See ?geom_bar for examples. (Defunct; last used in version 0.9.2)
```
# Suggested fix

The latter two lines could be replaced with

``` r
cars + stat_bin2d(aes(fill=..count..), binwidth = c(3,1))
cars + stat_bin2d(aes(fill=..density..), binwidth = c(3,1))
```

which give graphs similar to those shown in http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.3.1/geom_tile.html.

It is of interest to note, though, that adding an explicit `geom="tile"` to the `stat_bin2d` call causes other errors to be thrown, which may mean that these are not good examples for `geom_tile`.

title: Is there a way to allow scales in facet_grid to be completely "free"?
description:
Suppose we have an n x m grid.

Currently:
- `scales = free_x` allows for m scales along the bottom, and 1 common scale for all rows.
- `scales = free_y` allows for n scales along the side, and 1 common scale for all columns.
- `scales = free` allows for n scales along the side, and m scales along the bottom.

Is there a way to have all scales free? i.e. this would result in n*m independent scales, one for each subplot?

title: stat_bin2d: doesn't handle integer-valued data
description:
When I make a `stat_bin2d` using integer data, I still get the "range / 30" bin width.

``` r
> df <- data.frame(x = 0:3, y = 0:3)
> str(df)
'data.frame':   4 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ x: int  0 1 2 3
 $ y: int  0 1 2 3
> g <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y))
> g + stat_bin2d()
```

![default stat_bin2d](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/229502/8314722/570a2eca-19b9-11e5-8ae9-7d07cf9fcf95.png)

However, in [stat-bin2d.r](https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/v1.0.1/R/stat-bin2d.r#L66), it looks like it is trying to handle integer data specially, to end up with something like this:

``` r
> g + stat_bin2d(binwidth=c(1,1), origin=c(-0.5,-0.5))
```

![explicit stat_bin2d](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/229502/8314782/b5650d00-19b9-11e5-848a-f68de732db72.png)

Maybe, at some point, `data$x` retained its R integer type, but now something switches it to just numeric, and so the `is.integer` tests fail?

Here's a failing test case:

``` r
df <- data.frame(x = 0:3, y = 0:3)
g <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y))
p <- ggplot_build(g + stat_bin2d())

want_xbin <- cut(df$x, seq(-0.5, 4, 1))
expect_equal(p$data[[1]]$xbin, want_xbin)
```

title: %+% only works if it's the first argument
description:
I don't know if this a bug or a deliberate design decision, but `%+%` only works if it's the first argument.  To show this in an example, say I'm plotting 5 straight lines, and then I want to omit 2 of them:

```
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Sample data: lines
df <- data.frame(
    x = rep(1:20, each = 5),
    grouping = factor(rep(1:5, 20))
    )
df <- within(df, y <- x * as.numeric(grouping))

# Plot the raw data
(p1 <- qplot(data = df, x = x, y = y, color = grouping, geom = "line"))

# Subset out 2 of the 5 lines.  This works:
p1 %+% filter(df, grouping != 3, grouping != 4) +
  scale_color_brewer(type = "div")

# But this doesn't.  Seems like this should throw an error, at minimum
p1 + scale_color_brewer(type = "div") %+%
  filter(df, grouping != 3, grouping != 4)
```

If this isn't a bug, it does seem like there should at least be a warning when the user puts in a `%+%` command that ggplot ignores, so that way I know which data the plot is using in cases where it might not be obvious.

Thanks!  Please let me know if I can help in any other way.

title: Semi-transparent borders around bars not consistent
description:
# Summary

The algorithms for drawing the lines around bars in `geom_bar` assume that the color is completely opaque and can lead to different colors due to overplotting when semi-transparent.
# Example

``` r
library("ggplot2")
library("scales")
ggplot(mtcars[1:8,], aes(x = factor(carb), y = disp)) +
geom_bar(stat = "identity", lwd = 7, colour = alpha("white", 0.5)) +
theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue"))
```

![](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/463252/7579755/bc780682-f81d-11e4-92b2-ecf9bde65461.png)

The borders are 50% transparent white and absurdly large to make the effects more obvious. The borders between the stacked bars are not all the same color.
# Discussion

Fixing this completely would be very hard, especially the double plotting that occurs at the corners. I submit this bug more to mark it as a known issue than to get (or submit) a fix. What I might suggest is a comment in the details section of `geom_bar` such as

> Borders around bars (defined by the `colour` aesthetic) are drawn assuming a completely opaque color. A semi-transparent color can be used, but the effects will not be as expected.

title: Minimum number of points for boxplots
description:
Here is an issue I have struggled with repeatedly. When using geom_boxplot, a boxplot is done, irrespective of the number of data points that are available. This is especially a problem when doing boxplots across various groups (e.g. timepoints) where not always the same number of samples is available. In plotting, all the boxplots look equivalent, although it can easily be the case that some are only based on 2-3 points (or even 1).

Therefore I have the following feature request: Add a parameter to geom_boxplot that requires a minimum number of points for the boxplot to be done. By default it can be set to 0 not to change current behavior. then
1. If minimum number of points reached - do the boxplot as usual
2. If minimum number of points not reached - plot the available data as points instead (with color being equal to the fill color of the boxplot).

Thanks!

P.S. The same argument is also true for geom_violin.
P.P.S. I guess the easiest way to implement this practically is to declare all data points "outliers" if there are less than the request minimum and set the outlier color to the fill color in this case.

title: print(ggplot_obj) not returning a ggplot object
description:
The documentation of `print.default` states that 

```
 'print' prints its argument and returns it _invisibly_ (via
 'invisible(x)').
```

Hence I expected the following to work:

```
plot_obj <- ggplot(data = data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10), aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
plot_obj2 <- print(plot_obj)
print(plot_obj2 + ggtitle("testplot"))
```

... but it doesn't (`Error in plot_obj2 + ggtitle("testplot") : non-numeric argument to binary operator`), since `plot_obj2` is of class `list` and not `ggplot` (as is `plot_obj`).

A quick look at [plot-render.r](https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/4bb9270ef4d5d5062353438fd99d17b6f6de98a2/R/plot-render.r#L179-L195) confirms that `print.ggplot(x)` does not return `x` but rather `ggplot_build(x)` (invisibly).

So to summarise,
- the behavior of `print.ggplot` is not in tune with the documentation of `print.default` and
- it is not documented.

A little bit of context on why I wanted to do this: I have various custom functions that construct ggplot objects and print them. I found it very convenient to just have `print(obj)` as the final statement in my function, believing that this would also invisibly return the object, s.t. I could further modify it outside of the function if necessary. Now I have to do `print(obj); invisible(obj)`.

Is there a reason for this choice of implementation? If yes, I'd think it should at least be documented.

title: Histograms for multiple distributions in one plot
description:
I've been looking for a way to plot histograms for multiple distributions in a single plot. I've tried to use position="dodge" but in case of my data it's very hard to see anything.

Then I came across this SO thread: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/3541713/how-to-plot-two-histograms-together-in-r (the first couple of plots are density but the rest are actual histograms) and all solutions there are based on using transparency. It occurred to me that a more universal way to do it would be to use solid bars but for each bin, plot the bars in the order from highest to lowest so that all of them are visible (hope this makes sense). I've had a cursory look at the ggplot code and couldn't see a simple way of implementing this that would be compatible with how things are organised. 

I would really appreciate any suggestions on how to get this kind of plot to work.

title: stat_km and geom_km for Kaplan-Meier Survival curves
description:
People occasionally ask about plotting survival curves with ggplot2. While it is possible, [see here for some examples](https://stackoverflow.com/search?q=%5Bggplot2%5D+survival), it's not done in the "ggplot way" and people often revert to the base plot because it's so much easier (but not nearly as powerful).  

I've worked a bit on adding a stat and geom for computing and plotting survival curves [here](https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/compare/master...sachsmc:feature/kmcurve). I view it as along the same lines as `stat_ecdf` but for censored data. Before submitting a pull request I wanted to ask if this would be suitable for inclusion in ggplot2, or if it would be better as a standalone package?

Here's an example code and plot: 

``` r
df <- survival::lung
ggplot(df, aes(x = time, status = status, color = factor(sex))) + geom_km()
```

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5464185/6966565/17a8f7ce-d928-11e4-9b02-1a517c532614.png)

title: stat_contour fill - 2 issues
description:
Hello everyone,

I have been using ggplot2  for quite sometime now it's a great library! But I am stuck on some (known from what I have searched) issues of stat_contour. 

1) When I set geom="polygon" the levels that are not fully closed are not filled correctly.
2) Higher levels cover/hide the lower levels.

Straight to a simple example to show you what I mean:
### Creating the data

> library(ggplot2)
> x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 100)
> y = x
> R = expand.grid(x, y)
> dim(R)
> names(R) = c("x", "y")
> R$z = R$x^2 + R$y^2
> head(R)
### Ploting contour

> ggplot(R, aes(x = x, y = y, z = z)) + stat_contour()
> ![stat_contour1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8446323/6605024/6ad40550-c835-11e4-9528-9361885931e0.png)
### Ploting filled contour by setting geom="polygon"

> ggplot(R, aes(x = x, y = y, z = z)) + stat_contour(geom="polygon")
> ![stat_contour2](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8446323/6605028/72b6195c-c835-11e4-8c19-c0faf60e9553.png)
### In order to see what is filled correctly and what is not

> ggplot(R, aes(x = x, y = y, z = z, fill=..level..)) +
>   stat_contour(geom="polygon") + 
>   stat_contour() + 
>   scale_fill_gradient(low = "blue", high = "red") +
>   coord_map(xlim=c(-1,1),ylim=c(-1,1))
> ![stat_contour3](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8446323/6605033/77587982-c835-11e4-9cde-aa6f3b24065c.png)
### And if we reverse the values of R$z we can display the inner/hidden levels (multiply *-1)

> ggplot(R*-1, aes(x = x, y = y, z = z, fill=..level..)) +
>   stat_contour(geom="polygon") + 
>   stat_contour() + 
>   scale_fill_gradient(low = "blue", high = "red") +
>   coord_map(xlim=c(-1,1),ylim=c(-1,1))
> ![stat_contour4](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8446323/6605037/7f0b83cc-c835-11e4-8c41-ef94b5d90a92.png)
### The first problem is somehow fixed (not completely) by expanding my grid with the same values that has in each side. Something like this:

> R_fill <- subset(R, x==1 | x==-1 | y==1 | y==-1)
> R_fill[R_fill$x==1,]$x=5
> R_fill[R_fill$x==-1,]$x=-5
> R_fill[R_fill$y==1,]$y=5
> R_fill[R_fill$y==-1,]$y=-5
> R_fill <- rbind(R_fill,R)
> ggplot(R_fill*-1, aes(x = x, y = y, z = z, fill=..level..)) +
>   stat_contour(geom="polygon") + 
>   stat_contour() + 
>   scale_fill_gradient(low = "blue", high = "red") +
>   coord_map(xlim=c(-1,1),ylim=c(-1,1))
> ![stat_contour5](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8446323/6605039/84390388-c835-11e4-8267-a9047de12f63.png)

To sum up, (1) every level that is higher than 1 is not filled correctly since the level line is not closed on the edges. So whenever the level is not closed, ggplot is forcing a closure by connecting the two edges of the semi-circles. Maybe the only way to correct the above problem is to handle and plot the levels in stat_contour as polygons with certain coordination. Can I somehow obtain the exact point position that belong to each contour line? If I could then I would be able to plot them as polygons and set a certain box around the region I want to plot and "close" the "un-closed" levels in order to be filled correctly.

And (2) since ggplot (to my understanding) is plotting lower to higher levels, the lower levels are obscured. I have no idea how this could be fixed, since some datasets contain regions of lower values around higher levels.

I don't know how hard is to tackle and correct these problems since I have no experience on the ggplot code. It would be really useful if stat_contour acted as filled.contour, since ggplot2 has some many possibilities. So I would like to hear your thoughts and your suggestions.

Thank you in advance,
Thanos

title: OHLC and Themes
description:
Hello,  
  Let me start with Thanks for ggplot.  

  I am working on automating a process that will gather financial data from Yahoo! Finance and after using a series of checks will list suitable stock, mainly as financial style charts. This is entirely for personal use, I have no intention to turn this into a product.  

  My questions/comments/request are:  
- I know about quantmod, but I cannot modify or create something on top of it (without modifying quantmod itself, which I not interested or capable of doing, and would be beyond what I can spend in time.  
- Any chance to have a new chart type OHLC (Open, High, Low, Close)? Normally it also comes with a pairing Candlestick chart, which I don't care for my project.  
- As there is no such geom_ohlc yet :smile: , I am doing it all by myself, creating it all bit-by-bit.  
- something generic that would be nice: be able to move the y axis to the right, just move, no need for a second in this case.  
- I am using gridExtra to have charts combined (common in these financial charts) and the scales (x) do not align perfectly.  
- mere for the looks, any change to have themes plot.background and panel.background to produce a gradient fill?  

Here is an example:
![screen shot 2015-03-02 at 23 18 44](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/2324700/6440599/c9f45800-c132-11e4-91b6-cc427e5182b8.png)
- To create this chart I have a function that is about 200 lines of code. A good 50 are ggplot specific, so again, a geom_ohlc would be great (if we could still have the ability to play with the elements);  
- Doing it all by hand is fine, but I would like the y axis on the right;  
- I would like to be able to align the x scale. In this case it is a 1:55 for both (it is the same data.frame).  
- Again, just for the looks, a gradient for panel and plot areas would be nice.  

![screen shot 2015-03-02 at 23 28 33](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/2324700/6440698/eb446594-c133-11e4-96d9-ab3bbbc328a8.png)
- The panels do not align, if the range/format of the y axis is different;  
- For the RSI (bottom chart) I could not make the stat_ribbon to work for the red fill under the line of 30, so I had to create a second series changing the numbers. I am still having problems when it crosses the line of 30. 
- There is a minor gap between the two charts, probably gridExtra or simply the ways things are underneath.  

For the top chart:

```
g <- ggplot(Chart)
g <- g + geom_linerange(aes(x=Timeline, ymin=Low, ymax=High, colour=Colour), size=1.5) # High/Low bar
g <- g + geom_segment(aes(x=Timeline, xend=Timeline-0.4, y=Open,  yend=Open,  colour=Colour), size=1.5) # Open
g <- g + geom_segment(aes(x=Timeline, xend=Timeline+0.4, y=Close, yend=Close, colour=Colour), size=1.5) # Close
g <- g + scale_colour_manual(name="", values=c(Down=DC, Flat=FC, Up=UC)) # set the colour
g <- g + theme_ohlc
g <- g + geom_line(aes(x=Timeline, y=Trail), colour="darkred", size=1.3) # Trailing Stop
g <- g + geom_line(aes(x=Timeline, y=Profit.Taker), colour="green", size=1.3) # Profit Taker
# . . .
g <- g + scale_x_continuous(breaks=which(Chart$Timeline %% axis.x.interval == 0))
g <- g + theme(axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
g <- g + theme(plot.margin  = unit(c(1, 5, -22, 15), units = "points"))
y.top <- ggplot_build(g)$panel$ranges[[1]]$y.range[2] # high y limit from the chart internal structure
g <- g + annotate("text", x = 1, y = y.top, label = code) # put title inside the chart
```

For the bottom chart:

```
r <- ggplot(Chart)
r <- r + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=70), colour="black", linetype="dashed", size=0.5, alpha=0.5) # Upper line
r <- r + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=30), colour="black", linetype="dashed", size=0.5, alpha=0.5) # Lower line
```

title: stat_bin() does not seem to work for integer data
description:
Creating a simple data.frame with integers and binning it with stat_bin, should bin the integers.

``` R
df <- data.frame(xint = sample.int(10,size = 100,replace=TRUE))
is.integer(df$xint)
ggplot() + stat_bin(data = df,aes(x=xint),geom='line')
```

Code in `stat_bin.r` shows that for integers you should not get a `binwidth defaulted to range/30` msg and it should bin at:

``` R
  if (is.integer(x)) {
    bins <- x
    x <- sort(unique(bins))
    width <- width
```

Don't know the root cause but it seems integer data is no longer integer by the time it gets passed to `calculate` and `bin` functions, but shows up as an numeric.

Gabe Haarsma

description:
Hi,

I sometimes use the row names of a data frame to label the x axis of my plots. Today, this resulted in incorrect assignments of x axis labels to the data. Code for a (hopefully) reproducible example is below. I was using `fill` and `color` for an explorative analysis of two categorical variables,
and noticed that after adding facet_grid on a third variable, the assignment of the x axis labels
was off.

The small table (6 x 32) can be downloaded here: https://www.dropbox.com/s/zu4i7xbg0hl64l7/ggplot2.xls?dl=0.
The data looks like this:

```
Customer | UnitA | UnitB | Category | Change | Month | CEO
---------|-------|-------|----------|--------|-------|------
A1  | 23668 | 402393    | high|     6.491608782 | January   | John
A2  | 4098  | 83704 | high  | 7.798828697   | March | John
A3 |    19568   | 320138    | high  | 6.246519899   | January   | John
...
```

Now, this works:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
df = read.delim("ggplot2.xls")
## creating the plot based on df as is
p = ggplot(df,
       aes(x = Customer, y = log2(Change),
           fill = CEO, color = Category)) +
   geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
   theme(text = element_text(size = 8),
         axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 1, angle = 45)) +
   scale_color_manual(values = c("firebrick3", "darkblue")) +
   scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "grey80"))

## no difference in "Category" between simple barplot,
p
## and after adding facets
p + facet_grid(. ~ Month, scales = "free")
```

See images 1 and 2.

![image1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1090101/6322840/6cc78892-baec-11e4-8dd2-fd1d122467dd.png)
![image2](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1090101/6322842/6ccc6d94-baec-11e4-9486-004629555cbe.png)

Redrawing the plot using data.frame row names to label the x axis, everything is fine
without adding facets (image3.png), but 

``` r
rownames(df) = df$Customer

p = ggplot(df,
       aes(x = rownames(df), y = log2(Change),
           fill = CEO, color = Category)) +
   geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
   theme(text = element_text(size = 8),
         axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 1, angle = 45)) +
   scale_color_manual(values = c("firebrick3", "darkblue")) +
   scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "grey80"))

## simple barplot correct, see image3.png
p
## now Customer and Category do not match! (image4.png)
p + facet_grid(. ~ Month, scales = "free")
```

![image3](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1090101/6322841/6ccbedba-baec-11e4-8eef-c3a4cd2af53b.png)
![image4](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1090101/6322843/6cccd00e-baec-11e4-91a6-d4e91b433a09.png)

Thanks!

title: geom_vline requires converting to numeric when intercept is a POSIXct
description:
Even though ggplot successfully plots points where the x-axis is a POSIXct, calling "geom_vline" with the x-intercept being set to the same x values gives the error "Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale".

It seems like a bug that the code below labeled "Does NOT work."  would produce this error.

This issue is similar but not the quite the same as other issues I have seen in "hadley / ggplot2".

Thanks,

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

xdf <- data.frame(datetime = seq(as.POSIXct('2015-01-01 15:00:00'), length.out = 5, by = 'day'),
                  count = 1:5)
### Grab subset of xdf

ydf <- xdf %>% filter(count >= 3, count <= 4)
###### 
### Does NOT work.
###### 

ggplot(xdf, aes(datetime, count)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = datetime))
# Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale
###### 
### Does NOT work.
###### 

ggplot(xdf, aes(datetime, count)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = datetime), data = ydf)
# Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale
###### 
### Works (i.e. plots correctly)
###### 

ggplot(xdf, aes(datetime, count)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.numeric(datetime)))
### Also works.

ggplot(xdf, aes(datetime, count)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.numeric(datetime)), data = ydf)

title: Custom geom with custom grob not working
Update stat_summary fun.data documentation
description:
In  issue #929 you mentioned that the documentation for `fun.data` in `stat_summary` is wrong because the function only gets a single vector, but can return a data frame. You corrected this [here](https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/commit/1cdf2339ca98d8732427640015f35867ae6da20d).

I think the following part of the current documentation needs to be updated too:

`fun.data   Complete summary function. Should take data frame as input and return data frame as output`

Instead it should say:

`fun.data    Complete summary function. Should take numeric vector as input and return data frame as output`

title: Need to explicitly import density() from stats?
description:
You call it here: https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/254327c99cbfe061ba6c3fcc30bbb6115768a722/R/stat-ydensity.r#L80

Interestingly, if it is not imported explicitly, then `ggplot2` will just call the first `density` on the search path, and if an attached package defines a `density` function, then that one is called. I guess this is true for all functions from the base packages. (?)

Willing to submit a PR if you want.

title: Documentation trans argument in continuous_scale
description:
In `?scale_x_continuous` `trans` is mentioned in the **Arguments** section, and it is referred to `continuous_scale` for more details. However, in `?continuous_scale` there are no details to be found - `trans` only appears in **Usage** (`trans = "identity"`). Back in `?scale_x_continuous`, a few 'shortcuts' are mentioned (`scale_y_log10`, `scale_y_sqrt`, `scale_y_reverse`) and there is a pointer to `?scale::trans_new` (shouldn't it be `scales`, with an 's'?), but examples of `trans` itself and valid transformer names, such as those in Table 6.2 in the ggplot book, are lacking. Furthermore, in the book it says "Table 6.2 list **some of the more common** transformers", which I interpret as there are even more, albeit less common, but still potentially useful transformers.

I believe it would be nice with an exhaustive table of valid `trans`former names in the help text.

title: Change default guide_legend to reverse=TRUE
description:
A common complaint of new ggplot users is that the stacking order of bar plots is different in the main plot and the legend (see, for example, http://learnr.wordpress.com/2010/03/23/ggplot2-changing-the-default-order-of-legend-labels-and-stacking-of-data/).  

The `guide_legend(reverse=TRUE)` option enables users to change this behaviour but it would be nice if this was the default behaviour.  Aligned ordering is both the default in other plotting packages (e.g. Excel), is more intuitive, and makes it easier to interpret figures printed in black and white (because, like it or not, too many shades of grey will be used from time to time).

title: scale_colour_manual fails when elements of named matrix are passed to values
description:
I tried to pass a subset of a matrix with named dimensions to the values argument of scale_colour_manual, but no colours appeared in the relevant elements, not even defaults - instead the elements disappeared. Confusingly, passing elements of the same matrix as an argument to theme() has the expected (normal) effect.

Here is a reproducible example of the problem:

```
library(ggplot2)

colourmatrix <- structure(c("#f79646", "#4f81bd", "#f9b074", "#7ba0cd"),
                          .Dim = c(2L,2L),
                          .Dimnames = list(NULL, c("", "coltint")))

# Doesn't work - no error, no colour in the scale, but works in theme
qplot(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, colour=factor(mtcars$vs)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c(colourmatrix[1,1],colourmatrix[2,1])) +
  theme(plot.background=element_rect(fill=colourmatrix[2,1]))

# Works
qplot(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, colour=factor(mtcars$vs)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c(colourmatrix[1,1][[1]],colourmatrix[2,1][[1]])) +
  theme(plot.background=element_rect(fill=colourmatrix[2,1]))

# Works
qplot(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, colour=factor(mtcars$vs)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c(colourmatrix[c(1,2),1])) +
  theme(plot.background=element_rect(fill=colourmatrix[2,1]))

# Works when names are removed
dimnames(colourmatrix) <- NULL
qplot(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, colour=factor(mtcars$vs)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c(colourmatrix[1,1],colourmatrix[2,1])) +
  theme(plot.background=element_rect(fill=colourmatrix[2,1]))
```

title: rqss in stat_quantile ignore the quantile with large number of values
description:
When dealing with a large number of values (more than 1e4), then the rqss method seems to discard the quantile parameter. Here is a minimal example (with a non-linear relationship):

```
library(ggplot2)
X <- runif(1e4)
V <- data.frame(x=X, y=log(X+runif(length(X))))
p <- ggplot(data = V, aes(x=x, y=y))
p + stat_quantile(quantiles = c(0.05, 0.95), method = "rqss")
```

Instead of doing the quantile regression for 0.05, it may do it for 0.5. This occurs at least half the time (decreasing the number of values reduces the frequency of this problem).

This problem disappear when using the rq method.

It would be nice to be able to change the facet background fill colour depending on the facet, in a similar way to other categorical variable mappings.

An example use-case: I have a dataset of hydrological data that has measurements at 20 different sites. Each site can be categorised into different vegetation types (e.g. savannah, conifer, rainforest, etc.). I have a plot of some of the data, facetted by site. I would like to change the background colour to match the vegetation type (light pastels, with various hues) to allow easier distinction between the site types, to aid in pattern detection. so: 

```
site_types <- c(site1='rainforest', site2='evergreen', ...)

veg_colours <- c(rainforest='lightgreen', savannah='tan', ...)

ggplot(df, aes(x=var1, y=var2)) + facet_wrap(facets=c(site), nrow=5, aes(background=site_types[site])) +
  scale_facet_background(values=veg_colours)
```

Not sure if that would be the way to implement it. 

If something like this isn't practical to implement, is there any way to implement something like this manually?

title: Segfault in annotate when using wrong positioning aesthetics
description:
When using `<annotate>` the positioning aesthetics change depending on they type of annotation. The listed options include x, y, yend, xend, ymin, ymax, xmin and xmax. 

Unless you have memorized which aesthetic goes with which annotation geom you'll get a segfault if you chose the wrong one. 

 `<annotate>` should check that the supplied aesthetics match those required by the chosen geom and issue an error if they do not.

I have encountered this problem on Mac OS X Mavericks with R 3.1.0 Mavericks and ggplot2 1.0.0. I imagine this problem is cross platform.

title: size in geom_point using variable with all but 1 as NAs
description:
When passing a variable in the data.frame to the size argument in geom_point, if the column to be all but one as NA, all values get plotted equally, i.e. NAs are not dropped. If two non-NA values exist, the plot looks as expected.

Wanted to know if it is an unavoidable consequence of how size is calculated, or really a bug. It the later I could try finding/fixing it.

``` R
  df <- data.frame(year=rep(10:14, each=3), age=1:3, data=runif(15))

  # points sized as expected
  ggplot(df, aes(year, age)) + geom_point(aes(size=data))

  # convert all values but 2 into NAs
  df$data[1:13] <- NA
  #2 points sized and shown
  ggplot(df, aes(year, age)) + geom_point(aes(size=data), na.rm=TRUE)

  # convert all but one value into NA
  df$data[1:14] <- NA

  # plot shows equal-sized dots for all datapoints
  ggplot(df, aes(year, age)) + geom_point(aes(size=data), na.rm=TRUE)
```

I tried with different names for the data column, but it made no difference. Tested in both ggplot2 1.0.0 from CRAN and 1.0.0.99 from github.

Thanks

title: sqrt_trans, scale limit expansion, and missing breaks
description:
Prompted by a posting on the mailing list (https://groups.google.com/d/topic/ggplot2/IUje5H0jwm4).
# Summary

Specific problem: Breaks near 0 are not displayed when the square root transformation is applied to a scale.

General problem: Scale expansion in transformed coordinate space can lead to values which are not meaningfully (or correctly) invertable to data space leading to improperly excluded breaks.
# Reproducible example:

``` r
library("ggplot2")
library("scales")

DF <- data.frame(x = seq(0,1,by=0.1),
                 y = seq(0,1,by=0.1))

ggplot(DF, aes(x=x, y=y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  scale_x_sqrt() +
  scale_y_continuous()
```
# Expected result

A plot with breaks labeled at 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, and 1.00
# Actual results

![Actual results](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/463252/3401986/6130d7b2-fd56-11e3-8b1f-8c62e15899fd.png)

Note that there is no 0 break on the x-axis.
# Discussion

The error occurs because when the limits (in coordinate space) are expanded, there are negative values which, when transformed back to data space, give the incorrect limits from which breaks are determined (or at least limited). Stepping through the effective steps that occur for getting the breaks shows:

``` r
st <- sqrt_trans()
(x<-st$transform(c(0,1)))
## [1] 0 1
(x<-expand_range(x, 0.05, 0))
## [1] -0.05  1.05
(limits<-st$inverse(x))
## [1] 0.0025 1.1025
(breaks<-st$breaks(limits))
## [1] 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00
st$trans(breaks)
## [1] 0.0000 0.5000 0.7071 0.8660 1.0000
st$trans(limits)
## [1] 0.05 1.05
censor(st$trans(breaks), st$trans(limits))
## [1]     NA 0.5000 0.7071 0.8660 1.0000
```

The real problem is that the result of the `expand_range` call lies outside the domain of the transformation. How should extra-domain values be treated? 
# Workarounds
## Don't square negative values

One solution to this problem is an alternative transformation, one that does not invert negative values. A transformation should be one-to-one (within its domain) and `sqrt_trans` is, but it happily will run the inverse on negative values which can not occur if everything is constrained within the domain. A simple approach is to just map all negative values to 0

``` r
mysqrt_trans <- function() {
  trans_new("mysqrt", 
            transform = base::sqrt,
            inverse = function(x) ifelse(x<0, 0, x^2),
            domain = c(0, Inf))
}
```
## Squish range before inverting

If we assume that all transformations are monotonic (I'm not sure if ggplot2/scales assume transformations are monotonic or just one-to-one; I can not come up with a useful transformation which is not, though I can create a pathological one.), then it is reasonable to squish any values outside the range (not domain) of the transformation. Bringing them back to the nearest extreme should be sufficient. Therefore a more general approach for an inverse would be

``` r
mysqrt_trans <- function() {
  domain <- c(0, Inf)
  transform <- base::sqrt
  range <- transform(domain)
  trans_new("mysqrt", 
            transform = transform,
            inverse = function(x) squish(x, range=range)^2,
            domain = domain)
}
```
## Squish to range whenever values are extended

This approach makes it the responsibility of the code which manipulates transformed (coordinate space) values to squish those to the appropriate range if there is any chance that that range is violated. If monotonicity is assumed, I think any interpolations should be safe, but any operation which can result in a value more extreme than the existing most extreme values would need to be squished. If this approach is taken, it would be worth adding an additional component `range` to the `trans` which is just the result of `transform(domain)`.

The transformation, then, could have its inverse just assume that the data is in the range or it can check that before proceeding (just as now transform may or may not check domain before proceeding). Ideally, the transformation should throw an error if either `transform` is called with values outside `domain` or `inverse` is called with values outside `range` and this would help pick out places where calling code is not behaving appropriately.

title: Setting variable to NULL within `aes_string()`
description:
I'm wondering if a recent commit (possibly 7fdb328e73a3bfa60e6dd294468fa9566ceb6820) changed the way `aes_string()` responds when a variable is set to NULL.  

```
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE)) called by knitr, because it's above the first chunk.
require(ggplot2)
require(datasets)

#Create a simple dataset for the line
dsLine <- mtcars[ c("mpg", "wt")]

#Create a dataset for the ribbon and REMOVE the y variable
dsRibbon <- dsLine
dsRibbon$upper <- dsRibbon$wt + .5
dsRibbon$lower <- dsRibbon$wt - .5
dsRibbon$waylower <- dsRibbon$wt - 10

dsRibbon$wt <- NULL

(g <- ggplot(dsLine, aes_string(x="mpg", y="wt")) + geom_line())
```

Setting y to NULL works with `aes` (unlike `aes_string` below).

```
g + geom_ribbon(mapping=aes(y=NULL, ymin=lower, ymax=upper), data=dsRibbon, alpha=.1)
```

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1372890/3043493/381e1922-e107-11e3-84d1-fd9c19e089c5.png)

This still looks for 'wt', even though y is set to NULL.

```
#   The error is "Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'wt' not found"
g + geom_ribbon(mapping=aes_string(y=NULL, ymin="lower", ymax="upper"), data=dsRibbon, alpha=.1)
```

This looks for `wt`, even though the the geom_ribbon doesn't need it. (Am I correct that y isn't needed?)

```
#   The error is "Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'wt' not found"
g + geom_ribbon(mapping=aes_string(ymin="lower", ymax="upper"), data=dsRibbon, alpha=.1)
```

This changes y to some variable that is present in the dataset, but not used by geom_ribbon. This produces the intended graph.

```
g + geom_ribbon(mapping=aes_string(y="lower", ymin="lower", ymax="upper"), data=dsRibbon, alpha=.1)
```

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1372890/3043546/9bf87ffa-e107-11e3-90b2-67db62a2594c.png)

This changes y to some variable that is present in the dataset, but not used by geom_ribbon. However the low value still affects the y coordinates.

```
g + geom_ribbon(mapping=aes_string(y="waylower", ymin="lower", ymax="upper"), data=dsRibbon, alpha=.1)
```

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1372890/3043540/9456e7d2-e107-11e3-805b-8213bef748af.png)

(Brian Ripley was kind enough to point this out to me this morning that my [Wats](https://github.com/wibeasley/Wats) package will break with ggplot2 1.0.0.  I'm sorry for that I didn't notice from your April ggplot2 1.0 RC announcement that my package was causing  a trouble maker.)

title: Error that seems misleading when using geom_line(stat="density") without enough data
description:
Hello,

In a regular EDA of a specific type of results, I found an error using ggplot() + geom_line(stat="density"). At first I was confused by the error because the plot was working for other data sets. Tracing things, I realized that the real problem was because there was not enough data to calculate the density.

I'll change my EDA analysis so this doesn't happen again (attempting to plot without enough data), but it'd be nice if the ggplot2 error was more informative.

Here's a small reproducible example:

``` S
> library(ggplot2)
> df <- data.frame(width = c(2806, 320, 287, 132, 214, 202, 235, 266, 156, 210), 
    seqnames=factor(c("chr20", "chr1", "chr6", "chr16", "chr17", "chr4", "chr1", "chr19", "chrX", "chr17")))
> ggplot(df, aes(x=log10(width), colour=seqnames)) + geom_line(stat="density")
Error in exists(name, env) : argument "env" is missing, with no default
> traceback()
6: exists(name, env)
5: find_global(scale_name, env)
```

title: Documentation link to date_breaks is broken
description:
Not sure this was the proper place to report, but the fix should be easy.

On the documentation for [scale_x_datetime](http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.3.1/scale_datetime.html), the `breaks` documentation is like so:

> **breaks**
> A vector of breaks, a function that given the scale limits returns a vector of breaks, or a character vector, specifying the width between breaks. For more information about the first two, see continuous_scale, for more information about the last, see [date_breaks](http://www.inside-r.org/r-doc/scales/date_breaks)`.

I think inside-r has redone their URL scheme, so the link for `date_breaks` is dead.

It should point [here](http://www.inside-r.org/packages/cran/ggplot2/docs/date_breaks) (at least, it appears that's the analogous site on inside-r).

---

As an aside, this still seems to be an issue since inside-r features the 0.8.9 documentation, and I'm using time data so I thought to myself, "I wonder if there's an equivalent, like `time_breaks`?" Guess what, [there is](http://www.inside-r.org/packages/cran/ggplot2/docs/time_breaks), or at least used to be, but it's not featured in the [0.9.3 documentation on CRAN](http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggplot2/ggplot2.pdf).

And as a last aside, why does the `ggplot2` documentation feature _usage_ information for `date_break`, but never actually give any formal documentation of what the argument(s) need to be? Clicking the hyperref in the PDF for `date_breaks` with in a browser or the downloaded file just takes me to the top of the file.

title: `stat_function` catches errors without rethrowing
description:
If an error occurs in a function called by `stat_function` the error is written to the screen but no error is thrown in the sense that R continues along and there is no `.Traceback` or `last.dump` (if the option is set).

A small example is below

```
library(ggplot2)

reg_fn <- function(argument) {
        argmuent^2
}

plot_ <- ggplot(data.frame(x = rnorm(10), y = rnorm(10)), aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + stat_function(fun = reg_fn)
print(plot_)

print('we kept going')
```

which produces the output

```
> source('example.R')
Error in (function (argument)  : object 'argmuent' not found
[1] "we kept going"
> 
```

Should an error be thrown?

```
)
```

title: Accept different quantile types in stat_boxplot
description:
(_Spun off from #108_)

This is so trivial, I'm reluctant to bring it up.  But it seems like it would require  a small change, and could avoid unnecessary debates if ggplot uses the best way to calculate the hinges of a boxplot.

R's `quantile()` function currently supports [9 variations](http://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/quantile.html).  In [`stat_boxplot()`](https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/c181c8ce5c0b95149b98a861810120f5696e212c/R/stat-boxplot.r#L51), could line 51 be adapted to accept a parameter value from 1 to 9?  

```
} else {
   stats <- as.numeric(quantile(y, qs))
}
```

I don't understand all the internal functions of ggplot2, so I don't know if there would be downstream problems.  In #108, it was mentioned that it's not easy to allow the user to specify `fivenum()` instead of `quantile()`.  Hopefully this won't be as difficult, since it's the same function, and only an optional parameter changes.

The [`quantile()`](http://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/quantile.html) documentation apparently concedes that its default isn't the recommendation of people who have thought about the differences. I guess they kept it way for backward compatibility.  Notice the authors of the function are Ivan Frohne and Rob J **Hyndman**.

> Further details are provided in **Hyndman** and Fan (1996) who recommended type 8. The default method is type 7, as used by S and by R < 2.0.0.

title: To remove plot margins, why are both axis.title = element_blank() and labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) required?
description:
In trying to remove all borders from a plot, I applied all relevant [theme options](http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/theme.html) that seemed pertinent. It took stumbling on [a related SO question](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17786197/plot-margins-in-ggplot2) to find that in addition to `theme(axis.title = element_blank())`, I also need to pass `labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)` to my plot.

If one has set the titles to blank elements, why must they also be set to `NULL`?

P.S. As an aside, why does `labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)` work, but not `scale_x_continuous(NULL)`? They seem to do the same thing when passing strings, so if I really want axis text removed, it would be nice to be able to pass `NULL` for the title along with other `scale_continuous` options (`limits = c()`, etc.) vs. having to add a completely separate `labs()` command to do this.

title: Should axis.ticks = element_blank() and axis.ticks.margin = element_blank() imply axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "unit")?
description:
I was trying to remove all margins from a plot and was hung up on why I couldn't get the left and bottom sides to completely fill the plot space. I was focusing on anything related to removing text and margins from the [theme documentation](http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/theme.html).

My first attempts:

``` r
plot <- data.frame(x = 1:10)
plot$y <- plot$x^2

p <- ggplot(plot, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
p <- p + scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))
p <- p + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))
p <- p + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
               plot.margin = unit(c(0, 0, 0, 0), "cm"), axis.title = element_blank(),
               axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "cm"))
p <- p + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
p
```

That gets really close, but I stumbled on [a related SO question](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17786197/plot-margins-in-ggplot2) and in using trial and error on some of the options, figured out that I need to set `axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "cm")` as well, which completely removes the margins.

Might be a nuance, but if someone sets the ticks and tick labels to blank elements, why is there still a margin for non-existent tick lengths?

Feel free to disregards; just wanted to at least make note of the situation in case there was any interest in this scenario.

title: Add a new "just touching" position option for geom_bar
description:
geom_bar does not handle variable width bars well. If they are wide they overlap; if they are thin, large gaps are left between them. This is rarely useful. Instead, a "just touching" option allows for neat 'horizontal' stacking of the bars. This can be done using cumsums (see here http://stackoverflow.com/questions/20688376/how-to-make-variable-bar-widths-in-ggplot2-not-overlap-or-gap/20690333?noredirect=1#comment30993310_20690333 ) 

x <- c("a","b","c")
w <- c(1.2, 1.3, 4) # variable widths
y <- c(9, 10, 6) # variable heights

pos <- 0.5 \* (cumsum(w) + cumsum(c(0, w[-length(w)])))

ggplot() + 
geom_bar(aes(x = pos, y = y, width = w, fill=x), stat="identity")

My request is that a new position option (1ouching) should be created, such that the following code would result in the same plot as above:

ggplot() + 
geom_bar(aes(x = x, y = y, width = w, fill=x), stat="identity", position = "touching")

in addition, the function position_touching(gapwidth = 0) could be used to set the width of the gaps in a consistent way. Just ideas, that I'm actually up for trying to implement if someone gives me an idea of where to start. Sure this would be of use if it ever gets implemented. Thanks!

title: geom_text captions are useless for scatter plots
description:
I love ggplot2, but, my god, it has terrible captioning options.

Take a look at the manual page for geom_text:

http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/geom_text.html

Not one of the examples that actually uses geom_text is legible. They are in fact uniformly _terrible_. 

The problem isn't the manual; the problem is with geom_text, which does not have anything like a reliable means of positioning the labels next to (rather that on) data points. 

Even something that would reliably let you position the text at a fixed number of units above or to the side of the datapoint would be better than what exists now. Obviously something that positioned them in a non-overlapping way would be ideal, but that's no doubt a lot of work. 

Monkeying with the position tag produces nothing any more legible from what I have been able to produce or find online.

Surely just making a reliable offset for geom_text should be feasible? This strikes me as so patently obvious that I'm kind of surprised that it has never been done, especially when even the manual makes it clear that geom_text is woefully unacceptable in its current form.

title: annotate() doesn't transform xend/yend

``` R
        aes( x = x, y = y ) ) +
    geom_point() +
    annotate( 'segment', x = 0, xend = 1, y = 1E-2, yend = 1E-2, color = "red", type = 2 ) +
```

title: Border spacing depends on zooming vs. subsetting
description:
The spacing around the borders of ggplots depend on whether you are using `ylim` or `coord_cartesian`. If you are plotting a single plot, this difference is negligible. However, when faceting plots, the differences become noticeable because the labels overlap each other. 

I understand the difference in subsetting vs. zooming using `ylim` vs. `coord_cartesian`, respectively, but at the end of the day all you are doing in either case is changing the range of an axis. I think you should expect the same plot output regardless of whether you are subsetting or zooming. 

Currently, `coord_cartesian` causes the labels to overlap, while `ylim` looks ok.

For example,

```
library(ggplot2) 
# Data to plot
df <- data.frame(A = 1:6, B = 1:6, F = rep(c("H", "L"), times = 3))
# Default case. The axis labels for the H and L facets 2 and 6, respectively, do not overlap.
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = A, y = B)) + geom_point() + facet_grid(F ~ .)
# Using ylim, things continue to look good. There is a bit of spacing below the 0 in H and 5 and L 
# so that they don't overlap.
p + ylim(0, 5)
# But I don't want to subset the data, I want to zoom in. In this example it does not matter, but 
# my real data is much different. To do this I need to use coord_cartesian...
p + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 5))
# As you can see, none of that nice spacing between the values and the border exist anymore so the 0 and 5 
# sit directly on top of each other.
```

title: Please fix stat_bin documentation: default is `right = FALSE`, not vice versa
description:
From [the documentation for stat_bin](http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/stat_bin.html):

```
simple <- data.frame(x = rep(1:10, each = 2))
base <- ggplot(simple, aes(x))
# By default, right = TRUE, and intervals are of the form (a, b]
base + stat_bin(binwidth = 1, drop = FALSE, right = TRUE, col = "black")
```

But try this out:

```
simple <- data.frame(x = rep(1:10, each = 2))
ggplot(simple, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, col = "black")
```

![2013-09-29_182806](https://f.cloud.github.com/assets/379357/1234155/d03f1730-295e-11e3-804c-55daf479554d.png)

```
ggplot(simple, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(right = F, binwidth = 1, col = "black")
```

![2013-09-29_182806](https://f.cloud.github.com/assets/379357/1234155/d03f1730-295e-11e3-804c-55daf479554d.png)

```
ggplot(simple, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(right = T, binwidth = 1, col = "black")
```

![2013-09-29_182927](https://f.cloud.github.com/assets/379357/1234157/fffc6068-295e-11e3-84c6-bb938b1047d8.png)

So... no option is the same as explicitly setting `right = F`, and `right = T` obviously looks different than the other two. The argument summary at the top of the page actually has it right, but I was looking at the example to get more clarification on what it did -- caused me quite a lot of confusion lately!

title: Possible issue with floating point precision and facetted tile plot
description:
I created [a full example on StackOverflow](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/18157975/combine-geom-tile-and-facet-grid-facet-wrap-and-remove-space-between-tiles-gg/18164691#18164691) demonstrating my experience (the answer (user name _Hendy_) I posted contains it).

The gist:
- I created a linear model with `fit <- lm(x ~ y, ...)` with four inputs (`x`s) and one response
- I created a new set of data to generated a facetted tile plot of each combination of two `x`s vs. response (`fill = z`) over a range of values, holding the other two variables not pictured in each tile plot at constant values when using `predict()` to generate the data set. This was done with `lapply` and `expand.grid`.
- I used the following to create my tile plot:

```
head(plot_data)
           x y var1 var2     resp
1 -3.0000000 0   x1   x2 69.05287
2 -2.3333333 0   x1   x2 70.37217
3 -1.6666667 0   x1   x2 71.69147

tail(plot_data)
           x y var1 var2      resp
595 11.66667 7   x3   x4  92.37510
596 13.33333 7   x3   x4  99.02534
597 15.00000 7   x3   x4 105.67558
```

My ggplot call was like so

```
p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_tile(aes(fill = resp))
p <- p + facet_wrap(var2 ~ var1, scales = "free", ncol = 3)
```

I got a blank plot as a result.

![blank plot](http://i.stack.imgur.com/zqcQD.png)

If I round `plot_data$x` and `plot_data$y`, it works (though I also ended up having to create `height` and `width` values using `ddply` for each unique combination of `var1` and `var2` in order to get the tiles to fill the space... but that's a separate issue):

```
plot_data_round <- plot_data
plot_data_round[, c("x", "y")] <- round(plot_data_round[, c("x", "y")], 5)

# same plot call as above
p <- ggplot(plot_data_round, aes(x = x, y = y, z = resp))
p <- p + geom_tile(aes(fill = resp))
p <- p + facet_wrap(var2 ~ var1, scales = "free", ncol = 3) + theme_bw()
```

![plot fills in some tiles](http://i.stack.imgur.com/YBKZi.png)

Why would the output of my `expand.grid` call not create a plot, but rounding those vectors would?

---

P.S. If you need the full code here, I am happy to provide it. Since I already copied it elsewhere, I figured linking to the SO post would be sufficient.

**Edit:** Providing the full code just in case that helps this get an answer/resolution:

``` R
set.seed(42)
x1 <- rnorm(20)
x2 <- runif(20)
x3 <- rpois(20,10)
x4 <- rexp(20)
y <- 10 + 2*x1 + 3*x2^2 + 4*x3 +5*x4 + rnorm(20, sd=0.1)

dat <- data.frame(x1, x2, x3, x4, y)

# vector of variable names for easy data.frame column naming later
var_names <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4")

# possible combinations of four variables
combis <- combn(1:4, 2)
combis <- rbind(combis, combis[, 6:1])

# steps to generate for the contour using `rep(min, max, length.out = n)`
n <- 100

#fit the model
fit <- lm(y~x1+I(x2^2)+x3+x4, data=dat)

# range values for when variable is featured on an axis
mins_maxs <- data.frame(x1 = c(-3, 3),
                        x2 = c(0, 1),
                        x3 = c(5, 20),
                        x4 = c(0, 7))

# values to hold for plots in which variables are not on an axis
holds <- c(0, 0.5, 10, 5)

sim_data <- list()
sim_data <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(combis)), function (i) {
  sim_data[[i]] <- expand.grid(seq(mins_maxs[1, combis[1, i]], 
                                   mins_maxs[2, combis[1, i]], length.out = n),
                               seq(mins_maxs[1, combis[2, i]], 
                                   mins_maxs[2, combis[2, i]], length.out = n),
                               holds[combis[3, i]],
                               holds[combis[4, i]])
} )

# we create a new data frame for the data set we want to plot
# for each contour of interest, we want the first two columns, as the second two
# were only created for the sake of feeding into our fit lm 
# we'll also create a vector for facetting using paste()
plot_data <- list()
plot_data <- lapply(1:ncol(combis), function(i) {
  plot_data[[i]] <- sim_data[[i]][, 1:2]
  plot_data[[i]]$var1 <- rep(var_names[combis[1, i]],
                             nrow(plot_data[[i]]))
  plot_data[[i]]$var2 <- rep(var_names[combis[2, i]],
                                   nrow(plot_data[[i]]))
  return(plot_data[[i]])
} )

# now we rename the columns of plot_data
plot_data <- lapply(1:length(plot_data), function(i) {
  names(plot_data[[i]]) <- c("x", "y", "var1", "var2")
  return(plot_data[[i]])
} )

# similarly, we need to re-name the sim_data columns so we can rbind them
# and predict new values using our fit lm
sim_data <- lapply(1:length(sim_data), function(i) {
  names(sim_data[[i]]) <- var_names[combis[, i]]
  return(sim_data[[i]])
} )


# collapse the separate lists into one data.frame
plot_data <- do.call(rbind, plot_data)
sim_data <- do.call(rbind, sim_data)

# create a vector of predictions using sim_data
plot_data$resp <- predict(fit, sim_data)
```

Creates empty facets:

``` R
library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = x, y = y, z = resp))
p <- p + geom_tile(aes(fill = resp))
p <- p + facet_wrap(var2 ~ var1, scales = "free", ncol = 3) + theme_bw()
p
```

Creates plots simply by rounding the `x` and `y` data to 5 digits. It doesn't expand the tiles to fill the region, though (either by design or that would be a separate issue to file):

``` R
plot_data_round <- plot_data
plot_data_round[, c("x", "y")] <- round(plot_data_round[, c("x", "y")], 5)

# same plot call as above
p <- ggplot(plot_data_round, aes(x = x, y = y, z = resp))
p <- p + geom_tile(aes(fill = resp))
p <- p + facet_wrap(var2 ~ var1, scales = "free", ncol = 3) + theme_bw()
```

I _can_ create a separate vector for both `height` and `width` to get `ggplot` to make the tiles fill in the full region like so (in case anyone was curious):

``` R
library(plyr)
hw <- ddply(plot_data, .(var1, var2), summarize,
            height = (max(y) - min(y))/n, width = (max(x) - min(x))/n)

plot_data_hw_round <- merge(plot_data_round, hw, by = c("var1", "var2"), all.x = T)
p <- ggplot(plot_data_hw_round, aes(x = x, y = y, z = resp))
p <- p + geom_tile(aes(fill = resp, height = height, width = width))
p <- p + facet_wrap(var2 ~ var1, scales = "free", ncol = 3) + theme_bw()
```

title: Bars start at 1 in log scale
description:
Test cases:

```
qplot(c(1, 2), c(1, -1), geom = "bar", stat = "identity")
qplot(c(1, 2), c(10, 0.1), geom = "bar", stat = "identity") + scale_y_log10()
```

In the first case, the zero value may be considered as a reference value, however, in the second case, I would have expected the bar to go from below to 0.1 (rather than from 0.1 to 1). A solution would be to make the reference adjustable. Another would be to change the computation of the min value in the case of log scale by changing geom-bar.r from

```
ymin = pmin(y, 0), ymax = pmax(y, 0),
```

to

```
ymin = min(y), ymax = pmax(y),
```

Furthermore, in both cases (negative values or values lower than 1 in log scale) the following warning messages is produced even though not stacking is actually performed:

```
Stacking not well defined when ymin != 0
```

title: faceting with a variable named ROW or COL results in an error
description:
Attempting to facet with a variable named `ROW` or `COL` results in a cryptic error.

``` r-lang
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, ROW=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~ROW)
```

gives

```
Error in scale_apply(layer_data, x_vars, scale_train, SCALE_X, panel$x_scales) : 

```

The problem is that the `panels` data.frame contains two instances of `ROW` and when the `PANEL` column is added to `data`, it get the wrong one at https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/R/facet-locate.r#L76. 

The problem is not limited to `ROW`. The same (or the same with additional warnings) error happens for any variable which has the same name as one of the internal `panels` columns:

``` r-lang
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, ROW=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~ROW)
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, COL=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~COL)
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, PANEL=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~PANEL)
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, SCALE_X=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~SCALE_X)
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, SCALE_Y=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~SCALE_Y)
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, AXIS_X=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~AXIS_X)
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, AXIS_Y=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_wrap(~AXIS_Y)
```

It also is not limited to `facet_wrap`; `facet_grid` has the same issues:

``` r-lang
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, ROW=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_grid(~ROW)
ggplot(data=transform(mtcars, ROW=am), aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_blank() +
  facet_grid(ROW~.)
```

title: clipping of objects in ggplot using zoom limits
description:
Example follows of the bug that occurs when overplotting qmap with a SpatialPolygons\* object that extend beyond the zoom limit of the map. 

I think the same issue was noted last year in stack overflow: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/13469566/polygons-nicely-cropping-ggplot2-ggmap-at-different-zoom-levels 

I'm wondering if a built-in fix is in the pipeline?

```
# reproducible example of issue when overplotting qmap with a
# SpatialPolygons* object that extends beyond the edge of the map 

library(ggmap)
library(grid)
library(sp)

# function to create a SpatialPointsDataFrame (with dummy data)
# that represents a single box polygon centered around 'coordinate',
# with box sides of length 'size'
pt2box <- function(coordinate, size) {
    lowerleft <- coordinate-(size/2)
    coords <- rbind(
        lowerleft,
        lowerleft + c(0, size),
        lowerleft + size,
        lowerleft + c(size, 0),
        lowerleft
    )
    SpatialPolygonsDataFrame(
        SpatialPolygons(list(
            Polygons(list(
                Polygon(coords)
            ), 1)
        )
    ), data.frame(x=1))
}

# grab Google map of the region around Baylor University
baylor <- qmap("baylor university", zoom=8)

# lat/lon for city of austin
austin <- c(-97.7428, 30.2669)

# this works -- box fits on plot
baylor + geom_polygon(aes(x=long, y=lat), fill=NA, colour="black",
    data=pt2box(austin, 0.4))
# this doesn't -- box doesn't fit on plot
baylor + geom_polygon(aes(x=long, y=lat), fill=NA, colour="black",
    data=pt2box(austin, 0.5))
```

title: In stat_summary_hex and stat_binhex, hexagons overlap when z values are factors
description:
In the data set below, thing1 is numeric, and thing2 is a factor (but otherwise identical to thing1). For simplicity, the summary function is just the max value in the bin. When the z element is a factor, the hexagons overlap. 

```
library(ggplot2)
library(hexbin)
DF=data.frame(xpos=rnorm(1000),
              ypos=rnorm(1000),
              thing1=rep(1:9,length.out=100),
              thing2=as.factor(rep(1:9,length.out=100)))
ggplot(DF, aes(x=xpos, y=ypos, z=thing1)) +  
  stat_summary_hex(fun=function(x){x[which.max(x)]})
ggplot(DF, aes(x=xpos, y=ypos, z=thing2)) +  
  stat_summary_hex(fun=function(x){x[which.max(x)]})
```

![thing1](http://i.stack.imgur.com/lbZzU.png)
![thing2](http://i.stack.imgur.com/CV8BN.png)

This also occurs with `ggplot(DF, aes(x=xpos, y=ypos, z=thing2)) + stat_binhex()`.

This is [cross posted](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17373751/in-stat-summary-hex-why-do-hexagons-overlap-if-z-is-a-factor) on stackoverflow.com.

title: Strange scale_x_datetime offset
description:
I often plot data from a data frame that has both a POSIXct and a
numeric column.  The following code creates such a data frame and plots
the data:

```
require(ggplot2)
require(scales)
require(lubridate)
timelist <- ymd_hm(c("2013-05-01 12:00","2013-05-02 18:00","2013-05-03 06:00"),tz="America/Los_Angeles")
sampleDF <- data.frame(time = timelist, values = c(3,4,2))
qplot(time, values, data = sampleDF)+scale_x_datetime(minor_breaks=date_breaks("6 hour"))
```

When I run the code above, I get a plot with the three points at the
right times, but the minor break lines are offset apparently by 3 hours
from the axis.  I expected the minor breaks to coincide with the major
breaks.  That is, I expected minor breaks at 0:00, 6:00, 12:00, 18:00,
..., with major breaks as scales chose, but I get minor breaks at 3:00,
9:00, ....

My time zone is "America/Los_Angeles", but I get the same result when I
use "UTC" for the data instead.  

There was a discussion about this at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/ggplot2/Kvdx70hF51A.  While Brian Waismeyer's solution seems to work, it seems more than a bit unintuitive and thus out of character for ggplot2 and a bit fidgety.

title: The str function fails with error on ggplot2 objects
description:
When trying to debug https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/817 I noticed in some cases
that str gives an error when run on certain ggplot2 objects. 
My feeling is that this is a separate issue from 817, so I'm creating a different issue for it.
For example

```
library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:10,
  y = 1:10,
  colour = factor(sample(1:3, 10, replace = TRUE)),
  size = factor(sample(1:3, 10, replace = TRUE)))

p <- ggplot(data = df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = size)) +
  theme_bw()
pg = ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p))
str(pg)
```

The output ends with 

$ NA:Error in object[[i]] : subscript out of bounds

See also the Stack Overflow question [calling `str` on a object errors out if the ggplot2 package is loaded](http://stackoverflow.com/q/17127339/350713),  This has a different example by DWin, see http://stackoverflow.com/a/17128951/350713

title: missing `guide.margin`(s) theme parameter
description: I believe the theme parameters are not fully covering the margin options for guides. In this [SO question](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17073772/ggplot2-legend-on-top-and-margin), I discovered an extra margin that is being [set to a default value](https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/R/guides-.r#L228) and cannot be specified in `theme()`.

Details of the problem and possible fixes are on the R-help thread:
https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2013-May/353856.html
https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2013-June/354717.html

title: multiple calls to annotation_custom fail in certain cases
description:
I'm copying the example from Sandy Musgrove in
http://stackoverflow.com/a/13327793/350713

In the following code, two calls to `annotation_custom` result in the object `plotNew`.
But the two legends that should show up in that plot don't, 
(We can call up the display by simply typing `plotNew`.)
Only the first added shows up, namely `leg2`.
However, in the case of `plotNew2`, both circles added via `annotation_custom` show up.

```
library(ggplot2)
library(gtable)
## The proto package needs to be loaded for more detailed printing of proto objects
## I assume this replaces the `print` method for proto objects
## Without this package loaded you don't see `str` errors below.
library(proto)

##Some data
df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:10,
  y = 1:10,
  colour = factor(sample(1:3, 10, replace = TRUE)),
  size = factor(sample(1:3, 10, replace = TRUE)))

### Step 1
# Draw a plot with the colour legend
(p1 <- ggplot(data = df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
   geom_point(aes(colour = colour)) +
   theme_bw() +
   theme(legend.position = "top"))

## Extract the colour legend - leg1
leg1 <- gtable_filter(ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p1)), "guide-box") 

## Step 2
## Draw a plot with the size legend
(p2 <- ggplot(data = df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
   geom_point(aes(size = size)) +
   theme_bw())

## Extract the size legend - leg2
leg2 <- gtable_filter(ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p2)), "guide-box") 

## Step 3
```

title: `stat_contour` shouldn't return any break if `binwidth >> range(data$z)`
description:
Consider the following code,

```
b = data.frame(energy = rep(c(1,2),5), 
               R = rep(c(1-1e-10, 1), each=5), 
               N = c(55, 55, 65, 65, 75, 75, 85, 85, 95, 95))

ggplot(b)+ 
  geom_line(aes(energy, N, z=R), binwidth=1,
            alpha=0.5, stat="contour")
```

I suggest that there shouldn't be any level line in this plot because the z data is practically constant across the panel, and showing a level line suggests that there is some variation commensurate with the chosen binwidth. For more context, see the SO question:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/16863647/stat-contour-binwidth-oddity

title: Breaks misalignment with scale_x_date
description:
I'm seeing a misalignment between the major and minor breaks when they use different units.

```

                     to=as.Date("2013-04-30"), by="day"))
df$y=rnorm(nrow(df))

ggplot(df) +
  geom_path(aes(x=Date, y=y)) +
  scale_x_date(expand=c(0, 0), breaks=date_breaks("1 year"), 
               labels=date_format("%Y"),
               minor_breaks=date_breaks("3 months"))
```

```
  geom_path(aes(x=Date, y=y)) +
```

title: qplot does not facet factor correctly if it is passed without data argument
description:

x <- c(0, 0, 1, 1)
y <- c(0, 1, 0, 1)
f1 <- c("a", "a", "b", "b")
f2 <- c("c", "d", "c", "d")
F1 <- factor(f1)
F2 <- factor(f2)
F11 <- factor(f1, levels = c("b", "a"))
F22 <- factor(f2, levels = c("d", "c"))

df <- data.frame(x, y, F1, F2, F11, F22)

qplot(x, y, facets = F1 ~ F2) # correct
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(color = "red", size = 4) + facet_grid(F1 ~ F2) # correct
qplot(x, y, facets = F11 ~ F22) # wrong
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(color = "blue", size = 4) + facet_grid(F11 ~ F22) # correct
qplot(x, y, facets = F11 ~ F22, data = df) # correct

title: [feature request] Less strict check on element_xxx class for user-customised elements
description:
Periodically people have requested using a [different type of axis label](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/14070953/photo-alignment-with-graph-in-r/14078391#14078391), e.g. an image, or [a facet title that spans multiple lines with expressions](http://stackoverflow.com/a/16491363/471093), etc. In all these cases, a possible solution is to replace the default theme element (text, in both of these cases), with a completely different beast of a grob. Lattice allows such unpredictable changes to the default functions, but ggplot2 has internal checks for the class of objects that can be displayed, making the operation very difficult. 

I suggest that such changes should be a bit easier if ggplot2 wasn't so strict on checking the class of theme elements.

title: Checking for sensible nrow, ncol in facet_wrap
description:
The `nrow` and `ncol` arguments to `facet_wrap` only make sense as positive integers, but `ggplot2` curerntly does not check their values when the plot variable is assigned.  For example

```
p1 <- ggplot(CO2, aes(conc, uptake)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~ Type, nrow = 0)
```

is allowed, an even

```
p2 <- ggplot(CO2, aes(conc, uptake)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~ Type, nrow = -2)
```

It is only when these plots come to be printed that the problem manifests.

I suggest adding a check that `nrow` and `ncol` are positive integers into the `facet_wrap` function.

title: Make it possible to wrap geom and scale defaults in theme definitions
description:
This isn't an issue, this is more of a question about the paradigm being created for overall theme management. 

It would be nice if one could wrap geom and scale defaults in theme definitions. As it is now, one can define a theme for most attributes associated with the plot. 

```
theme_example <- function(base_size = 12) { 
   structure(list(
      ...
   ), class=c("theme","gg"), complete=TRUE/FALSE)
}
```

However, defaults for scale and geom are instantiated seperately. 

```
update_geom_defaults("geom", list(...))
scale_colour_discrete <- function(...) scale_colour_brewer(..., palette="Dark2")
```

This instantiation forces the user to remember to add the theme elements, and forces the user to repeat themselves by writing out the defaults over and over for each use case (think reporting via knitr). 

Perhaps there's a better way to manage this process that I'm not seeing?

```
    pp <- function (n,r=4) {
```

To borrow an example from [stackoverflow](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/3541713/how-to-plot-two-histograms-together-in-r):

```
chicks <- data.frame(length = rnorm(100, 4, 2), animal = 2)
carrots <- data.frame(length = rnorm(500, 9, 3), animal = 1)

measured_things <- rbind(chicks, carrots)

ggplot(measured_things, aes(x=length, fill=animal)) + geom_bar()
```

Which produces the flabbergasting error message:

> Error in unit(tic_pos.c, "mm") : 'x' and 'units' must have length > 0

```
measured_things$status = c('animal', 'not')[measured_things$animal]
# or measured_things$status = as.factor(measured_things$animal)

ggplot(measured_things, aes(x=length, fill=status)) + geom_bar()
```

Which works beautifully! Seems like `aes(fill=...)` and `aes(colour=...)` could very well force conversion to factor, but there might be other use-cases I'm not aware of, but at least the error message could be more helpful.

title: Subset in geom leaves empty panels in grid
description:
Hi,

I'm playing with the subset argument of `geom_*` and I'm finding that I end up with empty panels in the grid. I'm using version 0.9.3 of ggplot2.

Here is my toy-example:

``` R
d = data.frame(
  x=ceiling(seq(1, 30) / 3), y=runif(30),
  group=as.factor(rep(c('A', 'B', 'C'), 10))
)

ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y, group=group, color=group)) +
geom_point(subset=.(group != 'B')) +
facet_grid(group ~ ., drop=TRUE)
```

Note: It makes no difference if group is a `factor` or not.

![image](https://f.cloud.github.com/assets/878107/85606/0774e2a0-646d-11e2-8925-efc3db9c0adb.png)

The legend correctly omits B, but the empty panel for B is still present.

The obvious workaround is to subset the data upfront, e.g.

``` R
ggplot(subset(d, group != 'B'), aes(x=x, y=y, group=group, color=group)) +
geom_point() +
facet_grid(group ~ .)
```

Note: If I set `drop=FALSE` in `facet_grid` in the workaround example, then I end up with the same result as above.

However, it seems to me like the subset argument of `geom_*` could potentially take care of this. If this is not a bug, I would like to make it a feature request (and if I get my head around the code-base, I might take a stab :)

Cheers,
Josh

title: Use default aesthetics from geom_point as defaults for goem_boxplot outliers
description:
Currently, the default values for the outlier arguments to geom_boxplot, that control the shape, colour and size of outliers, cannot be changed with update_geom_defaults. It makes sense because technically these parameters are not aesthetics. On the other hand, if the user changes, say, the default shape of geom_point, the result will be that geom_point and geom_boxplot will produce points with different shapes, which probably is not desirable or entirely expected.

One solution is to use the default values from geom_point as defaults for the outlier arguments in geom_boxplot, so that

update_geom_defaults("point", list(shape = 1, colour='blue',size=4))

also affects the shape, colour and size of the outlier points produced by geom_boxplot. Find patch attached.

title: aesthetic inheritance and annotation_custom
description:
I posted this at SO and bring it here since it seems to be a real issue (and not just my confusion).  SO post: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/14415073/inheritance-of-aesthetics-in-ggplot2-0-9-3-the-behavior-of-annotation-custom

I looked at the code for annotation_custom and it has a hard-wired inherit.aes = TRUE which I think is the problem. I don't see why this function needs any aesthetic at all. I did try several ways to override it and set inherit.aes = FALSE but I was unable to fully penetrate the namespace and make it stick.

Here is a MWE which illustrates the problem:

```
library("ggplot2")
library("grid")

# Case 1, works as expected

td1 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(10), y = rnorm(10))

tf1 <- function(df) { # works as expected
    p <- ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y), data = df)
    p <- p + geom_point(color = "red")
    p <- p + annotation_custom(circleGrob())
    print(p)
}

tf1(td1)

tf2 <- function(df) { # circle isn't draw, but no error either
    p <- ggplot()
    p <- p + geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "red")

    f1 = c(rep("L", 5), rep("H", 5)), f2 = rep(c("A", "B"), 5))

tf3 <- function(df) {
    p <- ggplot()
    p <- p + geom_point(data = df, 
        aes(x = f1, y = r, color = f2, group = f2))

tf3(td3)
```

title: Wrong evaluation environment for expressions in aes()
description:
Expressions in `aes()` are evaluated in the global environment, but they should be evaluated in the calling environment. Example:

``` R
library(ggplot2)

foo <- 4
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt + foo, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()
# Works


f <- function() {
  foo2 <- 4
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt + foo2, y = mpg)) +
    geom_point()
}

f()
# Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'foo2' not found
```

It can be worked around by using `environment=environment()`:

``` R
g <- function() {
  foo3 <- 4
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt + foo3, y = mpg),
         environment = environment()) +
    geom_point()
}

g()
# Works
```

I think that should be the default behavior. @hadley, is the current behavior a bug or a feature?

The problem is the definition of `ggplot.data.frame` in plot.r:

``` R
ggplot.data.frame <- function(data, mapping=aes(), ...,
  environment = globalenv())
```

Changing it to use `parent.env()` fixes the problem:

``` R
ggplot.data.frame <- function(data, mapping=aes(), ...,
  environment = parent.env())
```

Specifically,

``` r
library("MASS")

  geom_point() + xlim(0.5, 6) + ylim(40, 110)
```
